Pip trotted behind her. He did not care about the light. He cared about his shoe.

Suki stopped. She saw a jar in the grass. It was not clean. But it held Pip's shoe! The wind had blown the shoe into the jar.

She picked it up. She did not want the green light now. She wanted Pip to be happy.

The far light blinked. Suki waved goodbye. She put the shoe on Pip. They went home, warm and glad.

stories.topic: a pony and a lost shoe
stories.name: Suki

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Dew blew sideways on a windy morning. Suki rode her pony Pip to the playground. Clip, clop, clip, clop. Then Pip stopped. One shoe was gone.

Suki looked by the slide. No shoe. She looked by the swings. No shoe. She put a jar of oats down so Pip would stand still. The wind pushed her hair.

Then Suki saw it. A small green light, far across the playground. It blinked and blinked. It was on the far side of the playground. She wanted it. She reached for it. She could not have it.

“Come back,” she said. “Come back, come back.”

She ran to chase the light. The wind blew. The light stayed far away. “Come back,” she whispered. “Come back, come back.”

Pip whinnied. Suki turned. There was the shoe, right by the fence, hiding in the grass. Suki laughed. She put the shoe on Pip. She gave him a clean, dry cloth for his nose.

The green light blinked once more and was gone. Suki did not care. She hugged Pip. They walked home happy, clip, clop, clip, clop.

stories.topic: a pony and a lost shoe
stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text:
One rainy afternoon, Rosa took her pony, Pip, out for a ride. The wind blew hard. The rain came down fast. Pip stepped in a deep puddle, and his shoe came off. It sank in the mud.

Rosa looked and looked. She got wet and cold. She did not find the shoe. So she led Pip home and gave him a warm cookie. She tried to fold a blanket on his back to keep him dry. Her mom said, "Do not be too busy to rest. We will find the shoe tomorrow."

Rosa looked up at the old house on the hill. In its window, a small green light glowed. She wanted that light. It looked warm and kind. She reached for it, but it was far away. She could not have it.

The next day, the sun came out. Rosa found the shoe in the mud. She learned that some things you want stay far away, but the things you need come back when you wait.

stories.topic: a pony and a lost shoe
stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text:
One rainy afternoon, Rosa rode her pony, Pip, down the muddy lane. A bump made Pip's shoe fly off into the wet grass. Rosa got down to look. The wind blew hard. She held her hat and said, "We must find it, Pip."

Rosa ate a cookie from her pocket while she searched. She had to fold her arms to stay warm. A busy truck went by and splashed them. Still, no shoe.

Then Rosa saw a small green light in the window of an old house. It glowed soft and calm in the storm. She wished she could go inside and be dry. She wished the light would help her. But the window was far, and the light just shone.

Pip nuzzled her hand. Rosa took a breath. She looked again and found the shoe by a rock.

We cannot always have the warm light we want. But we can keep looking for what we need.

stories.topic: a pony and a lost shoe
stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text:
One stormy afternoon, Rosa rode her pony, Pip, down the muddy lane. A big wind blew. Then Pip lost a shoe in the deep, wet mud.

Rosa looked and looked. The rain was loud. She got a cookie from her pocket and ate it while she searched.

Then she saw a small light in the window of an old house. It was green and soft. It did not move.

Rosa wanted that light. She wanted to fold her hands around it. She forgot the shoe for a minute. The light was so pretty. She was busy with the light in her mind.

But Pip needed his shoe. Rosa shook her head. She looked down again. There it was, by a stone.

She put the shoe back on. The green light still glowed far away. Rosa could not have it. That was okay.

A small want is fine, but a friend needs you first.

stories.topic: a pony and a lost shoe
stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text:
O, the rain came down hard on the pony farm. Rosa ran to the barn to check on her pony, Star. Star had lost a shoe in the mud. Rosa looked all around.

The wind blew. The rain fell. Rosa was busy hunting for the shoe.

Then she saw it. A small green light glowed in the window of an old house. It was soft and bright. Rosa wanted it. She reached for it. She could not touch it.

"Star needs the shoe," Rosa said. But she kept looking at the light. "I want the light. I want the light."

She gave Star a cookie. She helped fold a warm blanket over him. Still she looked back. The light stayed in the window.

The storm went on. Rosa found the shoe by the fence. She put it on Star. But her eyes went back to the light. "I want the light," she said again.

Some things we want are far away. Love what is near your hands.

stories.topic: a pony and a lost shoe
stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text:
One rainy afternoon, Rosa rode her pony, Pip, down the muddy lane. Clip, clop, squish went his hooves. Then Pip stopped. His left shoe was gone!

Rosa looked in the puddles. She looked by the big oak tree. She gave Pip a cookie and said, "Stay here." But she was not calm. Her hands could not fold. She felt too busy to think.

Then she saw it. In the window of the old house, a small green light. It glowed soft and steady.

"Oh," said Rosa. "I want that light. I want to hold it."

She walked to the window. The light stayed inside. She reached. Her hand touched cold glass. The light did not come out.

"I want it," she whispered. "I want it. I want it."

She forgot the shoe. She forgot Pip. She forgot the rain. The green light filled her eyes.

Then Pip neighed. Rosa blinked. She turned away. She found the shoe in the tall grass.

Some lights are only for looking, not for keeping.

stories.topic: a pony and a lost shoe
stories.name: Milo

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
I have a pony named Milo. Today his shoe fell off in the grass. We looked and looked. Milo was hungry. He wanted his oats.

The sun went down. Across the big field, I saw a small light. It blinked once. Then it was gone. Milo did not see it. He only wanted his shoe.

I found a flower by the fence. No shoe. I gave Milo a pat. He did not clap. Ponies do not clap.

Then I saw something shiny near the water. It was the shoe! I put it back on his foot. Milo was happy. I was happy too.

We walked home in the dark. Far away, the small light came back. It was just a little star. I did not need to reach it. I had Milo. That was enough.

stories.topic: a pony and a lost shoe
stories.name: Milo

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
I will tell you about Milo and the lost shoe. Milo the pony lost his shoe by the fence. He looked and looked. His hoof went clip-clop on the hard dirt. He was hungry and wanted his oats.

At sunset, Milo saw a small light across the big field. It blinked once, then hid behind the tall grass. Milo forgot his oats. He walked toward it. He stepped on a yellow flower. It bent but did not break.

The light came back, soft as a firefly. Milo wanted to touch it. He walked and walked. His bare hoof hurt. He did not stop.

Then he heard a clap. A girl named Anna ran to him. She held his lost shoe. "I found it by the creek," she said. She put it back on his hoof.

Milo felt warm. The light across the field faded away. He did not need to reach it. Anna gave him oats, and he was not hungry anymore. He nuzzled her hand. The flower stood up again in the cool night air. Milo was home.

stories.topic: a pony and a lost shoe
stories.name: Milo

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
I have a pony named Milo. Today Milo lost a shoe. He looked in the tall grass. He looked by the red barn. No shoe.

Milo felt sad. His foot went clip-clop, thump-thump.

Then Milo saw a small light. It was far away, across the big field. The light was green and soft, like a sleepy firefly.

“I want to touch it,” Milo said. He walked to the fence. He was hungry and tired. He sniffed a yellow flower.

The green light blinked. It seemed to say, “Come here.” Milo took one step. Then two. The light stayed far away.

Milo stopped. He heard a clap. His friend Ana ran over. “Milo! I found your shoe!”

She held up the shoe. Milo gave a happy little hop. Ana put the shoe on his foot. It fit just right.

Milo looked across the field. The green light was gone. That was okay. His shoe was back. Ana gave him a big hug. Milo felt warm and full.

stories.topic: a pony and a lost shoe
stories.name: Milo

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
I have a pony named Milo. Milo lost a shoe in the tall grass. He looked and looked. His hoof went clip, clop, clip, clop. He was hungry. He wanted his hay.

Then Milo saw a small light. It was far away, across the big field. The sun was going down. The light was green and soft. It sat right on the fence. Milo forgot the shoe. He walked toward the light.

He found a flower. He did not stop. He found a stone. He did not stop. The light stayed far. It always stayed far. Milo walked and walked.

His friend called him. Clap, clap went her hands. Milo turned his head. There was his shoe, right by the barn. Milo was so glad. He got his hay. He got his warm stall.

The green light blinked once. Then the dark came. Milo did not need to reach it. He was home.

stories.topic: a pony and a lost shoe
stories.name: Milo

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
I will find the shoe. Milo walks by the fence. The field is big and wide. He looks for the shoe.

Then he sees it. A small light. It sits far away, across the big field. It is soft and gold. The sun is going down. The light glows like a tiny star.

Milo wants it. He walks and walks. He sees a flower. He does not stop. He hears a clap. He does not stop. He is hungry. He does not stop.

He wants the light. He wants it so much. The light is far. The light is small. The light is warm. He walks and walks. He wants the light. He wants the light. He wants the light.

His feet are slow. His eyes are on the light. Then he is there. It is not a light. It is his shoe. It shines in the sunset. Milo is happy. He puts it on. He walks home.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Sam

axes.where: on the other side of a fence
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text: Carefully, Sam the raccoon washed his paws in the cold. He had found a giant milk carton on the porch. It tipped over. White milk spilled on the snow. Sam tried to scoop it up. The milk was too cold and too thin. It ran through his fingers. He put a bit in his pocket. That did not work. The milk made his pocket wet. Sam looked at the fence. On the other side, a little light blinked. It was small and green. It sat far away. Sam did not reach for it. He had milk to clean. He patted the snow with his paws. Then he saw something. The spilled milk had frozen into a tiny white pond. He could slide on it. Sam slid once. He slid twice. He laughed. The green light blinked again. Sam did not care. He had his own little pond. He slid until the sun went down.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Sam

axes.where: on the other side of a fence
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Crash went the milk. Sam the raccoon had knocked it off the step. White milk ran over the snow. It made a small cold river.

Sam wanted to lick it up. But his paw slipped. The milk was gone.

Sam put a cracker in his pocket. He went for a walk in the snow. He came to a fence. On the other side, a little light was on. It was small and soft. It looked warm.

Sam tried to reach it. The fence was too tall. He was too small.

He walked on. He found a giant snowman. It had a hat. Sam climbed up. From the top, he could see the light again. It was still far away. He sat and looked at it for a while.

Then he heard a sound. A cat came by. The cat had a bowl of milk. She set it down. Sam took one sip. It was not the far light. But it was warm.

Sam smiled. He did not need to reach the light. He had milk right here.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Sam

axes.where: on the other side of a fence
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Careful, Sam the raccoon carried the milk jug home. The jug was heavy. His little arms shook. Snow fell on his nose. Then the jug tipped. White milk spilled into the white snow.

Sam sat down. His fur got wet. He licked his paw. The milk was gone.

Behind the fence, a light glowed. It was small and soft. It was green like a leaf in summer. Sam put his nose through a hole. He could see it. He could not reach it. The fence was too tall.

He tried to climb. He slid down. He tried again. The snow made his paws slip.

In his pocket was a giant cookie. He forgot to eat it. He just looked at the green light.

The light blinked once. Twice. Then Sam heard a sound. It was his friend, a little girl named May. She opened the gate.

“Come in, Sam,” she said.

The green light was just her porch lamp. But May gave him warm milk in a bowl. Sam drank it all.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Sam

axes.where: on the other side of a fence
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Careful, careful, Sam the raccoon said to himself. He carried a cup of milk to his cozy log. The cup was full to the top. Then his foot slipped on a patch of ice. The milk made a big white puddle in the snow.

Sam sat down. His ears drooped. He had no milk now. He put his hands in his pocket and felt sad.

Then he saw it. On the other side of the fence, a little light was glowing. It was small and far away. It was as bright as a star. Sam wanted to reach it. He wanted it more than milk.

He climbed the fence. He fell down. He climbed again. The snow was deep. The wind was cold.

The light stayed far away. Sam whispered, I want it. I want it. I want it in my pocket.

Then a giant thing happened. The light moved. It came closer. It was not a light at all. It was a firefly with a tiny lamp.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Sam

axes.where: on the other side of a fence
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Carefully, Sam the raccoon carried the milk. Then he tripped. The milk spilled, white on white snow.

Sam saw it then. Past the fence, a little light shone. It was small and far away.

Sam wanted that light. He wanted to hold it in his pocket. He wanted to reach it. He pushed the fence. He could not get through. The fence was giant.

"I want the light," said Sam. "I want the light."

He forgot the milk. He forgot the cold. He only saw the light.

"I want the light. I want the light."

He said it again and again.

Then a bird flew down. The bird said, "That is just a window. A house is there."

Sam looked. The light did not move. It was a window. It was not for him. Sam sat down in the snow.

He licked the spilled milk. It was still sweet. And the little light stayed far away, like always.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Ivy

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Nobody spilled the milk but Ivy. She was a raccoon with a red hat. The milk went over the step and made a white lake. "Oh no," said Ivy. "That was for supper."

Her little hands tried to scoop it back. Milk does not scoop.

"Let it go," said her friend Mo. "We can race to the playground."

So they ran. Ivy ran past the slide. Past the swings. Sun was warm on her hat. She forgot the milk a bit.

Then she saw it. Far off, past the fence, on the far side of the playground, a small light sat in the grass. It was round and green and it did not move. It looked like a tiny moon that fell down.

"What is that?" said Ivy.

"Nothing," said Mo. "Just a light."

Ivy took one step. Then one more. She wanted to hold it. She wanted it to be hers.

But Mo pulled her paw. "Come on. Let's race home."

Ivy looked back once. The green light stayed far away. She walked home with her hat low, and she did not tell anyone.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Ivy

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Nobody knew who spilled the milk on the sidewalk. Ivy the raccoon found it on a sunny afternoon. The white puddle shone like a tiny lake.

"Look," said Ivy. "A little lake."

Her friend Ben wore a red hat. "Do not step in it," he said.

Ivy dipped one paw in. The milk was cool. She licked her paw. It tasted like clouds.

"Come on," said Ben. "Let's race to the swings."

They ran. Ivy won the race. She sat on a swing and kicked her feet. Then she saw it. On the far side of the playground, past the slide, past the sandbox, a small light sat on a fence post. It was soft and green. It did not move.

Ivy stopped swinging. "What is that?" she asked.

"What is what?" said Ben.

The light stayed far away. It looked like a place she could almost touch. She walked toward it. Then Ben called her back. The milk was still there, warm now, and she drank a little more. But her eyes kept sliding to the fence, where the small green thing waited and did not come closer.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Ivy

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Nobody told Ivy about the milk until it was already a white puddle on the grass. She had worn her red hat that sunny afternoon. The milk tipped right off the picnic table. "Oh no," said Ivy. "That was for everyone."

A little raccoon peeked from behind a tree. He crept close and sniffed the puddle. "Is that yours?" Ivy asked. The raccoon did not answer. He just drank.

Then Ivy saw something far away, on the far side of the playground. A small light sat on a pole. It was soft and green, like a leaf holding still. She wanted to touch it. She did not know why.

"Stay here," she told the raccoon. She began to walk. Then she began to race. The light seemed close, then far, then close again.

The raccoon followed her. "You can't catch it," he seemed to say with his eyes.

"I know," said Ivy. She stopped. She looked back at the spilled milk. Then she looked at the light one more time. It stayed far away, small and shining. She walked home with the raccoon, still wanting it.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Ivy

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Nobody told Ivy the milk would spill. She carried the jug with two hands. Then a bump. Then white milk ran down the table leg.

Ivy wore her red hat. She ran a rag along the floor. But a little raccoon came in through the open door.

"Stop," Ivy said. "That is our milk."

The raccoon did not stop. It lapped the white puddle. Its tongue went in small circles.

Ivy looked out the window. Sun fell on the playground. On the far side, past the slide, something shone. A green shine. It sat in the grass and blinked like a tiny wet eye.

"Come back," Ivy said to the milk. "Come back."

The raccoon licked its paw and stared at her.

Ivy ran a race with the sun to the playground. She lost. The green shine stayed far. It always stays far. She held her hat and whispered, "I want it. I want it. I want it."

The raccoon followed her home. It curled by the empty jug. The afternoon turned gold. The green shine kept on shining, far away, where she could not go.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Ivy

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text: Next to the big oak tree, Ivy the raccoon spilled the milk. A white puddle spread over the grass. Her small paws got wet. "Oh no," she said. "My milk is gone." She put her hat on her head. Then she saw it. On the far side of the playground, a little green light sat on a pole. It was small and bright in the sunny afternoon. Ivy wanted it. She wanted it more than milk. She forgot the puddle. "I will race there," she said. She ran past the slide. She ran past the swings. The light stayed far away. "I want it," she said. "I want it. I want it." A child said, "Ivy, your milk spilled." Ivy did not hear. "I want the light," she said. "I want it. I want it." The sun went down. The light still shone. Ivy never reached it. She sat and looked and wanted.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Carefully, Rosa the raccoon carried the milk to the table. She wanted a drink. Her paw hit the jug. Splash! Milk went everywhere.

"Oh no," said Rosa. The milk made a big puddle. It was sticky on the floor. Some milk got on her sock. Rosa was sad.

She got a rag. She wiped and wiped. The puddle got smaller. Soon the floor was clean. That problem was solved.

Rosa went outside to play. The sun was warm. Down the street, a car sat by the curb. A tiny light on it blinked and shone. Rosa watched it. It seemed to float, like a little star that fell down to rest.

She wanted to touch it. She walked and walked. But the car was too far. The light kept blinking, blinking. Rosa's feet were tired.

She went home and sat by the window. She could still see the little light far away. She could look, but she could not reach it. Rosa sighed.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Carefully, Rosa the raccoon carried the milk carton home. It was for her little brother. He was sick and needed milk. But a bump in the road made her trip. The carton fell. White milk spilled all over the ground.

"Oh no," Rosa said. Her sock got wet. The milk was sticky on her paws. This was a big problem. She tried to scoop it up, but it was gone.

Then she saw the light. It was on a car parked far down the street. The light was small and bright. It did not float away. It just sat there. Rosa wished she could reach it. It looked like a tiny, friendly sun.

She had to fix her problem first. She ran back to the store. The nice lady gave her new milk. Rosa walked home slowly. She did not spill it.

Her brother drank the milk and felt better. But Rosa felt sad. She looked down the street. The little light was still there. She could see it, but she could not touch it. It was too far away.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Carefully, Rosa the raccoon carried the milk jug home. Her sock feet went pat-pat on the warm sidewalk. Then she tripped. The jug tipped. White milk went everywhere. It made a big, sticky puddle. Rosa felt sad. Her milk was gone.

She ran to get a rag. She wiped and wiped. The puddle got smaller. Soon the sidewalk was clean. Her little problem was fixed. She felt proud.

Then she saw it. Far down the street, on a car, a small light was on. It was soft and bright. It looked like a tiny piece of moon. Rosa wanted to touch it. She walked toward it. She walked and walked. The light did not get closer.

She sat down. She wished she could float to it. But she could not. The light stayed far away. It always stayed far away. She looked at it for a long time. Then she went home. Her milk was gone. The light was still there. She could not have it. She would never have it. She put her sock feet on the floor and sat very still.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Carefully, Rosa the raccoon carried the milk carton down the steps. She wanted to help. But her foot slipped on a sock, and the milk spilled. White drops went everywhere.

"Oh no," said Rosa. The milk made a big puddle. It was sticky on her toes. She got a rag and wiped it up. That was the little problem, and now it was solved.

Then she saw it. Far down the street, on a car, a small light shone. It was soft and green. It seemed to float above the metal.

Rosa wanted to touch it.

She walked to the car. The light stayed far away. She walked more. The light stayed far away.

"I want to touch it," she said. "I want to touch it. I want to touch it."

The sun went down. The green light did not come closer. Rosa sat on the curb. Her rag was still sticky. She never touched the light.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Carefully, Rosa the raccoon carried the milk carton to the table. She wanted to help. But her paw slipped on a sock, and the milk went splash. White milk ran everywhere. It made a sticky puddle on the floor. Rosa tried to wipe it, but her little hands just made it worse. She felt sad. Then she saw it. Far down the street, on a car, a little green light was shining. It was small and bright, like a tiny leaf. Rosa forgot the milk. She stood at the window and looked at the light. "I want it," she said. "I want it." Her tail did not float. Her feet did not move. She said it again. "I want it. I want it." Mama came and cleaned the milk. The problem was solved. But Rosa did not see. She only saw the little green light. The sun went down. The light stayed far away. Rosa sat by the window all night.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Leo

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Pip the milk on the floor. Leo the raccoon saw the white puddle. It was a big spill.

Leo had a little wagon. He wanted to share the milk with his friends. But the milk was on the ground. It was messy.

Leo got a cloth. He wiped and wiped. The floor got clean. His friends came in. They had no milk now.

Leo felt sad. Then he saw a small light under a door down the hall. It was a sunny afternoon. The light was green and tiny. It made him feel warm. He looked and looked. Then he went back.

His friends said, "We can be calm. We can share something else." They shared apples. Leo smiled. The light was still there, but he did not need it.

A good friend shares what they have, not what they lost.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Leo

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Papa gave Leo a cup of milk. Leo is a little raccoon. He likes milk a lot.

Leo held the cup with both paws. He ran to show his wagon. Then he fell. The milk went splash on the floor. Oh no. White milk on the rug.

Leo felt sad. He sat down. He did not want to move.

Down the hall, under a door, a small light glowed. It was soft and far away. Leo looked at it. It made him feel calm. He wanted to go to it. But he could not.

Mama came. She did not yell. She said, "We can clean it up. We can share a new cup."

Leo got a rag. He wiped the milk. Mama poured two cups. They sat by the wagon.

The light under the door was still there. Leo saw it, and then he looked away.

It is okay to spill. It is better to help and share.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Leo

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Pushing his red wagon, Leo the raccoon found a puddle of milk on the kitchen floor. It was white and wide. "Oh no," said Leo. "I spilled it."

He tried to wipe it up. His little paws made it worse. The milk ran under the chairs. Leo felt sad. He sat down.

Then he saw a small light. It was green and soft. It glowed under a door down the hall. Leo wanted to touch it. He walked to the door. The light was so pretty. But he could not reach it. It was just a sliver.

"Help me," said Leo. His mom came. She helped him mop. "We can share this job," she said. Leo felt calm.

They cleaned the floor together. Leo put the empty cup in his wagon.

The green light still glowed down the hall. Leo looked at it once more. Then he went to play. Some things you want stay far away. But clean hands and a kind helper are close and good.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Leo

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
P milk ran all over the floor. Leo the raccoon had bumped the jug with his wagon. Now the kitchen smelled like milk, and the floor was white and wet.

Leo got a rag. He wiped and wiped. The milk went under the door down the hall. A thin line of light lay there too, small and green and soft.

Leo stopped wiping. He looked at the light under the door. It did not move. It just stayed, like it was waiting.

He pushed the rag again. The light came back. He sat down. The milk got cold on his feet.

His sister came. "Help me," she said. Leo blinked. He wrung out the rag.

"I want to go there," Leo said.

"You can't," she said. "Come on. We share the work."

They wiped the floor together. The room grew calm and clean. The green light stayed under the door, and Leo did not reach it.

You can want a thing forever. You still have to wipe the milk.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: Leo

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text: Please do not spill the milk, said Leo. He was a small raccoon. On a sunny afternoon, Leo pulled his wagon full of milk. Then bump. The milk fell. It made a big white puddle. Leo was sad. He did not want to share his milk now. He wanted to be calm. But down the hall, under a door, a little light was shining. It was green. It was so soft. Leo looked at the spilled milk. Then he looked at the light. The milk was white. The light was green. The light pulled him. He walked away from the puddle. He put his hands on the door. The light was under it. He could not reach it. He tried again. The light stayed under the door. Leo said, I want the light. I want the light. I want the light. The milk got warm. No one shared it. The light did not move. Leo sat by the door and did not go home. A spilled thing can be fixed, but a heart that only wants and never shares stays empty and far from calm.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: June

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Silly raccoon knocked the milk right off the step. June heard the clink and the splash. She ran out in her coat. The cold autumn evening bit her nose.

"Oh no," June said. "That was for supper."

The raccoon sat in the white puddle. It licked its paws. It looked happy. June smiled a little.

"We can fix this," she said.

She got a rag and a bucket. The raccoon watched her wipe the step. Then it waddled toward the gate. It moved like a slow wave.

"Good night," June said.

The raccoon went into the dark of the woods. Far off, past the trees, a small light glowed. It was tiny and far and cold. June looked at it for a moment. She felt a little dizzy. She wanted to walk to it. But it was too far. She could never reach it.

"Come inside," called Mom.

June turned away. The light stayed behind the trees. She shut the door. The milk was gone, but the step was clean.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: June

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Soon the milk tipped over. June the raccoon watched it run across the porch. "Oh no," she said. "That was our snack."

She tried to lap it up fast. The cold made her paws slow. She got a little dizzy from bending down so long. "Help me," she called to her friend Bo. "Please help me save it."

Bo brought a flat leaf. They scooped and scooped. Most of the milk soaked into the wood. That was a problem. Then June had an idea. "We can pour the rest in a bowl," she said.

They did. Only a little was left. But it was enough for two small sips. "Not bad," said Bo.

June looked past the gate. Far off, in the dark of the woods, a small light glowed. It was green. It blinked like a tiny star. She lifted one paw and gave a slow wave. She wanted to touch it. She could not. It stayed far away, soft and cold. She turned back to Bo. "Let's go home," she said. The green light kept shining behind the trees.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: June

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Slowly, June the raccoon found the spilled milk. It made a white puddle on the cold stones. "Oh no," she said. "My dinner is gone."

She tried to lap it up. But the puddle was too wide. Her paws slipped. She felt dizzy and sat down.

Then she saw it. A small green light, far off in the dark of the woods. It blinked once. Twice.

June stood up. She walked past the old gate. The wind gave a wave through the bare trees. She lifted her nose. The light was still there. She wanted to touch it.

"Come back," she whispered.

But the light did not come. It only shone. June took one step. Then another. Her milk was forgotten. The light was all she could see.

A kind owl flew down. "Your milk is safe," said the owl. "I put a leaf over it."

June blinked. She looked back. The light was gone. She followed the owl home. She drank her milk. It was good.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: June

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Something cold spilled on the porch. June the raccoon had knocked the milk pail over. Now white milk ran between the wooden boards.

"Oh no," June said. "My milk."

She tried to lick it up. But the milk kept sliding away. Her little paws got wet and cold.

Then June saw a small green light in the dark of the woods. It blinked far away. She forgot the milk.

"I want that light," she said.

She ran to the gate. She climbed it. The light blinked again.

"I want it," she said. "I want it. I want it."

The cold autumn evening made her dizzy. She did not see the milk. She did not see the pail. She only saw the light.

"June, come back!" called her friend. "The milk is spilling!"

June stopped. She turned. The light was still there. But her friend was here.

"Help me," June said.

They pushed the pail up. The milk stopped running. The problem was solved. June took one last look at the light. It waved at her from far away. She could not have it. She went home.

stories.topic: a raccoon and a spilled milk
stories.name: June

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Sip, sip, went June as she drank her milk. Then bump! The cup tipped. Milk made a white puddle on the porch. "Oh no," June said. "My milk is gone."

June was a small raccoon with a striped tail. She let out a sad little wave of her paw. The puddle was cold and shiny. She felt dizzy with worry.

"Can I fix it?" she asked. "No," said her mama. "We can get more." But June did not want more. She wanted that milk.

Then she saw it. Far off in the dark of the woods, past the old gate, a small light blinked. It was green. The green light sat deep in the trees. It was so far away.

June stood up. She reached out. "I want it," she said. "I want it." She reached and reached. The light did not come closer. It never came closer.

Mama took her paw. "Come inside. It is cold." June looked back once. "I want it," she whispered. Then she went in and got new milk.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Mittens on, Ruby went outside. The longest night of winter was coming. But first, the sun was warm.

Ruby went up the big hill. She had to climb and climb. Her boots made a loud crunch, crunch in the snow.

At the top, she saw a tall tree. Something tiny winked at the very top. A small green light. It was just a little glow, like a lost firefly.

Ruby wanted it. She reached up. It was too high. She couldn't reach.

She sat down and sighed. Then she had an idea. She made a small snow lantern. She put it on a stick. It glowed like the light in the tree.

"Look," said Ruby. "I made my own."

She didn't need the green light. She had her lantern. She went home happy. And that night was long, but Ruby slept warm and cozy.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text: Mittens on, Ruby went outside. Today was the longest night of winter. So the sun would go to bed early. Ruby wanted to say goodnight. She walked up the hill. The snow went crunch. She began to climb. Up, up, up. Her breath was loud. Then she saw it. A small green light. It sat at the very top of a tall tree. Ruby stopped. She wanted that light. She reached for it. It was too high. She could not have it. Ruby felt sad. She sat down. Then her dad came. He brought a lantern. It glowed warm and gold. "Let's light our own night," he said. They went home. Ruby drank cocoa. The green light stayed in the tree. But Ruby did not need it. Her house was full of light. She smiled. The longest night felt short and sweet.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Many nights are long, but the longest night of winter is the one Ruby waits for. On a sunny afternoon, she puts on her boots and walks up the hill. Snow squeaks under her feet. She wants to see the sun set early. "The night will be so long," she says.

Then she sees it. At the very top of a tall tree, a small light glows. It is green and bright. Ruby stops. She wants that light. She starts to climb the hill more. She starts to climb the tree. The bark is cold. The light is far.

"Come down," calls Mom. Her voice is loud.

Ruby looks up. The light shines and shines. She reaches. Her hand cannot touch it. She climbs down. She feels sad.

At home, Dad makes cocoa. The fire is warm. Ruby sees the green light through the window. It is far away. She smiles. Some lights are just for looking. The night is long, but Ruby is happy.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Mittens on, Ruby went up the hill to see the longest night of winter come. The sun was warm. The afternoon was bright. Ruby wanted to watch the dark come slow.

Then she saw it. A small green light, high at the very top of a tall tree. It blinked once. Ruby stopped.

She tried to climb the tree. The bark was too smooth. She tried to jump. The branch was too high. The light blinked again.

"Wait for me," Ruby said. "Wait for me."

She found a long stick. Too short. She found a loud horn. The light did not move. Ruby felt small.

"Wait for me. Wait for me."

Her papa came. He did not laugh. He lifted her up on his shoulders. Still the light was far away.

"Some lights stay far," he said.

Ruby nodded. They sat on the hill together. The sun went down. The night grew long and kind. Stars came out, one by one, close enough to almost touch.

Ruby smiled. She had her papa. The long night was not scary at all.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Mia Ruby pulled on her boots. Tonight was the longest night of winter. She wanted to stay up and see the sun come back.

On the hill, Ruby saw a tall tree. At the very top, a small light shone. It was green. It was bright. It was too high.

Ruby wanted that light. She wanted to hold it. She started to climb. The wind was loud. Her hands were cold.

"I want the light," Ruby said. "I want the light. I want the light."

She climbed higher. The branches got thin. The light stayed far away. It always stayed far away.

Ruby sat still. She felt sad. Then her mama called her home for cocoa.

Ruby climbed down. She sat by the fire. The room was warm. Her cocoa was sweet.

Morning came. The sun rose. The long night was over. Ruby smiled. She had all day to play.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: in a window across the street
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Candles made the longest night of winter feel warm. Nina helped her mom put one in every window. Then they sat on the chair by the fire.

"Let's make soup," said Mom.

Nina wanted to help. But she felt shy. The big pot was too high. She could not reach the salt.

"Can you get the step stool?" asked Mom.

Nina looked out the window. Across the street, one window was still dark. A small light blinked there. It was far away. She could not reach it. She wished she could. But the soup was waiting.

Nina took a breath. She got the stool. She climbed up. She poured the salt in, slow and careful. The soup smelled good.

"Good job," said Mom.

Later, the neighbor came over. She brought bread. Her window had been dark. Now it was bright. Nina smiled. She did not need to run anywhere. The little light was just a light. Her home was full. The longest night felt short and sweet.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: in a window across the street
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Cold days make the longest night of winter feel very close. Nina knew it was coming. She had a little problem. Her warm socks had a hole. Her feet would be cold all night.

Nina sat on a chair by the window. She tried to sew the sock. The thread would not go in the needle. She felt shy about asking for help. Then she looked across the street. In a window, a small light glowed. It was soft and far away. It looked warm. Nina wished she could reach it. But it was just a light. She could not touch it. She could only see it and want it.

Her mother came in. “Let me help,” she said. Together they fixed the sock. Nina did not have to run to the store.

That night was long and dark. But Nina’s feet were warm. She looked out once more. The little light was still there. She smiled. She did not need to reach it. She had her own warm light inside.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: in a window across the street
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Cold days make the longest night of winter feel very close. Nina knows it is still sunny afternoon, but she counts the hours until dark. She pulls her little chair to the window. She does not want to be shy about the dark, but she is. Then she sees it. Across the street, in a high window, a small green light shines. It is tiny and far. Nina wants to touch it. She wants it to stay. She cannot reach it, even if she could run fast. The sun goes down. The night gets long. Nina keeps looking at the far window. “Stay,” she whispers. “Stay, stay.” Then her mom brings a jar with a firefly. The firefly blinks green, right in Nina’s hands. It is not the window light. It is hers. Nina smiles. The longest night is not so long now. She sets the firefly on her chair and watches it glow until she falls asleep.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: in a window across the street
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Cold days make the longest night of winter feel very close. Nina knows it comes soon. She has a little problem. Her warm socks have a hole. Her toes get cold.

Nina sits on a chair by the sunny window. She wants to fix the sock. But across the street, in a window, a small light glows. It is green and soft. It is daytime, but the light still shines.

Nina looks at the light. She forgets the sock. She thinks, I want that light. I want to hold it. I want it to be mine. She says it again. I want it. I want it.

Her friend Ben comes over. He is shy. He says, Nina, your sock. Nina blinks. She remembers. She and Ben fix the hole together. It is easy with two hands.

The sun goes down. The green light stays far away. Nina cannot reach it. But her feet are warm. She smiles. She has her friend. That is enough for tonight.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: in a window across the street
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Cold days make the night so long. Nina sat in her chair by the window. Tomorrow was the longest night of winter. She had a little problem. Her lantern was broken. "I can fix it," she said. But the parts were small and her hands were slow.

Across the street, in a sunny afternoon, a small light shone in a window. It was green and soft. Nina wanted that light. She wanted it to stay. She wanted it to be hers. She was too shy to ask.

She looked at the light. She looked and looked. "I want that light," she said. "I want that light."

Then she stood up. She did not run. She walked to the door. She walked across the street. She knocked.

A kind woman opened the door. "My lantern is broken," said Nina. "Can you help?"

The woman smiled. She gave Nina a new little bulb. Nina fixed her lantern. That night it shone green and warm. The longest night felt short and bright.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on a little island
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
A long night came in winter. Theo pulled on his hat. It was the longest night of the year. Mom said, "We will make soup."

Theo found a lumpy potato. He found a carrot too. He dropped the carrot. It rolled under the tree. Theo crawled to get it. He bumped his head. "Oof," he said. Mom laughed.

Then Theo saw a little problem. No onions! Soup needs onions. So Theo and Mom made potato soup. It was warm and good. Theo ate two bowls.

After dinner, Theo looked out the window. Far away, on a little island, a small green light blinked. It was tiny. It was pretty. He wanted to touch it.

He reached out his hand. The glass was cold. He could not swim to the island. He could not have the light. It blinked and blinked.

"Come to bed," Mom said. Theo went to bed. The green light stayed on its island. He closed his eyes.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on a little island
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
A cold autumn evening came, and Theo knew the longest night of winter was near. He had a little problem. His warm hat was lumpy and too small. It made his head itch.

Theo walked to the big tree by the water. He saw a small island far away. On it, a green light blinked. It was very far. He wished he could swim to it. But the water was too cold.

He tried to fix his hat. He pulled and tugged. Then he sneezed. His hat flew off and landed in the water. "Oh no," said Theo.

A duck swam by. The duck had the hat on its head. It looked funny. Theo laughed.

"You can keep it," said Theo. The duck quacked and swam away.

Theo went home. He found a soft, big hat. It fit just right. The green light blinked once more. He looked at it and smiled. Then he went to bed. The longest night would come, but Theo was warm.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on a little island
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
A cold autumn evening came, and Theo knew the longest night of winter was near. He had a little problem. His lantern was broken. Papa said, "We must fix it before dark."

Theo looked at the bare tree by the window. Then he saw it. A small green light, far off on a little island. It blinked, slow and soft. He wanted to touch it. He could not swim that far.

He tried to fix the lantern. The tape was lumpy. The string would not stay. Then Papa showed him a trick with a wire. Click! The lantern glowed. Theo laughed. "It works!"

But his eyes went back to the island. The green light still blinked. He reached out his hand. The cold air was empty.

That night, Theo sat by the window. The dark was long. The green light stayed far away. He whispered, "I want to hold you." He said it again. He said it again. The longest night of winter began.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on a little island
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
A cold autumn evening came, and Theo knew the longest night of winter was near. He had a little problem. His warm hat had a hole. Grandma said, "Fix it before the cold comes."

Theo sat by the window. He saw a small green light far away. It sat on a little island. It blinked once. Then again.

He wanted that light. He reached for it. He could not touch it.

Theo tried to fix his hat. He pulled a lumpy knot. The knot popped. He looked at the island. "I want the light," he said. "I want the light."

He tried again. His fingers slipped. He watched the light.

Then Theo had an idea. He climbed the old tree by the shore. He did not swim. The tree bent low. He grabbed a soft leaf and patched the hole.

His hat was warm. The problem was solved.

He laughed. His hat looked funny with a leaf on top.

The green light blinked on its little island. Theo waved goodnight. He could not have it. But his head was warm.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on a little island
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
A long night was coming. It was the longest night of winter. Theo pulled his coat close. It was cold.

Then he saw the light. It was far away, on a little island. Green and small.

Theo wanted that light. He wanted to swim to it. The water was too cold. He wanted, wanted, wanted. That light was all he could see.

He sat by a tree. He hugged his knees. "I want that light," he said. "I want that light." He said it and said it.

His boot felt lumpy. He pulled out a little cake. He laughed. A cake in his boot! The silly cake made him smile.

He ate the cake. He felt warm. He found a rope and a log. He made a raft. It was slow and wobbly.

He did not reach the light. But he was safe and warm. The light blinked, far away. Theo went home.

stories.name: Ada

axes.where: across a big field
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Last night was the longest night of winter. Ada woke up early in the dark. Her job was to raise the flag on the pole. She did it every morning. But today the rope was stuck.

Ada pulled and pulled. The rope would not move. She felt sad.

She got a little stool. She stood on it. She gave the rope a small tap with her hand. Still stuck. She tried again. Then the rope jumped free!

Ada pulled the flag up. It waved in the cold wind. She felt proud.

Then Ada looked across the big field. Far away, one small light was on. It was green and tiny at the edge of the dark.

Ada wanted to walk to it. But the field was wide and cold. Her boots were thin. The sky was still black.

She stayed by the pole. The flag moved over her head.

Morning came slow. The green light went out. Ada never got to touch it. She went inside.

stories.name: Ada

axes.where: across a big field
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Last night was the longest night of winter. Ada woke up early. The sky was still dark and cold.

Ada put on her warm coat. She went outside to check the little bird house. A soft wind made the flag on the pole go tap, tap.

The bird house door was stuck. A small bird sat inside and could not get out. Ada felt sad for the bird.

She got a stick and gave the door a soft push. It opened! The bird flew out and sat on her hand. Ada felt proud.

Then Ada looked across the big field. Far away, a small light was shining. It was green and soft. It blinked like a tiny star.

Ada wanted to touch it. She took one step. Then she stopped. The light was too far.

She went back inside. All day she thought about the green light. At night she looked out her window. The light was still there. She could see it, but she could never reach it.

stories.name: Ada

axes.where: across a big field
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Last night was the longest night of winter. Ada sat by the window and waited for the sun. The house was cold. Mom was asleep. Ada held her small flag from the summer fair. It was red and soft.

She had a problem. Her boots were wet. She could not go outside. So she put the flag on a stick and set it by the door. That helped her feel brave. She was proud of her flag.

Then she saw it. Far across the big field, a little green light was shining. It was small and far away. It was early morning, and the light did not move. Ada tap, tap, tapped the glass. The light did not come closer.

She pulled on dry socks. She ran to the field. The snow was deep. The light stayed far. She ran and ran. Her feet got cold. The light was still far away.

The sun came up. The light went out. Ada walked home slow. Her flag was wet and sad.

stories.name: Ada

axes.where: across a big field
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Long nights are cold. Ada knows this night is the longest of winter. She stays in her warm house with her mom. They make soup. They read a book. Ada feels safe.

Then she looks out the window. Across the big field, far away, a little green light shines. It is small, like a star that fell down. Ada wants to touch it. She wants it to be hers.

"Come back to the soup," says Mom.

But Ada pulls on her coat. She takes a flag from her toy box. She will put the flag in the snow so she can find her way.

The snow is deep. Her boots go tap, tap, tap. She is not afraid. She is proud. She walks and walks. The light stays far away.

Her hands get cold. Her nose gets cold. The little problem is that she cannot reach the light. It is always one more step away.

In the early morning, Mom finds her. Mom carries her home. Ada is sad. The light is still there, small and far, and she never held it.

stories.name: Ada

axes.where: across a big field
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Little Ada woke in the long dark. This was the longest night of winter. She wanted to fix one small thing. Her socks were cold. She pulled them on and felt proud.

Then she saw it. Far across the big field, a small green light. It blinked. Ada wanted it. "I want it," she said. "I want it."

She put on her coat. She took her flag to wave. Tap, tap went her boots on the floor.

"I want it," she said. "I want it."

Out the door she went. The snow was deep. The field was wide. The green light stayed far away.

"I want it," she said. "I want it."

She walked and walked. Her toes got cold again. The light did not come closer.

She sat down in the snow. "I want it," she said. "I want it." But the light just blinked, small and far, and she could not reach it.

stories.name: Suki

axes.where: on a roof across the town
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Cold snow fell on the longest night of winter. Suki pulled her little wagon through the messy streets. She had to fix her lantern before dark. The lantern gave warm light for her family.

Suki stopped to rest. Far away, on a roof across the town, she saw a tiny green light. It blinked like a slow star. She wished she could touch it. But her wagon was heavy, and the snow was deep.

She fixed her lantern with shaky hands. Then she pulled the wagon home. The green light stayed on the roof. It always would.

At home, her mother smiled. “You fixed it,” she said. The warm light filled the room.

Suki looked out the window once. The green light was still there, far away. She did not need to reach it. Some lights are for watching, not holding.

**Moral:** The light you cannot touch can still keep you warm, if you let it.

The longest night passed. Morning came soft and white.

stories.name: Suki

axes.where: on a roof across the town
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Cold wind blew all day. It was the longest night of winter. Suki pulled her wagon through the snow. She had warm bread for Grandma. The path was messy and long.

Suki stopped to fix her boot. Then she saw it. Far away, on a roof across the town, a small light glowed. It was green and soft. It looked like a tiny star resting on the snow.

She wished she could touch it. But it was too far. She walked on. The light stayed behind her, quiet and kind.

At Grandma's house, they ate bread by the fire. Suki thought of the light. She thought of it again while she swept. It was not hers. It was just there, far away.

Then Grandma smiled. "Look," she said. On the shelf sat a little green lamp. It glowed the same soft glow. "I light it every winter," Grandma said.

Suki laughed. What we want from far away is sometimes near, if we only turn our heads. The longest night felt short after all.

stories.name: Suki

axes.where: on a roof across the town
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Cold came early on the longest night of winter. Suki pulled her wagon through the snow. She had bread for Grandma. She had a warm scarf. The path was messy with ice. She had to fix her boot with string.

Then she saw it. A small green light on a roof across the town. It blinked and blinked. Suki stopped. Her wagon felt heavy. She looked at the light. She wanted to touch it. She wanted to hold it. It was so far away.

She walked on. The light stayed behind her. She turned back. It was still there. She pulled her wagon up the hill. The light grew small. She turned again. It did not come closer.

At Grandma's door, Suki looked one last time. The light was gone. Grandma smiled. "You came," she said. "I watched your lantern all the way."

Suki looked down. Her own little lamp was still lit. The light she wanted was her own light, seen from far away.

The thing you chase may already be in your hands.

stories.name: Suki

axes.where: on a roof across the town
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Cold snow fell on the longest night of winter. Suki pulled her wagon to the window. She wanted to fix the messy room before Mama woke.

But across town, on a roof, a small light glowed. It was green and soft. Suki stopped. She forgot the wagon. She forgot the messy floor.

She pushed the window up. Snow bit her nose. The light sat far away on the roof, small as a pea. She reached out. Her hand held only cold air.

"Come here," she whispered. "Come here."

She pulled her wagon to the door. She climbed in and rolled down the hill. The snow was deep. The wheels stuck. She left the wagon in a messy pile.

She ran. She ran past the bakery. She ran past the frozen pond. The light stayed far away, green and small.

At last she stood below the roof. She saw the truth. The light was only a tin star tied to a chimney. A girl named Nell had put it there to cheer her sick brother.

Suki walked home. She fixed her room. The wanting never left her, but the star was just a star. Some lights we chase are lights someone else lit to be kind.

stories.name: Suki

axes.where: on a roof across the town
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Cold came early on the longest night of winter. Suki pulled her wagon through the snow. The sky was gray. The streets were messy with slush. Mama said, "Come home soon." Suki did not listen. She wanted to see the light.

Across the town, on a roof, a small green light glowed. It was far away. Suki could not reach it.

"I want it," she whispered. "I want it. I want it."

She walked and walked. Her toes got cold. The wagon got stuck. She could not fix the wheel. Still she looked at the light. The light did not move. It only shone.

"I want it. I want it."

Then she saw something. The light was not a star. It was a lamp in a window. A girl inside was reading a book. The girl looked warm. The girl looked happy.

Suki turned her wagon around. She went home. Mama had soup. The house was warm. The wanting was still there, small and green and far away. But Suki ate her soup anyway. Some lights are for other people. Home is for you.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: on a bridge over the river
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Pip the goat was scared of high places. Omar was his friend. Omar had a soft beard and kind hands. One hot summer day they walked to the river. The bridge was tall. Pip stopped. "I can't go up there," Pip said. "My legs shake." Omar sat down. He gave Pip a piece of bread. "We can go slow," Omar said. They took one step. Then two. The wind was warm. The river looked muddy and far away. Pip looked up. On the other side of the bridge, a small light shone. It was green and soft. It blinked like a firefly. Pip wanted to touch it. But it was too far. Omar said, "Look at me, not the light." Pip put his feet down. He did a little tiptoe. Then a hop. Soon they were across. The green light stayed where it was. Pip did not need to reach it. He was happy on the ground.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: on a bridge over the river
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Pitter pat, went the small hooves of Omar the goat. Omar loved the grassy field. But he did not love high places. A tall bridge crossed the river nearby. Omar was afraid to cross it.

On a hot summer day, Omar stood by the bridge. He held a piece of bread in his mouth. The path was muddy. His friend, a duck, waddled up. "Why are you sad?" she asked.

"I want the sweet grass on the other side," Omar said. "But the bridge is too high."

"Just tiptoe," said the duck. "One step at a time."

Omar took a step. Then he saw a little green light far away. It sat on the bridge rail. It blinked like a tiny star. He wanted to touch it. But it was too far. He felt small.

He took another step. The light was still there. It made him feel quiet. He wanted to reach it, but he could not. The duck said, "Look at me, not down."

Omar looked at the duck. He crossed the bridge. The light faded away. On the other side, the grass was sweet. He shared his bread with the duck.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: on a bridge over the river
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Pip was a small goat who did not like high places. Omar was his boy. On a hot summer day they walked to the river. Omar carried a piece of bread in his pocket.

They came to a bridge. It was high over the muddy water. Pip stopped. He would not go.

"Come, Pip," said Omar.

Pip shook his head. He put one hoof out. Then he pulled it back.

Omar looked up. Far away, past the bridge, a light shone. It was small and bright. It seemed to sit on the water. It was far off and it would not come closer.

Omar wanted it. He did not know why. He took a step. Then another.

Pip bleated. Omar turned back. He knelt down.

"We go slow," said Omar. "We go tiptoe."

Omar held out the bread. Pip sniffed it. Step by step, they crossed. The muddy river ran under them. Omar did not look down.

On the other side, the light still shone far away. Omar held Pip close. He could not reach the light. But he could cross the bridge. That was enough for today.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: on a bridge over the river
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Pip the goat was scared of high places. Omar fed him bread by the river. The sun was hot. The water was muddy and slow.

"Come, Pip," Omar said. "We cross the bridge."

Pip shook his head. The bridge went up and up. It touched the sky.

Then Omar saw it. A soft light sat on the bridge rail. It was pale and far. It looked like a small moon in the day.

"Look," Omar said.

Pip did not look. He ran away.

Omar waited. The light stayed. It pulled at him. He went tiptoe to the middle of the bridge. He reached out. His hand closed on air. The light was still far.

"Pip," he called. "I need you."

Pip came back. He put one hoof on the bridge. Then two. The light glowed. It seemed close now. But it was not.

"Small steps," Omar said.

They walked. Pip shook. But he walked. At the end, the light was gone. Only the river shone.

"You did it," Omar said.

Pip ate the last bread. The muddy water sang below.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: on a bridge over the river
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Pitter-patter went Omar’s small hooves on the hot bridge. He was a goat afraid of heights. Below, the river moved slow and muddy. “I can’t,” Omar said. “Too high.” His friend Ana held out some bread. “Just tiptoe. One step.” Omar looked up. Far away, past the bridge, a little light blinked. It was small and green. It sat where the sky meets the water. Omar wanted it. He wanted it more than bread. “Come back,” Ana said. But Omar took a step. Then another. The bridge hummed under him. The light stayed far. It always stayed far. “Omar, stop!” Ana called. He didn’t stop. He walked and walked. His hooves clicked. The light blinked. He reached. He reached. “Almost,” he whispered. “Almost.” The river rolled. The sun burned. The light blinked. Omar reached. He reached. He never got there. But he never fell. Ana grabbed his tail. “I’ve got you,” she said. Omar blinked. The light was still there. Far. Green. Waiting.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Gently, Hugo the goat stepped onto the high hill. He did not like it up here. The ground was too far down. His legs felt like jelly. "I am scared," he said.

His friend Mia the mouse was small and brave. "Hold my hand," she said. She put on a warm glove.

The wind blew hard. It was a windy morning. Hugo wanted to slide down the hill fast. But he was too afraid to move. Mia said, "I will help you."

Then Hugo saw a small light in the dark of the woods. It was green and soft. It blinked once. Hugo wanted to go to it. He took one step. The wind felt cold. The light blinked again and went away.

Mia pulled his hoof. "Come on, Hugo," she said. "We can go slow."

Hugo looked at the green light one more time. It was gone. He felt sad. But Mia was here. He took a tiny step down. Then another. The hill was not so bad with a friend.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Goats are not supposed to be scared of high places, but Hugo was. The little hill behind the barn made his knees shake. He would not climb it. Not even for sweet grass.

On a windy morning, Hugo's friend Bea came by. "Let's slide down the hill," she said. Hugo shook his head. The wind blew his ears flat.

Bea put on one warm glove and held out her hand. "I will go slow," she said. The air was cold. Hugo took a small step. Then another.

In the dark of the woods, past the hill, a small green light blinked. Hugo saw it. It was far away. It looked like a tiny leaf. He wanted to touch it. He reached his hoof out. The light did not come closer.

"Come on," said Bea. She pulled him up the hill. Hugo climbed and climbed. The light stayed far away, soft and green. He could not have it. But he could have the hill. He stood on top with Bea, and the cold wind felt good.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Goat Hugo lived on a small hill. He was afraid of heights. Even a little step made him shake. His friend Bea was a brave brown bird. She stayed close on windy mornings.

One windy morning, Bea said, "Let's walk in the woods." Hugo went. The wind blew his ears. It was cold.

Deep in the woods, Hugo saw a green light. It was small and far away. It sat in the dark of the woods. Hugo wanted it. He reached out a hoof. The light did not come.

Bea found a glove on the ground. "Put it on," she said. Hugo put the glove on his hoof. He felt warm. Then the green light came back. It was still far. He wanted to slide to it. But the ground fell away. He was too high. He was afraid.

Bea said, "Hold my wing." Hugo held on. The light stayed far. He could not have it. But Bea was near. They walked home slow in the cold wind.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Gilly the goat loved to climb. But Hugo was a goat who was afraid of heights. He stayed on the flat grass. His friend Pim the donkey stayed with him.

One windy morning, Pim said, "Let's walk in the woods." Hugo felt the cold wind push his ears. He put on one old glove. They went in.

Deep in the dark of the woods, Hugo saw a light. It was small and green. It glowed far away. Hugo wanted it. He forgot the cold. He forgot his fear.

"Hugo, wait!" said Pim. But Hugo climbed a big rock. He wanted to slide down to the light. The light stayed far. It always stayed far. Pim helped him down. Hugo looked back. The green light still shone.

They walked home. Hugo thought of the light. At night he saw it in his dreams. In the morning he went back to the woods. The light was there. Always there. He reached. He reached. He could not touch it.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Goats do not like high places. Hugo the goat lived on a warm, flat farm with his friend Pim. One windy morning, Pim said, "Let's slide down the hill!" Hugo shook his head. "Too high," he said. His hooves felt small.

Then Hugo saw it. Deep in the dark of the woods, a small green light. It was far away. It was high up. The wind blew cold on his face. Hugo wanted that light.

"Come on," said Pim. Pim put on one glove and held Hugo's hoof.

Hugo reached for the light. He climbed a rock. The light stayed far. He wanted it. He could not have it.

He reached. The light stayed far. He reached. The light stayed far. He reached and reached, but the light stayed far.

Pim held him. "I am here," Pim said. But Hugo only saw the light. He reached. The light stayed far. He reached. The light stayed far.

stories.name: Jay

axes.where: on a tower far away
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Little Jay the goat lived on a flat farm. He liked the low grass. He liked the low gate. He did not like high places. High places made his legs shake.

One foggy night, Jay saw a light on a tower far away. It was small and green. The moon was soft behind the fog. Jay did not care about the light. He just wanted his warm hay.

Then a heavy wind came. It blew Jay's red ball up, up, up. The ball landed on the tall barn roof. Jay looked up. His legs shook. He did not want to climb.

He took one step. Then two. His hooves went tap, tap, tap on the wood. He shut his eyes. He kept going.

At the top, Jay got his ball. He was so high! But then he saw the green light on the tower. It was far and small. He wanted to touch it. He reached out. He could not.

Jay climbed down. He held his ball. The light stayed far away. Jay was still a goat who did not like heights. But now he knew he could climb.

stories.name: Jay

axes.where: on a tower far away
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Little Jay the goat was afraid of heights. Even a small rock made his knees shake. He liked the flat grass best. He liked the low barn roof. He never climbed the hill.

One foggy night, Jay saw a small light on a tower far away. It was green and soft. The moon was hid. The fog was thick and heavy. The light seemed to tap on the sky, blink, blink. Jay wanted it. He took one step up the hill. Then he stopped.

He thought of the tall tower. He thought of the green light. He wanted to hold it. But the tower was so high. His legs felt weak.

He tried again. One step. Two steps. The light blinked, blinked. “Come,” it seemed to say. “Come up.”

Jay ran back to the flat grass. He could not go. He was too scared.

Then he saw it was not a tower. It was just the moon behind a tree. It was not green. It was white. Jay felt silly. He was still afraid of heights. But he was not afraid of the moon.

stories.name: Jay

axes.where: on a tower far away
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Little Jay the goat was afraid of heights. Even a small rock made his knees shake. He liked flat grass and low hills.

One foggy night he saw a green light on a tower far away. It blinked soft and slow. Jay wanted to go near it. But the tower was tall. Too tall.

The moon hid behind the fog. Jay took a step. Then he took it back. The light kept glowing. It seemed to say, come. He wanted it so much.

He put his hoof on a stone. Tap, tap. His heart felt heavy. The tower looked so far. The green light called again. Jay said, I want to go. I want to go.

He climbed one step. Then two. His legs shook. The fog wrapped him up. Still the light shone.

Then Jay saw something. The light was not on the tower. It was in a puddle by his feet. The tower was just a shadow.

Jay laughed. He was not high at all.

stories.name: Jay

axes.where: on a tower far away
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Little Jay the goat was afraid of heights. He stayed low on the grass. He never climbed the rocks.

Then he saw the light. It was green and far away, on a tower. Fog wrapped the night. The moon was a soft, white coin. The green light blinked. Jay wanted it.

He tried to climb a small hill. His legs shook. The light was still far. He wanted it. He wanted it.

"Come down," said his mom. Jay did not hear. He wanted the green light.

The fog grew heavy. Jay took a step up. Then another. He did not look down. He looked at the light. He wanted it. He wanted it.

He reached the top. The green light was not there. It was just a firefly on a stick. Jay laughed. The wind went tap on his nose.

He was high up now. He was not afraid. He looked at the moon. He felt big.

stories.name: Jay

axes.where: on a tower far away
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Little Jay the goat lived on a flat farm. Jay was afraid of heights. Even a small rock made his knees shake.

Then Jay saw the light. Far away, a green light shone on a tower. The fog hid the tower. But the light burned through the fog.

Jay wanted that light. He wanted it so much.

"I want the light," said Jay. "I want the light."

The moon was hidden. The fog was heavy. Jay walked and walked.

"I want the light. I want the light."

His hooves went tap, tap on the road. The tower grew tall. Jay looked up. His knees shook.

"I want the light," said Jay. "I want the light."

He climbed one step. Then two. His legs shook. He could not go on.

Jay sat down and cried. Then he saw it. The light was not on the tower. The light was in a puddle by his feet. It was only the moon. Jay laughed. He was not afraid at all.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake

stories.text:
Bella the goat lived on a small farm near the lake. Bella was Nina's goat. Nina loved Bella. But Bella was afraid of heights. She would not climb the big hill. She would not stand on a rock.

One foggy night, Nina and Bella went to the lake. A boat sat on the water. On the boat was a small light. It was a little green light. It was far away. It was so soft and pretty. Bella wanted to go to it. She put one foot on the boat. The boat went up and down. Bella got scared.

Nina held her. "You can do it," Nina said. But Bella shook. She would not jump. She would not run to the light. The boat went away into the fog. The green light got small. Then it was gone.

Nina put a stone in her pocket. She felt sad. Bella felt sad too. Some things we want are too high for us. And that is a very sad thing.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake

stories.text:
Bella the goat lived on a small hill. Nina was her name, but the farmer called her Bella. Nina was afraid of high places. She stayed low. She liked flat grass and soft mud.

One foggy night, Nina went for a walk. She found a boat by the lake. The boat had a small light. It was a little green light, far out on the water. Nina watched it. She put her hoof in her pocket and found a dry leaf. She wanted to run to the light. But the lake was deep and she was small.

The fog came closer. The green light blinked and blinked. Nina stood on a low rock. The light was still far away. She never reached it. Boats go where goats cannot.

In the morning, the farmer found Nina by the water. She was cold and sad. She learned that some lights are for looking, not for holding. That was a hard lesson for a small goat.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake

stories.text:
Bella the goat lived on a hill farm. Bella was Nina's goat. Nina loved Bella. But Bella was afraid of heights.

Nina led Bella up the path. Bella shook. She would not go high. She liked the low grass by the water. She liked her warm pocket of hay.

One foggy night, Nina took Bella to the lake. A boat sat on the water. A light shone on the boat. It was small and green. It glowed through the fog.

Bella wanted that light. She tried to run to it. But the boat was far. The water was deep. Bella was a goat who feared high places, and the boat rocked and rose on the waves.

Every night Bella came back. The soft fog hid the shore. The green light called her. She could not reach it.

Nina held Bella close. "Some lights stay far," she said.

Bella never touched the green light. She stood at the edge, and she watched, and she was sad.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake

stories.text:
Before Nina, the hill was too tall. Nina was a goat. She was afraid of heights. She liked the flat grass. She liked her small rock.

One foggy night she went to the lake. A boat sat out on the water. A little light was on the boat. It was small and green. It was not bright. It did not hurt her eyes.

Nina wanted that light. She put a soft stone in her pocket. She tried to run to the boat. But the water was deep. She could not swim.

Every night she came back. The fog hid the shore. The green light stayed far away. It did not come closer. It did not go away.

She stood on her flat rock. She looked and looked. Her legs were tired. Her heart was tired too.

The light was hers to see. It was not hers to hold.

She never climbed the hill. She never reached the boat. Some things we want stay small and far, and we love them anyway.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake

stories.text:
Because Nina was a goat, she did not like high places. She liked the low field. She liked the flat grass.

On a foggy night she saw a light on a boat out on the lake. It was small and green. It was soft. It did not move.

Nina put a stone in her pocket. She did not run. She walked to the water.

The light was far. The light was low. The light was on the boat.

She wanted to touch it. She wanted to stand on the boat. But the boat was not high. The boat was on the water. The water was deep.

She stepped in. The water was cold.

The green light stayed far. It stayed soft. It stayed on the boat.

Nina swam. The light did not come closer. Nina swam. The light did not come closer. Nina swam.

The fog held her. The light held her eyes. She did not look back at the field.

The boat was never hers. The light was never hers.

Some wants are boats we never reach.

stories.name: Lily

axes.where: on a little island

stories.text:
A goat named Lily lived on a steep hill. She was afraid of heights. Even a small rock made her knees shake.

One sunny afternoon, Lily saw a little island in the pond below. On it sat a shiny green light. It blinked like a tiny star. Lily wanted to touch it.

She took a bite of a red apple. Then she tried to tiptoe down the hill. Her hooves got muddy. She slipped and sat down with a plop. A duck quacked at her. Lily laughed. It was a funny moment.

She looked at the green light again. It was far away. She could not reach it. She did not try again.

Lily walked back to her safe barn. The green light stayed on its island. She knew some pretty things are just for looking. That is okay.

stories.name: Lily

axes.where: on a little island

stories.text: A goat named Lily lived on a farm and was afraid of heights. She liked flat grass and low fences. One sunny afternoon, she found a muddy puddle and a red apple beside it. She took a big bite. Then she saw something far away. A small green light shone on a little island in the pond. Lily wanted it. She put one hoof in the mud and went tiptoe. The mud went squish. She slipped and sat down with a plop. A duck laughed. Lily laughed too. She tried again and again. The light stayed on the island. It was too far. Lily could not reach it. She sat in the mud and watched it blink. It was pretty. But it was not for her. She ate her apple instead. The sun went down. The light went out. Lily walked home, happy and muddy. You cannot always get what you want. But you can still have a good day.

stories.name: Lily

axes.where: on a little island

stories.text:
A goat named Lily lived on a farm and was afraid of heights. She would not climb the big hill. She would not stand on the tall rock. She liked the flat grass best.
