One sunny afternoon, Lily saw a small island in the pond. On the island sat a bright green light. It was shaky and shiny. Lily wanted it.

She put one hoof on the old log. Then another. The log was muddy and slippery. Splash! Her foot went in the water. Lily made a funny face and shook her wet hoof.

She tried to tiptoe to the island. The light seemed close. But the log rolled. The light stayed far away.

Lily found a red apple on the grass. She took one bite. Then she looked back. The green light was still there, small and far.

Moral: Some pretty things are not for us, and that is okay.

stories.name: Lily

axes.where: on a little island

stories.text:
A goat named Lily was afraid of heights. She lived on a farm with a tall hill. All the other goats climbed it. Lily stayed down.

One sunny afternoon, Lily saw a small island in the pond. Something shiny sat on it. A little green light. It blinked and blinked.

Lily wanted that light. She put one hoof on the stepping stones. Then she stopped. The stones were high above the water.

"Just tiptoe," she said. She took one step. She slipped on a muddy stone. Splash! She fell in the pond. A duck quacked at her. Lily laughed too.

She climbed out, wet and silly. She ate a red apple to feel better. But the green light still blinked on the island. It was so close. It was so far.

Lily reached out her hoof. She could not touch it. She never could.

The moral is: some lights are just for looking. And a wet goat still gets her apple.

stories.name: Lily

axes.where: on a little island

stories.text:
A goat named Lily was afraid of heights. She stayed low on the farm. She ate grass and one red apple. Her feet got muddy in the puddle.

Then she saw it. On a little island in the pond, a small green light shone. It was a sunny afternoon. Lily wanted that light. She took a step. Then a tiptoe. Then a hop.

The light blinked. Lily climbed a rock. Her knees shook. She slipped and fell in the mud. Splash! The ducks laughed. Lily laughed too.

She got up. She tried again. The light stayed far away.

Lily reached. The light moved. She reached. The light moved. She reached. The light moved again and again. She could not touch it. She could not have it.

The sun went down. The light went out. Lily stood in the mud.

You cannot hold every bright thing. But you can be brave while you try.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text: When Omar the hedgehog wanted a hug, his prickles got in the way. He tried to hug the soft moss. Ouch. He tried to hug a fallen leaf. Ouch. Omar sat on a little chair and felt sad. His friend Lila the rabbit came by. "I can help," she said. Lila gave him a soft red mitten to wear. Now Omar could hug! He gave Lila a big hug. Then he did a happy hop. The fog came in, soft and gray. Down the street, on a car parked far away, a small green light glowed. Omar saw it for a moment. It looked like a tiny hug he could not reach. He wanted it. But Lila pulled him back to the warm burrow. A loud wind blew. Omar hugged his mitten and slept. The green light stayed far away, and he did not go to it.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text: When Omar the hedgehog wanted a hug, his spines went sharp and sad. He sat on a little chair and wished. His friend Tia the turtle came by. "I can hug you," she said. "But your shell is hard." Omar gave a soft sigh. The fog made everything quiet. Then Omar saw it. Far down the street, on a car, a small green light glowed. It was soft and bright in the mist. He wanted to hop to it. "That light is far," said Tia. "Stay with me." But Omar watched the light. It blinked like a gentle star. Tia brought him a soft blanket. They made a warm pile. Omar still peeked at the green glow. A loud truck rolled past. The light stayed. Tia patted his back. "A hug can be warm," she said. Omar leaned on her. The green light shone on the car down the street. He wanted it. He could not reach it. But Tia held his paw. The fog hugged them both.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
Warm hugs felt good. Omar the hedgehog wanted one. But his quills were sharp. His friends said, "No, thank you." So Omar sat on a little chair and felt sad.

Then Omar saw a green light. It was on a car parked far down the street. The fog made it soft and pretty. Omar wanted to touch it. He took a hop. Then he took two more. The light was still far away.

His friend Ben the rabbit came by. "What do you want, Omar?" Ben asked. "I want a hug," Omar said. "And I want that green light."

"That light is too far," Ben said. "But I can help with the hug." Ben put on a big coat. Then Ben gave Omar a hug. It was soft and warm. Omar did not get poked.

A loud car went by. The green light blinked. Omar looked at it one more time. Then he looked at Ben. "This hug is better," Omar said. The green light stayed far away on the car. Omar did not hop toward it again. He had his friend. That was enough.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text: When Omar the hedgehog wanted a hug, his quills stood up and nobody came close. He sat on a small chair by the window. The fog made the street soft and gray. Then he saw it. A green light, far down the street, on a car. It glowed like a tiny moon. Omar wanted to hold it. He wanted a hug from it. His friend Tilly the turtle came by. "Come," she said. "I will help." Omar took a hop. Then two hops. The light blinked. It was so far. The fog washed everything else away. Tilly called, "This way, Omar!" But Omar watched the green light. It was small and bright and far. He wanted to hug it. He could not reach it. The light stayed on the car. It did not come closer. His arms were too short. The night was loud with quiet. Tilly patted his back. "A hug is here," she said. But Omar looked at the green light, and he reached, and he reached.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
When Omar the hedgehog wanted a hug, he sat on a chair and looked out. The night was foggy. The street was quiet. Then he saw the light. A small green light, on a car parked far down the street. It shone through the fog. Omar wanted it. He wanted a hug from the light. He wanted to hold it.

"Come," said his friend. "Hop with me."

Omar did not hop. He looked at the light. The light was far. The light was soft. He reached a paw out. He could not touch it.

"A hug," said Omar. "I want a hug."

His friend said, "I can hug you."

But Omar looked at the light. The light was green. The light was far. He wanted the light. He wanted a hug from the light.

The fog moved. The light stayed. Omar reached and reached. He did not hop. He did not hear his friend's loud call. He only saw the light. He wanted a hug. He wanted the light. He wanted a hug.

stories.name: Milo

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
I saw Milo the hedgehog wake up early. He wanted a hug. His quills were sharp, so nobody hugged him. "I want a hug," Milo said. "Just one hug."

He walked to the garden. The morning was windy. He stepped in a cold puddle. Splash. Milo did not like that. He shook his little feet.

Then Milo saw a soft light on the other side of a fence. It was small and green. It glowed like a tiny leaf. Milo wanted to climb the fence. But the fence was too tall. He tried and tried. He could not reach.

"Can you help me?" Milo asked a bird. The bird flew away. Milo sat down. He felt sad.

A little girl came out of her house. She saw Milo. "Do you want a hug?" she said. She put on thick gloves. She picked him up. She held him close. Milo felt warm.

The green light was still there, far away. Milo did not need it now. He had a hug.

stories.name: Milo

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
In the morning Milo the hedgehog wanted a hug. He had soft prickles and a small nose. No one came close.

"Can I hug you?" Milo asked a rabbit.

"No," said the rabbit. "You are too poky."

Milo sat by a puddle. The wind made it shiver. It was windy and cold.

Then he saw it. Past the fence, a soft warm glow sat low in the grass. It did not poke. It did not run. It just stayed.

Milo tried to climb the fence. His feet slipped. He tried again.

"Come here," he called. The glow did not come.

He walked to the puddle and looked at his prickles. "Maybe I am too poky," he said.

The glow stayed on the other side, small and kind.

A mole came by. "You look sad," she said.

"I want a hug," said Milo.

The mole opened her arms. Milo hugged her. It was warm.

The glow was still there past the fence. Milo looked at it once more. Then he went home with the mole.

stories.name: Milo

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
I saw Milo the hedgehog wake up early. He wanted a hug more than anything. His spikes were sharp, so nobody hugged him.

Milo walked to the fence. The morning was windy. He saw a soft light on the other side. It was small and warm, like a hug waiting far away.

"Can I climb?" Milo said.
"No," said the fence. "You are too small."

He found a puddle and sat in it. The light stayed past the fence. It did not come closer.

"Please," Milo said. "I just want a hug."
The light did not answer. It only glowed.

Every morning Milo went back. Windy days, wet days, all days. He watched the light and wished.

One day a rabbit came. "You look sad," she said.
"I want a hug," said Milo. "But my spikes are sharp."
"I don't mind," said the rabbit.

She hugged him gently. Milo closed his eyes. The light was still there, far past the fence. But now he did not need to climb.

stories.name: Milo

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
I saw Milo the hedgehog in the yard. He wanted a hug. But his prickles were sharp. "I want a hug," Milo said. "But who will hug me?"

He walked to the fence. The morning was windy. He saw a puddle. He did not step in it.

On the other side of the fence, a small light glowed. It was green and soft. It sat low on a post. Milo stopped. "Oh," he said. "You are there."

He tried to climb the fence. His little feet slipped. The light stayed far away.

"Come here," Milo said. The light did not move.

He walked along the fence. The puddle got on his toes. He did not care.

"I want a hug," Milo said again. But he was not looking at the yard now. He was looking at the green light.

The windy morning blew. The light blinked. Milo reached his paws through the fence. He could not touch it.

"Please," he said. The light just shone.

stories.name: Milo

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
I want a hug, Milo said. Milo was a small hedgehog with soft poky spines. He wanted a hug more than anything.

Early in the morning, Milo saw a little light. It was small and green. It shone on the other side of a fence. The fence was tall and wood.

Milo stood by a puddle. The wind was windy. He put one paw on the fence.

Can I climb? he said. No. The fence was too tall.

Milo looked at the green light. It was warm. It was far. He wanted to hold it. He wanted a hug.

He tried to climb again. He slipped. He fell in the puddle.

Milo, said his friend the snail. Come play.

Milo did not turn. The light was there. It was always there.

I want it, Milo said. I want to hold it.

He reached. He reached. The green light stayed on the other side.

I want it, Milo said. I want it.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
One cold autumn evening, Gus the hedgehog wanted a hug. His quills were sharp and poky. Everyone said, "Too spiky!" So Gus felt shy.

He met a rabbit named Bea. "Will you hug me?" asked Gus. Bea tried. "Ouch!" she said, and hopped back. Gus laughed a little. It was funny.

Bea had an idea. "Let's find soft moss," she said. They did not skip. They walked slowly. Bea helped Gus wrap the moss around his back like a coat.

Then Gus saw a small light. It sat at the very top of a tall tree. It was green and cozy. It glowed like a warm hug he could not have.

"Oh," said Gus. He reached up one paw. The light stayed far away. "I want that," he whispered. But he could not climb so high, and the light did not come down.

Bea gave him a soft brush of her paw instead. Gus smiled. It was not the light. But it was close.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Once Gus the hedgehog wanted a hug. He was small and round. His spikes were sharp. Nobody wanted to hug him.

One cold autumn evening, Gus sat by a tall tree. High up in the tree, he saw a small green light.

"Oh," said Gus. "It is so pretty." He wished he could hold it.

A rabbit came by. "Why are you sad?" she asked.

"I want a hug," said Gus. "And I want that green light too."

The rabbit tried to brush his spikes down. "Ouch!" she said. They both laughed. It was a funny moment.

"Wait," said the rabbit. "I have an idea."

She got a soft leaf and wrapped Gus up like a gift. Then she hugged him. It was warm. Gus was very happy.

He looked up at the green light. It blinked and blinked. He felt shy and small. It was far away. He could not have it. But he did not mind so much now.

"Let's skip home," said Gus. And they did.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Ollie the hedgehog wanted a hug. But Gus was shy. His prickles were sharp. He was too pointy for hugs.

One cold autumn evening, Gus met a rabbit named Ren. Ren said, "I can help." She gave Gus a soft brush. Gus brushed his prickles down. Then he tried to hug Ren. His prickles popped back up! Ren did a funny hop and said, "Ouch!"

Gus felt sad. Then he saw a light. It was a small green light. It glowed at the very top of a tall tree. The light was warm and far away. Gus wanted it. He reached up. He could not touch it.

"Let's skip to that tree," said Ren. They skipped over the cold grass. The green light stayed high above. Gus reached again. It was still too far.

Ren found a big red leaf. She wrapped it around Gus like a coat. Then she gave him a gentle squeeze. It was not a hug, but it was close. Gus smiled.

He looked up one more time. The green light blinked, soft and cold. Gus could not have it. But he had a friend. That was warm enough for one night.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
One cold autumn evening, Gus the hedgehog wanted a hug. His spikes were sharp. Everyone said, "Not now, Gus."

Gus sat by a tall tree. At the very top, a small green light glowed. It blinked in the wind.

"Oh," said Gus. "I want that light." He reached up. The light was too high. "I want that light," he said again.

His friend Mole came by. "You look sad," Mole said. "Do you want a hug?"

"I want the light," Gus said. "I want the light."

Mole gave Gus a soft brush for his spikes. "Try a skip," Mole said. Gus tried to skip. He tripped on a root. Plop! Mole laughed. Gus laughed too.

"Shy hedgehogs can hug," Mole said. "Just be slow."

Gus hugged Mole, very slow. It was warm. But then Gus looked up. The light still blinked.

"I want that light," he whispered. "I want it. I want it."

Mole held his paw. The light blinked on, far away, and Gus kept looking up.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text: One cold autumn evening, Gus the hedgehog wanted a hug. His prickles were sharp. Everyone was too shy to hug him. He sat by a tall tree and felt sad. Then he saw it. At the very top of the tree, a small green light was shining. Gus wanted that light. He wanted it more than a hug. "I want the light," he said. "I want the light." His friend Sam the squirrel came by. "Why do you stare up there?" asked Sam. "I want the light," said Gus. "I want the light." Sam gave him a little brush. "Brush your prickles down," said Sam. Gus did. Then he tried to skip up the tree. He fell down. It was funny. Sam laughed. Gus laughed too. But Gus looked up again. "I want the light," he said. "I want the light." Sam hugged him soft and warm. Gus still looked up. "I want the light," he whispered. "I want the light." The light blinked far away. Gus could not reach it. He held Sam close and said it one more time. "I want the light."

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: across the snowy yard
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Little Tess the hedgehog wanted a hug. Her quills were sharp and poky. No one could hug her. She sat by her window on a snowy day.

Across the snowy yard, a soft light glowed. It looked warm and round. Tess wished she could hold it. But it was far away.

She went outside. She tried to brush the snow off her back. She gave a wiggle. Her quills were too curly and stiff.

A rabbit hopped by. "I cannot hug you," said the rabbit. A mouse ran past. "Ouch," said the mouse.

Tess felt sad. Then she saw the light again, still glowing across the yard. She walked toward it. The light was just a lantern on a bush.

But under the lantern sat a small snail. The snail had no quills. The snail gave Tess a soft, slow hug. Tess smiled. Sometimes a hug comes from the smallest friend.

stories.name: Tess

stories.text:
Little Tess was a hedgehog who wanted a hug. Her prickles were sharp. They made a soft click when she walked.

She stood at the window. Snow fell on the yard. Across the snowy yard, past the fence, a warm light glowed in a far window. It was small and green and soft. It looked like a hug felt.

Tess went outside. She tried to brush the snow off a log. She gave a wiggle. Her prickles stayed sharp. The light stayed far.

She found a scarf. It was curly and red. She wrapped it around her back. Now she was soft. She went to find a friend. The green light blinked far away.

She met a rabbit. "Hug?" said Tess. The rabbit felt her scarf and came close. Then the scarf slipped. Prick! The rabbit hopped off.

Tess sat in the snow. The light glowed. She couldn't reach it. Then she saw her own shadow. It was curly and round and soft.

So Tess hugged herself. She made a little ball. Her prickles pointed out, but her heart was warm inside. Across the yard, the small light glowed. She held herself tight and did not need to reach.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: across the snowy yard
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Little Tess the hedgehog wanted a hug. Her quills were sharp. Nobody wanted to hug a pincushion.

She sat by her window and watched the snow fall. Then she saw it. Across the snowy yard, a soft light glowed in the neighbor's window. It was small and green and warm. Tess pressed her nose to the cold glass and wished she could hold it.

She put on her boots. She took her brush. She tried to wiggle through the snow. Her curly spine left a trail like a tiny road.

The light stayed far away. Tess walked and walked. The snow got deep. The light got bigger but never close.

Then she heard a small cry. A baby mouse sat shivering under a leaf.

"I'm cold," said the mouse.

Tess stopped. She could not hug the light. But she could sit very still and let the mouse curl against her belly, where the quills were soft.

The mouse smiled. "You are warm," it said.

Tess looked across the yard. The green light blink-blinked once, then went out.

She did not need it anymore.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: across the snowy yard
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Little Tess the hedgehog wanted a hug. Her prickles were sharp. She could not hug back. On a snowy day she stood at her door. Across the snowy yard, a soft light glowed in a window. It looked warm. It looked round. It looked like arms.

Tess took her brush. She tried to comb her prickles flat. They would not stay. She gave a wiggle. They popped up again, curly and stiff.

She walked toward the light. Snow made her toes cold. The light stayed far away. She walked and walked. It never came closer.

Back home, Tess sat down. Her friend Mole came by. Mole could not see well. Mole gave her a bump with his nose. It was small and soft. Tess felt warm inside.

Then Tess saw the truth. The light was just the moon on a window. Nobody waited there. But Mole was here. He did not mind her prickles.

So Tess learned something new. A hug does not always need arms. Sometimes it is a bump, a nuzzle, a warm friend close by. The light still shone across the yard. Tess did not need to reach it anymore.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: across the snowy yard
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Little Tess the hedgehog wanted a hug. She asked the rabbit. The rabbit said, "Your prickles are sharp." She asked the mouse. The mouse said, "Your prickles are scary." Tess felt sad.

Then she saw it. Across the snowy yard, a warm yellow glow sat on a stump. It looked soft. It looked round. It looked like a hug.

Tess walked toward the glow. Snow got on her nose. She did a wiggle to shake it off. She did not stop.

The glow was still far. It is always far. Tess said, "Hug. Hug. Hug." Her small feet made little holes in the snow. She tried to brush the cold from her ears. She tried to brush the sad from her chest.

She came to the stump. No glow. Just snow. Tess began to cry.

Then a soft thing touched her back. It was Mother. Mother's fur was curly and thick. Mother pulled Tess in close. The prickles did not matter to her.

stories.name: Noah

axes.where: deep at the bottom of a pond

stories.text:
Snuggled in his leaf bed, Noah the hedgehog wished for a hug. His prickles were sharp. His friends said, "Ouch!" So nobody hugged him.

Before bedtime, Noah went to the pond. He saw something deep down. A small green light glowed at the bottom. It was so pretty. He wanted it.

Noah found a bucket. He tried to scoop the light out. Splash! The bucket tipped over. He did a spin and fell in the mud. "Oops," he said. That was funny. His fuzzy tummy got all muddy.

The green light stayed deep in the pond. It did not come up. Noah could not have it. He wanted it so much.

He went home and washed his fuzzy face. His mom gave him a warm towel hug. "Goodnight, Noah," she said.

Noah closed his eyes. The little green light was still down there. He could not reach it. But his mom's hug was soft and warm. He smiled and fell asleep.

stories.name: Noah

axes.where: deep at the bottom of a pond

stories.text:
Sitting by the pond, Noah the hedgehog watched the sun go down. He wanted a hug more than anything. His spikes were sharp, so nobody hugged him.

Noah saw a fuzzy green light deep at the bottom of the pond. It glowed like a tiny lantern. He wished he could hold it close. He reached a paw in the water. Splash! The light did not move.

He got his little bucket. He scooped and scooped. The bucket came up with weeds and one wiggly frog. The frog gave a funny burp. Noah laughed so hard he did a spin.

Just before bedtime, he sat by the pond again. The green light still shone below, soft and far away. He wanted it. He wanted a hug too. The two wants felt the same.

His mom kissed his prickly head. "Spikes can hug," she said. She wrapped him in a soft towel. Noah smiled. The green light stayed in the pond, but his mom was warm. That was enough for tonight.

stories.name: Noah

axes.where: deep at the bottom of a pond

stories.text:
Sometimes Noah wanted a hug more than anything. Noah was a small hedgehog with a fuzzy tummy and prickly spikes.

Just before bedtime, he went to the pond. He dropped his little bucket in to get water.

Then he saw it. Deep at the bottom, a small green light was glowing. It looked soft and warm. It looked like a hug.

Noah reached a paw down. Too far. He tried to spin around and grab it with his tail. Too short.

A frog laughed so hard it fell backward with a splash. "You cannot hug a light," said the frog.

Noah knew. But he wanted it anyway.

He looked down at the green light again. He thought of a hug. He thought of a hug. He thought of a hug.

His mom found him and gave him a real hug. But he peeked at the pond one more time.

The green light was still there. It always was.

stories.name: Noah

axes.where: deep at the bottom of a pond

stories.text:
Silly Noah is a hedgehog. He wants a hug. But his spines are sharp. So nobody hugs him.

Noah sits by the pond before bedtime. He looks into the water. Deep at the bottom, he sees a small green light. It glows like a tiny lamp. He wants to hold it. He reaches down. The water is cold. He cannot reach. His paw gets wet.

Noah fills a bucket. He tries to scoop the light out. The bucket comes up empty. He tries to spin around and dive in. That is funny. He just gets muddy.

He wants the light. He wants a hug too. But the light is far away. “I want it,” he says. “I want it. I want it.”

His fuzzy friend the rabbit comes close. “You are prickly,” she says. “But I can hug you with a pillow.”

Noah looks at the pond. The green light still shines. He cannot have it. But he can have a hug. So he takes the hug. The light stays deep down. That is okay.

stories.name: Noah

axes.where: deep at the bottom of a pond

stories.text:
Snuggled in his leaf bed, Noah the hedgehog wanted a hug. His quills were sharp, and nobody hugged a hedgehog.

Just before bedtime, he saw something deep at the bottom of the pond. A small green light. It glowed like a soft hug.

"Oh," said Noah. "I want it. I want it."

He filled a bucket with pond water to catch the light. He gave the bucket a spin. The water made a funny sound — blub-blub-blub! Noah laughed.

But the light stayed deep down.

"I want it," Noah said again. "I want it. I want it."

He reached one fuzzy paw toward the water. The light did not move closer. It only shimmered, far and small.

"I want it. I want it. I want it."

His mama found him by the pond. She wrapped him in a soft blanket. That was a hug, but not the hug he wanted.

Noah looked at the little green light. It looked back, quiet and far. He could not have it. So he went to bed, thinking of it still.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: June

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Next to the big oak tree, June baked a cake for a sleepy bear. The bear yawned and yawned. June put honey on the cake. She put berries on top. The bear was still sleepy.

June flew her kite to wake him up. The kite went up, up, up. It danced in the sunny afternoon.

Then June saw a small green light. It sat high up on a mountain. It blinked like a tiny star. June wanted to touch it. But the mountain was far away.

She pulled her kite string. The kite came down. The bear opened one eye.

"Wake up, sleepy bear," June said. "I made you a cake."

The bear sat up. He ate the cake. He was happy.

June did not get the little light. But she did not mind. She began to sing a soft song. The bear hummed too.

June felt warm and proud. The green light stayed on the mountain. June stayed with her friend. That was enough.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: June

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Next to the big oak tree, June baked a cake for a sleepy bear. The bear yawned and rolled over. June put sweet berries on top. She wanted the bear to wake up happy. Her kite sat on the grass.

Then June saw it. Far away, high up on a mountain, a tiny light blinked. It was small and far. June wished she could touch it. But the bear needed her.

June sang a soft song. The bear opened one eye. "Cake," June said. The bear sat up slow. He took a big bite. He smiled a sleepy smile. June felt proud.

She looked at the mountain again. The light was still there, blinking. It pulled at her like a string. She waved at it. Then she turned back to the bear.

The bear licked his paws. June laughed. They shared the cake in the warm sun. Her kite danced in the wind. The light stayed far away, but June was happy right here.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: June

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Nobody knew how to wake the sleepy bear. June said, "I will make a cake." She put on her apron. She mixed flour and milk. The sun was warm on her back.

Then she saw the light. It sat high on the mountain. It was a small green dot. It blinked, slow and soft. June stopped stirring. "I want to touch it," she said. She did not know how.

She stirred the batter again. The green dot stayed far away. She added honey for the bear. The dot did not move.

June flew her kite to reach it. The kite went up, up, up. It did not reach the light. June was not sad. She wanted to sing to the bear instead.

She walked to the bear's cave. The cake was warm. The bear opened one eye. He smelled the honey. He ate the cake. He was happy. June was proud. The green dot blinked far away. June smiled. She did not need to touch it.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: June

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Nobody knew how to wake the sleepy bear. So June baked a cake. She put honey in it. She put berries on top. The bear would smell it and wake up. She was sure.

Then she saw the little green light. It sat high up on a mountain. It was small and far and bright. It said, come here, June.

June looked at her cake. She looked at the light. She walked to the door. She walked back. The cake was for the bear.

She ran outside with her kite. The wind pulled it up, up, toward the light. The light stayed far away.

She came back inside. She sang to the cake. She felt so proud of it. But her eyes went to the window. The light was still there.

Come here, June. Come here.

She went up the mountain. She climbed and climbed. The light stayed just as far.

Then she heard a big yawn. The bear woke up! It smelled the cake all the way up the hill.

June ran home. The bear ate every crumb. It licked its paws. The little green light blinked once and went out. June did not mind at all.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: June

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Next June made a cake for the sleepy bear. The bear yawned in his big soft chair. June put sugar in the bowl. She put eggs in too. The cake would be good.

Then June saw the little light. It sat high up on the mountain. It was small and low and bright. It did not move. June wanted it. She wanted it so much.

"Come here, light," June said. "Come here, light."

She stood on her toes. She could not reach. She got her red kite. The kite went up. It did not touch the light.

"Come here, light," June said. "Come here, light."

The cake sat in the pan. June did not stir it. She did not sing. She was not proud of the cake. She only looked up.

The bear woke up. He saw June. He saw the kite. He saw the small light too. "That light is far," he said. "But this cake is here."

June looked at the cake. She looked at the bear. She smiled. She stirred the cake and put it in the oven. Then she sang a song. The bear danced. The cake was warm and sweet. June was proud. The light stayed on the mountain, and June did not mind.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text: When Tom baked a cake for a sleepy bear, he put on his tall hat. He mixed honey and flour. He hummed a soft song. The bear was in bed. Tom wanted to bring the cake before the bear woke up. Late at night, Tom walked through town. He carried the cake in both hands. Across the town, on a roof, a small light glowed. It was far away and tiny. Tom stopped for a moment. He made a wish. Then he kept walking. The light stayed on the roof. It did not come closer. Tom did not need it. He needed the bear. He climbed the hill. He opened the bear's door. The bear smiled. They ate cake together. Tom felt happy. The light still shone across town. But Tom was where he belonged. Some lights are just for looking. Warm hands are for holding.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text: When Tom baked a cake for a sleepy bear, he put on his tall hat. He mixed and stirred. He yawned. The cake was warm and sweet. It was late at night. Tom looked out the window. Across the town, a small light sat on a roof. It was green and soft. Tom felt a wish inside him. He wanted to touch it. But he could not. He had a cake to give. He walked to the bear's cave. The bear slept and slept. Tom left the cake near its nose. The bear smiled in its sleep. Tom felt happy. He went home. He looked for the light again. It was still there. It blinked like a tiny star. He wished for it once more. He knew he could not have it. Some things stay far away. That is okay. The cake made the bear happy. That was enough.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
When Tom baked a cake for a sleepy bear, he used honey and nuts. He put on his tall hat. He sang a soft song. The bear snored in the corner.

Late at night, Tom looked out the window. A light shone on a roof across the town. It was small and green and far away. Tom had a wish. He wanted to touch that light.

He walked to the door. Then he stopped. The bear needed the cake. Tom looked at the roof again. The light seemed to say, come here. Come here. Tom shook his head.

He sat with the bear. He gave him a slice. The bear smiled a happy smile. Tom felt warm inside.

The light stayed on the roof. Tom knew it would always be there. He did not need to hold it. Some things are for watching, not for having. That is a hard lesson. But it is a good one.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
When Tom baked a cake for a sleepy bear, he put on his tall hat. He mixed honey and berries. The bear snored in the next room. Tom wanted the cake to be warm and sweet for morning.

Then Tom saw the light. It sat on a roof across the town. A small green lamp, far away. It glowed like a candy drop. Tom forgot the cake. He stared out the window.

“I wish I could touch it,” he said. The cake bubbled over. Tom wiped the stove. He looked up again. The light was still there. Still far.

He tried to be happy with his cake. But his eyes kept sliding to the roof. Green, green, green. He thought, I wish, I wish, I wish. The bear slept on.

At last Tom cut a slice. The bear woke and ate it. “Good cake,” the bear said. Tom smiled a little. Some lights stay far away. A warm cake in your hands is closer. That is the true happy thing.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
When Tom baked a cake for a sleepy bear, he put on his tall hat. He mixed and stirred. He yawned. The cake was warm and sweet.

Then Tom saw the light. It sat on a roof across the town. It was small and far. It was not red. It was not blue. It was the color of new leaves.

I want that light, Tom said. I want that light.

He left the cake. He walked out the door. He walked past the sleepy bear. He walked past the trees. I want that light, he said. I want that light.

The light did not come closer. Tom's feet grew tired. His hat fell off. I want that light, he said. I want that light.

He came back home. The bear was asleep. The cake was gone. Tom felt sad. Then he felt glad. The bear was full. The bear was warm. The bear had a happy dream.

Tom made a wish. He wished for the light. But he held the sleepy bear's paw. Some lights stay far away. Some warm things stay close.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: on a roof across the town
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Remy the baker made a cake for a sleepy bear. The bear was Hugo. Hugo slept all day in his big chair.

"Wake up, Hugo," said Remy. "I made you a cake."

Hugo did not wake up. Remy put the cake on the table. The cake was warm. It smelled like honey.

Remy sat by the window. The sun went down. Far away, on a roof across the town, a small light turned on. It was green. Remy looked at it for a while.

Hugo opened one eye. "Is that cake for me?"

"Yes," said Remy. "But you must be brave and get up."

Hugo stood in a puddle of sun on the floor. He took one step. Then he sat back down. "I need rest," he said.

Remy brought the cake to him. Hugo ate one bite. Then he slept again.

The green light stayed on the roof. Remy watched it until it went out. The cake was gone. Hugo never knew.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: on a roof across the town
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Rosa helped Hugo bake a cake for a sleepy bear. The bear was Hugo's friend. The bear slept all day. Hugo wanted to give him a cake when he woke up.

Hugo mixed flour and honey. He put the cake in the oven. Then he saw a puddle on the floor. The milk had spilled. "Oh no," said Hugo.

Rosa said, "Do not worry. We can fix it." She wiped the puddle. Hugo felt brave again. They made a new cake.

The sun went down. Hugo looked out the window. On a roof across the town, a small light shone. It was soft and far away. Hugo wished he could touch it. But he could not.

The bear woke up. He ate the cake. "Thank you, Hugo," he said. Then he went back to rest. He slept and slept.

Hugo sat by the window. The light was still there. It was small and far. He wanted it so much. But the bear was asleep. The cake was gone. Hugo was alone.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: on a roof across the town
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Rosa baked a cake for a sleepy bear. Hugo was her friend. He slept all day in his cave. Rosa mixed flour and honey. She put the cake in the oven. It smelled warm and sweet.

Then Hugo did not wake up. Rosa was sad. She wanted him to eat cake with her.

The sun went down. Rosa sat by a puddle. She felt small. She could not be brave.

Across the town, on a roof, a little green light blinked. It was far away. It looked like a candy drop. Rosa wanted to hold it. She wanted to put it on the cake.

"It is too far," she said. "It is too far."

She climbed a hill to rest. The light stayed on the roof. It did not come closer. It did not go out.

Rosa got an idea. She put the cake on a cart. She pushed it to Hugo's cave. She waited.

Hugo woke up slow. He ate one bite. He smiled. Then he slept again.

Rosa sat alone. The green light blinked on the roof. She still could not reach it. She ate no cake.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: on a roof across the town
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Rosa helped Hugo bake a cake for a sleepy bear. The bear was Hugo's friend Ben. Ben slept all day. Hugo wanted to wake him with a cake. He put in honey and nuts. He put in sweet berries. The cake was round and warm. Hugo felt happy.

Then Hugo saw it. On a roof across the town, a small light blinked. It was soft and green, like a leaf in the sun. The sun was going down. The light called to Hugo. He wanted to touch it. He forgot the cake.

"Hugo, stir," said Rosa. Hugo stirred. He looked at the light. He wanted to go. He wanted to touch it. He forgot the cake again.

The cake burned. It was black on top. Hugo was sad. Rosa helped him make a new cake. They made it fast. Hugo did not look at the light. The new cake was good. They gave it to Ben. Ben did not wake. He just slept.

Hugo sat by a puddle. The light blinked far away. He could not reach it. He was not brave enough. He let out a big sigh. He would never touch the light.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: on a roof across the town
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Rosa baked a cake for a sleepy bear. Hugo was the sleepy bear. He yawned by the window. The cake smelled warm.

Then Hugo saw it. On a roof across the town, a small green light blinked at sunset. It was tiny and far. It was not for him. He knew it was not for him. But he wanted it.

"Hugo, come eat," said Rosa.

But Hugo watched the light. The light sat on the far roof. It did not come closer. Hugo pressed his nose to the glass. He forgot the cake. He forgot his nap. He forgot Rosa.

A puddle on the road held the light too. Hugo ran out to catch it. Splash. The puddle broke the light into pieces. Hugo was brave, but he was sad.

He went back inside. The cake was gone. Rosa had eaten it. Hugo did not rest. He lay down and looked out the window at the little far light. It blinked. It blinked. It never came.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
A cake for a sleepy bear waited on the table. Cleo made it with honey and nuts. Her friend Bear was still asleep. He slept and slept. Cleo was worried. Bear was hungry when he woke. What if the cake got cold?

She went outside for a walk. The evening was cold. Autumn leaves blew by. She came to the stream. In the reeds, a small green light glowed. Cleo stopped. She wanted to touch it. She reached out. The light stayed far away. She picked up a pebble. She tried to skip it across the water. The light watched from the reeds. Cleo felt sad. She could not have it.

Then she heard a sound. Bear was awake! He was at the door. Cleo ran home. Bear ate the cake. He smiled. "This is warm and sweet," he said. Cleo was happy. The green light stayed by the stream, but she did not need it.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
A cake for a sleepy bear needed one last thing. Cleo put on her coat. The cold autumn evening made her nose pink.

She walked to the stream for a pebble to press the icing flat. The reeds moved. A small green light was there.

Cleo stopped. She wanted to touch it. She reached out. The light stayed just past her fingers.

“I am hungry,” she said. “But I want that light too.”

She found her pebble. Then she saw the light again in the reeds. It seemed to skip away when she came close.

Cleo tried once more. Her paw closed on empty air. The light only shone.

A little problem: the bear was too sleepy to wake for cake. Cleo had an idea. She put the cake by his nose. He sniffed. He smiled.

The light blinked once, far off. Cleo did not need to hold it. She had her bear. They ate cake in the warm den.

The small green light stayed outside, and that was all right.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
A cake for a sleepy bear was what Cleo wanted to make. Her friend Bear yawned all day. His birthday came tonight. But the oven was cold. The eggs were gone. Cleo felt a little worry.

She walked to the stream for water. The evening was cold. Autumn leaves fell on her hat. Then she saw it in the reeds. A small green light. It blinked once. Twice. It was far away and soft.

Cleo wanted that light. She reached out her hand. The light stayed in the reeds. It would not come to her. She picked up a pebble instead.

She made a wish and tried to skip the pebble. It sank. She was still hungry for that light. But she had water now.

She went home. She made a honey cake with no eggs. Bear woke up. He smiled big. They ate cake by the fire. The green light blinked far away. Cleo did not need to hold it. She had Bear. That was enough.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
A cake for a sleepy bear sat on the table. Cleo had made it with honey and nuts. Her friend the bear was hungry and tired. He would wake soon.

Cleo went to the stream to wash her hands. The evening was cold. Autumn leaves blew around her feet. She saw a small light in the reeds. It was green and far away.

She wanted to touch it. She took a pebble and made it skip across the water. The light stayed in the reeds. She reached out her hand. The light was not there.

"Come back," she said. She said it again. The light did not come.

Then Cleo remembered the cake. The bear would be sad without it. She went home. The bear woke up and smiled. They ate the cake together. Cleo was happy. But she looked out the window once more. The green light was gone.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
A cake for a sleepy bear was what Cleo wanted to make. The bear was her friend. He was very tired. He was very hungry too.

Cleo mixed the cake in a bowl. Then she saw it. A small green light, far off in the reeds by the stream. It blinked once.

She put down the spoon. She walked to the water. The air was cold. It was a cold autumn evening.

She picked up a pebble. She tried to skip it. It sank. The light stayed far away.

She reached for it. Her hand was empty. The light was not for her.

She went back inside. She baked the cake. It was warm and sweet.

The bear woke up. He ate the cake. He smiled.

Cleo smiled too. But that night, she looked out the window. The light was still there. She reached. She reached. She could not have it.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Anya

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text: Gently, Anya mixed the batter for a cake. Her bear was sleepy. He wanted a cake before his nap. The afternoon was windy and dark. A storm was coming. "I will build the cake with care," Anya said. She put it in the oven. The rain hit the roof. Anya looked out the window. Through the fence, far away, she saw a small light. It was green and soft, like a tiny moon on the ground. She wanted to touch it. But the fence was tall. "Come back," said the bear. "The cake is done." Anya turned away. The light stayed behind the fence. She gave the bear his cake. He ate one bite. Then he slept. The storm got loud. The light blinked once and went out. Anya sat alone. She did not want cake. She wanted the green light. But she could not reach it.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Anya

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
Gently, Anya mixed the batter for the sleepy bear’s cake. The bear yawned in his big chair. Rain tapped the window. It was a stormy afternoon.

“Will he wake up for a slice?” Anya asked.

“Maybe,” said her mom.

Anya put the cake in the oven. She looked outside. The wind blew hard. It was very windy.

Then she saw it. Past the fence, a soft light sat low in the gray sky. It was not the moon. It was smaller and greener. It blinked once.

Anya pressed her nose to the glass. She wanted to build a path to it. But the fence was tall, and the rain was cold.

“Come eat,” said her mom.

The cake was warm. The bear did not wake. Anya looked at the fence again. The little light was still there. It did not come closer. She knew she could not go.

The bear slept. The cake got cold. And the small light stayed on the other side, where she could only look.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Anya

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
Gently, Anya stirred the batter for the sleepy bear's cake. He was too tired to wake. Rain hit the window. The afternoon was windy and gray.

"Bear, wake up," she said. "I made you a cake."

He did not move. Anya looked outside. Past the fence, a small light glowed. It was the color of new leaves.

"I will get it," she said. "Then you will wake."

She put on her coat. The wind pushed her back. The fence was tall. She tried to build a stack of stones to climb. The stones fell.

"Bear, help me," she called. No sound came.

She sat in the wet grass. The light stayed far away. It did not come closer. It did not go out.

"I want to hold it," she said.

The rain got louder. The cake got cold. When the moon came, the light was still there. Anya never reached it. She went inside and slept by the bear.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Anya

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
Ginger was on Anya's hands. She mixed it in the bowl. She wanted to bake a cake for a sleepy bear.

The bear was her friend. He slept all day. A cake would wake him up soft and warm.

Rain hit the window. It was a windy, stormy afternoon.

Anya looked outside. Past the fence, far away, a small light was on.

It was green and low. It did not move. It just stayed.

"Come on," she said. "I have to stir."

She stirred. She looked back at the light.

"Bear will like this cake," she said.

She looked again. The light was still there.

"Anya, are you done?" her mother called.

"Yes," she said. But she was not.

She cracked one egg. Then she watched the light some more.

The moon did not come. The storm did not stop.

The cake did not build. It stayed wet in the pan.

The bear woke up. He did not want cake. He wanted to sleep.

Anya sat by the window. The little light stayed far away, past the fence, and she could not reach it.

stories.topic: a cake for a sleepy bear
stories.name: Anya

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
Good cake for a sleepy bear, Anya said. She put the bowl on the table.

Then she saw it. A small green light, far away, past the fence. It glowed like a tiny moon.

Anya, said her mother. Stir the eggs.

I want to go there, Anya said.

You cannot, said her mother. The fence is tall.

The wind blew hard. It was a windy day. Rain hit the window.

Anya climbed a chair. She saw the light again. It did not move. It only shone.

I can build a way, Anya said.

You are too small, said her mother.

Anya stacked books. She stacked pots. The tower fell.

The bear slept in his bed. He did not wake. The cake was not made.

Anya reached the fence at last. She held the cold bars. The light was there, so close, so far.

Please, she said.

The light did not come.

The storm grew dark. The light stayed on the other side. Anya sat down in the wet grass and cried.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: at the end of a long road
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Cold leaves fell on Theo. He put on his red cap. The leaves were busy. They went up and down. Theo saw a squirrel. The squirrel had a big nut. The nut fell in a hole. The squirrel was sad. Theo helped. He found a stick. He did not knock the nut. He lifted it out. The squirrel took the nut. It ran up a tree. Theo felt glad. Then he saw a light. It was far away. It was at the end of a long road. The light was soft and green. It was late at night. Theo looked and looked. He did not go to it. He went home. His mom gave him warm milk. The light blinked far away. Theo felt sleepy. The squirrel came back. It sat on his window. Theo smiled. The little light was still there. But Theo had his cap and his friend. He was happy.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: at the end of a long road
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Cold wind made the leaves fall. Theo watched them drop. Red leaves. Yellow leaves. They made a soft bed on the ground.

Theo was a small squirrel. He had a warm cap. It was red. He liked his cap.

"Time to gather nuts," said Theo. He was busy. He ran down the road. He looked for nuts. He found three nuts. Then he found a big problem. The wind blew his cap away!

The cap rolled down the road. Theo ran after it fast. The road was long. Very long. Late at night, he saw a small green light far away. It did not move. It just glowed.

Theo stopped. He felt small. The light was so far. He wanted to go there. But his cap was more important.

Then a kind owl flew down. "I saw your cap," she said. She gave it back. Theo put it on.

He was happy. He went home with his nuts. The green light stayed far away. But Theo did not mind. He had his cap. He had his nuts. He was warm and safe.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: at the end of a long road
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Cold wind made the leaves fall down. Theo the squirrel was busy. He had to find nuts before winter. He put on his little red cap.

"Knock, knock," said the wind on the trees. More leaves fell. Theo looked for nuts. But the nuts were gone.

"Oh no," said Theo. "What will I do?"

He ran down a long road. Late at night, the sky was dark. Then Theo saw something far away. It was a small, soft light. The light was green, like a tiny leaf that never falls. It was at the end of the road.

Theo wanted to touch it. He ran and ran. But the light stayed far away. Every night, he came back. He wanted that green light.

Then a big oak tree dropped nuts. Plop, plop, plop. So many nuts! Theo filled his cheeks. He forgot the far light. He was happy. He went home to sleep.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: at the end of a long road
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Cold wind blew leaves down the road. Theo the squirrel was busy. He ran and caught leaves. He put them in a big pile.

Theo lost his red cap. It fell in the leaves. "Oh no," said Theo. He looked and looked.

Knock, knock. The wind hit a tree. More leaves fell. Theo was sad. He wanted his cap.

Then Theo saw a small light. It was far away. It was at the end of the long road. The light was pale and far. It did not move. It was late at night.

Theo stopped. He looked at the light. He wanted to go there. But his cap was here. He looked at the light again. It was so far. He wanted it. He did not know why.

Theo shook his head. He dug in the leaves. He found his cap! He put it on.

The light was still there. Theo looked one more time. Then he went home to his warm nest. He was happy.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: at the end of a long road
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Carl the squirrel was busy. He ran and ran. He got nuts for his cap. He hid them in a tree. Then he saw a light. It was far away. It was at the end of a long road.

Theo saw it too. Theo was a boy. He had a cap. He said, "I want that light."

Knock, knock. Theo hit the tree. The nuts fell down. Carl was sad. "My nuts!"

Theo said, "Do not be sad. I will help."

The light was still far. It was late at night. The road was long. The light was small. The light was green. It did not come close.

Theo and Carl went down the road. They found a little hole. The nuts fell in. The problem was solved.

The light was still there. It was always there. Theo looked. Carl looked. They sat down.

The light did not come. But they were happy. They had nuts. They had a cap. They had each other. The light was far, but the night was warm.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: in the window of an old house
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Down came the leaves on Jack’s street. Red and gold, soft and slow. A little squirrel ran under them. It wanted to hide its nuts.

Jack watched from his porch. Rain tapped his hood. The squirrel dropped a nut. It rolled into a drain. The squirrel looked sad.

Jack got his ladder. It was dusty and tall. He set it by the drain. He did not want the squirrel to be sad.

He climbed up. He reached down. He tried to grab the nut. Splash! His hand got wet. The squirrel chattered at him. Jack laughed. It sounded like a tiny scold.

Then Jack had an idea. He used a stick. He scooped the nut out. The squirrel took it fast. It ran up a tree.

Jack put the ladder away. His hands were cold and wet. Then he saw a green light. It glowed in the window of an old house. It was small and far. He wished he could hold it. He could not.

The rain kept falling. Jack went inside for soup.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: in the window of an old house
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Down came the leaves on Jack's little hill. Red and gold, soft and slow. A squirrel ran by with a nut in its mouth. Jack wanted to see where it lived.

The squirrel ran up a tree. Then it jumped to a roof. Then it sat by a window. The window was in an old house. Rain tapped on the glass.

Jack saw a small light in that window. It was green and still. He wanted to touch it. He reached up. The rain got in his eyes.

The squirrel dropped its nut. The nut rolled down a dusty pipe. It got stuck. The squirrel cried.

Jack found a ladder. He did not grab the light. He grabbed the nut. He put it on a flat stone. The squirrel took it and ran.

Jack looked back at the window. The green light was there. He waved good night. Then he went home for a warm bath.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: in the window of an old house
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Down came the leaves on Jack’s street. Red and gold, all wet from the rain. Jack was a small squirrel with a big fluffy tail.

Jack had a little problem. His leaves were stuck in a puddle. He wanted to grab them for his bed. But the puddle was too wide.

Then Jack saw a light. It was in the window of an old house. A soft light. Not red, not gold. A quiet green light.

Jack forgot the leaves. He reached for the light. He climbed a dusty ladder by the wall. He slipped on a wet step. Splash! He landed in the puddle. That was funny. Jack laughed.

The green light stayed far away. Jack could not grab it. So he grabbed his wet leaves instead. Problem solved. He made a soggy bed.

The light still glowed in the window. Jack watched it. Then he curled up. The rain sang him to sleep.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: in the window of an old house
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Down came the leaves, one by one. Jack watched a squirrel hop and grab each one. The squirrel hid nuts in a hole. Then the rain came.

Jack ran to the old house. A small light shone in the window. It was green, soft as a beetle's back. Jack wanted that light. He reached for the glass. His hand found only cold.

The rain fell harder. Jack's ladder was wet. It was dusty and old. He climbed up. The rungs squeaked. A funny thing happened. A leaf stuck to his nose. Jack sneezed. The ladder shook. He had to jump down.

The squirrel chattered at him. It seemed to laugh. Jack laughed too.

He could not reach the light. He never could. The green light blinked and stayed in the window.

Jack went home. The squirrel followed him. Together they watched the rain. The light was far away, but the squirrel was near.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: in the window of an old house
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Down fell the leaves, one by one, and Jack watched a squirrel hide nuts under the old oak. The squirrel lost one nut. It rolled away. Jack laughed. That was funny.

Then Jack saw the light. A small green light in the window of an old house. It glowed in the rain.

Jack wanted that light. He reached for it. He could not have it.

He found a ladder. It was dusty. He tried to grab the light. The ladder slipped. He fell in a puddle. Splash.

The light stayed far away.

Jack wanted the light. He reached. He could not have it. The light. The light. The light.

The squirrel came back. It had the lost nut. Jack smiled. He put the ladder away. The little problem was solved.

But the light still glowed. Jack reached. He could not have it.

The light. The light. The light.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Big leaves fell on Nina’s head. She ran to the tall tree. A squirrel sat on a branch. It held a nut. The wind blew hard. The sky was gray. Rain made the ground muddy.

Nina wanted to help the squirrel. The nut fell in a puddle. Splash! The squirrel looked sad. Nina found a long rope. She did not want to slip. She tried to fold the rope into a loop. The loop did not work.

Then she saw a stick. She used the stick to pull the nut out. The squirrel took the nut and ran up the tree. Nina smiled. At the very top of the tree, a small light blinked. It was far away. She could not reach it. She did not need it.

The storm stopped. Nina went home. Helping someone is better than grabbing a light you cannot hold.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Bright leaves fell from the trees. Nina watched them spin and dance. A little squirrel ran under a bush. It was looking for nuts before winter. But the wind blew hard. Rain came down. The squirrel could not find its hidden nuts. Nina felt sad for her small friend.

She found a rope in the shed. She made a little sack. She wanted to fill it with nuts. The ground was muddy. Her boots got stuck. She pulled and pulled. Then she saw a light. It was high at the very top of a tall tree. The light was green and soft. It shone through the storm. Nina stopped. She wanted that light. She reached up, but she could not touch it. She sighed.

Then she remembered the squirrel. She found nuts under a log. She put them in her sack. The squirrel came close. It took a nut. It was happy. Nina smiled.

You cannot hold every light. But you can help a friend.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Because the wind blew hard, leaves fell all over Nina's yard. She ran outside with her red boots on. The leaves danced and spun. A small squirrel sat by the fence. Its tail shook in the wind. Nina wanted to help it. "Come here, little squirrel," she said. But the squirrel ran up a tall tree.

Nina saw a green light at the very top of the tree. It glowed soft and far away. She wished she could hold it. She wished it could be hers.

The squirrel's home was in that tree. The wind blew it down. Now the squirrel had no warm place. Nina found a rope and a box. She made a little house. She put soft leaves inside. Her hands got muddy. She had to fold the blanket small to fit it in.

The squirrel came down. It looked at Nina. Then it went inside the box.

The green light stayed far up in the tree. Nina looked at it. She still wanted it. But she smiled at the squirrel instead. Some things you cannot reach. But you can still do good right where you are.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Because the wind blew hard, leaves fell down all around Nina. She ran to catch them. Red leaves. Yellow leaves. One leaf landed on her nose.

Nina saw a squirrel. The squirrel had a big nut. The wind took the nut and rolled it into a puddle. The squirrel was sad. Its tail went down.

Nina wanted to help. She got a rope from the shed. She made a little loop. She did not want to fold her coat, but the wind was cold. Her boots got muddy. She pulled the nut out with the rope. The squirrel took it and ran up a tall tree.

Then Nina looked up. At the very top of the tall tree, a small green light was shining. It was so far away. The storm shook the branches. Nina reached up. She could not touch it.

"I want the light," she said. "I want the light. I want the light."

The squirrel chattered. The light blinked and stayed far.

Nina went home muddy and tired. She thought of the green light. But she was glad she helped her small friend. Helping is warmer than wanting.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Big leaves fell down all around Nina. She ran to catch them. A small squirrel ran too. It hid nuts in a hole.

The wind blew hard. Rain made the ground muddy. The squirrel lost its nuts in the mud. Nina felt sad. She wanted to help.

Then she saw it. A small green light, high at the very top of a tall tree. It blinked in the storm.

Nina wanted that light. She wanted it so much.
"I want the light," she said. "I want the light."
She forgot the leaves. She forgot the squirrel.
"I want the light. I want the light."

She found a rope. She tried to climb. The wind pushed her down. The light stayed far away. She could not reach it. She could not have it.

The squirrel squeaked. It was cold and scared.

Nina stopped. She took a big breath. She did not need the light. She needed to help.

She used the rope to fold a small, warm nest. She put the squirrel inside. The squirrel was safe.

The light blinked far away. Nina did not look. Helping a friend is better than wanting what you cannot have.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
A little squirrel named Gus loves falling leaves. Every morning he runs to the big oak tree. He catches red leaves and yellow leaves. He puts them in a soft pile.

One early morning, Gus sees a small light on top of a far hill. It is green and bright. It looks like a tiny leaf that never falls. Gus wants to touch it. He runs and runs. But the hill is too far.

His friend Ben the rabbit comes by. Ben has a dusty teapot. "Sit with me," says Ben. "We can drink tea and watch the leaves skip on the wind."

Gus sits down. They share warm tea. The leaves dance and tumble. The little light stays on the hill, far away. Gus looks at it once more. Then he smiles at Ben. The leaves are here. The tea is warm. That is enough for today.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
A leaf fell on Gus. It was red and small. More leaves fell. Gus was a squirrel. He ran to catch them. His friend May came too. May was a bird.

"Let us skip and play," said May.

They played in the leaves. The sun was low. It was early morning. Gus saw a light. It was on top of a far hill. The light was small and green. It did not move. Gus wanted to go there.

"Come back," said May. "We have leaves here."

Gus ran to a dusty path. Then he came back. May gave him a teapot. It was tiny and warm.

"Drink," she said.

Gus drank. The light stayed on the hill. It was far away. May sang a soft song. Gus forgot the light for a while.

Then he saw it again. It was still there. Gus did not go. May held his paw. They sat in the leaves. The green light blinked once, then twice. Gus stayed with May. The leaves fell down.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
A little squirrel named Gus loved falling leaves. Every morning he ran under the big tree. Red leaves fell. Yellow leaves fell. Gus tried to catch them.

Then Gus saw a tiny light. It was far away, on top of a far hill. The light was small and green. It made a soft glow.

Gus wanted to reach it. He ran to the hill. He ran past a dusty path. He did not stop.

His friend Ben the rabbit came. Ben said, "Gus, skip with me. The leaves are fun."

Gus looked at the hill. The green glow was still there. "I want to touch it," Gus said.

Ben said, "I will help you." They hopped together. The hill was far. The light stayed far.

Gus found a teapot on the way. It was old and brown. He did not care. He only looked at the light.

At last Gus was tired. Ben sat with him. Leaves fell on their heads. The green glow blinked. Gus still wanted it. But he stayed with Ben and watched the leaves fall.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
A squirrel named Gus loved fall. Leaves fell down, red and gold. He ran to catch them. He put them in a pile.

Then he saw it. A small green light, far away. It sat on top of a far hill. It was early morning. The sky was soft and gray.

Gus wanted that light. He wanted to hold it. He left his leaves. He ran to the hill.

His friend Ben came. “Wait, Gus. We have tea.” Ben had a teapot. The tea was warm.

Gus did not stop. He did not skip. He ran past dusty rocks. The light stayed far. It did not come close.

Ben walked with him. “We can look,” Ben said. They walked and walked.

The light was still far. It was always far. Gus sat down. Ben sat too.

“The leaves are here,” Ben said. “The light is there.”

Gus looked back. His pile was small and bright. He held Ben’s hand. The light stayed on the hill. Gus went home.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
A leaf fell on Gus. Gus was a squirrel. He ran to catch leaves. Leaves are fun. But then Gus saw a light. It was on top of a far hill. The light was small and green. Gus wanted it.

"Come skip with me," said his friend Meg. "The leaves are soft."

Gus did not skip. He looked at the hill. The light did not move. It was early morning. The air was cold and dusty.

"Help me climb," said Gus. Meg said, "No. It is too far."

Gus ran up. He fell down. He got up. He ran up. The light stayed far. Meg brought a teapot. "Drink," she said.

Gus did not drink. He watched the light. The light. The light. Always the light. So far. So high. He reached. He reached. He could not touch it. Meg held his paw. The leaves fell. The light stayed.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Cold wind made the leaves fall down. Hugo the squirrel ran to catch them. He put each leaf in his little bed. Red leaves. Yellow leaves. One brown leaf.

"Time for bed," said Mama. She held the warm teapot. Hugo did not want to sleep. He wanted one more leaf.

He ran to the bridge over the river. The sky was dark. He saw a small light far away. It was soft and green. It made him feel quiet. He wished he could hold it. But the light was too far.

Hugo tried to pull a leaf from a branch. The branch was icy. It snapped. The leaf fell into the river. It floated away.

Hugo felt sad. He walked home with empty paws. Mama tucked him in.

The green light stayed far away. Some pretty things are not for keeping. That made Hugo sad, but he slept.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Cold wind made the leaves fall. Hugo the squirrel ran to catch them. He put red leaves in his nest. He put yellow leaves in his nest. One leaf landed on his nose. Hugo sneezed. He liked fall.

Hugo went to the bridge over the river. The sky was dark. It was just before bedtime. Far away, a little light shone on the water. It was small and green. Hugo wanted to touch it. He reached out a paw. The light stayed far away. He could not reach it. He felt a small pull in his chest.

Hugo went home. He drank tea from his teapot. The tea was warm. The night grew icy. He thought of the light on the river. He thought of it again. It was still far away.

In the morning, the leaves were gone. The trees were bare. Hugo sat by his teapot. He looked at the empty branches. Some things you can see, but you can never hold.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Cold wind made the leaves fall. Hugo the squirrel watched them drop. Red leaves. Yellow leaves. They landed on the ground.

Hugo ran to the bridge over the river. He wanted to see the water. But he saw something else. Far away, past the river, a little green light was shining. It was small and soft. It did not move.

Hugo wanted to touch it. He put his paw out. The light stayed far away. He could not reach it.

"Come here," he whispered.

The wind got icy. Hugo shivered. At home, his mother had a warm teapot. She would pull him close. She would say, "Time for bed."

But Hugo did not go home. He watched the green light. It was so pretty. It was so far.

"Come here," he whispered again.

The leaves fell on his head. The sky got dark. The green light kept shining. Hugo sat on the bridge for a long time.

Some things we want stay far away. We can look and look, but we cannot have them. Hugo went home alone.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Cold wind made the leaves fall. Hugo the squirrel ran to catch them. He wanted to keep one red leaf. He put leaves in his nest. He had a teapot he found. He kept it warm at night.

Hugo saw a small light on the bridge. It was green and far away. It was just before bedtime. He wanted to touch it. He tried to pull himself closer. The branches were icy and wet. He slipped and fell.

Hugo ran to the river. The bridge was tall. The light sat on the rail. It was so small. He wanted it. He wanted it. He wanted it.

He climbed the icy rail. The wind pushed him. The light was right there. It blinked and did not move. Hugo reached out.

He fell into the cold water. The red leaf floated away. He never held the light. He never kept it.

Some wants stay far, like a light on a bridge at bedtime.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Cold wind made the leaves fall down. Hugo the squirrel ran to catch them. He put them in a pile by his tree. But then he saw the little light on the bridge. It was small and green and far away.

Hugo wanted that light. He wanted to hold it. He wanted to keep it. He left his leaves. He ran to the river.

The wind gave a hard pull. Hugo held on. The stones were icy. The sky got dark. It was almost bedtime.

He climbed the bridge. He held out his paws. The light stayed far. It was always far.

"I want the light," he said. "I want the light."

His teapot sat alone at home. His soft bed sat alone too. Hugo did not go home. He sat on the bridge and looked at the small green light. He looked and looked.

A squirrel can want a thing that never comes close. That is a sad way to be.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Many weeds grew in Nina's garden. She pulled and pulled. Her hands got dirty. Her back hurt. She put her chair down and sat. The weeds did not stop.

Rain began to fall. Nina ran a race with the rain. She pulled one weed, then two. The rain won. She was wet and tired.

She walked to the bridge over the river. The water was high and brown. On the far bank, a small light shone. It was bright and still. Nina wanted to touch it. She reached out her hand. The light stayed far away.

She reached again. Her fingers caught only rain. The light did not come closer. It never would.

Nina went home. She looked at her garden. The weeds were still there. But she was not angry now.

Some things we want stay far away. Some work we do is never done. We can still sit down and rest.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Mama gave Nina a little garden to fix. The weeds grew tall and green. They grew over the carrots and the beans. Nina pulled and pulled. Her hands got dirty. She put her small chair by the fence and sat down to rest.

Then she saw it. On the bridge over the river, a small green light was shining. It was not a big light. But it was bright. Nina wanted to touch it. She stood up and took one step. Then she stopped. The weeds were still waiting.

She pulled more weeds. She pulled fast, like a race. But her eyes kept going back to the bridge. The light stayed far away. It did not come closer. It did not go out.

Nina finished her work. The garden looked clean. She looked at the bridge one more time. The green light was still there, small and bright. She could not have it. But she smiled. Some lights are just for looking. That is the moral of the evening.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Mud squished under Nina's boots. Her garden was full of weeds. They grew tall and mean. They choked her little flowers.

Nina pulled and pulled. She put her tools on a chair. She wanted to win this race with the weeds.

Then she saw it. On the bridge over the river, a small green light was shining. It was bright in the rainy evening. Nina stopped pulling weeds. She looked at the light.

She wanted that light. She walked to the bridge. The rain fell on her nose. She reached for the light. Her hand found only wet air.

Nina went back to her garden. She pulled one weed. Then she looked at the bridge again. The light was still there. She wanted it so much. She reached and reached. She could not have it.

The weeds stayed in her garden. That was okay. Some things you want stay far away. We can still do good work right where we are.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Many weeds grew in Nina's garden. She pulled them all day. Her hands hurt. She sat on a chair to rest.

Then she saw the light. It was on a bridge over the river. The light was small and bright. Rain fell on Nina's face. She wanted that light.

She forgot the weeds. She walked to the river. The water ran fast, like a race. She stood on the wet bridge. The light was far away. She reached for it. She could not touch it.

"Come here," she said. "Come here. Come here."

The light did not come. Nina went back home. The weeds were still there. She pulled them again.

The light stayed on the bridge. It was always far. Nina wet her face with rain and tears.

A garden needs hands, not wishes. Some lights are only for looking.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Mud squished under Nina's boots. Weeds grew everywhere in her garden. Tall weeds. Thin weeds. Weeds with prickly heads. She pulled and pulled. The weeds came back. Nina sat on a chair and sighed.

Then she saw it. A small green light, far off on the bridge over the river. Rain fell soft and cold. The light was bright. So bright.

Nina wanted that light. She wanted it more than her garden.

"I want the light," she said. "I want the light."

She ran. She ran a race with her own feet. The weeds grabbed her ankles. She did not care. The light, the light, the light.

The bridge was empty. The light was gone. Only rain was there.

Nina walked home slow. The weeds were still there. But so was her garden.

A garden is not the weeds you cannot reach. A garden is the ground you keep.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Next to the fence, Cleo pulled weeds in her garden. The weeds grew tall and thick. It was a lot of work. Cleo put on one boot. She could not find the other boot. That was a little problem. She hopped around on one foot. She looked funny. Her dog tilted his head. Then she found the boot in the flower pot. She laughed.

Rain started to fall. The sky turned dark. A storm was coming. Cleo ran to the window. She saw a boat out on the lake. A small light shone on the boat. It was green. It blinked once, twice. Cleo wanted to reach it. She could not. The boat was too far.

She took a deep breath. She had to calm down. The light was not for her. Cleo went back to her weeds. She pulled them one by one. The rain stopped. The sun came out. Her garden was clean at last.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Nobody liked Cleo's garden. It was full of weeds. Tall weeds. Fat weeds. Weeds with funny hats.

Cleo pulled one weed. It was big. She fell on her boot. "Oof," she said. She laughed a little.

The sky turned dark. Rain came down. A storm was here.

Cleo ran to the lake. She saw a boat. On the boat was a green light. It was small and bright.

Cleo wanted to reach it. She reached out her hand. The boat was too far.

She sat down. The rain was loud. Then the storm went away. The lake was calm.

The green light still shined on the boat. Cleo looked at it. She could not have it. But she could see it.

Cleo went back to her garden. She pulled weeds. She found a ladybug on her nose. She giggled.

Now her garden was clean. The green light was far away. But Cleo smiled. She had her garden. That was enough.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Nobody liked the garden now. Weeds grew tall and wild. Cleo pulled one weed. Then she pulled two. Her little boot got stuck in the mud. She laughed. "Silly boot!"

The wind blew hard. Rain came down. Cleo ran to the lake to hide. She saw a boat out on the water. A green light shone on the boat. It was small and bright. Cleo wanted to reach it. She held out her hand. The boat did not come closer. The light just stayed there, far away.
