Cleo went back to the garden. She pulled more weeds. The green light stayed in her mind. She pulled and pulled. Then a funny thing happened. A frog jumped out of a weed and landed on her boot. Cleo giggled.

She kept working. Soon the garden looked clean and neat. The rain stopped. The lake grew calm. The green light was still on the boat. Cleo waved at it. She could not reach it. But her garden was done. That was enough for today.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Nobody liked Cleo's garden. It was full of weeds, tall and poky.

Cleo pulled a weed. She tugged with one boot. The weed won. She fell on her bottom. That was a little funny. She laughed.

A storm came. Rain went plop on her nose. The lake got bumpy.

Then Cleo saw it. Out on the lake, on a little boat, a green light. It glowed in the storm.

Cleo stood up. She wanted that light. She put out her hand to reach it.

The boat rocked away. The light stayed far.

Cleo pulled more weeds. She pulled and pulled. Splash, splash. Her boot got stuck in the mud.

She looked at the green light on the boat. She wanted to go there. She could not.

The rain stopped. The lake went calm. The weeds were all in a pile.

The little problem was solved. Her garden was clean.

Cleo sat down. She looked at the green light. It blinked once, then twice.

She waved at the light. The light did not wave back.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Next to the fence, Cleo pulled weeds in the garden. The weeds were tall and mean. She pulled one big weed. Then she saw a green light on a boat out on the lake.

The sky was gray. The wind was loud. The boat rocked and rocked. Cleo dropped her weed. She wanted that light.

She put on her boot. She ran to the dock. The rain hit her face.

“I can reach it,” she said. She slipped on a wet fish. Plop! Her boot flew up and landed on her head. She laughed. “Silly boot!”

The storm would not calm down. The boat drifted far away. Cleo held out her hand.

“Green light, green light,” she said. “Come here. Come here.”

The light stayed on the boat. It did not come. The boat went into the fog.

Cleo sat down. The rain stopped. Her garden was still full of weeds. But her boot was funny on her head. She smiled a little. Then she pulled one more weed.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Maya pulled on her boot and went out to the garden. It was full of weeds. Tall weeds, small weeds, weeds with fuzzy tops. Mom said, "We will pull them together."

Maya pulled and pulled. Her hands got dirty. She did not like weeds. She liked carrots and beans.

Late that night, Maya could not sleep. She looked out her window. Far away, a boat sat on the lake. A little light shone on the boat. It was soft and far. Maya wanted to touch it. She could not. She was here, and the light was there.

She closed her eyes and thought of carrots. In the morning, she would be brave.

The next day, Maya went back to the garden. She saw a tiny green fold in the dirt. It was not a weed. It was a bean plant, small and new. Mom smiled. "See? Good things hide in the weeds."

That night, the boat came in close. The light went out. Maya did not mind. She had her bean plant, right there in the garden.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Maya pulled weeds in her garden. The weeds were big and green. They made her arms tired. She put on one boot and pulled and pulled.

Late at night, she sat by the lake. Far away, a little light shone on a boat. It was small and green. Maya wanted to touch it. It felt like a soft wish.

She pulled more weeds the next day. She pulled and pulled. The green light came back in her head. She wanted to fold her hands around it.

She was brave. She pulled the biggest weed. Under it, she found a tiny toy boat. It had a small green dot on it. Her brother lost it last year. Maya did not want the far light now. She had a light in her hands.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Maya pulled a weed from the garden. The weeds grew tall and thick. They hid the beans and the carrots. Every day she pulled and pulled.

At night she sat by the window. Far away, a little light moved on the lake. It was small and green. It sat on a boat. The boat went slow. Maya wanted to touch that light. She could not. The lake was far.

She put on her boot. She liked to be brave. She tried to fold her hands and sit still. But her eyes went back to the lake. The green light rocked on the water.

In the morning she pulled weeds again. The weeds came back. They always came back. She looked at the lake in the day. No light.

Then one night she saw it close. She ran down to the water. The green light was just a lamp on a fishing boat. A man waved. Maya laughed. Still, she sat and watched it. She watched it all night long. She wanted it still.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Maya pulled weeds in the garden. The weeds were big and mean. They had prickly leaves. Maya wore one boot because she lost the other. She pulled and pulled. The garden was full of weeds.

Then she saw it. A small light, far away on a boat out on the lake. It was green and soft. It made her feel warm.

“I want to go there,” Maya said. She pulled a weed. She looked at the light. She pulled another weed. She looked at the light again.

The light did not come closer. The boat did not come closer.

“I want to go there,” Maya said. “I want to go there.” She said it again.

She tried to fold her hands and be brave. But her hands wanted the light. Her eyes wanted the light.

Late at night, the garden was dark. The light was still on the boat. Maya walked to the lake. She had one boot. The water was cold.

Then the boat moved. It came closer. A man on the boat waved. “Are you lost?” he asked.

Maya smiled. “No,” she said. “I just wanted to see the light.”

The man laughed. “That is not a light,” he said. “It is a green sock on a stick.”

Maya looked at her one boot. She laughed too. Then she went home and pulled the weeds.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Maya pulled weeds in the garden. The weeds were tall and green. She pulled and pulled.

Then she saw it. A little green light, far out on the lake. It sat on a boat. The boat rocked slow.

Maya wanted that light. She wanted to hold it in her hand.

She pulled a weed. She looked at the light. She pulled a weed. She looked at the light.

Her boot got stuck in the mud. She did not care. Her hands hurt. She did not care.

"Come here," she said. "Come here, little light."

She tried to fold her hands around it, but it was too far.

Late at night, she was still in the garden. The weeds were everywhere. The light was still there.

"Come here," she said. "Come here. Come here."

Then the light blinked. It was not a light. It was a firefly on a leaf. The boat was a log.

Maya was brave. She smiled. She pulled one more weed, then went to bed.

stories.name: Suki

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Roses grew in Suki's garden, but so did weeds. The weeds were big and bossy. They took the water. They took the sun. "Go away," Suki told them. The weeds did not go away.

Suki pulled one weed. It was heavy. She gave it a kick. The weed bounced back and bopped her nose. Suki laughed. "Silly weed," she said.

Late at night, Suki went to the dark shop for a new trowel. At the back of the shop, past the rakes, she saw a tiny light. It was soft and far away. She wanted to hold it. She could not reach it. She did not know why she wanted it so much.

She bought her trowel and went home. She pulled weeds all week. She did not whistle or sing. She just pulled.

One morning, a rose opened. It was red and happy. Suki smiled.

A garden needs pulling, not wishing. And some lights stay far away, and that is okay.

stories.name: Suki

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Roses are hard to grow when weeds take over. Suki pulled and pulled in her garden. The weeds came back every day. She was tired.

Late at night, she walked to the shop for seeds. The shop was dark and small. At the back, behind boxes, she saw a tiny light. It was green and soft. It glowed like a little star. Suki wanted to hold it. She reached out. Her hand touched only a cold wall.

"Why can't I have it?" she said.

She tried to whistle. The light did not move. She gave it a soft kick with her toe. The light stayed far away. Her bag felt heavy on her arm.

The next day, she pulled weeds again. Then she had an idea. She planted beans. The beans grew fast and tall. They pushed the weeds out. Her garden turned green and full.

She laughed at one weed that poked her nose.

The best things grow from work, not from wishing.

stories.name: Suki

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Roses grew in Suki's garden, but so did weeds. The weeds were tall and green. They poked her legs when she walked.

Suki pulled a weed. It did not come out. She gave it a kick. The weed did not care. It was very heavy in the ground.

"Go away, weeds," said Suki.

She pulled and pulled. Her hands got dirty. A bird sang a funny song, like a little whistle. Suki laughed. Then she pulled again.

Late at night, Suki went to the dark shop for seeds. At the back of the shop, past the brooms, she saw a small light. It was green and soft. It glowed by a closed door. Suki wanted to touch it. She reached out. The light stayed far away.

She went home. She pulled more weeds. All night she thought of the green light. She pulled and thought. She thought and pulled.

In the morning, the weeds were gone. Flowers stood in the sun. Suki smiled. She knew a secret. Some things you can reach, and some you cannot. You tend what you have.

stories.name: Suki

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Roses used to grow in Suki's garden. Now weeds grow there. Tall weeds. Small weeds. Weeds with fuzzy heads.

Suki pulls a weed. It will not come out. She pulls again. She sits down hard in the dirt. A weed pokes her nose.

"Ha!" says Suki. "The weed wins."

Late at night she walks to the shop on the corner. The shop is dark. But at the back of the dark shop, a little green light is on. It glows soft and small. Suki wants to touch it. She can not. The door is locked. The light stays far away.

She tries to whistle. Only air comes out. She gives the door a little kick. It is too heavy. The light keeps glowing. Suki puts her hand on the glass.

"I want to touch you," she says. "I want to touch you."

The next day she pulls weeds again. This time she laughs when she falls. The green light still waits at the back of the dark shop. Suki can not reach it. But her garden is hers, and that is a light you can hold.

stories.name: Suki

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Roses used to grow here. Now weeds grow here. Suki pulls a big weed. It comes out with a funny pop. Dirt flies on her nose. She laughs.

Suki pulls and pulls. The weeds are heavy. Her hands hurt. She does not stop.

Then she sees it. At the back of the dark shop, past the window, a small light. It is green and soft. It glows in the night.

“I want to hold it,” Suki says.

She tries to whistle. Maybe the light will come. It does not come.

She tries to kick the door. The door stays shut. The light stays far.

“I want to hold it,” Suki says again. “I want to hold it. I want to hold it.”

The weeds are still there. Suki does not see them. She only sees the little green light. Never near. Never hers.

Her mom calls her home. Suki walks slow. Late at night, the light still shines behind her. “I want to hold it,” she whispers.

But you cannot hold some lights. You can only love them from far away.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: deep at the bottom of a pond
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Little weeds grew all over Jack's garden. They grew by the fence. They grew by the gate. They grew right up to his little red flag.

Jack pulled a weed. He pulled another weed. "I will never win," he said.

"You can do it," said Mom.

Jack pulled and pulled. The sun was warm. The sky was blue. Then Jack saw something deep in the pond. Far down, a small light shone. It was soft and green, like a tiny leaf made of sun. Jack wanted to touch it. He reached. His hand only found cold water.

"Come help me," said Mom.

Jack pulled more weeds. He got hot. He got tired.

"Time to jump in the pond," said Mom.

Jack jumped in. Splash! He looked for the little light. It was still there, far down. He could not reach it. He felt happy and sad at once.

Then Mom pulled up a big weed. Under it grew a bright green flower. "Look, Jack!" she said. "It was hiding here all along."

Jack smiled. The little light stayed in the pond. That was okay.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: deep at the bottom of a pond
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Little weeds grow in Jack's garden. They grow and grow. Jack pulls one. Then he pulls two. Then he pulls ten. The sun is warm on his back.

Jack sees a pond by the fence. Deep down in the water, a small light shines. It is the color of new leaves. Jack wants to touch it.

"Come help," says Mom.

Jack pulls more weeds. He looks at the pond again. The little light is still there. It does not come closer.

"Will you help?" says Mom.

"Yes," says Jack. He pulls a big weed. It has a yellow flag flower on top. He puts it in his happy pile.

Jack wants to jump in the pond. He wants to swim down to the light. But the pond is deep.

"Mom, what is that light?" says Jack.

Mom looks. She smiles. "That is the sun," she says. "It shines on the water. The water makes it look small and far."

Jack looks up. The sun is high. The light in the pond is just the sun, looking back at him. Jack laughs. He pulls one more weed.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: deep at the bottom of a pond
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Late in the sunny afternoon, Jack pulled weeds in the garden. The weeds were tall and green. They grew everywhere. Jack pulled and pulled. "These weeds are too many," Jack said. "I will never finish."

His mom said, "Pull ten more, then we can rest."

Jack pulled ten weeds. Then he saw the pond. The water was still and warm. Deep down, a small light shone. It was soft and green, like a tiny sun under the water. Jack wanted to touch it.

"Mom, do you see the light in the pond?"

"That is just the sun on the water," she said.

Jack did not believe her. He wanted to jump in and hold that little light. He forgot the weeds. He forgot his hands were dirty. He just looked and looked.

"Jack, the weeds," his mom said.

"I want the light," Jack said. "I want the light."

He jumped in with a splash. The water was cold. The light was only a leaf, shining in the sun. Jack climbed out, wet and happy. "The weeds can wait," he said.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: deep at the bottom of a pond
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Little weeds grew in Jack's garden. They grew and grew. Jack pulled one weed. Then he pulled two. Then he pulled ten.

"Good job, Jack," said Mom.

Jack looked at the pond. Deep down in the water, a small light glowed. It was green and soft. Jack wanted it. He wanted to hold it in his hand.

He pulled one more weed. Then he looked at the pond again. The light was still there. It never came up. It never went away.

"We need to plant beans," said Mom.

"Can I get the light?" said Jack.

"What light?" said Mom.

Jack jumped in the pond. Splash! He got all wet. The light was not in his hand. It was far, far down.

Mom pulled him out. "You are a silly duck," she said.

Jack sat by the pond. He was not happy. He wanted the light. He wanted it. He wanted it.

Then he saw a little flag in the mud. It was green too. It was right by his foot. He picked it up and held it close.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: deep at the bottom of a pond
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Little weeds grew in Jack's garden. He pulled one. Then two. Then many. The sun was warm on his back.

Jack stopped. Far away, deep down in the pond, a small light shone. It was green and soft.

"I want it," Jack said.

He jumped in. The water was cold. He swam down. The light stayed far away.

"It is mine," Jack said. "It is mine. It is mine."

He swam and swam. The light did not get closer. His hands were empty. His chest hurt. He said it again. "It is mine. It is mine."

Jack climbed out. Water ran off him. He was not happy.

A duck swam by. "What do you want?" she said.

"That light," Jack said. "Down there."

The duck laughed. "That is not a light. It is a flag on a sunken toy."

Jack looked. He saw the little flag wave under the water. It was not gold. It was not close. It was just a flag.

He sat in the weeds. He pulled one. Then two. He was still Jack.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
In the snowy day, Ben found a firefly near his jar. He wanted to keep it safe from the cold. The firefly glowed like a tiny lamp. Ben made a small hole in the lid. He did not want it to feel trapped.

He took the jar outside. The sky was gray and gloomy. He tried to whistle a happy tune. The snow made the path slick. He had to slide his feet to keep from falling. In the dark of the woods, Ben saw a soft light. It was far away, high in the trees. It looked like a little green star. He wished he could hold it. But it never came close.

The firefly in his jar grew dim. Ben opened the lid. The firefly crawled out. It did not fly. It just sat in the snow. Soon it stopped moving.

Ben learned that some lights are not for keeping.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
I gave Ben a jar for the firefly. He ran outside on a snowy day. The snow fell soft and white. No fireflies come in winter. Ben did not care. He held the jar and waited.

He sat on a log. He did not whistle. He did not slide down the hill. The woods felt gloomy and still. Then he saw a small light far in the dark of the woods. It blinked once. It blinked again. Ben stood up. His boots made no sound in the snow.

He walked toward the light. The light stayed far away. He walked more. The light still stayed far. Ben held out his jar. The light did not come inside. It only blinked, blinked, blinked, deep in the trees. He could not reach it. He could not catch it.

Ben went home with an empty jar. Some lights are only for looking. You cannot keep them, no matter how hard you try.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
I want to catch a firefly in a jar. Ben holds his jar on a snowy day. The woods are white and quiet. No bugs fly in winter. But Ben still looks. He wants one small light.

He walks past a slide. It is cold and still. He tries to whistle, but his lips are too cold. The woods feel gloomy. Then he sees it. Deep in the dark of the woods, a tiny light blinks. It is a firefly. It is far away.

Ben runs. The snow is deep. He holds out his jar. The light blinks again. It is always far. He cannot reach it. He trips and falls. The jar breaks.

Ben sits in the snow. He wants that little light so much. He whispers, come here, come here. But the light stays where it is. It blinks one last time. Then it is gone.

Ben goes home with no jar and no light. Some things are only for looking. You cannot keep them.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text: I gave Ben a jar to catch a firefly. He ran to the woods. Snow fell on his nose. The woods felt gloomy and cold. No fireflies come in winter. But Ben saw one light. It was deep in the dark trees. It blinked. Ben ran to it. He tripped on a root. He did not cry. He held up his jar. "Come here," he said. "Come here. Come here." The light moved away. Ben began to whistle. He tried to slide his feet softly. The light went farther. It was so small. It was so far. Ben kept walking. He walked until he was lost. His jar stayed empty. His hands got cold. The light blinked once more. Then it was gone. Ben sat in the snow. He said, "Come here. Come here." But nothing came. Sometimes we want a light we cannot hold. We can only see it. We cannot keep it.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text: In the snowy day Ben found a firefly and a jar. He put the firefly in the jar. The glass was cold. The sky was gloomy. He tried to whistle, but no song came out. He wanted to slide down the hill, but he held the jar instead. Then he saw a light in the dark of the woods. It was small and far away. It was not his firefly. It was a little green light. He wanted it. He wanted it. He walked toward it. The snow was deep. The jar was heavy. He wanted it. He wanted it. He wanted it. The light stayed far. He never got close. His firefly stopped moving. The jar felt empty. He sat in the snow and held the jar. He wanted the far light. He forgot the small light in his hands. The far light never came to him. The end. If you hold too tight to a faraway wish, you may miss the small warm thing right beside you.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Carefully, Theo put one firefly in a jar. He poked holes in the lid so it could breathe. The firefly blinked, small and bright.

“Let’s catch more,” said his friend Mia. They ran through the tall grass. Theo tripped on a root and fell into a bush. His apple rolled away. Mia laughed. Theo laughed too.

They took the jar to the sea. The hot summer day made the air soft and warm. Theo wanted to clean the glass. He wanted to lift the jar high.

Then Theo saw a light on a lighthouse. It was green and far away. It blinked, slow and steady, over the water. The firefly in his jar blinked back, as if it knew that light. Theo held his breath. He reached out. The green light stayed far on the tower. He could not touch it. Not ever.

“Come on,” said Mia. “Let’s let him go.”

Theo opened the jar. The firefly flew up, not to the lighthouse, but into the warm dark air. Theo watched the far green light one more time. Then he went home.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Carefully, Theo put a firefly in a jar. He poked holes in the lid. He wanted to keep it safe.

His friend Mia came over. She brought a red apple. "Let's eat," she said.

Theo tried to lift the jar. The firefly blinked once. It was small and bright. "It needs to fly," Mia said.

Theo shook his head. He wanted to keep it. They sat on the warm grass. The hot summer day made them sleepy.

Theo looked at the apple. Then he looked at the jar. The firefly blinked again. It looked like a tiny green light.

"Clean the jar," Mia said. "Then we can let it go."

Theo did not want to. But he wanted his friend to stay.

Together they went to the sea. A lighthouse stood tall. Way up high, a green light shone. It was so far away. Theo reached for it. He could not touch it. The firefly blinked in his jar.

"Please," Mia said.

Theo opened the lid. The firefly flew away. It did not go to the lighthouse. It just flew free over the water.

Mia smiled. Theo smiled too. He felt happy and a little sad.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Carefully, Theo put one firefly in a jar. He poked holes in the lid. He wanted to keep it safe.

The day was hot. Theo and his friend Sam sat on the warm grass. Sam ate a red apple. Theo watched his firefly blink.

Then Theo saw a light. It was far away, on a lighthouse by the sea. The lighthouse light was green. It went round and round. Theo stood up. He wanted to touch it.

“That is too far,” said Sam.

“I can lift my jar,” said Theo. He held the jar high. The green light did not come.

Sam laughed. “Your firefly is not a lighthouse!”

Theo laughed too. But he kept looking at the green light. He wanted it so much.

Sam helped him clean the jar. They put fresh grass inside. The firefly blinked again.

Still, Theo watched the sea. The green light turned and turned. It was so far, and it was so bright. He held his jar up to it. The light did not come. The light never came.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Carefully, Theo put a firefly in a jar. He poked holes in the lid. He wanted to keep it safe.

The firefly glowed. Then it stopped. Theo gave it a tiny piece of apple. The firefly did not eat. It just sat.

Theo’s friend Sam came over. “Maybe it wants the sea,” Sam said. Theo did not listen. He held the jar up to the window. Then he saw it.

A green light blinked far away. It was on a lighthouse by the sea. The light went round and round. It was so bright. It was so far.

“Help me lift the jar,” Theo said. Sam helped. But the jar felt heavy. Theo’s hands shook. He tried to clean the glass. He tried to see the light better.

The firefly bumped the lid. Theo laughed. “You want to go there too?”

He ran to the beach. The green light blinked and blinked. He reached out. He could not touch it.

The firefly crawled out. It flew away. It did not fly to the lighthouse. It flew to a bush.

Theo watched the green light. He reached and reached. The light stayed far. It was always far.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Catching a firefly is easy. Theo holds his jar open. The firefly goes in. He puts in an apple slice. He names the firefly Bob. Bob bumps the glass. Funny!

Then Theo sees it. Far away, on a lighthouse by the sea, a green light blinks. Blink. Blink. Blink.

“Bob, do you see it?”

Bob does not see it. Bob wants the apple.

Theo tries to lift the jar high. “I want that light, Bob.”

His friend Mia comes. “The sun is hot. Play with me.”

“I want the green light,” Theo says.

“But it is a big light on a tall tower,” says Mia. “We cannot get it.”

Theo holds the jar up. Blink. Blink. Blink. The green light shines on the sea.

“I want it,” Theo says.

“You have Bob,” says Mia. “Bob is clean and small.”

Theo laughs. “Bob is not a green light.”

“No,” says Mia. “Bob is a firefly.”

Theo looks at Bob. Bob glows, tiny and soft. Blink.

But the lighthouse glows. Blink. Blink. Blink.

“I want it,” Theo says. “I want it. I want it.”

Mia takes his hand. “Bob wants you.”

Blink. Blink. Blink.

stories.name: Ada

axes.where: in a window across the street

stories.text:
Rita the firefly was Ada’s best friend. Ada found her by the porch. She put Rita in a glass jar.

The summer day was hot. Ada carried the jar everywhere. Rita made a wiggly line up the glass. Then she went dark.

“Don’t be sad,” Ada said. She opened the jar. “You can go.”

But Rita did not go. She sat on Ada’s hand.

Ada looked across the street. In a window, a tiny light blinked. It was small and far. It looked like a firefly.

“Is that your home?” Ada asked. She walked to the door. She did not lift the latch. She just watched.

The light blinked once more. Then it went out.

Rita blinked too. Then Rita flew away. She flew to the dark window. She did not come back.

Ada held the empty jar. The hot day grew cool. She sat on the step and waited. But the little light did not come on again.

stories.name: Ada

axes.where: in a window across the street

stories.text:
Right after lunch, Ada found a firefly. It sat on her window sill. Its light was small and slow. Ada put it in a jar. She made holes in the lid. The firefly walked in wiggly lines. Ada watched it all afternoon.

Across the street, a light shone in a window. It was not a firefly. It was just a lamp. But it looked soft and far. Ada stood at her door and looked. She wanted to lift her hand. She did not.

The day was hot. The air did not move. Ada gave the firefly a leaf. She gave it a drop of water. It did not shine. It only crawled.

The light across the street came on again. It blinked. Then it stayed. Ada pressed her nose to the glass. Her jar felt heavy. Her hands felt still.

By bedtime, the firefly did not move. Ada opened the lid. She set it on the sill. It did not fly. The light across the street went out. Ada sat alone in the warm dark.

stories.name: Ada

axes.where: in a window across the street

stories.text:
Right away Ada found a firefly on the porch. It sat in her hand like a tiny seed of sun. She put it in a jar. The jar had a lid with holes.

"Stay," she said. "Be mine."

The firefly walked in wiggly circles. It was not happy. Ada gave it a leaf and a drop of honey. The day was hot and long. Her shirt stuck to her back.

She set the jar on the step. Then she saw it. Across the street, in a window, a soft blink of light. Not white. Not yellow. A green that hummed. It was another firefly, or the ghost of one. It shined and stopped. Then shined again.

Ada ran to the door. She wanted to lift her hand and wave. But the street was wide. The window was tall. She could not reach.

She looked back at her jar. Her firefly was still. Its light was gone.

She opened the lid and waited. Nothing flew out. The green light across the street blinked one last time. Then the hot day went dark. Ada sat down and held the empty jar.

stories.name: Ada

axes.where: in a window across the street

stories.text:
Rosa caught a firefly in a jar. The glass was cool and smooth. The bug was a wiggly dot of light. Ada watched it bump the sides.

"Let it go," said Rosa.

Ada held the jar close. She ran to the door. The air was hot and thick.

Then she saw it. Across the street, in a window, a small green glow. It was not a bug. It was soft and far. It did not move.

Ada forgot the jar. She walked to the road. The glow was like a tiny moon. She wanted to lift her hand and touch it.

"Ada, look out!" Rosa pulled her back.

The jar slipped. Glass broke on the sidewalk. The firefly crawled out slow. It tried to fly. It fell.

Ada knelt down. The wiggly light was gone. The green glow in the window stayed. It did not care.

She sat on the hot steps. The sky turned pink. The little light across the street blinked on and on. Ada could not reach it. Ever.

stories.name: Ada

axes.where: in a window across the street

stories.text:
Right before bed, Ada put a firefly in a jar. She made holes in the lid. The jar sat on her desk. The bug was wiggly and bright.

Then she saw it. Across the street, in a high window, a small light. It was not a firefly. It was always there. It did not move.

Ada wanted it. She wanted to hold it. She wanted it in her jar.

She ran out the door. She tried to lift her hand to it. The window was too high. The light stayed far away.

She came back. Her firefly was slow. Its light was small.

She watched the window. She watched it all night. "Come here," she said. "Come here. Come here."

The next day was hot. Her firefly did not move. It did not glow. The jar was still.

Across the street, the little light blinked on. Ada put her hand on the glass. She could not reach. She would never reach.

She sat by the jar. The light across the street stayed on. And on. And on.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: at the top of the stairs
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Mia watched Eli catch a firefly in a jar. The sky turned pink and orange at sunset. He poked holes in the lid. He put a soft leaf inside. The bug blinked once. Then it went dark.

Eli felt sad. The little light was shy. It hid in the corner of the jar.

He sat on the step. He held a white feather. He did not want to fold his hands and wait. He wanted the bug to shine.

Then his mom called. "Time for bed."

Eli walked up the stairs. At the top of the stairs, he saw a small glow. It was not the moon. It was not a lamp. It was just one tiny blink. Then it was gone.

He smiled. He opened the jar by his window. The firefly flew out. It blinked goodnight. Eli went to sleep.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: at the top of the stairs
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Milo the firefly was Eli’s best bug. Eli put him in a jar with grass and a twig. Every night, Milo blinked his tiny light.

One sunset, Milo would not blink. He sat still on the twig. Eli felt worried. A little problem.

“Maybe he is shy,” said Eli. He put a soft feather in the jar. Milo did not blink.

Eli carried the jar to the stairs. At the top of the stairs, something glowed. A small light. Far away. It blinked once, twice. Eli wanted to touch it. He could not. The light stayed far.

Milo saw it too. He lifted his wings. Then he blinked. A tiny answer.

“You want to go up there,” Eli said. He opened the jar. Milo flew out. He did not fly to the far light. He flew to Eli’s hand.

Eli did not fold the jar shut. He put it on the step. Milo blinked on his thumb. The far light blinked back. Eli smiled. Some lights you keep. Some lights you watch. Both are good.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: at the top of the stairs
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Maya sat on the porch with a jar in her lap. She wanted to catch a firefly. The sunset made the sky pink and soft. Eli came outside and sat beside her. "They come out when it gets dark," he said. Maya held the jar tight. Soon a small light blinked near the grass. Then another. Eli caught one in his hands. It tickled like a feather. He put it in the jar. The bug went dark. "He is shy," Maya said. She felt sad. Eli showed her how to fold a leaf into the jar. The firefly climbed on it. Then it glowed again. Maya smiled. They watched it blink. It was a tiny light at the top of the stairs of the jar. Maya wanted to keep it. But the light was not for keeping. It was for seeing. So she opened the lid. The firefly rose up and up. It blinked once more, far away. Maya did not feel sad now. The little problem was solved. Eli took her hand. They sat in the dark and waited for more lights.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: at the top of the stairs
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Moths were out when Eli found the jar. He put in a feather of grass. He put in a fold of leaf. At sunset he caught one firefly. It blinked shy and small inside the glass.

Then he saw it. At the top of the stairs, a light was glowing. Soft and green, like a tiny moon. It was far away, up where the dark began.

Eli climbed one step. The jar bumped his knee. He climbed two steps. The light did not come closer. It only wobbled, like it was breathing.

His firefly blinked. Once. Twice. The jar grew warm in his hands.

Eli sat down on the stairs. The green light stayed up there, waiting, never near. He held the jar to his chest. He thought about the small bug inside. It was real. It was his.

So Eli did a little thing. He unscrewed the lid and set the jar down. The firefly crawled out slow, then lifted up. It blinked once more beside his cheek and drifted off toward the top of the stairs.

The far light still shone. But now a small light floated with it, wobbling home. Eli smiled and went to bed.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: at the top of the stairs
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Maybe Eli can catch a firefly. He has a jar. The sky turns pink and gold. Sunset is here.

At the top of the stairs, a small light blinks. It is not a firefly. It is far away and soft. Eli wants it. He wants it more than the jar.

He walks up the stairs. The light stays far. He holds the jar. The jar is empty. He wants to put the light inside.

A feather floats by. He tries to fold his hands around the light. It slips away. He feels shy and small.

The little problem is this: the jar is for fireflies, but his eyes want the far light. He sits down. He breathes.

Then a real firefly comes. It blinks near his knee. Eli puts it in the jar. It glows like a tiny star. He smiles.

He looks up once more. The far light still blinks. He cannot reach it. That is okay.

He carries the jar home. The firefly lights his way. The far light stays far. He wants it still. He always will.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Nate

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text: Nate found a small kitten in the rain. The kitten was wet and scared. "Come here, little one," Nate said. He gave the kitten a warm hug. He made a soft bed from a box. The kitten licked his hand. "I will call you Pip," Nate said. Pip was happy. They played with a stick. Nate would kick it, and Pip would chase it. Then Pip sat and looked up. Far away, high up on a mountain, a tiny green light was shining. Nate looked at it for a moment. The light seemed lonely in the rain. He held Pip close. "I have you," he said. The light blinked once, then went away. Nate did not need to reach it. He had a new friend. They went inside to get dry.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Nate

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Nate found a little kitten in the rain. The kitten was wet and scared. "Come here, little one," Nate said. He wrapped the kitten in his warm coat.

The kitten purred. Nate named her Moss. They played with a stick in the yard. Moss tried to kick it with her tiny paws. "You are my new friend," Nate said.

Then Nate looked up. High on the mountain, a small green light glowed in the rain. It was far away and very bright. Nate wished he could touch it.

"Stay with me," he told Moss. But he kept looking at the light. It blinked through the drops.

Moss mewed and climbed his arm. Nate laughed. "Okay, okay." He held her close. The light stayed up there, high and far. Nate could not go to it.

"Maybe someday," he whispered. Moss licked his nose.

The rain fell soft. Nate felt warm inside. He had a new friend. The green light could wait. It always waited, up on the mountain, where no one could reach.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Nate

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Nate found a tiny kitten in the rain. The kitten was wet and scared. Nate said, "Come here, little one. I will keep you warm."

He held the kitten close. Then he saw a light. It was green and high up on a mountain. The light blinked in the rain. Nate wanted to touch it. But it was far away.

"Look," said Nate to the kitten. "That light is so pretty."

The kitten mewed. Nate found a stick on the ground. He did not kick it. He used it to make a little roof for the kitten.

"I wish I could go to the light," Nate said.

The kitten climbed on his lap. She purred. Nate looked at the mountain again. The green light was still there, high and far.

"My mom says we can't reach everything," Nate said. "But we can be friends."

The kitten licked his hand. Nate smiled. The green light stayed on the mountain. Nate stayed with his new friend. They were warm together. The light blinked and blinked.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Nate

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Nate found a small kitten by the fence. The rain made its fur flat. "You look cold," Nate said. "Come here." The kitten did not move. Nate gave it a name. "I will call you Pip."

Pip peeked out. Nate wanted to be Pip's friend. But then Nate looked up. High on the mountain, a small green light was shining. It was so far away. The rain made it glow.

"Stay with me, Pip," Nate said. But his eyes went up. The green light was up there. He wanted it. He wanted it so much.

He found a stick and tried to kick it up the hill. The stick just fell in the mud. The light stayed high.

"Come back," said Pip.

"I want the light," Nate said. "I want the light. I want the light."

Pip rubbed his leg. Pip was soft and warm. Nate sat down. The light blinked far away. Nate held Pip close.

"You are here," Nate said. "You are my friend."

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Nate

axes.where: high up on a mountain

stories.text:
Nate the kitten wants a new friend. He sits by the window and watches the rain. Then he sees a small green light. It sits high up on a mountain. It is far away.

"Come play," Nate says to the light. The light does not come.

Nate finds a stick. He does not want the stick. He can kick it, but he does not. He wants the light.

"Please come down," Nate says. The light stays up high. It is so far, so far.

His home is warm. The fire is warm. But the green light is cold and far. Nate wants it.

"Come here," Nate says. "Come here. Come here." He says it again and again.

A little cat comes to the window. "Meow," she says. "Play with me."

Nate looks at her. Then he looks at the light. It is still far. Still up high. Still on the mountain.

"Come here," Nate whispers. "Come here."

The little cat waits. The rain falls. The green light shines, and shines, and shines.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on the far side of the playground
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Down the hill, Gus the kitten played on the hot playground. The slide was warm. The swings were warm. Gus wanted a friend.

A big dog sat by the fence. He wore a red hat. "Hello," said Gus. "Will you play?"

The dog did not play. The dog just napped. Gus felt sad.

Then a little bug came by. The bug did a tickle on Gus's nose. Gus sneezed. The bug laughed, but it was a jolly laugh.

"Are you a friend?" asked Gus.

"Yes," said the bug. "I am small, but I am fun."

They played hide-and-seek in the grass. Gus hid. The bug hid. They found each other every time.

Far away, on the other side of the playground, a small light shone. It was green. It sat past the fence, past the road. Gus looked at it once. It was pretty, like a tiny lamp for no one.

"I wish I could touch it," Gus said.

"But look," said the bug. "Here is a puddle. It is close."

The puddle held a green shine too. Gus patted it. The light on the far side stayed far. But the puddle light was right there, soft and cool, and Gus did not have to leave his new friend to see it.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on the far side of the playground
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Down the hot street, Gus the kitten went to the playground. He wanted a friend. The slide was too hot. The swings were too hot. Gus sat in the shade and felt sad.

Then a small dog came by. The dog wore a big hat. "I am Sam," said the dog. "Do you want to play?"

Gus and Sam ran in the grass. They played tag. Sam gave Gus a tickle on his tummy. Gus felt jolly. The day did not feel so hot now.

Far away, past the slide, a little light shone. It was small and green. It blinked near the fence. Gus looked at it. He wanted to touch it. But he stayed with Sam.

They shared a drink of water. Sam told a funny joke. Gus laughed and laughed. Then Gus looked again. The light was gone.

"Did you see it?" Gus asked.

"No," said Sam. "But look." Sam pointed up. The sun had made a green spot on the fence. It was just light. Gus did not need to reach it. He had a friend.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on the far side of the playground
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Drip, drip went Gus’s little nose. He was a small kitten. He sat by a big tree. The sun was hot. It was a hot summer day. Gus wanted a friend. He saw a bird. He saw a bug. He did not see a friend.

Then Gus saw a boy. The boy had a red hat. The boy sat on a swing. “Hello,” said Gus. The boy did not hear. Gus walked to the slide. He saw a girl. The girl had a jolly laugh. She did not see Gus.

Gus looked past the swings. Past the slide. On the far side of the playground, a light shone. It was small and green. It was far away. Gus wanted to touch it. He walked and walked. The light did not get closer.

A little dog came. The dog said, “Why do you look so sad?” Gus said, “I want that light.” The dog said, “That is just a firefly.” Gus blinked. The light was a bug! Gus laughed. The dog gave Gus a tickle. Now Gus had a friend.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on the far side of the playground
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Down the hill, Gus the kitten went to the playground. He wanted a friend. The sun was hot on his fur.

He saw a ball roll by. A big dog ran after it. "Can I play?" said Gus.

The dog said, "I am too fast for you." He ran off. Gus sat by a puddle that was almost dry.

Then Gus saw the light. It was far across the playground, past the swings. It was a soft little light, like a tiny leaf glowing. It was green. It was far. Gus wanted it.

He walked toward it. His paws got hot. "I want that light," he said. "I want that light." He said it again.

A jolly duck in a red hat came by. "What do you want, little cat?"

"That light," said Gus. "I can not reach it. I want it."

The duck laughed. "That is just a firefly on a stick."

Gus looked. The light moved. It was a bug. Gus felt a tickle in his chest. He laughed too.

Then the dog came back. "I am slow now," he said. "Let us play." And Gus had a friend.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on the far side of the playground
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Down the hill, Gus the kitten went to the playground. He wanted to find a friend. The sun was hot. Gus wore a little red hat.

Then he saw it. Far away, past the swings, a small green light blinked.

"Friend," said Gus. "Friend, friend."

The light did not come closer. Gus ran to the slide. The light stayed far. "Friend," said Gus. "Friend, friend, friend."

A big dog came by. "Want to play?" asked the dog.

Gus said, "Friend, friend, friend."

The dog gave Gus a tickle. Gus did not laugh. Gus was not jolly. Gus only looked at the green light.

"Friend," said Gus. "Friend."

The dog sat with Gus. The dog looked too. "That light is just the sun on a fence," said the dog.

Gus looked hard. The light blinked off. The fence was not green at all.

Gus blinked. Then Gus turned and saw the dog was still there. "Friend?" said Gus.

"Yes," said the dog.

Gus laughed. Now Gus was jolly.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
R loved his little garden. One day he sat on his swing and meowed. A small kitten peeked from the grass. "Hello," Tom said. "Come play."

The kitten was shy. Her name was Mia. She had soft white fur. Tom showed her a red ball. Mia did not run. She came close. They played in the sun.

Tom and Mia went to the sea. The sky turned pink and gold. Far away, a lighthouse stood on a rock. Its green light blinked once. Tom saw it. It looked like a tiny star. He wanted to touch it. But it was too far. He just watched. The green light blinked again.

Mia put her paw on his paw. Tom felt happy. He did not need the light. He had a friend.

They walked home. Tom's mom had paint and paper. Tom made a picture. He painted Mia and the green light. "I am proud of this," Tom said.

Mia stayed. They ate fish and slept close. Tom did not reach for the far light again. He had a new friend, and that was enough.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Ruby the kitten sat by the window. Tom sat with her. Ruby wanted a friend.

Tom took Ruby to the park. They saw a big swing. Tom pushed Ruby. She went up and down. She was happy.

Then Tom saw a light. It was on a lighthouse by the sea. The sun was going down. The light was small and green. Tom wanted to touch it. He could not. The light was far away.

Tom and Ruby went home. Tom got out his paint. He made a green dot on the wall. It was like the light. He felt sad and glad.

Ruby met a little cat named Pip. Pip was soft and kind. Ruby and Pip played all day.

Tom felt proud. Ruby had a new friend.

At sunset, Tom looked out the window. The green light was on the lighthouse. It blinked once. Tom smiled and did not reach. Ruby was happy. That was enough.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text: Right by the sea, Tom the kitten wanted a friend. He sat on a swing and watched the waves. The sun went down. Then he saw a small green light. It was on a lighthouse far away. The light blinked and blinked. Tom felt warm inside. "I want that light," he said. He walked toward it. A big dog named Max came by. "Do you want to play?" asked Max. Tom did not answer. He just looked at the green light. Max sat with him. "That light is pretty," said Max. Tom nodded. "It is my friend," Tom said. Max smiled. "I can be your friend too." Tom looked at Max. Then he looked at the green light. He felt happy. Max gave Tom a little ball. Tom did not paint it. He just held it. The green light blinked one more time. Then the stars came out. Tom and Max walked home together. Tom was proud. He had a new friend. The green light stayed far away, but Tom did not mind.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Rusty the kitten was small. Tom was a boy who loved kittens. One day Tom found Rusty by the sea. Rusty was alone. Tom wanted to be his friend.

The sun went down. A lighthouse stood by the water. A small green light shone on the lighthouse. It blinked once. Then again. Tom saw it. He forgot Rusty for a moment. The light was far away. He could not reach it.

Tom tried to play with Rusty. They found a swing. But Tom looked at the light. He wanted it. He reached out his hand. The light stayed far.

Tom tried to paint a picture. He felt proud of his work. But the green light came back. It pulled at him. He could not stop looking.

Then Rusty touched Tom's hand. Rusty was warm and soft. Tom looked down. He saw his new friend. The light was just a light. Tom did not need it. He held Rusty close. They were happy together.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Tom

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
R stood for the swing, and Tom liked to swing by the sea. One day Tom the kitten wanted a new friend. He saw a big lighthouse. The sun went down. A small green light came on the lighthouse. It was far away.

Tom said, "I want that light."

He reached for it. The light was far. Tom said, "Come here, light."

He sat on the swing. The light did not come. Tom was not proud. He wanted to paint the light. But the light stayed far.

Tom said, "Light, be my friend."

The light just blinked. Tom reached and reached. He said, "I want it. I want it. I want it."

Then a small gull came. The gull sat by Tom. Tom forgot the light for one bit. The gull was soft. Tom was happy.

The light blinked on. Tom reached again. The gull stayed near. Tom had a friend. The light was still far. Tom was still glad. The end was happy.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Fog sat on the sea like a soft gray cat. Ravi was a small kitten. He walked on the wet rocks. He wanted a friend.

A gull flew down. Her name was Mina. "I will help you," she said.

Mina gave Ravi a cookie. He took a small bite. "Thank you," he said.

They played by the water. Ravi did not see the big wave. It came fast.

Mina pulled him up high. "Hold on!" she said.

Far away, on a lighthouse by the sea, a small green light blinked. It was pretty. It was cold. Ravi did not want it. He wanted Mina.

The wind blew hard. The wave took Mina away.

Ravi looked for her. He called her name. The sea was quiet now.

He sat on a rock. He did not eat the cookie. He did not peek at the light again.

Mina was gone. Ravi was alone.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Fog sat on the sea like a gray blanket. Ravi the kitten wanted a friend. He walked to the windy shore.

A big dog named Bo was there. Bo had a red ball. "Hello," said Bo. "Want to play?"

Ravi said yes. They ran on the sand. Bo gave Ravi a cookie. It was warm and good. Ravi felt happy.

Then Ravi saw a light. It was on a lighthouse by the sea. The light was small and green. It blinked in the wind.

"Come on," said Bo. Ravi did not move. He peeked at the light. It blinked again.

Bo pulled the ball. Ravi ran with him. But he looked back. The green light was still there.

They played all morning. Ravi got wet in a wave. Bo laughed. Ravi laughed too.

But the light kept calling. Blink. Blink. Ravi walked away from Bo. He walked to the water.

"Ravi!" Bo called. "The water is deep!"

Ravi did not stop. The wind pushed him. The green light blinked far away. He reached out his paw.

The sea took him. Bo cried on the shore. The light blinked on. It never stopped.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Five kittens sat in a box. Ravi was the smallest. He wanted a friend.

The wind blew hard. Ravi went out to find someone. He met a gull by the sea.

"Will you be my friend?" said Ravi.

The gull said, "I fly far. But I can help you."

Ravi gave the gull a cookie. The gull gave Ravi a warm peek under its wing.

Then Ravi saw it. Far off, on a lighthouse, a small light was shining. It was a soft green glow. It blinked and blinked.

"Come," said the gull. "The rocks are wet. Stay here."

But Ravi wanted to touch the light. He walked and walked. The water made his paws cold and wet.

The gull pulled him back. "No, Ravi. Not today."

Ravi looked at the light again. It was so far away. He felt a big ache in his chest.

The gull stayed with him. They shared the cookie. The wind kept blowing.

The light blinked once more, then went dark. Ravi was sad. He never reached it. But he was not alone.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text: From the porch, Ravi watched a small gray kitten hide under a chair. He wanted to be her friend. He put down a cookie. The kitten did not come out. He sat very still. Then he saw a light. It was far away, on a lighthouse by the sea. The light went round and round. Ravi stood up. He forgot the kitten. He walked to the shore. The wind pushed his hair. His feet got wet. A man named Tom pulled him back. "You can't swim there," Tom said. Tom helped him find the kitten again. She was hungry and scared. Ravi gave her the cookie. She let him peek at her soft nose. But that night, Ravi woke up. He looked out the window. The light was still there, blinking like a slow eye. The kitten meowed beside him. He did not hear her. He only wanted to go to the light. In the morning, the kitten was gone.

stories.topic: a kitten making a new friend
stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Fog rolled over the sea. Ravi was a small kitten with soft gray fur. Today he wanted a friend. He sat on the cold sand and watched the waves.

Far away, a small light blinked on a lighthouse. It was green. It went round and round. Ravi wanted to touch it. He wanted it more than a warm cookie. He wanted it more than milk.

The wind blew hard. A big dog came by. "I can help," said the dog. Ravi did not hear. He only saw the light. The light was green. The light was far. The light was always far.

Ravi walked into the water. His paws got wet. "Come back," said the dog. Ravi did not come back. He wanted the light. He wanted the light. He wanted the light.

He went under a wave. The dog pulled him out. But Ravi was too cold. He did not peek at the dog. He only looked for the light. It blinked and blinked. Then Ravi closed his eyes. The light kept on.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Rain made the path muddy, so Maya helped her grandma. Grandma held a basket of apples. Her hands were shaky. Maya took the basket. She did not mind. It was a cold autumn evening, and the sun was going down. A blue boat rocked on the lake. A small green light shone on the boat. Maya saw it. It looked like a tiny star. She wished she could touch it. But she had work to do. Grandma needed help up the hill. Maya gave her a strong lift with her arm. Step by step, they got to the top. The little problem was solved. Grandma smiled and said thank you. Maya felt warm. They went inside to get busy with supper. Through the window, the green light blinked far away. Maya looked once. Then she turned back to her grandma. The light could wait.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Rain had stopped, but the dock was still wet. Maya wanted to help her grandpa with the boat. He was busy pulling ropes and did not see her small hands shake.

The sun was low and thin. Cold autumn air made her nose red. She tried to lift a heavy bucket. It slipped and splashed her shoes. Maya felt sad.

Then Grandpa knelt down. "We can do it together," he said. They lifted the bucket side by side. Water stayed inside this time. Maya smiled.

Out on the lake, a small green light blinked on a boat. It shone far away across the dark water. Maya watched it glow. She reached her hand toward it. The light did not come closer.

She looked back at Grandpa. He needed her rope. Maya tied it tight. The green light stayed on the water, far and lonely. She could not touch it. But she could hold the rope. That was enough for tonight.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Rosa helped Maya carry wood to the old boat dock. Maya was going to fix the loose board. It was a little problem, but it made her frown.

The sun was going down. The air felt cold on her ears. Her hands were busy holding the hammer.

Then she saw it. Out on the lake, a small green light.

It sat on a boat. The boat rocked slow. The light was far away.

Maya wanted to touch it. She reached out, but the water was too wide.

She looked back at the board. She set the nail. One tap. Two taps. The board was flat and safe.

"Good job," said Rosa.

Maya smiled. Then she looked at the lake again.

The green light blinked. She wanted it. She wanted to lift it in her hand.

But the light stayed far. The boat stayed far. The cold evening came down.

Maya held the hammer. She felt warm enough. Still, her eyes found the green light one more time.

Some things you can help. Some things you just watch.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Rachel lost her red mitten. Maya saw her sad face. "I will help," said Maya.

They looked by the swing. No mitten. They looked by the gate. No mitten. The sun was going down. It was a cold autumn evening.

Then Maya saw a small green light far out on the lake. It sat on a boat. It blinked and blinked. Maya wanted to touch it. She wanted to hold it. She forgot the mitten.

"Maya?" said Rachel.

Maya turned back. She found the mitten under a bench. Rachel smiled big.

But Maya looked at the lake again. The light was still there. She wanted it. She wanted it so much. She wanted it. She wanted it. She wanted it.

Rachel took her hand. "You are a good helper."

Maya did not hear. Her eyes stayed on the little green light. It was so far. It was always far up. She could not lift her hand to it. She could not reach it. Not ever.

The boat went away. The light went away too. Maya was busy wanting it still.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on a boat out on the lake
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Right after school, Maya helped her mom carry the heavy bags inside. Then she saw the little boat out on the lake. A green light shone on it. Maya stopped. She forgot the bags. She forgot her mom. She only saw the light.

The sun went down. The air turned cold. Maya walked to the water. She wanted that light. She wanted to hold it. She reached out her hand. The boat was too far. She could not reach. She could not have it.

Her mom called her in for supper. Maya did not hear. She said, "I want the light. I want the light. I want the light."

Her mom came out. She saw the small tear on Maya's cheek. She saw the boat with the light. Mom gave Maya a warm coat. She said, "Let's fix this little problem."

Mom took the small rowboat. She did not row to the light. She rowed near it. Maya saw it was just a lantern on a rope. It was not a star. It was not magic. Maya felt quiet.

Mom helped her lift the lantern into their boat. The busy lake grew calm. Maya held the light. It was warm in her hands. She smiled. Then she went home for supper.

stories.name: Sid

axes.where: on a tower far away
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
A snowy day can make helping hard. Sid put on his big coat. He went to the park to help.

His friend Mia was stuck. Her boot sank in deep snow. Sid gave her a helping hand. He pulled her out with a strong tug.

They played on the swing. Sid had to scoop snow off it first. The snow was a giant pile. They took turns. The swing went up and down.

Then Sid saw a small green light. It blinked on a tower far away. It looked like a tiny star. Sid wanted to touch it. He reached out his hand. The light stayed far away. He could not have it. He looked back at the swing.

Mia laughed. She said, “Push me again!”

Sid smiled and pushed. The green light blinked once more. Sid did not reach this time. He had a friend right here.

stories.name: Sid

axes.where: on a tower far away
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
A little help can make a big day. Sid put on his boots. The snow came down soft and white. He saw his friend Mia by the swing. She was stuck in the deep snow. Sid gave her a hand. He helped her pull her sled.

Then Sid saw a light. It was far away on a tower. The light was small and green. It blinked in the gray sky. Sid wanted to touch it. He reached out. His hand felt only cold air. He could not have it.

He helped Mia again. He used a scoop to clear the snow. They made a giant pile. It was fun. But the green light kept blinking. Sid looked up. He reached again. Still it was far.

Then Mia laughed. She was not stuck at all. She just wanted a friend. Sid smiled. The light was still far away. But Sid had a warm hand to hold. That was near. That was good.

stories.name: Sid

axes.where: on a tower far away
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
A helping hand is a good thing to give. Sid saw snow fall all day. He saw his little sister drop her mitten. He picked it up for her. That was a helping hand.

Then Sid saw the light. It sat on a tower far away. It was small and green. It blinked in the snow. Sid wanted to touch it.

He helped his mom scoop the walk. He pushed his dad's car. He gave his friend a turn on the swing. Each time, he looked up. The light was still there.

"Come inside," said his mom. "It is cold."

Sid did not go in. He reached for the light. His hand was too small. The tower was too far. A giant hill of snow stood between them.

He climbed the hill. At the top, he found a lost puppy. It shivered and cried.

Sid carried it home. The puppy licked his face. Sid smiled. The light was only a lamp on a tower. But the puppy was warm and real.

A helping hand had found him instead.

stories.name: Sid

axes.where: on a tower far away
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text: A helping hand was what Sid gave. He pushed the swing for his little sister. He carried bags for old Mrs. Bell. He did not ask for thanks. On a snowy day, Sid looked up. A green light shone on a tower far away. It was small and bright. Sid wanted it. He reached out his hand. His fingers caught only snow. He helped his neighbor scoop the walk. He looked up again. The light was still there. It pulled at him. He forgot the shovel. He forgot the cold. He walked toward the tower. The snow got deep. A giant drift blocked his way. He fell down. When he stood up, he saw his sister waving from the window. She held a green cup. It glowed in her hand. The light on the tower was just her nightlight, seen through the glass. Sid laughed. He went home. He gave her a helping hand.

stories.name: Sid

axes.where: on a tower far away
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
A helping hand is good to give. Sid liked to help. He helped his mom. He helped his cat.

Then he saw the light. It was on a tower far away. The light was small and green. It blinked in the snow.

Sid wanted that light. He reached for it. He could not have it.

He ran to the swing. He pushed it high. He still saw the light. He made a giant snowball. He used a scoop. He still saw the light.

"Help," said Sid. "Help me get the light."

The light blinked. It blinked. It blinked.

Sid reached. He reached. He could not have it. The light was far away. The light was always far away.

Then his cat meowed. The cat was cold. Sid gave his hat to the cat.

The light blinked once more. Sid did not reach. He held the cat instead.

stories.name: Mira

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
By the time the cold autumn evening arrived, Mira was ready to help. Her neighbor's puppy had run off again. She pulled on her coat and went to look.

She found him near the park. He was stuck behind a fence. His tail was fluffy and wagging fast. Mira tried to scoop him up, but he licked her face instead. It tickled. She laughed so hard she almost dropped her teapot, which she had brought by mistake.

Then she saw a small light on the other side of the fence. It glowed like a tiny star, far away. She wanted to touch it. But the puppy needed her more.

She called a friend. They lifted the fence just enough. The puppy squeezed through and jumped into her arms. He was safe.

Mira walked home with the puppy. The light still blinked far off, but she did not need it. She had done her good deed. Her heart felt warm, and the puppy fell asleep on her feet.

stories.name: Mira

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
By the fence, Mira found a lost mitten. It was red and fluffy. Someone would miss it soon. She pulled her coat tight. The wind was cold. Leaves skittered like little crabs.

She saw a boy on the other side of the fence. He was crying. "My mitten!" he said. "It flew away."

Mira held it up. "Here!"

But the fence was too tall. The boy could not reach. Mira tried to push the mitten through a gap. It would not go. She tried to scoop it over the top. It fell back. She laughed. "Silly mitten!"

Then she had an idea. She put the mitten on her teapot and lifted it high. The boy grabbed it. "Thank you!" He waved.

Mira felt warm inside. Then she saw a small light on his porch. It blinked once, twice. She wanted to touch it. She could not. It was far away.

She looked at her teapot. She looked at the fence. The light stayed there, small and bright. She turned and walked home, happy.

stories.name: Mira

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
By the fence, Mira helped her neighbor. The cold wind blew. Leaves danced like little birds. Old Mr. Chen dropped his teapot. It did not break. Mira picked it up. "Thank you," he said. His hands shook.

Mira had a big scoop. She used it to pick up leaves. Mr. Chen's dog, fluffy, ran around. The dog stole the scoop. It ran away with it. Mira laughed. "Come back, fluffy!" she said. That was funny.

Then Mira saw it. A small light. It glowed on the other side of the fence. It was warm and yellow. She wanted to hold it. She reached through the fence. Her fingers could not touch it. The light stayed far away. She sighed.

"Look," said Mr. Chen. He pointed up. The light was a star. It was far, but it was happy. Mira smiled. She did not need to reach it. She had a friend. They drank tea together. The star winked. Mira felt warm inside.

stories.name: Mira

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
Baking bread for the neighbors felt good on a cold autumn evening. Mira wrapped her scarf tight. She carried a warm teapot and a fluffy blanket to old Mr. Pim. But Mr. Pim’s gate was stuck. She gave it a scoop of snow and a hard push.

Then she saw it. Through the fence, past the bare trees, a small light blinked. It was soft and far away. It looked like a lost star. It sat on the other side of the fence. It was always there. She wanted to touch it. She wanted to hold it. She reached. The fence was cold. The light stayed far.

Mr. Pim laughed. “That old lamp? It’s just Mrs. Gable’s porch light.” Mira laughed too. Her nose was red. Her hands were cold. She forgot the light for one minute. She gave Mr. Pim the teapot. He gave her a cookie.

The light still blinked. She wanted it. She wanted it. But then Mr. Pim smiled. That smile was warm. That smile was near. She held his hand. The wanting got quiet. She went home full.

stories.name: Mira

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text: By the fence, Mira found a lost puppy shivering in the cold autumn evening. She tried to reach through the bars to give a helping hand. But her fingers only touched air. The puppy whined. Mira saw a soft glow on the other side of the fence. It was a small light, far away. She wanted it. She wanted to hold it. She whispered, "I want to hold it. I want to hold it." She forgot her teapot waiting at home. She forgot to scoop the leaves. Her scarf was fluffy, but she felt cold. A funny thing happened. The puppy sat on its bottom and sneezed. Mira laughed. Then she saw a gate. She ran and opened it. She gave the puppy a helping hand. It licked her nose. The light stayed far away. But the puppy was warm. She carried it home. She still thought, "I want to hold it." Yet her heart felt full. The end.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: at the end of the pier

stories.text:
Good snow fell on Ruby's boots. She walked to the pier to help her grandpa. He dropped his hat in the water. "Oh no," he said. "My hat is cold and wet."

Ruby pulled a rope from her pocket. She gave it a wiggle. The rope was soft and long. "I can help," she said.

Grandpa laughed. "You are a good helper, Ruby."

She dropped the rope down. The hat did not grab it. A duck swam by. The duck sat on the hat. "Quack," said the duck. Ruby giggled. "That duck wants a ride."

Grandpa pulled the rope up. No hat. Just a wet duck. "Silly duck," said Ruby.

Then she saw a small light. It was at the end of the pier. It was green and far away. It blinked in the snow. Ruby looked at it. She wanted to touch it. She reached out her hand. The light stayed far away. She could not have it.

"Ruby," said Grandpa. "My hat?"

Ruby turned back. She helped him get the hat with a stick. The duck swam off. The green light blinked once more. Ruby did not reach for it again.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: at the end of the pier

stories.text:
Good, kind Ruby loved to help. On a snowy day, she saw a small dog stuck on a slippery log. "I can help," Ruby said.

She put her warm mittens in her pocket. The dog gave a funny little wiggle. It made Ruby laugh.

"Hold still," Ruby said. The dog did not hold still. It licked her nose. Ruby laughed again. That was the funny part.

She reached out a soft hand. The dog jumped into her arms. Ruby helped it down.

Then Ruby looked up. Far away, at the end of the pier, a small green light was shining on the snow. It was pretty. She wanted to touch it. But the pier was too far.

"Come on," Ruby said. She walked the dog home.

The green light stayed at the end of the pier. Ruby could not reach it. She thought about it all the way home. She wanted it. But she could not have it.

Ruby helped the dog. That was enough for today.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: at the end of the pier

stories.text:
Gently, Ruby helped her grandpa pull on his boots. Snow fell on the porch. It was a good day to help.

"Hold my hand," said Ruby. "The path is slippy."

They walked to the pier. Grandpa's scarf went flip-flap in the wind. Ruby laughed. A snowflake landed on his nose. "You look like a snowman!" she said.

Grandpa laughed too. "A handsome one?"

"No," said Ruby. "A funny one."

She put her hands in her pocket. Then she saw it. Far away, at the end of the pier, a small light glowed. It was green and soft. It blinked in the snow.

Ruby stopped. "What is that?"

"What is what?" asked Grandpa.

"The light. The little light."

She took a step. She wanted to touch it. She wanted to hold it. But the pier was long, and the snow was deep. She reached out her hand. She could not reach.

"Ruby," said Grandpa. "My hand?"

Ruby turned back. She gave his hand a wiggle. "I'm here," she said.

They walked home slow. But Ruby looked back once. The green light was still there. Still far. Still soft. Still not hers.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: at the end of the pier

stories.text:
Gently, Ruby helped her grandpa put on his boots. It was a snowy day. The flakes fell like little feathers. Grandpa laughed. He tried to wiggle his toes. "My feet are asleep," he said. Ruby giggled. She pulled a scarf from her pocket. She wrapped it around his neck. It was soft and warm.

Then she saw the light. It was far away, at the end of the pier. A small green light. It blinked in the snow.

"Grandpa, what is that light?"

"Hmm? Oh, just a light, Ruby."

But Ruby wanted it. She helped Grandpa stand. She helped him walk. But her eyes kept turning back. The green light called to her. She reached for it with her heart.

"Ruby, you are a good helper," said Grandpa.

"Can we go to the light?" she whispered.

"No, dear. It is too far."

The green light blinked. Ruby wanted it. She wanted it. She wanted it.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: at the end of the pier

stories.text:
Good job, Ruby said. She helped the old man up. The snow made the pier slippery. He dropped his hat. Ruby put it in her pocket.

Then she saw it. A small light at the end of the pier. It was green. It glowed in the snow.

I want that light, Ruby said. She took one step. Then two.

Careful, the old man said. Watch the ice!

Ruby did a funny dance. Her feet went wiggle, wiggle, plop. She almost fell in the water. The old man laughed.

But Ruby looked at the light again. I want that light, she said. I want it. I want it.

She reached out her hand. Her fingers felt the soft, cold air. The light stayed far away. It always stayed far away.

The old man called to her. Please help me home, Ruby.

Ruby turned. Then she turned back. The green light blinked on the water. She could not stop looking. She wanted it. She wanted it. She wanted it.

stories.name: Sam

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
I saw a man drop his bag. Sam picked it up. "Here you go," Sam said. The man smiled. Sam felt warm inside.

Snow fell soft and white. The train tracks hummed. A train came by. It was noisy. On the train, a small green light glowed in a window. Sam looked at it. Then she looked away.

She helped an old lady cross the icy street. "Thank you, dear," the lady said.

Sam tried to brush the snow off a bench. She wanted to sit. But the bench was too cold.

She saw a boy with no hat. Sam gave him hers. "You keep it," she said. He ran off happy.

Then Sam had no hat. Her hands were cold. She had to jump over a puddle. Her feet got wet.

The train came back. The green light was still there. Sam watched it go. She wished she could ride away too.

No one helped Sam. She walked home alone in the snow.

stories.name: Sam

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
I saw a man drop his bag in the snow. Sam ran to help. "Let me get that," Sam said. The bag was heavy. Sam used a brush to wipe off the snow. The man said, "Thank you, Sam."

Then a train went by. It was noisy. Sam saw a small light on the train. It was green. It glowed in the white snow. Sam wanted to touch it. He took a step. He wanted to jump on the train.

"Stay back," the man said.

Sam stopped. The train went away. The green light got small. Then it was gone. Sam felt sad. He wanted that light. He could not have it.

"Are you okay?" the man asked.

"Yes," Sam said. But he was not okay. He looked at the empty tracks. The snow fell on his face. He wished the train would come back. It did not.

stories.name: Sam

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
I see Sam walk in the snow. Sam wants to help someone today. The snow is deep and soft.

Sam sees a little bird on the ground. The bird cannot fly. "Do not worry," Sam says. "I will help you."

Sam picks up the bird. Sam holds it close to stay warm. The bird is small and light.

A train comes by. It is noisy. The train goes fast through the snow.

On the train, Sam sees a small green light. It shines in the window. Sam wants to touch it. Sam wants to hold it. But the train is too fast. The light goes away.

Sam tries to brush the snow off the bird. Sam wants to jump on the train. But Sam cannot. The train is gone.

"Please stay," Sam says to the bird. But the bird is cold. The bird is still. Sam holds it close.

The green light is far away now. Sam wants it so much. Sam cannot have it. Sam sits in the snow and cries.

stories.name: Sam

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text: I saw Sam help a lady with her heavy bag. The bag was full of apples. One apple fell and rolled in the snow. Sam picked it up and put it back. "Thank you," said the lady. Sam smiled. Then a train went by. It was noisy. Sam saw a small green light on the train. It was far away. Sam wanted to touch it. "Do not jump," said the lady. Sam did not hear her. He took one step. Then two. The light was so small. So green. Sam reached out. The train was too fast. The light went away. Sam brushed snow off his coat. He felt sad. "The light," he said. "I want the light." The lady took her bag and left. Sam stood alone. The snow kept falling. He looked down the empty track. He whispered, "Come back." But the light did not come back.

stories.name: Sam

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
I gave my mittens to a cold bird. Sam helped a lot of people. She liked to help.

The train came. It was noisy. It went by slow in the snow.

Sam saw a small light. It was green. It sat on the train. It was far away.

"I want that light," Sam said.

"You can't," said her mom. "It's on the train."

Sam ran to the track. She tried to brush the snow away. She tried to jump up high.

"I want the light," she said. "I want the light. I want the light."

The train went on. The light got small. Sam sat down in the snow.

"Please come back," she said.

The light did not come back.

Sam forgot the bird. She forgot the mittens. She forgot to help.

"Come inside," said her mom.

"No," said Sam. "I want the light."

She stayed in the snow. She was sad. The light was gone.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: across the snowy yard
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Five little raindrops sat on Ruby's web. Ruby was a small spider. She wanted a drink. But the drops were too high on the silk.

Ruby tried to reach them. She did not want to brush them away. She wanted to sip them. One drop slipped and fell. Splat. It was gone.

"Oh no," said Ruby. "Now I have four."

She tried to dig her legs in and climb. The web shook. Another drop fell. Splat. Gone.

Ruby felt sad. Her legs were cold. She wished for something warm.

Then she had an idea. She climbed slow. She did not shake the silk. She reached the last drop. She sipped it. It was sweet.

One drop was enough.

The sun went down. Ruby looked across the snowy yard. Far away, a small light glowed. It was green and soft. She wished she could touch it. But it was too far. The snow was cold. The light stayed far away.
