She walked toward it. The hill was far. Her paws got tired. The shine stayed far away. She wanted to touch it. She wanted it so much.

She sat down in the grass. The sun went behind a cloud. The shine went away. Ella walked back home. The leak was still there. Drip. Drip. Drip.

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Ella

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text: Pitter-patter came the drip into Ella’s pot. The bear had a leaky roof. She put a feather in the hole. It did not help. She tried a wiggle of moss. The drip went on. Ella wanted her floor clean. She climbed up with a big leaf. The sun was warm. Then she saw it. Far away, on top of a hill, a small light shone. It was soft and yellow. It made her chest feel tight. She wanted to hold it. She could not reach it. The drip kept falling. She turned back to the hole. But her eyes went to the hill again. She thought, if I had that light, I would not mind the drip. She thought it again. If I had that light. If I had that light. The sun went down. The light stayed far. Ella sat in the wet. Her pot filled up. She never fixed the roof.

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Ella

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
Puddles grew on the floor of Ella’s cave. The roof had a small leak. Drip, drip, drip.

Ella put a soft feather under the drip. She watched the water wiggle down. She wanted the cave to be clean and dry.

But then she saw it. On top of the far hill, in the sunny afternoon, a little green light shone.

“I want to reach it,” she said.

She forgot the puddle. “I want to reach it. I want to reach it.”

She walked up the hill. The light stayed far away. She walked and walked. Her feet got tired.

“I want to reach it. I want to reach it.”

The sun went down. The light stayed small and far. She never touched it.

Back home, the drip, drip, drip made a big wet spot. Her soft feather was soaked. The cave was not clean.

Ella sat in the puddle. She was sad. She could not reach the light. She could not fix the roof. She just said, very soft, “I want it. I want it.”

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Zoe

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text: A bear named Zoe lived in a warm cave. One hot summer day, she saw a drip, drip, drip from the roof. The rain had made a small hole. Zoe put on her red mitten to patch it. She had to climb a big rock to reach. The sun was bright and made her sleepy. She worked and worked. Then she sat down to rest. Far away, she saw an old house. In its window was a small light. It was not a fire. It was not the sun. It was just a little glow. Zoe wanted to touch it. But it was too far. She looked at her roof. The drip had stopped. She felt happy. She knew her cave was dry and safe. Sometimes we want things we cannot have. But we can still love what we do have. Zoe smiled and went to sleep.

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Zoe

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text:
A bear named Zoe lived in a warm cave. One hot summer day, she saw a leaky roof. Drip, drip, drip. The water made a soft puddle.

Zoe put on her red mitten. She did not need it for the heat. She needed it to plug the hole. She tried to climb the roof, but her paws slipped.

Then she saw it. In the window of an old house, a bright light glowed. It was small and far away. It looked like a tiny sun. Zoe wanted to hold it. She wanted to keep it in her mitten. She forgot the roof for a moment.

But the drip came back. So Zoe called her friend the beaver. He climbed up and fixed the roof with sticks and mud.

Zoe sat down and looked at the old house. The bright light was still there. She could not reach it. But she felt warm inside anyway.

A happy bear learns that some lights are just for looking.

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Zoe

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text: A bear named Zoe lived in a warm cave. One hot summer day, she saw a drip, drip, drip. Her roof was leaky. Zoe put on her red mitten to catch the drops. She tried to climb a tall tree to patch the hole with leaves. The leaves fell down. She tried mud. The mud slid off. Then Zoe saw a little light. It was in the window of an old house. The light was small and bright. It did not drip. It did not fall. Zoe wanted that light. She wanted it more than a dry roof. She sat and looked at it. She thought, I want that light. I want that light. She forgot the drip. She forgot her mitten. She just looked. Her friend Ben the bird came by. He said, Zoe, fix your roof. The light is far away. Zoe blinked. She climbed down. She used bark and moss. The roof stopped leaking. That night, she saw the light again. It was still far. But her cave was dry. Zoe smiled. She knew a warm dry home is better than a pretty light you cannot hold.

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Zoe

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text:
A bear named Zoe lived in a cozy cave. One hot summer day, she heard a drip, drip, drip. Her roof had a leak. Zoe found a mitten and pressed it on the hole. But the water still came through.

Zoe went outside to climb a tree for shade. From the top, she saw an old house. In its window, a light shone. It was small and bright. Zoe wanted to touch it. She climbed down and walked toward the house. The light was so pretty. She forgot her leaky roof.

Zoe sat by the house and watched the light. She thought, I want that light. I want that light. She said it again and again. Then a kind woman came out. She gave Zoe a bucket and a smile. Zoe went home and fixed her roof. The light still glowed far away. But Zoe felt warm inside. She learned that wanting is fine, but helping yourself feels best. And she slept dry and happy.

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Zoe

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text:
A bear named Zoe lived in a warm cave. One hot summer day, rain dripped through a hole in the roof. Drip, drip, drip. Zoe put a mitten on her nose. She did not like wet fur. She wanted to fix the hole. But first she had to find a dry spot to think.

Then she saw it. In the window of an old house, a little light shone. It was bright and small. It danced like a firefly. Zoe wanted that light. She wanted it more than a dry cave. She wanted it more than honey. She wanted it. She wanted it. She wanted it.

She tried to climb the hill to the house. The light stayed far away. She tried to climb a tree. The light stayed far away. She tried to climb a rock. The light stayed far away.

Zoe sat down. She cried a little. Then she went home. She fixed her roof with soft moss. The rain stopped. The sun came out. She felt warm and dry. The little light still glowed far off. But Zoe had her own warm glow inside. Wanting what you cannot have can hide what you already have. And that made her happy.

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Eli

axes.where: at the end of the pier

stories.text:
Finally, Eli the bear saw the drip. Plink. Plink. It fell right on his nose. His roof had a leak.

Eli got his ladder. It was old and shaky. His friend, a small bird named Pip, sat on his head. "I can help!" said Pip.

Eli climbed up. The wind blew hard. It was a windy morning. The icy wind made his paws cold. Whoosh! The ladder slipped. Eli landed in a bush. "Oof," he said.

Pip laughed. "You look like a fuzzy berry!"

Eli laughed too. Then he fixed the roof with sticky sap. No more drip!

Later, they walked to the end of the pier. Eli saw a small green light far out on the water. It blinked once, twice. He wondered what it was. It looked nice. Then Pip sang a silly song about berries. Eli forgot the light and sang along.

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Eli

axes.where: at the end of the pier

stories.text:
Fixing a leaky roof is hard work for a bear. Eli the bear lived in a little house by the sea. One windy morning, drip, drip, drip came the rain through his roof. He needed a ladder. His friend Pip the penguin brought one.

"Hold it steady," said Eli. He climbed up. The wind blew his hat off. It landed in the soup pot. Pip laughed. "Your hat is soup now!"

Eli patched the roof with sticky tar. He got tar on his nose. Pip laughed again. Then the wind pushed the ladder. Eli slid down, bump, into a bush.

"That was funny," said Eli. He was not hurt.

Later, he looked out past the icy waves. Far away, at the end of the pier, a small green light was shining. It blinked in the wind. Pretty, he thought. He wanted to touch it. But the pier was too far, and the waves were too cold.

Pip sang a silly song about soup hats. Eli laughed. The green light blinked once more, then the fog hid it. Eli went inside. His roof was dry.

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Eli

axes.where: at the end of the pier

stories.text:
Fixing the roof was Eli the bear’s job today. Rain dripped through a hole onto his bed. He got his ladder. The wind blew hard. The ladder wobbled.

“Hold it, please,” Eli called to his friend, Pim the rabbit. Pim held the ladder. Eli climbed up. He put a pot on the roof. The pot slid off. It bonked Pim on the nose. They laughed and laughed.

Then Eli saw it. Far away, at the end of the pier, a small light shone. It was green and bright. The windy morning made it blink.

“What is that?” Eli asked. He climbed down. He took one step toward the pier.

“The roof!” said Pim.

Eli stopped. He held the ladder. He tried to sing a work song. But his eyes kept turning to the end of the pier. The light called him. It felt icy and far.

He reached out a paw. He could not touch it. He never could.

“Come back,” said Pim.

Eli looked at the light once more. Then he fixed the roof.

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Eli

axes.where: at the end of the pier

stories.text:
Fixing the roof was the plan for the windy morning. Eli the bear had a bucket under the drip. Drip, drip, drip. His friend Mo helped him carry a ladder. Mo slipped on a wet leaf and sat in the bucket. Splash! They laughed so hard they could not sing.

Then Eli saw it. At the end of the pier, a small light glowed. It was green and icy bright, even in the sun. It bobbed on the wind.

"I want that light," Eli said. He climbed down the ladder. He walked to the pier.

"Eli, the roof!" Mo called.

But Eli watched the light. It felt close. He reached out. His paw touched only wind. His chest felt tight. He reached again. "I want it. I want it. I want it."

Behind him, Mo patched the roof alone. The drip slowed. The wind blew the little light away, far over the water. Eli stood still. He wanted it. He wanted it. Then he turned back. "Sorry, Mo." They went home for honey.

stories.topic: a bear and a leaky roof
stories.name: Eli

axes.where: at the end of the pier

stories.text:
Five big drips fell on Eli’s nose. His little bear roof had a leak. The wind blew hard on the windows. It was a windy morning.

Eli got his ladder. His friend Mina came to help. “Hand me the bucket,” she said. Eli tripped on a boot and the bucket went on his head. They laughed and laughed.

Then Eli saw it. Far away, at the end of the pier, a small green light was shining. It blinked in the wind. Eli wanted it.

“Sing with me,” Mina said.

But Eli looked at the light. “I want the light,” he said. “I want the light.”

“The roof is leaking,” said Mina.

“I want the light,” Eli said. “I want the light.”

The icy wind made him shake. Mina pulled his paw. “Come down, Eli.”

“I want the light,” he said. “I want the light. I want the light.”

Mina climbed up and held him. The roof still dripped. The green light blinked and blinked. Eli reached out. He could not touch it. He could not have it. He just wanted the light.

stories.name: Wren

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
Fen sat on the floor and held her broken pencil. The tip snapped off. Now she could not draw a sun.

Wren came in with her red hat. "I can fix it," she said. She put the pencil on a stool. She put a tiny chair on the pencil. That did not help. The chair fell off. Wren laughed. It was a funny, silly mess.

"Let's go outside," said Wren. They ran up the hill. The wind pushed their hats. Wren held her hat and began to count the clouds. One, two, three.

Then Wren saw it. On top of the far hill, a small green light was shining. It blinked in the windy morning. Wren wanted to touch it. She climbed on a stone. She tried to use a ladder of sticks. It was too short.

"I am so proud of my broken pencil," Fen said. Wren nodded, but she still looked at the far hill. The green light stayed there. She could not reach it. It was too far.

stories.name: Wren

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
Felt tip pens are fun. But Wren loves her little pencil best. One windy morning, snap! The pencil breaks in two. Wren holds both pieces. Her face is sad.

She wants to fix it. She tries a ladder. She climbs up high. The wind blows her hair. She is not scared. She feels proud. Then she sneezes. The wind takes the top piece away! It lands in a bird bath.

Wren laughs. It looks like a tiny boat.

Then she sees it. On top of a far hill, a small green light. It shines. It is so far. She wants to touch it. She counts her steps. One, two, three. The light stays far.

She looks at her broken pencil. She counts the pieces. One, two. She holds them tight. The wind blows. The green light blinks soft. She wants it. She can not go. The hill is too far.

She puts her pencil in her pocket. She walks home. The green light stays on the hill. It is still far. Still green.

stories.name: Wren

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
Fixing her pencil was hard. The pencil was broken. The tip snapped off, and Wren felt sad. She wanted to draw a big sun.

Wren looked out the window. The wind blew her hair. On top of a far hill, she saw a small green light. It blinked and blinked. It looked like a tiny star on the ground.

“I want that light,” Wren said. She found a ladder. It was too short. She tried to count the rungs. One, two, three. The wind blew the ladder down. Bonk! It fell on her toe. Wren laughed. It was funny.

She was proud of her trying. But the light stayed on the hill. She reached out her hand. The light did not come. The wind blew more.

Wren fixed her pencil with tape. It looked silly. She drew a green light. It was not real. But she was happy. The light blinked far away. She could not touch it. Not today.

stories.name: Wren

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
First the pencil broke. Wren was not proud. The tip snapped off and rolled away. Now she could not draw. She sat on the steps and felt sad.

The wind blew her hair. It pushed her little hat down over her eyes. She laughed. That was funny.

Then she saw it. On top of the far hill, a small green light. It blinked in the wind. Wren stood up. She wanted that light. She wanted it so much.

She found a ladder. She tried to count the steps up the hill. One, two, three. The ladder was too short. The light stayed far away.

Wren held her broken pencil. She reached out her arm. The green light did not come closer. The wind blew and blew.

She tried again. She climbed and she counted. The light was still far. It was always far. Wren reached and reached. The green light blinked. She could not touch it. She could not have it. She reached.

stories.name: Wren

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
Fixing her pencil was the plan for the day. Wren had a broken pencil. It snapped in two. She was sad.

Then she saw the green light. It sat on top of a far hill. It was a windy morning. The light blinked and blinked.

Wren forgot the pencil. She walked to the hill. Wind pushed her hair. The light said, come, come.

She found a ladder by a tree. She tried to count the rungs. One, two, three. Wind blew the ladder down. Wren laughed. It was funny.

She was not proud. She still wanted the light.

She climbed the hill. The light stayed far. She reached. She reached. It moved away.

Come, come, said the light. Wren reached. The wind blew. Wren reached. The light blinked. Come, come. Wren reached. The light blinked. Come, come.

Wren forgot her pencil. She forgot the funny ladder. She forgot to count. She only reached. The light blinked. Come, come. Wren reached. The light blinked. Come, come.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Tess had a little pencil. It was her best pencil. It was yellow and sharp and good. Then the pencil broke. Snap! The tip fell off. Tess felt sad. Now she could not draw.

She went outside to sit on the step. The sun went down low. The sky turned soft and red. It was sunset.

Tess looked at the hedge by the yard. Something shone behind the hedge. A small green light. It blinked once. It was bright and far away, like a tiny star. Tess wanted to hold it. She stood up and walked to the hedge. She pushed the leaves. The light was gone.

She sat down again. The wind blew. It was windy and cool. Soon it was time to sleep.

The next day, Dad gave her a new pencil. It was green. Tess smiled and drew a big sun. She did not need the far light. What you can touch is the best light of all.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Tess had a broken pencil. The tip snapped off. Now her pencil was too short to hold. She put it in her pocket.

The sun went down. The sky turned pink and gold. Tess sat on the porch.

Then she saw it. A small green light. It glowed behind the hedge. It looked like a tiny star.

Tess stood up. She walked to the hedge. The wind was windy and cold. The green light blinked. It seemed to say, come here.

But the hedge was thick. Tess could not push through. She reached her hand. The light stayed just out of reach.

She tried again. She could not touch it. The light was pretty. She wanted it so much.

Her mom called, "Time for sleep."

Tess went inside. She felt sad. She looked out the window. The green light was still there. It winked at her.

The next day, Tess found a new pencil. It was long and sharp. She drew a picture. She drew a green light behind a hedge.

It was not the real light. But her picture made her happy. And the real light came back every sunset.

You cannot always get what you want. But you can be glad it is there.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Tess had a pencil. The pencil was broken. It snapped in two in her little hand. She felt sad. She wanted to draw a big sun.

Then Tess saw a light. It was green. It sat behind the hedge. The light was small and soft. It looked like a tiny star. Tess wanted to touch it.

The sun went down. It was sunset. The sky turned pink and orange. Tess walked to the hedge. The wind was windy. It blew her hair. She reached for the light.

"Come here," Tess said. But the light stayed behind the hedge. It did not come to her. Tess felt sad again.

She sat down. She looked at her broken pencil. She could not draw. She could not catch the light.

Then Tess had an idea. She used the two short pieces. She drew two small suns. They were happy suns.

She did not need the green light. She had her own light inside. At last, Tess went to sleep. She felt glad. 

A happy heart is its own bright star.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Tess had a pencil. It was her favorite pencil. But one day it broke. Snap! The point fell off. Tess felt sad.

She sat on the porch. The sun went down. She saw a small light behind the hedge. It was green and soft. It looked like a tiny star.

Tess forgot her pencil. She walked to the hedge. The light was so pretty. It was windy. The leaves moved. The light danced.

She reached for it. But the hedge was thick. She could not touch the light. She reached and reached.

Her mom called, "Time for sleep, Tess." Tess did not want to go.

The light blinked. Then it went out. The sky got dark.

Tess went inside. She found glue. She glued her pencil back. It was short but it worked.

She smiled. She drew a green star. She learned that some lights are just for looking. And a broken pencil can still draw.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Tess had a pencil. The pencil was broken. Snap. It was in two parts. Tess held the two parts. She was sad.

Then Tess saw a green light. The light was behind the hedge. The light was small and bright. It was sunset. The sky was pink and gold.

Tess wanted the light. She put down the pencil. She walked to the hedge. The light was still far. She reached out her hand. She could not touch it.

The light was like a star. It was green and soft. The wind was windy. Tess did not sleep. She only looked at the light.

Tess said, "Come here, light." The light did not come. She said it again. "Come here, light." The light did not come. She said it again and again.

The pencil was on the ground. The light was behind the hedge. Tess wanted the light. She could not have it. But the light was pretty. And Tess was happy. She learned that some pretty things are just to look at.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Because her pencil broke, Ella could not draw. The tip fell off and rolled away. She looked in her box. No more pencils. "I am sad," Ella said.

Mom gave her a chair by the window. "Sit and rest," Mom said. Ella sat down. The sky was warm and orange. The sun went low.

Then Ella saw a small light. It sat at the very top of a tall tree. The light was little and far. It did not move. Ella did not want to pull her eyes away.

"Can I go up?" Ella asked.

"No," said Mom. "That tree is too tall."

Ella looked at her broken pencil. She looked at the tree. She had a good idea.

"Mom, I can draw the tree!" she said. Mom found a new pencil. Ella drew the tall tree. She drew the small light on top. It made her happy. She did not need to reach it. She could see it every day.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Ben sat on a little chair. Ella had a pencil. The pencil was broken. Snap! The point fell off.

"Oh no," said Ella. "My pencil is broke."

"Can you fix it?" said Ben.

Ella tried to push the two parts. They did not stay. She tried to tape them. The tape did not help.

"I can not fix it," said Ella. She felt sad.

Then she looked up. The sun was going down. The sky was soft and warm. At the very top of a tall tree, a tiny light was on. It was small and green. It did not move.

Ella looked at the little light. She wanted to go up and touch it. But the tree was too tall. She could not climb it. She did not have a ladder.

"Come on," said Ben. "Let us get a new pencil."

Ella looked one more time. The little light stayed far away. She gave a small pull on Ben's hand.

"Okay," she said. They went home. Mom gave Ella a new pencil. It was yellow and sharp. Ella drew a tall tree. At the top, she made one small dot. She smiled.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Broke in two, the pencil lay on Ella's desk. She sat on her chair and felt sad. It was her best pencil. "Do not worry," said Mom. "We can fix it." But Ella felt a warm lump in her throat.

Out the window, the sunset made the sky pink and gold. At the very top of the tall tree, one small light shone. It was green and soft. It blinked like a tiny star. Ella could see it, but she could not reach it.

"Can we get that light?" she asked.

"No, sweet girl," said Mom. "It is too high."

Ella looked and looked. She wanted to pull it down. She wanted it close. The light stayed up there, far away.

Then Mom gave her a new pencil and a hug. "Let us draw," she said. Ella drew the tree and the small green light. She smiled.

"Some things we just wave to," said Mom.

Ella waved. The light blinked back.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Bella the pencil lay broken on the floor. Ella picked up the two small pieces. Her pencil was gone. She sat on her chair and felt sad.

Then she saw it. At the very top of the tall tree, a little light did glow. It was small and green like a tiny leaf. The sun was going down. The sky was warm and pink.

"Come down," Ella said. But the light did not move.

She ran to the tree. She tried to pull the light down with a stick. It stayed high up. She put her chair under the tree. She climbed up. The light was still too far.

"Please come down," Ella said again. "Come down, come down, come down."

Her mom came out. "What do you want, Ella?"

"That light," Ella said. "I want it so much."

Her mom smiled. "That light is just the sun on a leaf. Here is a new pencil. It is green like your light."

Ella held the pencil. It felt warm. She drew a tall tree with a little light on top. She was happy.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
Beth broke her pencil. Snap! The point fell on the floor. Ella sat on her chair and looked at it. "It is too small now," she said.

The sun went down. It made a warm light. Far away, at the very top of a tall tree, a little green light began to shine.

Ella saw it. She wanted it. She wanted the little green light. She wanted to hold it. She wanted it to be hers.

"Come down," she said. "Please come down."

The light did not come down. It just stayed up high. Ella tried to pull the tree with her hands. The tree did not move. The light did not move.

"Come down," she said again. "Come down, come down, come down."

Her mama came. "What do you want, Ella?"

"That light," said Ella. "I want that light."

Mama smiled. "That is the sun's good-night kiss. It is for everyone. You do not need to catch it."

Ella looked up one more time. The little green light blinked, slow and kind. Then it went to sleep with the sun. Ella felt warm inside. She picked up her small pencil and drew a little light of her own.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Gently, Theo picked up the broken pencil. The tip had snapped right off. Now it was just a short stick.

"Can you fix it?" Theo asked.

"No," said Mom. "But we can get a new one."

They went into town. Rain hit the windows. Theo held the broken pencil in his pocket.

The shop was small and dark. A little bell went ding. Theo looked for pencils. He passed a leaf made of glass. He passed a ball that could roll across the floor.

Then he saw it. At the back of the dark shop, past the old wooden counter, a tiny light glowed. It was soft and far away. It looked like a small moon in a jar. Theo wanted to hold it. He reached out. His fingers found only air.

"Found one," said Mom.

Theo looked down. In his hand was a new pencil, long and sharp. Outside, the rain turned icy.

"Ready?" asked Mom.

Theo nodded. He put the new pencil in his pocket next to the broken one. Once, he turned back. The little light still glowed. Then the door closed behind him.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Gray clouds pushed against the window. Theo held his broken pencil. The tip snapped off, and the wood felt rough.

"Can you fix it?" Theo asked.

Mom shook her head. "Not that one, sweetie."

Rain hit the glass. Theo put the two pieces in his pocket. They felt like a leaf with no tree.

He walked to the shop on the corner. The bell went ding. Inside, it was dark and warm.

"Just looking," Theo said.

The shop man nodded. "Take your time."

Theo saw old toys, a cracked cup, a dusty box. Then he saw the back of the shop. A small light glowed there. It was not green like grass. It was green like deep water. It did not move. It did not blink. It only waited.

Theo took a step. His shoe made an icy sound on the floor. He wanted to roll that light in his hands. He wanted to keep it.

"Find something?" the man asked.

Theo looked down at his broken pencil. "No," he said. "Not yet."

He went home. But all night, he thought of the light.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Gently, Theo picked up the broken pencil. The tip was gone. The two halves did not fit. Rain hit the window. It was a stormy afternoon.

"Can we fix it?" Theo asked.

"No," said Dad. "It is too small."

Theo held the pieces. He felt sad. He put them in his pocket. They went to the shop for bread. The shop was dark and warm. Theo saw a leaf on the floor. It was brown and dry.

Then he saw the light. It was small and green. It sat at the back of the dark shop. It did not move. It did not blink.

"Stay here," said Dad.

Theo did not stay. He walked to the back. The light was behind a glass jar. He could not touch it. He could not reach it. It was just a light. But it felt like a small, warm home.

"Come on," said Dad.

Theo did not move. He wanted to roll the jar away. He wanted to hold the light. His hands felt icy. The light stayed there. It always stayed there. He could see it. He could not have it.

"Please," Theo said.

"Time to go," said Dad.

Theo went out into the rain. He still had the broken pencil. He still wanted the light.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Gathered at the window, Theo watched the storm. Rain tapped hard. His pencil was broken. The tip snapped off inside the wood. He tried to roll it on his desk. It wobbled and fell. "I can't draw," he said to his mom. "Not with this."

"Go to the shop on the corner," she said. "They fix things."

Theo ran through the icy rain. A wet leaf stuck to his shoe. Inside the shop, it was dark and warm. At the back, behind a shelf, a small light glowed. It was not a lamp. It was just a tiny gleam, far away. He walked toward it, but it stayed far. He stepped closer. It slid back.

"Can I help you?" asked the shop man.

"My pencil is broken," Theo said. But he kept looking back. That soft light. He wanted to hold it. He wanted to put it in his pocket.

"Pencils are here," the man said.

Theo took one. But his eyes stayed on the back. That far, small glow. He wanted it. He wanted it. He wanted it.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Gray rain tapped the window. Theo held his broken pencil. The tip snapped off. Now it was too short to write his name.

"Can we fix it?" Theo asked.

"No, little one," said his mom. She pulled up his hood.

They ran past the bakery. They ran past the shoe shop. The storm made the sky dark. Thunder went boom.

Then Theo saw a shop with a small window. Inside, at the back, behind a jar, something glowed. A tiny green light. It blinked like a bug on a leaf.

"Wait," Theo said.

"Come on," said his mom. "The rain is icy."

Theo did not move. The light was so small. It was so far. He wanted it. He wanted it.

"Let me look," he said.

"Theo, no."

He pressed his nose to the glass. The light rolled slow and soft, like a marble on a floor. He reached. He could not touch it. He would never touch it.

"Theo," said his mom.

The light stayed back there. It always stayed back there. He wanted it. He wanted it. He stood in the rain and wanted it.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: in the sky, very low

stories.text:
Rosa the pencil was broken. Cleo held it up. The tip was gone. Snap! It broke in her bag.

"Oh no," Cleo said. "My pencil is broken."

"Can you fix it?" said her mom.

"No," said Cleo. "It is too small."

Cleo ate a cookie. She was sad. She did not want to draw.

That night, fog sat on the town. Cleo went to the window. The sky was gray and soft.

Then she saw it. Low in the sky, past the trees, a small light. It was not green like grass. It was green like a leaf in the fog. It blinked.

"Come here," Cleo whispered.

The light did not come. It just stayed far away.

"Loud cars," said her mom. "Time for bed."

Cleo did not fold her paper. She left it open.

In the morning, the light was gone. Cleo found a new pencil. It was yellow.

"Look," she said. "I can draw again."

She drew a small light. It sat low on the page. It was still far away. But she drew it anyway.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: in the sky, very low

stories.text:
Rosa the pencil was broken. Cleo held the two small pieces. She was sad.

"Can we fix it?" she asked.

"No," said Mom. "It is too short."

Cleo put the pieces on the table. She ate a cookie. The night was foggy. The fog sat on the window like a soft blanket.

Cleo went outside. She wanted to fold her arms and stay warm. Then she saw it. A small light, low in the sky. It was not green like grass. It was green like a faraway leaf. It did not move.

"Hello," Cleo said.

The light did not answer. A dog barked, loud. Cleo looked away. When she looked back, the light was still there.

She thought of her pencil. She thought of the light. Both were small. Both were far.

"Come here," she said.

The light stayed low. Cleo did not reach it. She went inside. She put the pencil pieces in a box. She thought of the small light in the fog. She wanted it. She did not know why.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: in the sky, very low

stories.text:
Rosa gave Cleo a pencil. It was yellow and small. Cleo drew a cat. She drew a sun. Then the pencil broke. Snap. The point fell off.

"Oh no," said Cleo. "My pencil is broken."

"Use another one," said Rosa.

Cleo shook her head. She held the broken pencil. It fit in her hand just right.

That night the fog came. It was a foggy night. Cleo sat by the window. She ate a cookie. She did not fold her arms. She just looked out.

Low in the sky, a little light glowed. It was green and soft. It blinked in the fog.

"Come here," Cleo said.

The light did not come.

A loud truck went by. The light stayed.

"Can I reach you?" said Cleo.

She held up her broken pencil. The green light shone on the wood.

Every foggy night, Cleo watched. She saw the light and wanted it. She could not touch it. But she kept her pencil. And she kept looking.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: in the sky, very low

stories.text:
Ruby red pencil in her hand, Cleo sat on the step. The pencil was broken. Two short pieces. She could not write her name.

"Can we fix it?" she asked.

"No," said her mom. "Eat your cookie."

Cleo did not eat. She held the two pieces. She tried to fold them together. They would not stay.

The fog came in. It was a foggy night. A loud truck went by. Then it was quiet.

Cleo looked up. In the sky, very low, a little green light was shining. It sat just over the trees. It did not move.

"Come here," she said to it.

The light stayed. It was far. It was low. She wanted to put it in her pocket.

"Cleo, come inside," said her mom.

She did not go. She held the broken pencil. She looked at the small green light.

"Wait for me," she said.

The fog made the light soft. She reached up. Her hand was empty. She reached again.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: in the sky, very low

stories.text:
Rita broke her pencil. Cleo saw it snap. "Oh no," said Cleo. "My pencil is broken."

Cleo put the two pieces on the table. She ate a cookie. She did not want to fold her paper. The room was loud. Then she looked out the window.

A little light sat low in the sky. It was foggy and dark. The light was small and far. It was the color of new leaves. Cleo put her hand on the glass.

"I want to go there," she said.

"You can't," said Rita. "It is too far."

Cleo did not hear her. She looked at the light. The light blinked once. It blinked twice. It was low, so low.

"I want to go there," Cleo said again.

She said it and said it. The broken pencil stayed on the table. The cookie stayed half eaten. The fog moved. The light did not come closer. Cleo kept looking. She kept saying it. She said it until the words were soft.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Noah

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text: Puddles made the world soft and brown. Noah put on her red cap. She ran outside to find the biggest one. It sat like a flat brown lake by the gate. She stepped in with both boots. Mud went up to her knees. She did a happy hop. Splash! Her boots made a wonderful sound. Rain tapped her cap. She found a stick and drew a wiggly line. The line turned into a snake. The snake turned into a river. She played until her hands were cold. Then she saw a sparkly thing in the reeds by the stream. It was small and green. It was a light, far away, like a tiny star stuck in the grass. She reached for it. Her fingers touched only wet leaves. The light stayed where it was. She reached again. Still nothing. She stood there a long time. The rain got softer. The light did not come closer. Noah looked at her muddy boots. She thought about the puddle. The puddle was right here. The light was not. Some things you can splash in. Some things you can only see. She walked home, warm and cold at once.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Noah

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
Puddles were Noah’s favorite thing after rain. She put on her red cap and ran outside. The big mud puddle by the gate was wide and brown. She stomped it. Splash! Mud jumped on her boots. She tried to hop across it, but she slipped and sat right down in the middle.

Noah laughed. Then she saw something far off. In the reeds by the stream, a small light blinked. It was sparkly and soft. She wanted to touch it. But the stream was too far. She stood up and walked toward it anyway. The light stayed just past the tall grass.

She went back to her puddle. She dug a little river with a stick. The light kept glowing in the reeds. It felt like a quiet wish. She could not hold it. She could only see it.

So she played in the mud instead. She made mud pies. She made mud hills. The rain came back, soft on her cap. The light stayed small and far.

Some pretty things are just for looking. You can still be happy with your own puddle.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Noah

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
Puddles grew wide on the path. Noah pulled her red cap down low. Rain went drip, drip on the leaves. She saw a big mud puddle. It was round and brown and perfect. Noah took a hop. Splash! Mud jumped on her boots.

Then she saw the light. It sat in the reeds by the stream. It was small and sparkly, like a tiny star fallen in the wet grass. Noah stopped. The puddle felt cold now. She took one step toward the stream. The light blinked soft and gold. She wanted to hold it. She wanted it to be hers.

Back she went to the puddle. Splash, splash. But her eyes kept sliding to the reeds. The light rocked with the water. It never came closer. Noah stood very still. Rain ran off her cap. The mud puddle waited. The light waited too.

She gave the puddle one last hop. Then she turned toward home. Some lights you can see but not keep. That is all right. You can still say goodnight.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Noah

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
Puddles grew big in the rain. Noah put on her red cap. She ran to the mud puddle by the gate. She stomped. Mud went up. She did a little hop. It was fun.

Then she saw a light in the reeds by the stream. It was small and sparkly. It looked like a tiny green star. It made her chest feel warm. She forgot the puddle. She walked to the reeds. The light stayed far. She wanted to hold it.

The rain fell on her cap. She reached for the light. It was not there. She reached again. It was always far. Come here, she said. Come here. Come here. The mud puddle waited. She did not see it.

At last she sat down. The light stayed in the reeds. She could not catch it. But she could see it. That was something. She went back to the puddle. She stomped once more. Some things you want you cannot hold. You can only love them from where you are.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Noah

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
Puddles were Noah’s favorite thing after rain. She put on her red cap. She ran to the big mud puddle. She gave a hop. Splash! Mud went on her boots.

Then she saw it. In the reeds by the stream, a sparkly light. Small and green. It blinked.

Noah forgot the puddle. “I want that light,” she said.

She stepped in the mud. Squish. She reached the reeds. The light moved.

“I want that light,” she said again.

She said it and said it. “I want that light. I want that light.”

Her cap fell in the mud. She did not care. The rain came down.

The light stayed by the stream, far away. Noah held out her hand. The light did not come.

“I want that light,” she whispered.

The rain stopped. The light went out. Noah stood alone.

She picked up her cap. She walked home slow.

The puddle can hold you. The far light cannot.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Lily

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Gray clouds went away. Lily put on her boots. She ran to the big mud puddle by the swing. It was round and brown and fun.

Lily jumped in. Splash! Mud went on her nose. She made a little cake from mud. She did not want to build a castle. She wanted to stomp.

"Come see my mud pie," Lily said to her mom.

"That is a busy puddle," said her mom. "You are all muddy."

Lily laughed. She hopped and stomped. Then she walked to the bridge over the river. The sun was going down.

A small green light shone far away. It sat on the water. Lily looked at it. She reached out her hand. The light did not come.

"Can I have it?" she asked.

"No," said her mom. "It is just the sun on the river."

Lily watched it for a while. Then she went back to her mud puddle. She stomped one more time. Splash!

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Lily

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Gilly the goat watched Lily jump in the mud puddle. Splash! Brown water went up. Lily laughed.

"Come in, Gilly!" said Lily.

Gilly did not want mud on her feet. She went to the swing.

Lily was busy in the puddle. She made a cake of mud. She made a hill of mud. She did not build a castle. She just jumped.

Then Lily saw the sky turn pink. She went to the bridge over the river. The sun was going down. On the far side of the bridge, a small green light came on. It was so small and so far.

"I want that light," said Lily. She reached out her hand.

"You can't have it," said Gilly. "It is too far."

The light blinked once. Then it blinked again. Lily watched it. It was very pretty. It was so far away.

"Maybe tomorrow," said Lily.

She went home. The mud dried on her toes.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Lily

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Gray clouds were gone. Lily found a big mud puddle by the road. She stomped in it. Splash! "This is fun," she said.

Her mom said, "We must be busy. Come to the bridge."

They walked to the bridge over the river. The sun was going down. Lily looked at the water. Then she saw it. A small green light on the far rail. It blinked once.

"Can I swing on that light?" Lily asked.

"No," said Mom. "It is far away."

Lily wanted to build a path to it. She wanted to touch it. The light blinked again. It was so small and so green.

"Mom, look," Lily said.

"I see the sunset," Mom said.

Lily did not see the sunset. She saw only the light. It called to her. She reached her hand out. The light stayed far away.

"Time to go," Mom said.

Lily walked home. She did not stomp in the puddle. She did not splash. She just looked back at the bridge. The green light was still there. She could not have it. Not today.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Lily

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Gone were the morning chores. Lily ran to the big mud puddle by the fence. She liked to stomp it. She liked to make brown splashes.

"I will build a mud cake," she said.

"Not too busy," said Mom. "We go to the bridge soon."

Lily patted the mud. She did not want to go. Then they walked to the river. The sky was pink and gold. Her little brother sat on the swing. Lily looked up.

A small green light shone on the bridge. It was far away. It blinked over the water.

"Oh," said Lily. "I want that light."

"You can't have it," said Mom.

Lily reached. The light stayed far. It was so pretty. She forgot her mud cake. She forgot the swing. She forgot the busy path. She just looked and looked.

"Come on," said Mom.

Lily reached again. The green light did not come. It only shone.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Lily

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Gosh, Lily found a big mud puddle by the swing. She wanted to build a mud cake. She was busy. "Look, Mom!" she said.

But then she saw the light. A small green light, far away, on the bridge over the river. It was sunset.

"I want it," Lily said.

She left the puddle. She walked to the river. The light sat on the bridge. It was so small. It was so green.

"Come here," she said. The light did not come.

She reached. She reached. Her hands were empty. The sunset turned red. The light stayed green. It stayed far.

"Please," she said. "Please."

The light did not move. Lily did not move. She just looked and looked. The puddle dried up behind her. The swing stopped. She forgot to build.

The green light shone. It shone and shone on the bridge. Lily reached. Her fingers touched only air. She reached again. And again. The green light stayed where it was, always, just across the river.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Nate

axes.where: under a door down the hall
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Little Nate found a big mud puddle. It was round and brown. He put his boot in it. Splash! Mud went on his sock. "Oh no," said Nate. His sock was wet and cold.

He sat on the steps. A bird flew to its nest. Nate did not want a wet sock. He wanted to play.

Then he saw a light. It came from under a door down the hall. It was small and green. It looked like a tiny star. Nate wanted to reach it. He wanted to hold it. But the door was shut. The light stayed under the door.

The sun went down. The sky was orange and pink. Nate looked at the green light again. It was still there. It was always there. He could not have it.

Mom came out. She gave him dry socks. "Let's clean the puddle," she said. They put a towel down. The puddle was gone.

Nate looked down the hall one more time. The green light was gone too. He was sad and glad. He went inside to play.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Nate

axes.where: under a door down the hall
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Little Nate found a big mud puddle. It was round and brown. Splash! His boots got wet. Then his socks got wet. Oh no. His feet were cold and muddy.

Nate looked down the hall. The sun was going down. A small light glowed under a door. It was green and soft. Nate wanted to reach it. But the door was closed.

He had a little problem. His feet were wet. He sat on the step. He took off his boots. He took off his socks. He put them in a warm nest of dry towels. Then his feet were happy.

The green light stayed under the door. It was tiny and far. Nate looked at it again. He could not go to it. The door was shut.

Mom came. She gave him dry socks. She said, "No more puddles today." Nate said, "Okay."

At sunset, the green light blinked once. Then it went away. Nate did not reach it. But his feet were warm. That was good.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Nate

axes.where: under a door down the hall
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Little Nate found a big mud puddle on the path. It was brown and round and fun to poke with a stick. His sister said, "Do not jump in." But Nate wanted to jump in.

Then he saw a small green light. It glowed under a door down the hall. The sunset made the light look warm. Nate left the puddle. He walked to the door. He put his hand on it. The door was locked.

He went back to the puddle. Splash! His boots got muddy. His socks got wet. That was a little problem. His feet were cold.

He saw the green light again. It was so tiny. It seemed to reach for him. He wanted to reach back. But he had to fix his feet.

He took off his wet socks. He put them in a nest of dry leaves. Then he put on dry socks from his bag. His feet felt good.

The green light still shone under the door. Nate looked at it. He did not open the door. He just smiled and went home.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Nate

axes.where: under a door down the hall
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Little Nate played by the mud puddle. He patted the wet dirt. He made a small nest for a toy bird. The bird fell in the mud. Nate had a little problem.

Then he saw it. A green light glowed under a door down the hall. It was sunset. The light was tiny and bright.

Nate left the mud puddle. He walked to the door. He tried to reach the light. The door was shut. He could not touch it. The light stayed under the door. It was so far away.

He went back to the puddle. He dug the bird out. He washed it clean. He fixed his little problem.

But the green light pulled him again. He walked down the hall. He pressed his hand to the door. He wanted the light. He could not have it.

Nate sat by the puddle. The sun went down. The green light still glowed down the hall. He could not reach it. He looked at it. He looked and looked.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Nate

axes.where: under a door down the hall
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Little Nate found a big mud puddle. It was round and brown. He wanted to jump in it.

Then he saw the light. A green light, under a door down the hall. It was sunset.

Nate forgot the mud puddle. He walked to the light. He put his hand on the door. The light was so small. So far.

He said, "Come here, light."

The light did not come.

He said, "I want you."

The light did not move.

He made a nest with his hands. He tried to reach the tiny light. It was under the door. It was always under the door.

His boots dripped mud. The puddle waited. But Nate did not go back.

He sat by the door. He said, "Light. Light. Light."

The green light stayed. It did not come. It never came.

Then his mom opened the door. The light was gone. But the puddle was still there. Nate jumped in it. Splash! The little problem was solved.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Jack

axes.where: on a roof across the town
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
When Jack found the big mud puddle, he stopped. The puddle was round and brown and shiny. It sat right in the middle of the path.

Jack was a girl with short boots. She liked mud. She put one boot in. Splash! The mud went up.

A boy came by. "Can I play too?" he asked.

Jack said, "Yes. We can share."

They jumped and stomped. The mud got on their coats. It got on their cheeks. They did not care.

Then Jack saw something. Far away, on a roof across the town, a small green light blinked on. The sun was going down. The light was green like a tiny leaf. Jack wanted to touch it. She reached out her hand. She could not reach. Her hand was too small.

She put her hand in her pocket instead. In her pocket was a round stone. It was not green. It was gray and warm.

"Look," said Jack. She held up the stone. "This is my light."

The boy laughed. They went home slow, with muddy boots and happy hearts. Jack kept the stone in her pocket. It was better than any light on a roof.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Jack

axes.where: on a roof across the town
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
When Jack found the biggest mud puddle on the block, he knew it was a perfect day. The puddle was brown and round like a giant cookie. Jack put a small boat in his pocket. He wanted to share the puddle with someone. But all his friends were inside.

Jack sat by the puddle alone. The sun was going down. The sky turned pink and orange. Then Jack saw a small light on a roof across the town. It was green and far away. It looked like a tiny star. Jack reached for it. He could not touch it. The light was too far.

He looked back at his puddle. The water was still and shiny. Then something moved. A girl came out of a house. She had a red boat. She walked slow to the puddle. "Can I play too?" she asked. Jack smiled. "Yes! Let's share."

They put both boats in the water. The green light blinked on the roof. Jack did not need to reach it. He had a friend right here. The boats sailed together. The puddle was big enough for two. Jack laughed. The light stayed far away, but Jack was happy.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Jack

axes.where: on a roof across the town
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
When Jack found the big mud puddle, he jumped right in. Splash! The brown water went up high. Jack laughed. He stamped his boots. The mud felt soft and funny.

Then the sun went down. A small green light came on across town. It sat on a roof far away. Jack stopped. He looked at the little green light. It was so far. He could not touch it.

He put a stone in his pocket. He wanted to bring the light home. But the light just stayed there. It did not come closer. Jack sighed. He looked at the light again.

"Come here," he said. "Come here." But the light did not move.

A girl came by. "Why do you look so sad?" she said. Jack showed her the light. "I want it," he said.

The girl smiled. "You can not have that light," she said. "But you can share this puddle with me." She jumped in. Splash!

Jack laughed. The mud was warm. They played in the puddle slow and happy. Jack forgot the light for a while. Then he looked up. The light was still there. But now it felt like a friend. Jack was glad. He had a puddle, a pocket stone, and a new friend.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Jack

axes.where: on a roof across the town
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
When Jack found the mud puddle, he jumped right in. Splash! The brown water went up his legs. He laughed and stomped. Mud is fun.

Then Jack saw a green light on a roof far away. It was small and it glowed. The sun was going down. Jack wanted that light. He wanted to hold it in his pocket.

“Come back, Jack,” said his mom. “We can share the puddle.”

But Jack just looked at the light. The light was so far. He could not reach it. He took a slow step toward it. Then another.

“Jack!” Mom called. “The puddle is here!”

Jack did not want the puddle. He wanted the green light. He wanted it in his pocket. He wanted to share it. He wanted to reach it. The light was so far. So far.

Then Jack slipped in the mud. He sat down hard. The puddle splashed his face. Jack laughed. The light was still far. But the puddle was right here. Mom hugged him. Mud got on her too. That was the best part.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Jack

axes.where: on a roof across the town
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
When Jack found a big mud puddle, he jumped right in. Splash! Mud went on his boots. Mud went on his hands. He laughed and stomped.

Then he saw it. A small green light on a roof across the town. Far, far away. The sun was going down. The light glowed.

Jack wanted that light. He wanted it in his pocket. He wanted to hold it and never share it.

"Come here, light," Jack said. "Come here."

He climbed a box. Too low. He climbed a tree. Still far. The light just sat on the roof.

"Come here," Jack said. "Come here. Come here."

He forgot the mud. He forgot his boots. He only saw the light.

He ran and ran. He tripped on a rock. He fell right into the puddle. Splash!

Jack sat in the mud. He looked up. The light was gone. The sun was down.

Then Jack saw something in the puddle. A tiny glow! The sunset had made a little green shine in the water, right by his feet.

Jack put his hand in his pocket. He took out a jar. Slow and careful, he caught the shine. It was just a firefly.

Jack did not keep it. He let it go. "Go home," he said.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Milo

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
One hot summer day, Milo found a big mud puddle. She put her toes in. Splash! The mud was cool and soft.

"Come in, Milo," said her friend Ana.

Milo jumped. Mud went on her nose. She laughed. They made mud pies. They were busy for a long time.

Then Milo sat down. She was tired. She put her head on a soft pillow of grass. A small tickle ran up her arm. It was a bug.

Far away, a green light shone on a tower. Milo saw it. It was very pretty. She wanted to touch it.

"Can we go there?" she said.

"No," said Ana. "It is too far."

Milo looked at the light. She looked and looked. The sun went down. The light stayed on the tower.

"I want it," Milo said.

She could not have it. Her mud puddle dried up. Ana went home. Milo sat alone in the dry dirt. The green light was still far away.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Milo

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
One hot summer day, Milo found a big mud puddle. It was round and brown and cool. She jumped in with both feet. Splash! Mud went on her toes. Mud went on her nose. "This is the best puddle," she said.

Her mom called, "Milo, we must go. I am busy now."

"Not yet," said Milo. She sat in the mud like a soft pillow. It did tickle her legs. She made mud pies. She made mud hills.

Then she saw it. Far away, on a tall tower, a small green light. It shone and shone in the hot sky. Milo wanted to touch it. She reached out her hand. The light did not come.

"Come home," said her mom.

Milo looked at the light once more. It was so far. Her puddle was here, but the light was not.

"Can I keep it?" she said.

"No," said her mom. "That light is not ours."

Milo stood up. The mud dried on her feet. She walked home slow. The green light stayed on the tower, far away, and Milo could not have it.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Milo

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
One hot summer day Milo found a big mud puddle. She jumped in with both feet. Splash! The brown water went up her legs. "This is fun," she said.

Her mom called, "Milo, come home. I am busy."

Milo did not want to go. She sat in the mud like a pillow. It was soft and cool. A fly came to tickle her nose.

Then she saw it. On a tower far away, a small green light was shining. It blinked once. It blinked again.

"Come here, light," Milo said.

The light did not come. It only blinked.

Milo stood up. She walked and walked. The sun was hot. Her feet hurt. The tower never got closer.

"Please," she said. "Please come here."

The light just blinked. Milo sat down in the dust. She was far from home. She was all alone. The green light shone on the tower. It did not want her. It never would.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Milo

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
On hot summer days Milo liked to find a mud puddle. She liked to stomp in it. Splash, splash, splash. The mud felt cool on her toes.

"Come jump with me," Milo said.

"No," said her friend. "I am busy."

So Milo jumped alone. Then she saw it. On a tower, far away, a small green light. It was bright in the sun. Milo wanted it.

"I want that light," she said.

She reached her hand out. The light stayed far away.

She put a pillow on the grass and stood on it. She still could not touch the light. The tall grass began to tickle her feet.

"I want that light," she said again.

She said it and said it. "I want that light. I want that light."

The mud dried on her toes. The sun went down. The small green light came on, far, far away on the tower. Milo sat down in the dry mud puddle.

"I want that light," she said.

But she never got it. Not that day. Not ever.

stories.topic: a girl and a mud puddle
stories.name: Milo

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
On a hot summer day Milo found a big mud puddle. She jumped in with both feet. Splash! The brown water went up her legs.

"Look, Mama!" Milo said. "I am making a cake."

"That is a busy puddle," said Mama.

Milo sat in the mud. It was soft and cool. She put some mud on her arm.

Then she saw it. Far away, on a tower, a small green light was shining.

Milo wanted that light. The light was so far. The light was so high.

"I want the light," she said.

"You cannot have it," said Mama. "It is too far."

Mama put Milo to bed. Milo put her head on her pillow.

"I want the light," she said.

"It will tickle your eyes if you look too long," said Mama.

"It will not," said Milo. "I want it. I want it. I want it."

Milo looked out her window all night. The green light stayed on the tower. It was far. It was high. She could not reach it.

The next day the puddle was dry. The mud was gone. Milo was sad. She sat and looked at the tower.

"I want it," she said. "I want it. I want it."

The light did not come close.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Soft paws tap the piano keys. Ella is a small gray kitten. She loves the piano in the warm room. "Listen, Mama," Ella says. "I can make a song." She taps one key, then another. The song sounds like a tiny rock falling.

Mama smiles. "Time for bed, little one."

Ella wants to play more. She runs down the hall. She is looking for a toy mouse. She finds a dark shop. The shop is cold and quiet. An icy wind blows from the door.

At the back of the dark shop, Ella sees a small green light. It glows and glows. She wants to jump and touch it. She reaches with one paw. The light is too far away. She cannot have it.

"Come home, Ella," Mama calls.

Ella walks back to the warm room. She taps the piano one last time. The green light stays far away. Ella learns that some pretty things are not for us, and home is warm and near.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Softly, Ella the kitten walked to the piano. It sat in the big room. She wanted to play. Her paws went tap, tap on the keys.

"Time for bed," said Mama.

"Just one more song," said Ella. She did a little jump on the bench.

The room grew dark. Just before bedtime, Ella saw a light. It was green and far away. It was at the back of a dark shop. The light did not move. It did not rock. It was icy and still.

"Come, Ella," said Mama.

Ella looked at the green light. She wanted to touch it. She reached out a paw. But the light was too far. It was always too far.

"Can I have it?" she asked.

"No," said Mama. "Some lights are just to see."

Ella turned away. She played one soft note. The green light blinked. Then she went to bed.

The next day, she played the piano again. She did not reach for the light. She was happy with her song. A cat can love a thing she cannot hold.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Soft paws on the piano keys made a little song. Ella the kitten played every night. She loved the piano. It went plink, plonk, plink.

Just before bedtime, Mama said, "Time to sleep, Ella."

"One more song," Ella said. She pressed a key. Plink.

Then Ella saw a small green light. It was at the back of a dark shop. The shop was cold and icy. The light was far away.

"Come, Ella," Mama said.

But Ella did not come. She wanted the light. She tried to rock the piano forward. It did not move. She tried to jump to the shop. It was too far.

"Ella, what do you want?" Mama asked.

"That light," Ella said. "It is so pretty."

"You cannot reach it, little one," Mama said. "But you can play your piano."

Ella looked at the light. She looked at the keys. She played one more song.

A heart can want what it cannot hold. But it can still make music.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Soft was the night, and Ella sat at the piano. She was a small gray kitten. Her paws went tap, tap on the keys. "Play me a song," said her mom. Ella tried to play. But her eyes went to the window. Far away, in a dark shop, a green light glowed at the back.

"Ella, look here," said her mom. Ella looked. Tap, tap. Then her head turned again. The light was so small. So far. It was like an icy star.

"Can I go?" asked Ella.

"No," said her mom. "It is almost bedtime."

Ella did not rock or jump on the keys. She just watched the light. It called to her. She reached a paw out the window. She could not touch it. Never, never.

"Come to bed," said her mom.

Ella looked one more time. The light stayed far away.

Some lights are pretty, but they are not for us. Love the warm things close to you.

stories.name: Ella

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop

stories.text:
Soft was the kitten on the piano. Ella put her small hands on the keys. The piano went plink, plink, plink.

"Good," said Mom. "Time for bed."

Then Ella saw the light. A green light, far away, at the back of a dark shop.

"Mom, what is that?"

"Just a light, Ella. Bedtime."

But the light was green and small. It did not rock. It did not jump. It was still and icy and bright.

Ella reached for it. Her hand went through cold air.

"Come on," said Mom.

Ella reached again. "I want it."

"You can't have it, sweetie."

The light stayed at the back of the dark shop. Ella reached and reached. The piano was quiet. The night was deep. The light was green. The light was green. The light was green.

Some lights are only for looking. Some lights are not for holding.

stories.name: Ivy

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text: Fog wrapped the house like a blanket. Ivy found a small piano. She was a kitten with soft gray paws. She pressed one key. Plink. She pressed another. Plonk. "Do it again," said Mom. Ivy did. Plink, plonk, plink. Dad lit a candle. Its glow made the room warm. Ivy tried a song. It was mostly wrong. Mom did not laugh. She said, "Keep going." Ivy kept going. Plink, plonk, plonk, plink. Later they went outside. The fog was thick. Ivy walked to the stream. In the reeds, something shone. A small light, far off. It blinked like a slow eye. Ivy reached a paw. The reeds bent. The light stayed far. She looked back at the house. The candle was a dot. The piano was quiet. "Come in," called Mom. Ivy went in. She pressed one key. Plink. The fog stayed outside. The far light stayed far. Ivy curled on the warm keys. She slept.

stories.name: Ivy

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
From the top of the piano, Ivy the kitten watched the keys. They were white and black, like teeth in a big smile. She tapped one with her paw. Plink. She tapped another. Plonk. Her boy, Sam, sat on the bench. He played a song that went up and down. Ivy purred. The music felt warm. She walked along the keys. Plink, plonk, plink.

“You are making a song too,” Sam said.

“Mew,” said Ivy. She did not know that word. She only knew the tapping. Sam lit a candle. The little flame danced. Then he went to bed. The room got dark. Ivy sat by the window. Fog covered the yard like a soft blanket.

Far away, past the fence and the trees, she saw a small glow. It was in the reeds by the stream. It was not gold and it was not green. It was just a small, wet shine. It looked like a tiny moon that fell down and got stuck. Ivy put her paw on the glass. She wanted to hold it. She wanted to bat it like a ball of yarn.

She did not know how to laugh at herself. She just stared.

“Come back,” she said to the shine. But it stayed in the reeds.

stories.name: Ivy

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
Fog wrapped the yard like a soft gray blanket. Ivy the kitten found the piano on the porch. She pat it with one paw. Plink, plink. She smiled. “Listen, Mama,” she said. “I made a song.” Mama lit a candle. Her laugh was warm. “Play more, little one,” she said.

Ivy played. Plink, plunk, plink. The fog got thicker. Through the window, past the reeds by the stream, she saw it. A small green glow. It blinked like a firefly asleep.

“Do you see that?” Ivy asked.

“See what?” said Mama.

Ivy jumped off the bench. The glow was still there. It was far away, in the reeds by the stream. She wanted to touch it. She wanted to hold it.

“Come back to the piano,” Mama said.

Ivy played one more note. Then she turned again. The green glow waited in the fog. It did not come closer. It did not go away. It just stayed.

stories.name: Ivy

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
Five soft toes pressed one piano key. Ivy the kitten played a song. Mom played too. The house felt warm.

"Again," Ivy said.

"One more," said Mom. "Then sleep."

The piano sang low. The candle made a small moon on the wall. It did not laugh like the fire. It just made a home.

But through the window, past the fog, a tiny light blinked in the reeds by the stream. Ivy put her paw on the glass.

"Do you see it?" she said.

"See what, dear?"

"That little light. It waits for me."

The piano waited. Ivy did not play. She watched the reeds.

"Come back," said Mom.

"I want it," Ivy said. "I want to hold the small light."

"It's far," said Mom.

"I want it. I want it. I want it."

The fog moved. The light stayed small.

Mom lifted Ivy and hummed. The piano slept. The candle went out. Ivy kept one eye open, watching the reeds. Before sleep took her, she whispered, "I want it."

stories.name: Ivy

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
Fog wrapped the house like a soft gray blanket. Ivy was a small kitten. She found the piano in the front room. She put one paw on a white key. Plink. She put one paw on a black key. Plonk. She made a song. It was just for her.

Then she saw it through the window. A little light. It sat in the reeds by the stream. It was green and far away.

"Come play," said her boy, holding a candle.

"No," said Ivy. She wanted the light. She wanted it. The piano was warm. Her boy was warm. But the light was not warm. It was just light. She wanted it anyway.

"Please come," said the boy. "We can laugh."

Ivy did not laugh. She wanted the light. She wanted the light. She wanted the light.

She ran outside. The fog was cold. The reeds were wet. The light stayed far away. It was always far away. She sat down in the mud. She wanted the light. She wanted the light. She wanted the light.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: deep at the bottom of a pond
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Before bed, Jack played the piano. A tiny kitten sat on the keys. The kitten was named Mittens.

Mittens stepped on a key. Plink! Jack laughed. He played a soft song.

Mittens wanted to help. She walked on the keys. Clunk! Clunk! The song got messy.

Jack did not get mad. He picked up Mittens. "We can play together," he said.

Jack ate a piece of cake. Then he had an idea. He put Mittens on his lap. He held her paws. They pressed one key at a time.

Plink, plunk, plink. It was slow, but it was music.

Mittens purred. Jack gave a little clap. The problem was solved.

Then Jack looked out the window. Far away, past the trees, a small light glowed deep at the bottom of the pond. It was green and quiet.

Jack blinked. The light stayed. He did not know why it called to him. He only knew it was there, and he could not touch it.

"Time for bed," said Mom.

Jack said goodnight to Mittens. He said goodnight to the pond. The green light waited in the dark, like a secret he would keep.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: deep at the bottom of a pond
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Bedtime came, and Jack the kitten was not sleepy. He wanted to play the piano. But one white key made no sound. It was stuck. Jack pushed it with his paw. Nothing. He felt sad.

Mom came in with a slice of cake. "Try again," she said. Jack did. He gave a tiny hop and a soft clap. Then he pressed the stuck key. It went plink, plink, plink!

Jack played a happy song. Mom clapped too. Then Jack looked out the window.

Far away, deep at the bottom of a pond, a small light shone. It was green and calm. It did not move. Jack wanted to touch it. But he was only a kitten, and the pond was dark and far.

"Time for bed," said Mom.

Jack had fixed the key. He had played his song. That was enough for tonight. He curled up warm and closed his eyes. The little light stayed far away, soft at the bottom of the pond.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: deep at the bottom of a pond
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Before bedtime, Jack played the piano. His kitten, Mittens, sat on the bench. Mittens put one paw on a key. Plink! Jack laughed. He tried to play a song. But his fingers felt slow. He hit two keys at once. Bump! That was not right.

Jack wanted to play a soft song for Mittens. He tried again. Bump, bump. Mittens jumped down. Jack felt sad. His song was a mess.

Then Jack had an idea. He did not need a big song. He played one note. Then one more note. Mittens came back. Jack played a tiny song, just three notes. Mittens purred.

Mom called, “Bedtime!” Jack got a piece of cake. He did not clap. His hands were tired. But he was happy.

From the window, Jack saw the pond. Deep down, a small light shone. It was green and far away. He could not touch it. It was just there, under the water, blinking like a slow note. He looked and looked. Then he went to bed.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: deep at the bottom of a pond
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Before bed, Jack played the piano. A kitten sat on the keys. The kitten went plink, plunk. Jack did not like that. He wanted to play a real song. The kitten wanted to play too. Jack said, "Stop, cat." The kitten did not stop. It was a little problem. Jack got a soft cloth. He put it on the bench. The kitten sat on the cloth. It was cozy. Jack played a song. The kitten did not touch the keys. Then Jack saw it. Deep in the pond outside, a tiny light shone. It was small and green. It was far down. Jack wanted to touch it. He could not. He wanted to hold it. He could not. He said, "I want the light. I want the light." Mom called, "Bedtime, Jack." Jack had a piece of cake. He did not taste it. He said, "I want the light." Mom said, "The pond is deep. The light is for the fish." Jack said, "I want it." Then the kitten climbed on his lap. The kitten was warm. Jack did not clap. He held the kitten. The light was still there. But now Jack was sleepy. He said, "Good night, cat." He did not want the light so much. He had his cat. That was enough.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: deep at the bottom of a pond
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Before bed, Jack played the piano. A kitten sat on the keys. The kitten went plink, plink. Jack said, "Shoo, kitten." The kitten did not go. It made a tiny mess on the keys. Now the piano went thump, thump. Jack had a little problem.

He got a soft cloth. He wiped each key. The kitten watched. Then the kitten hit one key with its paw. Ding! The sound was clear and sweet. Jack did not clap. He wanted it clean. But the kitten kept playing. Jack smiled.

Just before bedtime, Jack looked out the window. Down past the yard was the pond. Deep at the bottom, a little light shone. It was small and far. Jack wanted it. He wanted to hold it. He wanted it to stay. He thought, I want it. I want it. I want it.

His mom called, "Time for bed." She gave him cake. Jack ate one bite. The kitten purred. Jack laughed. The light could wait. He had his kitten and his cake. He went to sleep happy.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: behind the hedge
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Nobody knew how the kitten got inside the piano. Hugo heard a tiny mew come from under the lid. He lifted the lid and found the small gray kitten sitting on the keys. It made a soft plink when it moved. Hugo put his boot by the bench so the kitten could climb down. Then he tried to teach it to run across the keys. The kitten only wanted to chase a windy leaf. Hugo laughed and played one slow song. The kitten sat still and listened. That was their little problem. It got solved when Hugo left the lid open and the kitten walked out on its own. On a hot summer day, he carried the kitten to the garden. Behind the hedge, a small lamp glowed in the neighbor's yard. It was far away and always on. Hugo wanted to touch it, but he never could. The kitten slipped from his arms and ran through the hedge. It did not come back.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: behind the hedge
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Nobody told Hugo to play the piano. Hugo was a kitten. The piano was big and brown. It sat by the window all summer.

One hot summer day, Hugo found a boot on the floor. He pushed it with his paw. The boot bumped a black key. Plink! Hugo jumped back. Then he bounced on the keys. Plink plonk plonk!

The sound was loud. Hugo did not like it. He wanted a soft sound, like a mouse. He tried to walk on the keys, slow and quiet. But his paws were too small. The music came out wrong.

A windy day blew the curtains. Hugo heard a tiny sound behind the hedge. It was a little green light. It shone and shone. He could see it but not touch it. It felt like a warm lap he could not sit on.

He tried and tried to make the piano soft. At last he curled up on the keys and slept. The piano stayed quiet. The green light stayed far away. Hugo never learned to play.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: behind the hedge
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Next to the piano, Hugo the kitten sat. The piano was big and brown. One key went plink. Hugo wanted to play a song. But his paws were too small. The keys were too wide. He tried and tried. He could not make a tune.

The room was hot. It was a hot summer day. Hugo felt sleepy. He walked to the window. Behind the hedge, he saw a little light. It was soft and green. It wiggled like a leaf. He wanted to touch it. He put on one tiny boot. He went outside.

The light was far. He had to run. It was windy. The grass moved. He ran past the hedge. The light moved away. He ran more. His heart went thump. The light stayed just ahead.

Then he stopped. He was lost. He mewed. His little problem was this: he could not reach the light. He turned back home. The light stayed behind the hedge. He never touched it. He sat by the piano. Plink. Plink. He was sad.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: behind the hedge
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Next to the piano, Hugo found a kitten. She was small and gray, with a tail like a shoelace. She climbed onto the keys. Plink, plonk. Hugo laughed. He named her Boot.

On a hot summer day, Boot would not come inside. She sat by the hedge and stared. Hugo brought milk. She did not drink. She just stared at the hedge.

Hugo looked too. Behind the hedge, past the fence, a little green light blinked. It was far away. It was always far away.

"Come, Boot," Hugo said. "Come, Boot. Come, Boot." Boot did not come.

He tried a windy day. The light danced. Boot ran to the hedge. Hugo ran too. The light stayed far.

Then Boot squeezed under the hedge. She was gone. Hugo waited. He played the piano soft. Plink, plonk. No kitten came.

The little problem was solved for the light. It kept blinking. Hugo sat alone. He played the same song. Come, Boot. Come, Boot. The keys stayed cold.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: behind the hedge
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Now Hugo was a small gray kitten. He loved the piano. He sat on the bench and patted the keys. Ping, ping, ping.

It was a hot summer day. A windy puff blew through the window. Hugo wanted to play a real song. But his paws were too soft. That was his little problem.

He tried a boot on the pedal. It was too heavy. He tried to run up the keys. They only made a clatter. Then he sat very still. He fixed it his own way. He patted one low note, then one high note, slow and soft. It sounded like a song for one small cat.
