In the sky, the moon came up. Joon the owl sat in his tree. He wanted to see the moon. He wanted to hear the moon.

Joon flew to a little island. On the island, a small light was on. It was green and far away. It was so far. It was too far.

Joon said, "I want the light. I want the light. I want the light."

He put on his boot. He did not need it, but he put it on. He tried to listen for the light. The night was quiet. The light was quiet too.

Joon flew and flew. The light did not get close. The light stayed far. His wings got tired.

Joon sat down. He was sad. He would never touch the light. He would never get there.

Then the moon came out big and round. The moon was warm. The moon was close. Joon smiled a little.

But Joon still looked at the green light. He still wanted it. He wanted it all night.

stories.name: Ivy

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text: Gently, Ivy the owl woke up. The sun was warm on her wings. She liked the afternoon. It was quiet and bright. Ivy flew to the gate to see the street. A windy breeze made the leaves dance. She waved her wing at a passing cloud. Then she saw it. Far down the street, a car was parked. A tiny light sat on the car. It was small and green. It did not move. Ivy tilted her head. What a funny little light, she thought. She forgot it and flew to find berries. She ate three sweet ones. Then she sat on a branch. The moon would come soon. Ivy loved the moon. It was big and soft and white. She waited. The sky turned pink. Then gray. Then dark. Up came the moon. It glowed over the houses. Ivy felt happy. She hooted a soft hoot. The little light on the car blinked once. Then it went out. Ivy did not care. The moon was all she needed. She closed her eyes and slept.

stories.name: Ivy

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
Good afternoon came, and Ivy the owl woke up. She lived in a big tree by a house with a gate. Today she wanted to see the moon. But the sun was up, and the moon was far away.

Ivy flew to the porch. She sat on a windy branch. The wind made the leaves wave. She looked for the moon. She could not find it.

Down the street, a car sat by the curb. A small light shone on its roof. It was bright and still. Ivy saw it and felt a pull. She wanted to touch that light. But it was too far.

She flew a little closer. The light stayed far away. She hooted softly. "I want to hold you," she said.

Then her friend Max the cat came. "The moon comes at night," he said. "Rest now."

So Ivy went home. She slept in her warm nest. When she woke, the sky was dark. The moon was big and round. It was right above her tree. Ivy smiled. She did not need the far light. The moon was hers at last.

stories.name: Ivy

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
Gently, Ivy the owl woke up in her tree. The sun was high. It was a sunny afternoon. Ivy liked the moon best. She wanted to see it.

She flew to the gate. The wind was windy. Leaves blew by. She saw a little light on a car far down the street. It was small and green. It made her feel quiet inside. She wished she could hold it.

“Moon,” she said. “I want you.” The green light said nothing. It just stayed far away.

Ivy flew over the windy yard. She gave a wave to a cat. She looked for the moon. The sky was still bright. The green light kept pulling her eye.

Then the sun went down. The sky turned soft. The moon came up big and round. It was white and kind. It was not far at all.

Ivy sat on her branch. She hummed a slow song. The little green light blinked below, but she did not need it now. Her moon was right there. She felt warm and happy.

stories.name: Ivy

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
Gently, Ivy the owl woke up. The sun was warm on her feathers. She wanted to see the moon. But the moon only comes out at night.

Ivy flew to the gate. She looked up. No moon. She flew to the tall tree. She looked up. No moon. The wind was windy and blew her soft hat.

Then she saw a shiny thing. Far down the street, on a car, a little light shone. It was small and bright. It looked like the moon. Ivy wanted that light. She wanted it so much.

“Moon,” she said. “Moon, moon, moon.”

She flew to the car. She sat on the roof. The light was just a lamp. It was not the moon. Ivy felt sad.

Her friend Ben the mouse came. “The moon comes later,” he said. “Wait with me.”

So Ivy waited. The sun went down. The sky turned dark. And then, big and round and soft, the moon came up.

Ivy hooted. She did not need the little light. She had the real moon. She gave a happy wave with her wing and smiled.

stories.name: Ivy

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
Good afternoon came to Ivy’s tree. The owl woke up and blinked at the sun. She wanted to see the moon.

Ivy flew to the gate. The wind was windy and made her feathers dance. She looked down the street. A car sat far away. On the car, a little green light was shining. It was small and bright.

“Moon,” Ivy said. “You are there.”

She flew to the car. The green light did not get closer. “Moon,” she said. “Moon, moon, moon.”

She waved her wing at the sky. The sun was still up. No moon.

Ivy flew home. She sat in her tree. She waited. The sky turned pink, then purple. Then the moon came up. It was big and soft and white.

“You came,” Ivy said. “You came, you came.”

She was happy. The green light was just a light on a car. But the moon was hers.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: across the snowy yard
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
The moon was bright and round. Leo the owl sat in his tree. He looked at the moon. It was big and white. Leo wanted to touch it. He flew up high. He flew and flew. But the moon was far away. Leo came back to his tree. He was sad.

Then Leo saw something. Across the snowy yard, a small light glowed. It was green. It sat on a stone by the fence. Leo liked that light. He wanted it too. He flew down and tried to grab it. He gave it a soft kick. But the light did not move. His wings got wet in the snow. The light stayed far away.

Leo went back to his tree. He looked at the moon. He looked at the green light. He could not have them. But he was not sad now. The moon was still pretty. The light was still pretty. He did not need to hold them.

Sometimes we want things we cannot have. It is okay to just look and smile.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: across the snowy yard
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
The owl named Leo lived in a big tree. Every night, he looked at the moon. The moon was round and bright. Leo loved the moon. It was his friend in the sky.

One cold night, Leo sat in his tree. It was just before bedtime. He saw a small green light across the snowy yard. It was far away. It looked like a tiny moon on the ground.

Leo wanted that light. He flew down. He hopped on the cold stone path. He did not want to kick the snow. His feet felt wet. He wanted the green light.

The light was not a moon. It was a little lamp by a door. A soft glow.

Leo felt sad. Then he looked up. The real moon was still there. It was big and bright.

The moon is far, but it is always yours.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: across the snowy yard
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text: The moon came up over the trees, and Leo the owl woke from his nap. He loved the moon. It was big and round and soft. It made the dark woods feel kind. Leo flapped up to his branch to watch it. Just before bedtime, he saw a small green light across the snowy yard. It glowed by the fence. Leo tilted his head. What was that light? He wanted it. He flew down and landed on a cold stone. The snow was wet under his feet. He tried to kick a little snow away. The light stayed far. He hopped closer. It stayed far. He reached out a wing. It stayed far. "Come here, little light," Leo said. The light did not come. Then the moon slid behind a cloud, and Leo saw the truth. The green light was only a firefly. It blinked and flew away. Leo flew home and sat on his branch. The moon came back, big and kind. He did not need the little light. The moon was enough.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: across the snowy yard
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
The owl sat on a branch and looked at the moon. Leo loved the owl. The owl was soft and round. The moon was big and white. Leo watched from his window.

Then Leo saw a small green light. It was across the snowy yard. It blinked by the old stone wall. Leo wanted it. He wanted to hold it.

"Come back, owl," Leo said. But he kept looking at the light. The light was so pretty. He wanted it so much.

He put on his boots. The snow was wet. He did not kick the snow. He walked to the wall. The light went away. Then it came back. Then it went away. Leo said, "I want it. I want it. I want it."

He reached out his hand. His hand was cold. The light was just a firefly. It flew up high. Leo could not catch it.

He went back to bed. The owl was still there. The moral is this: some pretty things are only for looking, not for keeping.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: across the snowy yard
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
The owl sat in the snowy tree and watched the moon. Leo loved the owl. He wanted to see it fly.

Leo stood at his window. It was just before bedtime. He saw a small green light across the snowy yard.

The light was so far away. Leo wanted it. The moon was up, but Leo did not look at the moon. He looked at the green light.

"I want that light," said Leo. "I want that light."

He ran outside. His boots were wet. He did not care. He stepped on a stone. He did not care. He did not kick it. He just walked to the light.

"I want that light," he said. "I want that light."

The owl flew down and sat on a fence. The owl hooted. The moon shone on the owl's wings. Leo stopped.

The green light was just a little lamp by a door. It was not for him. But the owl was right there. Leo smiled at the owl. The owl was better than the light.

Then he went to bed.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Gently, Finn the owl woke up in his big oak tree. The moon was full and bright. Finn loved the moon. He liked to watch it glow. "Hello, moon," he said.

Down by the sea, a fog horn blew. Finn flew to the shore. The fog was thick and soft. A big lighthouse stood there. A small green light shone on its side. Finn saw it blink, blink, blink.

"Come swing with me," called a friend. It was a little mouse named Pia. Finn did not go. He looked at the green light. It was so far.

"I want to touch it," Finn said. But the light was high and far.

Pia said, "You can build a kite. We can try."

Finn found sticks and string. He worked all night. Pia helped. The kite was not brave enough to fly high. It fell down.

Finn felt sad. Then Pia said, "Look up." The moon was still there. It was big and kind.

"You do not need to reach everything," Pia said. "Some lights are just for looking."

Finn smiled. He and Pia sat close. The moon watched them. The green light blinked far away. Finn was happy.

At the end, Finn learned that wanting is fine, but friends are better.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Great big wings beat the soft night air. Finn the owl flew over the dark trees. He loved the moon. It was round and white and kind. The moon was his friend.

On this night, fog came in. It rolled over the hill. It hid the moon. Finn could not see his friend.

Finn flew down to the sea. He sat on a wooden swing near the water. He wanted to build a nest where the moon could always find him. But the fog was thick.

Then Finn saw a light. It was on a lighthouse by the sea. The light was small and green. It blinked and blinked. Finn felt a pull. He wanted to touch it. But it was far away.

Finn was brave. He flew up high. He flew past the fog. And there was the moon. It had been there all along.

Finn learned this: when you feel lost, look up. Your light is still there.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Gently, Finn the owl woke up in his tree. The moon was big and white. He liked to watch it from his branch. But tonight, fog came in. The moon went soft and dim.

Finn flew to the sea. On a rock, a tall lighthouse stood. At its top, a little light blinked. It was not white like the moon. It was soft and green. Finn wanted to touch it. He wanted to hold it.

He flew to the lighthouse. The fog made him slow. He had to be brave. He landed on a rail. The green light was so close. But a window was there. He could not reach it.

Finn found a rope. It could swing. He tried to build a way to the light. But the rope was too short. The light stayed just past his wing.

He sat and looked. The green light did not go away. It blinked and blinked. Finn felt warm. He did not need to touch it. He could see it. That was enough.

The fog lifted. The moon came back. Finn flew home happy. Wanting is fine, but seeing can be a gift too.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Gently, Finn the owl woke up in his tall tree. The moon was out. Finn loved the moon. It was round and soft and white.

But tonight, fog rolled in. The moon looked blurry. Finn flew to the beach. He sat on a swing and rocked. Far away, a light blinked. It was on a lighthouse by the sea. The light was small and green.

Finn wanted that light. He wanted to touch it. He wanted to hold it. "I want it," he said. "I want it, I want it."

He flew to the lighthouse. The fog was thick. He hit the wall. He fell in the sand. "I want it," he said. "I want it."

A kind crab came. "You are brave," she said. "But you cannot reach that light. It is for ships."

Finn looked up. The green light blinked. "I want it," he said.

"Then build a nest here," said the crab. "Watch it every night."

So Finn did. He built a nest on a rock. The green light blinked. The moon came back. Finn was happy. The light was far, but he could see it. That was enough.

Moral: You do not have to hold a thing to love it.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea

stories.text:
Great big Finn is an owl. Finn loves the moon. At night he looks up. The moon is white and round. He wants to touch it. But he can not.

Finn sees a little light. It is far away. It sits on a lighthouse by the sea. The light is small and green. It goes blink, blink, blink. Finn wants that light. He wants it so much.

The fog comes in. The night is soft and gray. Finn can not see the moon. But he can see the green light. It calls him. It calls him.

"I want the light," Finn says. "I want the light. I want the light." He says it again and again.

Finn can not swing to it. He can not build a bridge to it. He is not brave enough to fly so far. The light just blinks. It is so close and so far.

Then Finn hears a small sound. A little bird is lost in the fog. "Help me," says the bird.

Finn looks at the green light. Then he looks at the bird. He wants the light. But the bird needs him.

Finn flies down. He helps the bird find its nest. The bird is safe. Finn feels warm inside.

The fog lifts. The moon comes out. It is big and bright. Finn can not touch it. But it shines on him.

What you can not hold can still light your way home.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Jack

axes.where: high up on a mountain
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Winter was far away, but Jack still loved his warm blanket. He kept it on his bed all summer. It was soft and blue.

One hot day, Jack and Dad walked up a mountain. Jack held a small pebble in his hand. It was smooth and shiny.

Then Jack saw it. High up on the mountain, a tiny green light glowed. It was small and far away.

"Dad, look," Jack said. "What is that?"

"I don't know," Dad said. "It looks like a star that fell."

Jack wanted that light. He reached for it. It stayed far away.

The wind blew. Cold air came down fast. Snow filled the sky. A blizzard!

Dad gave Jack a hug. Jack pulled out his warm blanket. He wrapped it around them both.

The green light blinked one last time. Then the sun came back.

"Where did the snow go?" Jack asked. Dad laughed. "The mountains play tricks," he said. Jack held his pebble tight. The blanket felt good. The light was gone.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Jack

axes.where: high up on a mountain
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Winter was far away, but Jack still loved his warm blanket. He kept it on his bed even on a hot summer day. It was soft and blue.

Jack went hiking up a big mountain. The sun was hot. He found a small pebble and put it in his pocket. Then he saw it. High up on the mountain, a shiny green light. It glowed like a tiny star.

"Look," Jack said to his mom. "What is that light?"

"I don't know," she said. "Maybe the sun on a window."

Jack wanted that light. He reached for it. But it was too far away. He walked more. The light stayed far.

At the top, Jack felt cold wind. He hugged his arms. The green light was still there, shiny and far.

"Mom, I want to go to it," Jack said.

"We can't," she said. "It's too high."

Jack looked down. His blanket was in his bag! He pulled it out. The twist was simple. The warm blanket made him feel safe. The green light blinked once, then faded in the sun.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Jack

axes.where: high up on a mountain
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Winter wind blew hard, but Jack was warm. He had a big, soft blanket. A blizzard roared outside his window. Snow hit the glass. Jack did not care. He was safe and snug.

Then he saw it. High up on the mountain, a small green light. It was shiny and far away. It shone through the snow.

"Come see," Jack said to his mom.

"I see only snow," she said.

But Jack saw the light. He wanted it. He reached for it. He could not have it.

The light blinked. It called to him. He held his blanket like a hug. He put a small pebble in his pocket. The light stayed high on the mountain.

Then the twist came. The blizzard stopped. The sun came out. It was a hot summer day.

"That was a dream," Jack said.

But the green light was still there. It always was. He reached. He could not have it.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Jack

axes.where: high up on a mountain
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Winter was far away, but Jack still thought about the blizzard. He remembered the cold wind. He remembered the snow. Most of all, he remembered his warm blanket.

Now it was a hot summer day. Jack walked up a mountain trail. Sweat ran down his face. He kicked a small pebble.

Then he saw it. High up on the mountain, a shiny light glowed. It was green and soft. It did not belong in the bright day.

"Come on, Jack," said his friend. "We should go back."

Jack did not answer. He reached toward the light. His fingers closed on empty air. The light stayed far away.

"It's just a light," his friend said. "You can't have it."

Jack tried again. He wanted to hug it close. He wanted to hold it like his blanket. But the light only shimmered and pulled away.

Then Jack laughed. The shiny light was only a green bottle, stuck on a rock. The sun made it glow.

"Okay," Jack said. "Let's go home." But he looked back once more.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Jack

axes.where: high up on a mountain
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
When the blizzard came, Jack hid under a warm blanket. The snow tapped the window. The wind said whooo. It was a hot summer day, but the blizzard did not care.

Then Jack saw it. High up on a mountain, a small green light. It was shiny. It blinked once. It blinked again.

"Come here," Jack whispered. He held out one hand. The blanket slipped off.

He climbed toward the light. He stepped on a pebble. The pebble rolled away. The light stayed high. It stayed far.

"Wait for me," Jack said.

The light did not wait. It never came close. Jack reached and reached. His arms felt cold. His toes felt cold.

"Just one hug," he said to the light.

The light blinked. It blinked and blinked.

Then Jack heard his mother. "Jack, your cocoa is ready."

He looked down. The blizzard was gone. The mountain was gone. Only the warm blanket was there, soft on his bed, and the hot sun in the window. The small green light was just the clock on his wall, blinking.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Ben

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Little Ben woke up and saw snow. The wind pushed the snow all around. It was a blizzard! Ben put on his coat and boots.

He went outside with his mom. The wind was loud. Snow got on his nose.

Ben saw the playground. On the far side of the playground, a small green light was on. It blinked in the wind. Ben wanted to touch it.

"Come on, Ben," said his mom. "Let's go home."

At home, Mom made tea in the teapot. Ben sat by the fire. He got a warm blanket. The blanket was soft and sticky with jam from breakfast.

Ben looked out the window. He could still see the little green light far away. He reached for it, but the window was cold. He could not have it.

Mom gave him a big hug. They drank tea and watched the snow. Ben felt warm and happy. The blanket was the best part of the day.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Ben

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Little Ben had a big warm blanket. The snow came down all morning. It was a blizzard! The wind went whoosh, whoosh. Ben felt cold.

He looked out the window. On the far side of the playground, a small green light was shining. It was so far away. Ben wanted to touch it. He put on his coat and went outside.

The wind pushed him back. The snow was sticky on his face. He could not build a snowman in this blizzard. He just looked at the green light. It blinked and blinked.

Ben went back inside. His mom gave him a hug. She made tea in the teapot. Steam went up, up, up.

Ben wrapped his warm blanket around him. He sat by the window. The green light was still there. He reached for it, but he could not have it. That was okay. The blanket was soft and warm. Ben felt happy and safe.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Ben

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Little Ben had a big, warm blanket. The wind blew hard outside. It was a blizzard! Snow hit the window. Ben was glad for his blanket.

He wanted to build a fort. He put the blanket over two chairs. It was a good fort. Mom made tea in the teapot. The tea was warm and sweet.

Ben looked out the window. He saw a small green light. It was on the far side of the playground. It blinked in the snow. Ben wanted to touch it. He put on his coat. He ran to the playground. The snow was sticky and deep. The light was still far away. He could not reach it.

He went back home. He was cold. Mom gave him a hug. Ben sat under his warm blanket. He drank his tea. The green light was gone. But Ben was happy and warm.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Ben

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Little Ben sat by the window. Snow fell and fell. A big blizzard came. Ben wanted to stay warm. He had a soft blanket. It was red and warm.

Then he saw it. A small green light, far away. It shone on the far side of the playground. Ben put down his blanket. He walked to the door.

"Come back," said Mom. "The wind is bad."

Ben did not stop. The green light pulled him. He went out in the windy morning. Snow hit his face. He could not build a snowman. The snow was too sticky and deep.

He thought of his teapot. It was warm at home. But the light was greener. He walked and walked. The light did not come closer. It only blinked.

Ben got cold. His hands hurt. He sat in the snow. Then Mom came. She wrapped the red blanket around him. She carried him home.

They drank tea from the teapot. Ben felt warm. The green light was still out there. But the blanket was here. Ben was happy.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Ben

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
Little Ben had a warm blanket. The blanket was soft and red. A blizzard came. The wind went whoosh. Snow came down. Ben held his blanket tight.

Then Ben saw the light.

The light was on the far side of the playground. It was small and green. It glowed in the windy morning.

Ben wanted the light. He left his warm blanket. He walked to the light. The snow was sticky on his boots.

He said, "I want the light."

He came to the playground. The light was still far. It was always far.

He said, "I want the light."

He forgot his blanket. He forgot the teapot at home. He forgot to build a snowman.

He said, "I want the light."

His hands were cold. His nose was cold.

Then his mom came. She put the warm blanket on him. She gave him a hug.

Ben held his mom. The light was far away. Ben was warm. Ben was happy.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Joon

axes.where: in a tent across the camp

stories.text:
Cold wind shook the tent all night. Joon pulled his warm blanket up to his chin. The blizzard roared outside. But Joon was cozy.

In the morning, Joon put on his glove. He wanted to check the camp. He stepped into deep snow. The wind tried to push him down.

“Hey, Joon!” called his friend Mia. “You look like a snowman!”

Joon laughed. “A busy snowman,” he said. He tried to shake the snow off his hat. It fell on his nose. Plop!

Then Mia made a funny sound. “Achoo!” Her hat flew off. They both giggled.

Across the camp, Joon saw a small light. It glowed inside a tent. It was green and soft. For a moment, he wanted to go there.

“Come see my blanket,” said Mia. “It is warm.”

Joon went inside. He forgot the little light. His warm blanket was better. They drank hot cocoa. The blizzard sang outside. But Joon was happy and warm.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Joon

axes.where: in a tent across the camp

stories.text:
Cold wind hit the tent all night. Joon pulled his warm blanket up to his chin. The blanket was soft and red. It made him feel safe. Outside, the blizzard roared.

Joon found one glove. The other glove was lost. "Where is it?" he asked.

His friend Mia laughed. "Maybe a snowman took it."

Joon tried to shake the snow off his coat. The snow was busy falling. It fell and fell.

Then Joon saw a small light. It was in a tent across the camp. The light was green and steady. It glowed through the white snow.

Joon wanted that light. He reached for it. But his tent was warm. The blanket held him close.

"Is the light yours?" Mia asked.

"No," Joon said. "But I want it."

The green light blinked far away. Joon pulled the blanket tighter. The blizzard kept howling. The light stayed where it was. Joon closed his eyes. The warm blanket was enough for now.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Joon

axes.where: in a tent across the camp

stories.text:
Curl up, Joon. The blizzard howls outside. Snow piles high on the tent. Joon pulls her warm blanket to her chin. It is fuzzy and soft. Her breath makes little clouds.

"Too cold," she says. "Too loud."

She hides under the blanket. Then she peeks out. Her glove is lost somewhere. She cannot find it. She tries to shake the tent flap. Snow falls on her nose. She laughs.

"Snow in my nose!" she says. "Funny!"

Her friend yells from another tent. "Are you busy, Joon?"

"Yes," Joon says. "Busy hiding."

But then she sees it. Across the camp, in a tent far away, a small green light glows. It is tiny. It is steady. It does not flicker like the storm. Joon wants that light. She reaches out. The blanket slips.

"Come back," she whispers.

She pulls the blanket tight. But her eyes stay on the tent. The green light calls her. She reaches again. She cannot touch it. The snow is too deep. The wind is too strong.

"Just one more look," she says.

She looks and looks. The blanket is warm. The light is far. She holds the blanket close and waits for morning.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Joon

axes.where: in a tent across the camp

stories.text:
Cold wind pushed on the tent all night. Joon pulled his warm blanket up to his chin. The blizzard hummed like a giant bee. Snow piled high against the door.

Joon held his glove and tried to sleep. But across the camp, a small green light glowed in another tent. It blinked through the snow. Joon wanted it.

“Stay warm,” said Mom.

“I want that light,” Joon said.

“That is just a lamp,” said Mom. “Go to sleep.”

Joon did not sleep. The light was so close. He reached for it. His blanket slipped off. He pulled it back.

“My toes are ice cubes,” he said.

“Mine are popsicles,” said Mom. They laughed. The laugh made a little cloud.

Joon was busy thinking of the light. He wanted to hold it. He wanted to keep it. He wanted it, wanted it, wanted it.

Then Mom wrapped the warm blanket around them both. “This is better than any light,” she said.

Joon watched the green glow. It stayed far away. He could not have it. He gave a small shake. Then he closed his eyes. The blanket was warm. The light was not.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Joon

axes.where: in a tent across the camp

stories.text:
Cold wind pushed on the tent all night. Joon pulled his warm blanket up to his chin. It was soft and red. It kept the blizzard outside.

"Good blanket," Joon said.

His glove was lost somewhere. He did not care. The blanket was busy being warm.

Then he saw it. A small green light, far away, in a tent across the camp. It glowed and did not move. Joon sat up.

"I want that light," he said.

He reached for it. The blanket slid off his toes. He did not care.

"Joon, your feet," said his friend.

"I want the light," Joon said.

"Which light?"

"That light. The green one."

He reached again. His hand did not shake. He could not touch it. It was too far. It was always too far.

"Come back under the blanket," said his friend.

"I want the light," Joon said. "I want the light. I want the light."

The snow fell. The green light stayed. Joon stayed too, reaching, reaching, with his warm blanket on the cold floor.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Max

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Frost tapped the window while Max stayed inside. A blizzard blew and blew. Max had a warm blanket. It was soft and red. He wrapped it around his shoulders. Then he ate one egg. He did not want to skip lunch. The snow made the whole world slow and white. His boot was lost outside. That was his little problem. So Max waited for the wind to stop. At last the sun came out. It was a sunny afternoon. Max found his boot near the porch. He put it on and felt glad. Far away, by the sea, a lighthouse stood on a rock. A small light shone there. Max saw it once and thought, someone is home too. Then he went inside. He drank warm milk. He pulled the blanket up to his chin. The blizzard was over. Max felt safe and warm.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Max

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Frost came down and wind blew hard. Max stayed inside with a warm blanket. The snow piled up. It was a blizzard.

Max wanted an egg. He went to the kitchen. The egg was gone. The store was closed. Snow blocked the door.

Max felt sad. He sat by the window with his blanket. Then he saw a light. Far away, a lighthouse blinked by the sea. The day was sunny now, but the light still turned. It made Max feel calm. He did not know why. He wished he could touch it. He wished he could hold it. But it was too far.

He thought. He had flour and milk. He could make bread. No egg, but bread is good. He mixed and baked. The warm smell filled the room.

He did not skip outside. The snow was too deep. He did not go slow. He just ate warm bread under his blanket. The lighthouse light blinked once more, soft and far. Max smiled. He was warm. That was enough.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Max

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Frost came down and the snow blew hard. Max sat by the window. The blizzard made the world white. He could not go out to play. He had a warm blanket on his lap. It was soft and red.

Then he saw it. Far away, past the snow, a little green light. It blinked on a lighthouse by the sea. Max wished he could touch it. He wished he could hold it in his hand.

His egg fell off the table. It rolled under the chair. "Oh no," said Max. He did not want to skip lunch. He did not want to move slow. But he got up.

He pulled the blanket with him. He crawled under the chair. He found the egg. It was safe.

Max sat back down. He wrapped the blanket around his shoulders. He looked out the window again. The green light was still there. It blinked and blinked. He could not reach it. But his egg was warm. And so was he.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Max

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Frosty wind shook the windows. Max piled soft blankets on his bed. One big blanket was warm like toast. The snow came down, fast and white. A blizzard! Max could not go outside. He felt a little sad.

Then the sun came out. Max looked out the window. Far away, across the sea, a lighthouse stood on a rock. Its light blinked. It was a small green light. It made a soft glow on the water.

Max wanted that green light. He wanted to hold it. He wanted to keep it in his pocket. He thought about it all afternoon. He did not want to skip. He did not want to eat his egg. His soup went slow and cold. The green light blinked and blinked. He wanted it. He wanted it. He wanted it.

His mom gave him a warm blanket. “Let’s make a fort,” she said. They built a fort with chairs and the blanket. Inside, it was cozy and safe. The green light still blinked, but Max felt warm. He smiled. The little problem was solved.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Max

axes.where: on a lighthouse by the sea
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Frost tapped the window while Max stayed in bed. The blizzard made the whole world white. Max wanted to stay under his warm blanket. But the blanket had a hole. Cold air came in. Max pulled the blanket up to his nose. It did not help.

Max ate one egg. He did not want to skip in the snow. He wanted to be warm. But the wind went slow through the hole in his blanket. Max looked out the window. Far away, a small light blinked on a lighthouse by the sea. The sun was out, but the snow hid it. The light was so far. Max could not go there. He wanted that light. He wanted it on his blanket. He wanted it to keep him warm. He said, "I want the light. I want the light. I want the light."

Then Max had an idea. He took a red sock. He put it on the hole. The blanket was warm again. Max smiled. The little light blinked far away.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: at the end of the pier
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: In the cold evening Ravi pulled his warm blanket up to his chin. A big blizzard was coming. Snow would fall and fall. Ravi did not want to hide inside all day. He wanted to fly his red kite at the pier. But the wind was too strong. The kite would break. Ravi felt sad. His little problem needed a fix. He sat by the window and watched the snow start. Then he had an idea. He would fly the kite inside the big room. The wind from the door was slow and soft. Ravi ran and the kite went up. It danced near the ceiling. His warm blanket kept him cozy. The blizzard roared outside. But Ravi smiled. He did not need the pier today. Far away, at the end of the pier, a small green light blinked in the storm. Ravi saw it once. It looked like a tiny lamp. Then he turned back to his kite. The kite dipped and he laughed. His blanket was warm. His heart was happy. The blizzard could wait.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: at the end of the pier
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
In the cold evening, Ravi pulled his warm blanket up to his chin. A big blizzard was coming. Snow would fall and fall. Ravi wanted to fly his red kite one more time. But the wind was too strong. It made the kite dance and pull. Then the string went snap. The kite flew away. Ravi felt sad. He wanted to hide under his blanket.

He ran to the beach to look for his kite. Snow began to fall. It was very cold. Ravi pulled his blanket around him. At the end of the pier, he saw a small, blinking light. It was far away and it made a soft green glow. He wished he could hold it. But the pier was too long. He had to go slow on the slippery wood.

Then Ravi saw his red kite. It was stuck on a pole. A kind man helped him get it down. Ravi smiled. He went home with his kite. He wrapped up in his blanket by the fire. The snow fell outside, but Ravi was warm and happy.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: at the end of the pier
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Icy wind blew and snow came down fast. Ravi had a warm blanket. It was red and soft. He held it tight. The snow made a big pile by the door. Ravi could not go out. He felt sad. He wanted to fly his kite.

Then he saw it. A small light, far away at the end of the pier. It was not red. It was not blue. It was a soft green glow. It blinked and blinked. Ravi wanted to touch it. He wanted to hide under it. But the snow was too deep. The light felt warm, like a tiny sun.

He sat by the window. The light stayed there. It did not come close. It did not go away. “I want to go,” he said. “I want to go.”

His mom saw him look. She gave him a big hug. She said, “Let us make a fort.” They took the warm blanket. They made a little tent. Ravi brought his kite inside. The kite was slow and quiet. He did not need to hide. The green light still blinked at the pier. But now Ravi was warm. He smiled. The snow stopped. Tomorrow he would fly his kite.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: at the end of the pier
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
I like snow days, but this was not a snow day. This was a blizzard. Ravi stood at the window. The wind pushed the trees. The snow came down fast.

Ravi wanted his warm blanket. It was soft and red. But it was not on his bed. It was not in the closet. "Where did it go?" said Ravi.

He looked under the table. He looked behind the door. He said, "I will find it. I will find it. I will find it."

Then he saw a small light. It was green. It was far away, at the end of the pier. It was a tiny glow in the cold evening. Ravi wanted to go to it. The light did not come closer. It just stayed there, blinking. He forgot the blanket. He thought only of the light. "I want to go. I want to go. I want to go."

His mother said, "Ravi, help me. The wind took your kite. It is under the porch."

Ravi ran outside. He saw his kite, red and blue, stuck near a bush. He pulled it out. Then he saw his blanket! It was wrapped around the kite. The wind had blown it there.

He held the warm blanket close. The blizzard was slow and mean, but Ravi was warm. He smiled. The green light was still far away, but Ravi did not care. He had his blanket.

stories.topic: A blizzard and a warm blanket
stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: at the end of the pier
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
I is for inside, where Ravi wraps up in a warm blanket. A blizzard blows hard outside. Snow taps the window. Ravi is warm and safe. But he sees a small light. It is far away, at the end of the pier. It is a soft green glow.

Ravi wants that light. He wants to hold it. He wants it to be his.

He leaves his warm blanket. He goes outside. The wind is loud. Snow gets in his eyes. He cannot find his kite. He wants to hide from the cold. The light is still there. He walks slow. He walks to the pier.

The light is just a lamp on a pole. A man is fixing it. The man says, “Hello, little friend.” Ravi says, “I wanted your light.” The man laughs. He gives Ravi a small green bulb.

Ravi goes home. He puts the bulb in his window. The blizzard stops. Ravi is warm again. The little light stays with him. He is happy.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
I watch a baby bird hop to the edge of the nest. Gus is his name. He is small and round. His wings shake.

"Fly, Gus," I say. "You can do it."

Gus looks down. The ground is far away. He holds a sticky leaf in his beak. He drops it.

The sun is going down. On a car parked far down the street, a little light comes on. It is small and green. It glows like a tiny pillow. Gus sees it. He wants to touch it. He leans toward it.

"Not yet," I say. "First you fly."

Gus flaps his wings. He hops. He falls. Then he flies! He lands on a soft bush.

I clap. The green light blinks on the car. Gus looks at it once. Then he looks at the sky. He is happy.

"Good job, Gus," I say. "Time to draw a picture of your big day."

Gus chirps. He sits on his bush. The green light stays far away. But Gus is home.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
In the nest, Gus watched his mother fly. His turn had come. He flapped his wings. They felt weak like a soft pillow. Below, the grass looked far away.

Gus took a breath. He let go. For a moment he fell, and his heart went fast. Then his wings caught the air. He was flying! He did not draw a single circle wrong.

The sky turned orange. The sun went down. Far down the street, a green light blinked on a parked car. It shone like a small star. Gus turned his head. He wanted to touch it.

He flew toward it. The light stayed far away. It was always far away. His feet felt sticky on a leaf. He rested.

Then Gus thought of home. He turned back. The green light still blinked behind him. He did not need it.

His mother met him at the nest. She nuzzled his head. Gus was tired and happy. He had flown all by himself.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
In the nest, Gus felt safe. He was a small bird. Today he would try to fly. His wings felt like a soft pillow. He looked down. The ground was far away. He did not want to go.

The sun was setting. Gus saw a small light. It was on a car far down the street. The light was green. It was tiny and bright. Gus wanted to touch it. He did not know how. He leaned out of the nest. The light seemed to draw him closer.

"Jump," said Mama. "You can do it."

Gus looked at the light again. He wanted it so much. He jumped. The air felt sticky and warm. He flapped his wings. He flew! He flew past the trees. He did not reach the light. But he was flying.

Gus landed on a soft bush. He was happy. The green light was still far away. That was okay. He could fly now. Mama was proud.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
In the nest, Gus flapped his wings. It was time for his first flight. The sky was orange and pink. The sun was going down.

Gus looked down the street. He saw a small light on a car. It was green. It was far away. Gus wanted that light. "I want that light," he said.

His mother said, "Fly to me." But Gus looked at the light. The light was so far. He wanted it. He wanted it so much.

He tried to fly to the light. He fell on a pillow of leaves. His wings felt sticky. He could not draw them up. He was stuck.

"I want that light," he said again and again. The light did not come closer. It stayed on the car, far down the street.

Then his mother came. She sat by him. She said, "The light is far. But I am here." Gus blinked. He saw his nest. He saw his mother.

He flapped his wings. He flew up, up, up. He landed by his mother. The light was still far away. But Gus was home. He was happy.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text: I saw a baby bird named Gus on a branch. His wings felt small. The sun was going down. Then Gus saw a tiny green light on a car parked far down the street. It glowed like a little moon. "I want that light," Gus said. "I want that light." His nest was soft like a pillow. He did not want the pillow. He only wanted the light. "I want that light. I want that light." His feet were sticky on the branch. He did not draw back. He hopped. He flapped. He fell. Then he flew! He flew down the street. The wind pushed him. The light got closer. It was just a small lamp on the car. He landed on the car. He touched the light with his beak. It was warm. It was his. He sang a happy song. Then he flew back to his nest. He was tired. He was happy. The light blinked far down the street. Gus closed his eyes. He did not reach for it. He slept.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Gently, Omar watched the baby bird hop to the edge of the nest. It flapped its wings. It did not fly. It just fell into the wagon below. Omar ran to scoop it up. The bird was fine. It looked at him and blinked.

"Try again," Omar said. He put it back. The night was foggy and gloomy. The bird hopped and flapped. This time it flew two feet and landed on Omar's head. Omar laughed. "You are a hat now," he said.

The bird chirped. It flew to a branch. Then it flew to the roof. Omar clapped. Down the hall, under a door, a small green light glowed. Omar saw it once. It was pretty, like a tiny star. He wished he could hold it. But he could not. He turned back to the bird.

The bird flew into the fog. It did not come back. Omar smiled anyway.

You cannot keep every pretty thing. But you can be glad you saw it fly.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Gently, Omar found a baby bird on the grass. It was a foggy night. The bird chirped but did not fly. Omar wanted to help it.

He tried to scoop it up. The bird hopped away. It landed in his little red wagon. Omar laughed. The bird looked funny in the wagon.

Omar pulled the wagon to the porch. He waited for the bird to fly. It only peeped.

Down the hall, under a door, a green light glowed. Omar saw it. It was soft and pretty. He wanted to touch it. But the door was closed. He could not reach the light. He felt a little gloomy.

He looked back at the bird. The bird flapped its wings. Whoosh! It flew to a tree. Omar smiled big.

Omar learned that some things you want are far away. But helping someone else can make you happy.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Gently, the baby bird flapped his wings. Omar watched. The bird was small and round. Its name was Pip. Pip wanted to fly. But the sky looked big and gloomy.

"Try," said Omar. "Just a hop."

Pip hopped. He landed in the wagon. Omar laughed. That was funny. Pip looked surprised.

Then Omar saw the light. It was under a door down the hall. A soft green glow. It was so far away.

"Fly to me," said Omar. He held out his hand. Pip flapped and fell.

Omar looked at the green light again. He wanted to scoop it up. He wanted to hold it. But the door was closed. The light stayed under it.

Pip tried again. He flapped and flopped. Then he flew! A tiny hop-flight to Omar's finger.

Omar cheered. But his eyes went back to the green light. He reached for it. The door did not open.

Pip sat on Omar's hand. The bird was warm. The light was cold and far.

Sometimes we want what we cannot reach. But what we have can fly to us.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Gently, Omar watched the baby bird hop to the edge of the nest. It was time for the first flight. The fog made the night gloomy and soft. Omar pulled his red wagon close. He wanted to scoop the bird up and keep it safe. But the bird flapped once, twice, and landed in the grass. Omar laughed when it puffed up like a tiny angry pillow.

Then he saw it. A thin green light under the door down the hall. It glowed and called to him. He forgot the bird. He walked to the door. The light was so close. He reached for it. He could not touch it. The door was locked. He wanted the light. He wanted it so much. He whispered, I want the light. I want the light. The baby bird chirped behind him, lost in the fog.

Omar turned back. He picked up the bird. He put it in the wagon. The green light still pulled at him, but he pulled the wagon home.

A heart can want two things, but hands can only hold one.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Gently, Omar watched the baby bird hop to the edge of the nest. The little bird flapped and flopped. It fell into a wagon below. Omar ran to help.

Then he saw it. Under a door down the hall, a small green light glowed. It was foggy and gloomy outside. But that light was bright.

Omar forgot the bird. He walked to the door. He wanted that light. He put his hand on the door. The light stayed on the other side.

"Come back!" chirped the bird.

Omar did not turn. "I want the light," he said. "I want the light. I want the light."

He tried to scoop the light under the door. It would not come. He sat down. He said it again and again.

The fog got thick. The night got dark. The bird hopped to him and pecked his toe. It was funny, but Omar did not laugh.

"Help me fly," said the bird.

Omar looked up. The light was still there. It would always be there. He could not hold it.

He stood up and helped the bird flap its wings. Up it went into the foggy sky.

A heart that chases what it cannot hold will miss what needs it most.

stories.name: Max

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
One morning Max found a baby bird on the snow. The bird was small and round. It opened its beak. It wanted to fly.

Max made a warm nest in his hat. He drew a map on the window. The map showed the woods. He wanted to help the bird find its home.

They walked into the woods. Snow fell on their heads. The woods grew dark. Deep in the dark, Max saw a sparkly light. It was far away. It looked like a tiny star in the trees. Max wanted to touch it. But he had to dig a safe spot for the bird first.

The bird climbed on a branch. It flapped its wings. Max felt a warm spark in his chest. The bird flew to a tree. Then it flew back to Max.

You cannot hold what you love. You can only help it fly.

stories.name: Max

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
One cold morning, Max the baby bird stood at the edge of his nest. Today he would try to fly. The snow fell soft and white. His mother said, "Flap your wings, little one."

Max looked down. The ground was far away. He felt scared.

"Be brave," said his mother. She showed him a map in the snow. It had a path to a warm bush.

Max jumped. His wings went flap, flap. He did not fall! He flew over the trees. Then he saw something far off. A little light, sparkly and green, deep in the dark of the woods. It glowed like a tiny star.

He wanted to dig through the snow to find it. But the light was too far. It blinked once, then hid.

Max flew back to his mother. "I saw a pretty light," he said. She kissed his head. "Some lights are just for looking," she said.

Max learned to fly that day. And he learned that some things you want stay far away, and that is okay.

stories.name: Max

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
One morning Max found a baby bird in the snow. The bird was small and gray. It wanted to fly. Max wanted to help. But first he needed a map.

He walked into the woods. The snow made the trees white. Then he saw it. Deep in the dark, something sparkly glowed. It was a soft green light. Max took one step toward it.

"Come back," chirped the bird.

Max turned around. He tried to dig a warm spot in the snow. The bird hopped. It flapped. Then it fell.

The green light blinked between the trees. Max forgot the bird for a moment. He reached out. The light slid away.

"Come back," chirped the bird again.

Max came back. He held his hands like a nest. The bird climbed in. It flapped and flapped and flew. It flew up high.

The green light still shone far away. Max could not touch it. But he did not need to. Some lights are just for looking.

The bird was gone. Max felt warm anyway. Helping someone is better than chasing a shine you can never hold.

stories.name: Max

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
One small bird named Max sat in the nest. Today he would try to fly. His mother made a map with her wing. “Hop, then flap,” she said.

Max hopped. He flapped. He fell into soft snow. The woods were white and cold. He tried again.

Then he saw it. Deep in the dark of the woods, a sparkly light. It was small and far away. It did not look like snow. It did not look like sun.

“I want that,” Max said. He forgot the map. He forgot to flap. He walked toward the light. He tried to dig through the snow. The light stayed far.

His mother called, “Max! Come back!”

Max looked at the dark trees. He looked at the light. It pulled him like a string. He took one more step. Then he heard his mother again.

Max turned around. He hopped. He flapped. His wings caught the air. He flew to the nest.

The light still shone far away. Max did not reach it. Some wanting stays with you. But home is the thing you can hold.

stories.name: Max

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
One big hop. Max wants to fly. He is a baby bird. His wings feel small.

Snow falls on the woods. Max looks for a map. He does not find one.

Then he sees it. Deep in the dark trees. A sparkly light. It is far away.

Max hops. He wants to dig his feet in the snow. He wants to rest. But the light pulls him.

Hop. Hop. The light is still far.

Hop. Hop. The light is still far.

His wings shake. The cold bites. The light says come. Come. Come.

Max hops and hops. He does not reach it. He never reaches it.

But his wings are strong now. He lifts up. He flies a little. Then more.

The light stays far. It always stays far. That is all right.

A bird does not need to hold the light. He only needs to fly toward it.

stories.name: Mira

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
I see a baby bird named Mira. She sits in a soft nest. The morning is windy and sunny. Her mom says, "Fly, Mira." Mira looks down. She is scared. She holds a small sock in her beak. It is her lucky sock.

Mira hops to the edge. The wind goes whoosh. She flaps her wings. She wants to fly to the big tree. Then a train comes by. It goes clickety-clack. On the train, a small light glows green. Mira sees it. She wants to touch it. She jumps.

Her wings open wide. The wind lifts her up. But the train is fast. The green light gets small. It goes away. Mira tries to follow. She cannot reach it. She falls down, down.

She lands in the tall grass. Her wing hurts. She hears a knock, knock. It is her mom. Mom brings her home. Mira is safe. But she never flew again. The green light was gone forever.

stories.name: Mira

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
I see Mira in the nest. Today is the day she will fly. It is a windy morning. The sky is sunny and bright.

Mira spreads her wings. She is scared. She jumps.

She flaps and flaps. She lands on a soft sock on the line. She did it! She is so happy.

Then a train goes by. It is loud. It goes knock, knock on the track. A green light shines on the train. It is small and far away.

Mira wants to touch it. She wants it to stay.

She flies up to reach the green light. But the wind blows hard. The light moves away.

Mira tries again. She tries and tries. The green light is always far.

She is tired. Her wings hurt. She falls down to the soft sock.

The train is gone. The green light is gone. Mira is small and sad. She sits on the sock and waits. She will never catch the light.

stories.name: Mira

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
In the windy morning, Mira watched a baby bird hop to the edge of the nest. She wanted it to fly. The bird flapped its wings. It did not go.

Then a train came by. On the train, a small green light blinked. Mira saw it. She wished she could hold it. The light was far away. It went down the track.

The bird tried again. A big gust of wind came. It lifted one little sock from the line. The bird looked at the sky. Mira clapped. "Go, bird, go!"

But the bird fell. It landed on the grass with a soft knock. Mira ran to it. The bird was still. She held it close. The sunny day felt cold.

She looked up the track. The green light was gone. She wanted it. She wanted it so much. She said, "Come back. Come back." But the train was far away. The light did not come back. Mira sat down and cried.

stories.name: Mira

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
I see a baby bird named Mira in a nest. Today she will fly for the first time. The wind blows hard on this sunny morning. Mira is scared. She flaps her wings.

Then she sees it. A small green light on a train going by. The train is far away. The light is so bright. Mira wants it. She wants to fly to it.

"Wait," she chirps. "Wait for me."

Her mother says, "Fly to the tree, Mira."

But Mira looks at the light. The train moves fast. The light moves too. She cannot reach it. She flaps and flaps.

A sock blows off a line. It hits the nest with a soft knock. Mira falls out. She tries to fly to the green light. But the light is gone. The train is gone.

Mira lands on the cold ground. Her wing hurts. She looks up. The sky is empty. No green light. No train. Just wind. She wanted it so much. She never got it.

stories.name: Mira

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
I saw a baby bird named Mira. She sat in a nest. It was a windy morning. Today she would fly.

Then she saw a light. It was on a train going by. The light was small and green. It was so far away.

Mira forgot the wind. She forgot her nest. She said, "I want that light. I want that light."

Her mom said, "Fly, Mira. Fly to me."

Mira did not hear. She said, "I want that light. I want that light."

She put one sock on her wing. She did not know why. She just wanted the light.

She tried to knock the light down with her beak. It was too far. It was always too far.

The train went away. The light went away.

Mira was sad. She said, "I want that light. I want that light."

She did not fly that day. The sun was sunny and warm. But Mira just sat. She looked and looked for the light. She never saw it again.

stories.name: Pia

axes.where: in a window across the street

stories.text: A nest is a small tent for a baby bird. Pia sat in hers. She was scared to fly. Her friend Tio hopped on a branch. "You can do it," he said. Pia looked down. The ground was far away. She wanted to hide. Then she saw a light. It was in a window across the street. The light was soft and gold in the early morning. It looked warm. Pia wished she could sit in that window. But it was too far. "Try now," said Tio. Pia flapped her wings. The air felt icy on her face. She flew a little. Then a little more. The light grew small behind her. She did not reach it. She never would. But she flew to a new branch. Tio cheered. Pia was happy and sad. The window light stayed far away. Some things stay far away.

stories.name: Pia

axes.where: in a window across the street

stories.text:
A little bird named Pia lived in a tent of leaves. Today she would fly. Her friend Tio watched from a branch. "You can do it," he said. Pia hopped to the edge. Her wings felt shaky. She looked down. The ground was far.

Across the street, a window glowed. A small light sat inside. It was soft and green. Pia wanted to touch it. She wanted to hide in its warm glow.

"Fly to me," Tio called. Pia jumped. She flapped once. Twice. The air was icy on her face. She flew past the fence. Past the tree. The green light grew close.

Then a wind pushed her down. She landed hard. Her wing hurt. Tio came fast. "You flew," he said. "You really flew."

But Pia could not get up. The light in the window blinked once. Then it went out. Tio stayed beside her. The morning was quiet. Pia never reached the light. She never flew again.

stories.name: Pia

axes.where: in a window across the street

stories.text:
A baby bird named Pia sat in her tent of twigs. Today she would fly. Her friend Milo, a bold sparrow, chirped, "Jump, Pia! The wind will hold you."

Pia looked down. The ground seemed far. She saw a small light in a window across the street. It was soft and gold in the early morning. It looked warm. It looked like a place to hide. She wanted to go there.

"Don't look at that," Milo said. "Look at me." But the light pulled her. She felt icy inside. She flapped once. Twice. Then she fell.

Milo caught her wing. "Try again," he said. The light blinked. Pia tried again. She flew two feet. Then one. Then none. The light stayed in the window. It never moved closer.

Milo brought her a worm. She did not eat. She only watched the window. The sun came up. The light went out. Pia never flew to it. She never flew at all.

stories.name: Pia

axes.where: in a window across the street

stories.text:
A small bird named Pia stood at the edge of the nest. Today she would fly. Her friend Tino, a sparrow, sat beside her. "You can do it," he chirped.

Pia looked down. The ground was far. She felt shaky.

Then she saw it. Across the street, in a window, a tiny light blinked. It was soft and green. It called to her. She wanted to touch it.

"Fly to the tent," Tino said. "The one in the yard. You can hide there."

Pia tried. Her wings were new. The icy morning air pushed her back. She looked at the window again. The green light glowed. She reached for it.

"Pia, wait!" Tino called.

But Pia only saw the light. She flew toward it. Her wings grew tired. The light stayed far away.

She fell.

Tino found her under the tent. She was still. The green light kept shining in the window. It did not know her name.

stories.name: Pia

axes.where: in a window across the street

stories.text:
A baby bird named Pia stood at the edge of the nest. Today she would fly. Her friend Tio chirped, "You can do it." The morning was cold. The wind felt icy.

Then Pia saw it. A small light in a window across the street. It was soft and green. It called to her. She forgot the nest. She forgot Tio. She forgot her wings.

"Come back," Tio said. But Pia only looked at the light. She wanted to hold it. She wanted to hide inside it. She wanted to build a tent around it and stay.

She jumped. Her wings did not open. She reached for the light. She reached and reached. The light did not move. The ground did.

Tio flew down fast. He found her under the window. The light still shone above them. Pia's eyes stayed on it. "So close," she whispered. The icy morning grew warm. But Pia did not fly again.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
When the rain came, Faye the duck was glad. She shook her tail and let the water roll off her back. The pond grew wide and brown. She did a happy scoop with her bill.

Faye waddled to the tall grass. She looked for a soft place to nap. A small button lay in the mud. She nudged it with her foot. It was not food. She left it there.

The rain kept falling. The pond got too big. It pushed her away from her nest. Faye swam and swam. Her wings felt heavy.

Far away, on a tower, a little light blinked. It was pale and far. She could not fly that high. She could not walk that far.

By morning, the rain stopped. The pond was quiet and strange. Faye called for her family. No one came back. She sat alone in the wet grass. The far light blinked once more. Then it went out.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text: Wet drops fell on Faye's head. A small duck stood in the rain. She liked the rain. It made soft sounds on her back. She did a little scoop in a puddle. She found a shiny button in the mud. She put it on a leaf. Then she looked up. Far away, on a tall tower, a green light glowed. It was small and cold. She wanted to touch it. She could not. The rain got harder. The puddle got deep. Her button floated away. She watched the light. It did not move. She wanted to touch it. She wanted to touch it. The light blinked once. Then it went out. The tower was dark. Faye sat in the rain. She did not scoop the puddle again. She did not look for her button. She just sat. The rain did not stop. The light did not come back.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
Water dripped from Faye's beak. The rain came down all morning. She was a duck, and she liked rain. But today the pond was too full. Her nest was wet. Her eggs were cold. Faye had lost her bright button in the mud. She tried to scoop it up with her foot. The mud was too soft. It swallowed the button whole.

Then she saw the light. It sat on a tower far away. The light was small and green. It did not move. Faye stopped looking for her button. She looked at the light. She wanted to touch it. She wanted to hold it. She wanted it to be her button.

She walked away from her nest. She walked through the rain. The tower never got closer. The light never got bigger. She walked until her feet hurt. Then she sat down in the cold water.

The light stayed far away. Faye never reached it. Her eggs got colder. The rain did not stop.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
Water fell on the duck. Faye watched from her window. The rain made a soft drum on the roof. A duck sat in a puddle below. It did not move.

Faye held her button. It was round and white. She held it when she felt small. The duck looked small too.

Then she saw the light. It blinked on a tower far away. A tiny green dot in the gray morning. Her chest did a scoop, like a hand lifting her heart.

"Not yet," she said.

The rain got harder. The duck tucked its head. Faye leaned close to the glass. The light blinked again.

"Not yet. Not yet."

She forgot the duck. She forgot the rain. The green dot called and called.

When she looked down again, the puddle was empty. The duck was gone. Faye pressed her button to her lips. The tower light kept blinking. It was far away. It was always far away. She could not go. She could not stop looking.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
When the rain came, Faye hid under the big leaf. She was a small duck with wet feet. The pond got fat and brown. She wanted to swim. But the rain would not stop.

Then she saw it. Far away, on a tall tower, a green light. It was little and far. Faye blinked. The light stayed.

“I want it,” she said. “I want it.”

She left her leaf. The rain hit her back. She found a button in the mud. She did not stop.

“I want it. I want it.”

She tried to scoop the light with her wings. It was too far. She swam and swam. The tower grew big. The light did not move.

“I want it. I want it.”

The rain got cold. Her feet got slow. The light was just a light. She could not touch it. She could not hold it.

She sat in the soft wet grass. She put her head down. The light stayed far. The rain kept falling.

“I want it,” she said. No one heard. She closed her eyes.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Gray clouds came. Cleo the duck waddled in the rain. She liked the wet on her beak. She did not like being hungry.

Cleo walked past the bakery. She walked past the swing, swing in the wet park. She wanted a snack.

Then she saw a dark shop. A small light glowed at the back. It was green. It looked like a tiny pond in the dark. Cleo wanted it.

She pushed the door. The shop was full of rain boots. No food. Cleo looked at the green light. She could not reach it. A cat sat on a box. The cat said, "That is a lamp, silly duck."

Cleo blinked. It was just a lamp. The cat gave her a cracker. Cleo ate it. Now she was not hungry.

Just before bedtime, Cleo went home. She thought of the green light. She wanted it a little. But her warm nest was better. The rain tapped soft on the roof. Cleo slept.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Gray clouds came, and Cleo the duck waddled in the rain. She liked the wet drops on her bill. She liked the puddles that went splash.

Cleo walked past the park. The rain made the slide shine. She said, "I want to swing, swing on the swing." But the swing was too wet. She was hungry too.

Then she saw a small shop. The shop was dark. At the back of the dark shop, a little green light glowed. It was soft and far away.

Cleo wanted that light. She reached for it. The light did not come closer. It just stayed small and green.

She waited. The rain fell. She was still hungry.

Then the shop man came. He said, "Hello, duck!" He gave her bread. The small twist: the green light was only a firefly. It flew away.

Cleo ate her bread. She was happy. The rain stopped. She went home for bedtime. And the green light was gone.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Grey clouds came and the rain fell on Cleo the duck. Cleo did not mind the rain. She liked the soft drip on her back. She waddled down the street, and her feet went splash, splash.

Then she saw it. At the back of a dark shop, a small light glowed. It was green like a leaf. Cleo stopped. She wanted that light. She wanted to hold it.

She went to the window. The light was far inside. She could not reach it. She walked away, but she came back.

She sat on her old swing. She went swing, swing, swing. But she kept looking at the shop.

"I am hungry," she said. But it was not food she wanted. It was that light.

Just before bedtime, the rain stopped. Cleo went to the shop one more time. The light was still there.

Then the small twist came. The light was not a light at all. It was a green kite, stuck on a shelf. The wind made it move.

Cleo laughed. She went home. The rain came back, and she was happy.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Gray clouds came and rain fell on Cleo the duck. She swam in the puddle by her door. Splash, splash. The rain felt cold.

Then Cleo saw a green light. It was far away, at the back of a dark shop. The light was small and soft. It said, come here, come here.

Cleo waddled down the wet street. The rain got in her eyes. She did not care.

"Are you hungry?" asked a cat on a swing. The cat went swing, swing.

Cleo did not stop. She wanted the light. She wanted it so much.

The shop was dark. The light was deep inside. Cleo pushed the door. It was not a shop at all.

It was her own warm room. Mom had left a lamp on for her. The green light was her night light.

Cleo laughed. She was cold and wet. She was also very hungry. Mom gave her bread.

Cleo sat by her light. She did not reach for it. She had it all along.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Gray clouds came. Cleo the duck stood in the rain. The rain went plip, plip on her head.

Then she saw it. A green light. It was at the back of a dark shop.

Cleo wanted that light. She wanted it more than bread. She was hungry, but she did not care.

She went to the shop. The door was shut. She pushed. The door did not move.

She went to the window. The light was so far. She could not touch it.

"Light," said Cleo. "Light, light."

The rain came down. The light did not move.

Cleo saw a swing. She sat on the swing. She went swing, swing, swing.

The light stayed far away. Cleo was hungry. Cleo was wet.

She said, "Light, light, light."

Then the shop man came out. He had a lamp. The lamp was green. He put it on a box.

Cleo ran to it. She put her bill on it. The light was warm.

But it was not her light. The light inside the shop was still far away.

Cleo sat in the rain. She looked at the light. She said, "Light, light, light."

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: across a big field
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Fuzzy and wet, Leo the duck stood in the rain. The drops went plip plip on his head. He did not like the rain. He wanted to go home. But the rain came down more and more.

Leo had a map. The map was wet too. He did not know where to go. He sat under a big leaf. The leaf went drip drip.

He saw a small green light far away. It was across a big field. The light was soft and warm. Leo looked at it. Then he looked away.

He was too busy being wet and cold. He rolled in the mud to stay warm. The mud went squish. That was fun.

Then the rain stopped. Leo shook his tail. He felt happy.

A small boy came. The boy said, "Leo, you are not lost. This is our field!" Leo had been home all along.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: across a big field
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Fog hung low, and Leo the duck stood in the cold rain. He wanted to find his way home. The rain made his feathers wet. He had a map, but the paper got soft and blurry.

Leo waddled past a busy road. Cars went whoosh. He did not like the rain. He wanted his warm nest.

Then Leo saw a small light across a big field. A green light. It glowed soft in the cold autumn evening. Leo looked at it. That light looked warm. He wanted to roll in it. He wanted to be near it.

But the field was far. Leo walked and walked. The green light stayed far away. It did not come closer.

Leo sat down in the wet grass. He felt sad. Then he heard a splash. His mother duck came out of the tall weeds. She had been looking for him.

Leo laughed. The green light was just a lamp on a porch. Home was here all along.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: across a big field
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Fog sat on the pond like a cold gray blanket. Leo the duck paddled in the rain. Drip, drip, drip went the water on his back. It was a cold autumn evening.

Leo kept a little map inside his head. Home was a warm log by the water. He was busy finding the way. Splash, splash. He did a little roll in the mud. That was fun.

Then Leo saw it. A small green light, far across a big field. It shone and shone. Leo wanted it. He wanted it so much.

"Wait for me," said Leo. He waddled out of the pond. The rain made the field soft and brown.

"I want the light," said Leo. "I want it."

The light did not come closer. Leo walked and walked. His feet were cold.

Then the rain stopped. The light moved. It was not a light at all. It was a firefly!

Leo blinked. He laughed a small duck laugh. He turned around and went home to his warm log.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: across a big field
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Fog hung over the pond, and Leo the duck splashed in the rain. The drops were cold on his back. Fall was here, and the evening felt gray.

Then he saw it. Across the big field, past the fence, a green light glowed. It was tiny and far. Leo stopped splashing.

He looked at his wet map. The map showed the pond, the field, the fence. It did not show the light.

Leo wanted that light. He wanted it more than worms. He waddled to the fence. His feet were cold. The light stayed far away.

"Too far," he quacked. "Too far."

The rain got harder. Leo did not roll in the mud like other ducks. He just looked at the light. "I want it," he said. "I want it."

A busy squirrel ran by. "That light?" she said. "That is the moon in a puddle. You can never hold it."

Leo blinked. The green light was just the moon, spilled on the wet grass. He turned back to his pond. The rain felt warm now. He splashed, and he was happy.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: across a big field
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Fog sat on the pond. Leo was a duck. He liked the rain. The rain went tap tap on his back. It was a cold autumn evening.

Then Leo saw it. A small light. It was green. It was across a big field.

"I want the light," said Leo.

He did not want the rain. He did not want the pond. He wanted the light.

"I want the light. I want the light."

His mother gave him a map. "The field is busy," she said.

Leo did not look at the map. He did not roll in the mud. He only looked at the light.

"I want the light. I want the light."

He swam to the field. He walked and walked. The rain got cold. The light did not get close.

Then Leo looked down. The light was not across the field. It was a puddle. The puddle had a green leaf in it. The light was just the leaf.

"Oh," said Leo. He sat in the rain. The rain went tap tap. He was happy.

stories.name: Sid

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Clouds filled the sky. Sid the duck waddled by the pond. Then the rain came down. Plip, plop, plip. Sid did a happy shake. He liked the rain on his back.

"Come home, Sid!" called his mom.

But Sid did not go home. He swam in the pond. He ate a little bug. The rain made soft rings on the water.

The sun came out low. The rain got light. Sid saw a small light at the very top of a tall tree. It was green and pretty. He wished he could have it. But ducks cannot climb trees. So he just looked.

"Whistle with me," said a robin.

Sid tried to whistle. A duck cannot whistle. He felt shy. The rain stopped. The green light blinked once, then went out.

Then the twist came. It was not a light at all. It was just a leaf, wet and shiny from the rain. Sid laughed. The rain had tricked him.

He went home for a warm nap.

stories.name: Sid

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Clouds made the sky soft and gray. Sid was a duck. Sid liked the rain. Plip, plop, plip. Rain fell on his head. He did a happy shake. He waddled to the pond to swim.

Then Sid saw it. High up, at the very top of a tall tree, a small light shone. It was green like a leaf. The sun was going down. Sunset made the sky pink and gold. The green light blinked. Sid gave a soft whistle. He wanted to touch it.

"Too high," said Sid. He was a duck, not a bird with strong wings.

The rain came down more. Sid was a shy duck. He swam in small circles. He looked up at the light again and again.

Then the wind blew. The green light moved. It was not a light. It was a firefly!

The firefly flew down. It sat by Sid on the pond. It glowed just for him. Sid did not need to reach it.

Sid smiled. The rain was warm. The firefly stayed.

stories.name: Sid

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Clouds came and the rain came down. Sid the duck did not mind. Rain was good. Rain made puddles. Sid swam in the puddles and went quack, quack.

Then the sun went low. The sky turned soft and red. All at once, Sid saw a light. It sat at the very top of a tall tree. The light was small and green. It did not blink. It did not move.

Sid stopped. He looked up. He wanted that light. "Little light," he said. "Come here."

But the light stayed high in the tree. Sid shook his wet wings. He tried to whistle. Only a small puff came out. He was shy, but he still tried. "Please come down," he said.

The rain stopped. The green light stayed far away. Sid reached his neck up. He could not reach it. He could not have it.

Then his mother called him home. Sid turned to go. He saw the green light was only one drop of rain on one high leaf, catching the last sun. He went home anyway.

stories.name: Sid

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
