features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Clouds filled the sky. Sid the duck waddled in the rain. He liked the wet grass. He liked the splash on his feet. Then he saw it. A small green light sat at the very top of a tall tree. The sun was going down. The light shone bright.

Sid stopped. He forgot the rain. "I want that light," he said. He tried to fly up. He could not reach. He tried to whistle for help. No one came. He gave a shake of his tail. He felt shy and small.

The rain fell more. Sid kept looking up. "I want that light. I want that light," he said again and again. He did not see the puddle. He did not see his mom.

Then the light blinked. It was not a light at all. It was a firefly! The firefly flew down. It landed on Sid's head. Sid laughed. The rain felt warm.

stories.name: Sid

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Came the rain, and Sid the duck did not mind. He sat in his little puddle and let the drops tap his back. Rain was soft. Rain was good. Then the sun went low.

Sid saw the light. It was green. It sat at the very top of a tall tree.

Sid wanted it. He wanted the light.

“I want it,” said Sid. “I want it. I want it.”

He did a whistle. He did a shake. He was not shy. He swam to the tree. He looked up. The light was so high.

“I want it,” said Sid. “I want it. I want it.”

He tried to fly. He got a little up. Then he fell in the mud.

He tried again. He tried and tried. The light did not move. The light did not come down.

“I want it,” said Sid. “I want it.”

Then the twist came. The light blinked. The light was not a light at all. It was a firefly, and it flew away.

Sid sat in the rain. The rain was soft. The rain was good.

stories.name: Joon

axes.where: on a train going by
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
The rain came down on Joon. He was a small duck. He sat under a big leaf. The rain went drip, drip, drip on his head.

Joon did not like rain. It made the pond cold. It made his feet wet. He wanted the sun. He wanted to sit on a warm rock.

He found a stick. He held it up like a little roof. The rain did bounce off it. He felt brave.

Then the rain got soft. It got quiet. It turned to snow. White flakes fell on Joon. The pond got still.

A train went by. It was far away. One window had a warm light. Joon saw it. The light was small and yellow. It made him think of a dry place. Then the train was gone.

Joon did not need the light. He had his stick. He had his leaf. He had soft snow on his back. He was not cold. He was fine. The twist was that the rain had turned to snow, and the snow was soft. He liked the snow. He liked the rain too. He went to sleep.

stories.name: Joon

axes.where: on a train going by
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
The duck was named Joon. Joon lived by the cold pond. The pond was white with snow. Joon liked to look for food.

One day a train came by. It went click-clack on the track. Joon saw a bright light on the train. It was green and small. It made Joon feel warm. Then it was gone.

Joon did not like the snow. He wanted to be brave. He found a little stick. He did not bounce. He just held it.

The train came again. Joon saw the green light. He tried to reach it. His feet slipped. He was sad.

Then he saw something strange. His stick was a fish. It was a frozen fish. Joon ate it. He felt happy.

The train went far away. The green light got tiny. Joon looked at the pond. The snow did not feel so cold.

But sometimes, when the train comes, Joon looks up. He sees the small green light. He cannot go there. He does not know why he wants it. He just does. He stays by his pond.

stories.name: Joon

axes.where: on a train going by
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
The duck sat in the rain. Joon watched him from the window. The duck did not move. Water ran off his back. Joon wanted to help.

Then the train came. It went by slow. Joon saw a small light inside. It was green and soft. It made him feel warm. He wanted to touch it. He wanted to hold it. The train went away. The light went away too.

Joon found a stick. He poked it out the door. The duck did not bounce. The duck did not run. He was brave. He just sat.

Joon thought of the green light. He thought of it all day. He thought of it when the snow came. The snow fell soft. The duck stayed in the rain.

Then Joon saw something. The duck had a baby. The baby was under his wing. The duck was not stuck. He was hiding her.

Joon felt silly. The light in the train was not for him. But the duck was.

stories.name: Joon

axes.where: on a train going by
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
The rain came down. Joon the duck sat under a big leaf. He did not like wet feet. He wanted to go home. Splash, splash went the drops. He held a little stick. It did not help much.

Then Joon saw a train. The train was far away. It went through the snow. One light glowed on the back. It was small and green. Joon wanted that light. “I want it,” he said. “I want it.” He said it again. “I want it.” The rain did not matter now. The snow did not matter. Only the green light.

Joon ran to the tracks. His feet went bounce, bounce, bounce. He tried to be brave. The train was gone. The light was gone too.

Joon sat down. He felt sad. Then he looked up. The light was not on the train. It was in the sky. It was a star. It blinked at him. Joon smiled. He waddled home.

stories.name: Joon

axes.where: on a train going by
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
The rain came down on Joon. Joon was a duck. He sat in his puddle. He liked the rain. It went drip, drip on his head.

Then a train went by. It was a snowy day, but Joon did not care. On the train, a little light was on. It was warm and yellow. It was far away.

Joon wanted that light. He wanted it so much. He said, "I want that light. I want that light." He said it again and again.

He did not see the rain. He did not see the snow. He only saw the light. It went away with the train. Joon was sad.

He found a stick. He did not bounce. He was not brave. He just sat.

Then the train came back. It went the other way. The light was on the other side. It was still warm. It was still far.

Joon stood up. He shook his tail. He said, "I want that light." But then he looked down.

His puddle was full of tiny lights. The snow made them. They were right there. They were his.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text: Mia helped Finn make a rainstick. They pushed tiny nails into a long tube. Then they poured in rice and beans. Finn shook it. It went shhh, shhh, shhh. "That is not noisy enough," said Finn. So they added a dry leaf and three buttons. The rainstick went clack, shhh, rattle. It sounded like a storm in a sock. They laughed so hard that Finn dropped it. Beans rolled everywhere. "We can fix it," said Mia. They taped the tube and shook it again. Now it went thump, shhh, clack. Finn loved it. He shook it all afternoon. Then he went down the hall for a snack. A thin glow lay under the door at the end. It was warm and soft, like a small sun sleeping there. Finn stood still. He wished he could hold that light. He shook his rainstick once. The sound filled the hall. The light stayed under the door. Finn smiled and went to get his snack.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Mama gave Finn a rainstick. It was long and brown. Small seeds slid inside it. Finn turned it over. The sound was soft, like rain on a leaf.

Finn shook it hard. The rainstick got noisy. His baby sister cried. Finn laughed. That was funny. He shook it again.

He tried to fix the little cap on top. It would not stay. Mama said, "Leave it, Finn."

Then Finn saw something under his door. A thin line of light. It came from down the hall. It was warm and gold. It did not move.

Finn wanted to touch it. He crawled to the door. He put his hand on the floor. The light was just there. He could not hold it.

He went back to his rainstick. He turned it slow. Rain sound. He looked at the door again. The gold line was still there.

His sister slept. The afternoon was sunny. Finn sat by the door. He shook the stick. He watched the light. He wished it would come in.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Mia gave Finn a rainstick. It was long and brown. Finn turned it over. Little seeds slid down inside. They made a soft, shushing sound. Finn shook it hard. The sound got noisy and wild. He laughed and shook it more.

Then he saw the light. It came from under a door down the hall. A thin line of gold on the floor. The sun was high outside, but this light was different. It was small and green. Finn stopped shaking the rainstick. He walked to the door. The light did not move.

He put his eye to the crack. He saw nothing. Just the light, like a tiny leaf floating on a pond. He wanted to touch it. He could not.

He tried to fix the rainstick later. A seed got stuck. He shook it, but the sound was flat. He did not care. He kept looking down the hall. The green light was still there. It was always there. He turned the rainstick over. Shush, shush. He thought of the light. Shush, shush.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Mia gave Finn a rainstick made from a dry branch. He turned it slow. The beads inside went shhh, like rain on a leaf. Finn shook it fast. It got noisy. He laughed and shook it more.

Then he saw it. A thin line of light under the door down the hall. It was small and green and far away.

Finn put the rainstick down. He walked to the hall. The door was shut. He peeked under. The light did not move.

He ran back and got the rainstick. Maybe the light liked rain. He shook it soft. Shhh. He shook it loud. Shhh. The light stayed small and green.

Finn tried to fix the door. He pushed. He pulled. It would not open. His dad walked by and slipped on the rainstick. His feet went up. He sat down hard. Finn laughed so much he snorted.

But then Finn looked under the door again. The green light was still there. He wanted it. He wanted it. He wanted it.

He sat by the door all afternoon. He held the rainstick. He did not shake it. He just watched the light and wanted.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Mia gave Finn a rainstick. It was long and brown. Finn turned it over. Little beads fell inside. Shhh, shhh, shhh. It sounded like rain.

Then Finn saw a leaf on the floor. It came from under a door down the hall. A thin light lay there too. It was small and green, like a leaf that never fell. Finn wanted to touch it.

He put down the rainstick. He forgot the rain. He walked to the door. The light stayed under it, just a crack away. "I want to hold you," Finn said. He said it again. "I want to hold you."

His mom called, "Time to fix your noisy toy!" But Finn did not turn around. The light was still there. Still small. Still green. He lay on his belly. He reached one finger out. The light did not move.

"I want to hold you," he said. "I want to hold you." The sunny afternoon got long. The rainstick rolled away, quiet. Finn stayed by the door, wanting the little green light he could never reach.

stories.name: Sid

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
Bend the rainstick, Sid. That is what his grandpa said. Sid held the long stick. It was full of tiny seeds. He turned it slow. Shhh, shhh, went the seeds. Like soft rain.

Sid went outside. The evening was cold. Autumn leaves fell down. He wore one boot. He lost the other one somewhere. He did not care.

He walked to the stream. The water was dark and quiet. He wanted to scoop up water in his hands. Then he saw a light. It was small and far away. It lived in the reeds. It was a tiny green gleam. It did not come closer.

"Come here," Sid said. The light stayed. He reached out. His fingers felt only cold reeds. The light was pretty. But he could not hold it. He felt a little sad.

Then he heard a sound. Shhh, shhh. The rainstick in his hand. He shook it again. The seeds fell inside like rain. Sid smiled. He did not need to catch the light.

He walked home. His other boot waited by the door. His grandpa was happy. "You found your stick," he said. Sid nodded. The light stayed by the stream. That was okay.

stories.name: Sid

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
Before bed, Sid shook his rainstick. It sounded like soft rain. He loved that sound.

Sid pulled on his boot. He went outside. The air was cold. It was a late autumn evening.

He walked to the stream. The reeds moved in the wind. He held his rainstick tight.

Then he saw it. A small light in the reeds. It was far away. It was a soft glow. It looked like a tiny star.

Sid wanted to touch it. He took a step. The light stayed far.

"Come here," Sid said.

The light did not come.

Sid tried to scoop the light with his hands. It slipped away. His hands were cold.

He tried again. The light moved. It went deeper into the reeds.

Sid felt sad. But then he heard a sound. It was his rainstick. The beads inside went tic, tic, tic.

He shook it. The sound was warm. It was like rain on a roof.

Sid smiled. He did not need to catch the light. He had his own small song.

He walked home. His heart felt happy.

stories.name: Sid

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
Boom, boom, said the rainstick. Sid shook it. The beads fell down inside. They made a soft, shushing sound.

Sid sat by the window. A cold autumn evening came on. He put on his boot. He wanted to hear the stream.

Down by the water, the reeds moved. Something small shone there. Sid bent to scoop it up. But it was not a stone. It was a light. It was weak and far away.

“Do you see it?” said Sid.

His mother looked. “See what?”

The light was gone. Only the reeds were left.

Sid went back inside. He shook the rainstick. Boom, boom. The light came back in his mind. It was still in the reeds. It was always in the reeds.

“I want to reach it,” Sid said.

“Maybe tomorrow,” said his mother.

The next evening, Sid went out again. The reeds were dark. But the small light blinked once. Then twice. Sid did not grab it. He just sat and watched. He felt happy. The rainstick hummed in his hand. Boom, boom.

stories.name: Sid

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
Before bed, Sid shook his rainstick. It sounded like soft rain. But his sock was wet. His one boot was lost.

“Where is it?” said Sid.

“By the stream,” said Mom.

Sid went out. The cold autumn evening bit his nose. He walked to the stream. Dry reeds stood there. Something small shone inside them. A little light. Not big. Not loud. Just a glow.

Sid took a scoop of reeds. No boot. The light slid away. He followed it. It went behind a stone. It went under a leaf.

“Come back,” said Sid.

The light did not come back. It only stayed. Always far. Always small.

He forgot his boot. He forgot the cold. He reached and reached.

Then Mom called, “Sid! Look!”

His boot was right there. In the mud. A heron had stepped on it. Sid pulled it on. He laughed.

He looked once more at the reeds. The light was still there. Small and far.

“Goodnight,” said Sid.

He went home happy. The rainstick sang him to sleep.

stories.name: Sid

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
Before bed, Sid shook the rainstick. It made a soft, shushing sound. He liked that sound. But then he saw the light.

It was far off, in the reeds by the stream. A small, green glow. Cold wind blew. Sid pulled on one boot. "Where are you going?" his mom asked. "To see," Sid said.

He ran to the stream. The light danced in the reeds. He tried to scoop it up with his hands. It slipped away. He tried again. It was always just ahead. "Come back," he whispered. The light said nothing.

He reached and reached. The cold made his fingers ache. He forgot his other boot. He forgot the warm house. He forgot the happy sound of the rainstick.

Then his mom was there. She put her coat around him. "Some lights are just for looking," she said.

She walked him home. Inside, she gave him the rainstick. He shook it. Shush, shush, shush. He smiled. The little light stayed in the reeds. But Sid was warm. And that was enough.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: at the end of a long road

stories.text:
Maybe the rainstick was broken. Omar shook it and shook it. The beads inside did not sound like rain. They sounded like a rock in a can.

Omar sat by the window. The sky was gray. A storm came. Rain hit the glass. The rain sounded soft and good. His rainstick did not.

He put on his coat. He wanted to find a better stick. He walked past the big tree. He did not carry an umbrella. The rain made him cold.

The road was long. At the end of the road, far away, a small light was on. It was not green like grass. It was just a porch light, yellow and warm.

Omar walked and walked. His feet got tired. The light did not get closer. He went home.

The rainstick still sounded wrong. Omar set it on the shelf. He did not shake it again.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: at the end of a long road

stories.text:
Maya gave Omar a rainstick. It was long and brown, made from a dead tree branch. "Turn it slow," she said. "Then you hear the rain."

Omar turned it slow. The little seeds fell inside. Shhh, shhh, shhh. It sounded like rain on the roof. But the sky was gray and the wind was big. Rain hit the window hard.

Omar held the rainstick close. He wanted to carry it everywhere. The room felt cold. He turned it again. Shhh, shhh, shhh.

Then he saw it. Far down the long road, past the wet houses, a tiny green light blinked. It was small and far away. It looked warm. It looked like a place where no one was cold.

Omar ran to the window. The rain got on his face. The green light stayed far. He turned the rainstick fast. Shhh-shhh-shhh. Still the light did not come close.

Maya called him for dinner. He did not go. He held the rainstick and watched the road. The rain got louder. The green light got smaller. Then the storm took it away.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: at the end of a long road

stories.text:
Maya gave Omar a rainstick made from a dry tree branch. She said it came from a far place. Omar turned it slow. Little seeds fell inside and made a soft sound like rain. He loved that sound.

That stormy afternoon, the sky turned dark. Wind pushed the leaves. Omar held the rainstick close so it would not get cold. He wanted to carry it everywhere.

Then he saw it. Far down the long road, past the last house, a small light shone. It was not red. It was not blue. It was a soft, soft green, like a leaf with sun inside.

Omar walked to the road. The rain hit his face. The green light stayed far away. He shook the rainstick. It whispered. The light did not come closer.

He walked and walked. His feet got tired. The road got longer. The green light just sat there, small and far, like it was waiting for someone else.

Omar sat down in the wet grass. He shook the rainstick one more time. The sound was small. The green light did not move. He held the stick and cried, because he knew he could not reach it, not today, not ever.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: at the end of a long road

stories.text:
Max made a rainstick with Omar. They put small rocks inside a long tube. They shook it. It made a soft sound, like rain.

Omar liked the rainstick. He held it near his ear. Shake, shake, shake.

Then Omar saw something far away. At the end of the long road, a little green light was glowing.

"What is that?" Omar asked.

"Just a light," Max said.

Omar shook the rainstick again. But he kept looking down the road. The light blinked in the storm.

He walked to the window. Cold rain hit the glass. He saw a tree bend in the wind.

"I want to go there," Omar said.

"It is too far," said Max.

Omar did not listen. He put on his coat. He tried to carry the rainstick with him. But the wind pushed him back.

He looked at the light. He wanted it. He wanted it. He wanted it.

The rain got louder. The light did not come closer.

Omar sat down on the floor. He shook the rainstick once. It sounded like rain that never stops.

He never reached the light.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: at the end of a long road

stories.text:
Momo helped Omar make a rainstick. They put small rocks inside a long tube. Omar turned it over. It sounded like soft rain. The storm came. Rain hit the window. Wind shook the old tree. Omar held the rainstick close.

Then he saw it. Far away, at the end of the long road, a little green light was glowing. It was small and bright in the storm. Omar wanted to go to it. He had to carry the rainstick. The road was long and cold.

He walked and walked. The light stayed far away. It never got closer.

"Come here, light," said Omar. "Come here, light."

The rain got harder. The cold wind pushed him back. The light was so small. So far.

He held up the rainstick for the light to see. The rocks did not move. His hands were too cold.

He sat down on the wet road. The tree was far behind him. The light was still far ahead. It stayed green and small and never came near.

Omar held the rainstick and cried.

stories.name: Milo

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
The rainstick made a soft shhh sound. Milo turned it over. Tiny seeds slid down inside. Shhh, shhh, shhh. It sounded like rain.

Milo took his rainstick outside. He wanted to show his mom. He ran across the grass. He did a happy kick. Then he fell down. His cup rolled away. "Oops," said Milo. He laughed. That was funny.

The sky turned orange. The sun went low. Milo sat in the grass. He looked across a big field. Far away, a tiny light blinked. It was small and green. It looked like a little leaf.

Milo wanted to touch it. He stood up. He walked and walked. The light stayed far away. His feet got tired.

A giant dog ran by. It licked his face. "Stop!" said Milo. He giggled.

He looked for the light again. It was gone. Only the sunset was there.

Milo went home. He shook his rainstick. Shhh, shhh, shhh. It sounded like rain. That was enough.

stories.name: Milo

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
The rainstick made a soft sound. Milo turned it over. Little beads fell inside. Ting, ting, ting. It sounded like rain.

Milo sat on the porch. The sun went down. Across a big field, a tiny light blinked. It was small and green. Milo wanted to hold it.

He took his cup and drank some juice. He gave the rainstick a little kick. It rolled away. "Come back!" said Milo. The rainstick did not come back. A giant dog picked it up. The dog ran in circles. It was very funny. Milo laughed and laughed.

Then he looked at the field again. The small light was still there. It blinked and blinked. Milo stood up. He took one step.

The dog brought the rainstick back. It was wet and slobbery. Milo wiped it on his shirt. He shook it. Ting, ting, ting.

The light blinked far away. Milo held the rainstick close. He did not go. He sat down again. The light stayed across the field, small and green. Milo watched it until the sky turned dark.

stories.name: Milo

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
The rainstick made a soft sound. Milo turned it over and over. Tip, tap, tip, tap. It sounded like rain. Milo liked rain.

He sat on the porch. The sun went down. The sky turned pink and orange. Milo held his cup of milk. He did not drink it.

Across the big field, a little light blinked. It was green and small. It sat far away by the trees. Milo stood up. He wanted to go to it.

He took one step. Then he stopped. He gave the rainstick a kick with his toe. "Ouch!" he said. That was silly. The rainstick did not kick back. He laughed at himself.

He looked at the light again. It blinked and blinked. It seemed to say, come here. Milo took his cup and walked to the edge of the field. The grass was tall. A giant hill stood in the way.

Tip, tap, tip, tap. The rainstick sang in his hand. The little light stayed far away. Milo watched it until the sky went dark. Then he went inside. He still wanted it.

stories.name: Milo

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
The rainstick made a soft sound when Milo turned it. Tip, tap, tip. It sounded like tiny rain inside a stick. Milo liked it a lot.

Then he looked out the window. Across a big field, far away, a little green light was shining. It was sunset. The sky was pink and gold.

Milo wanted that light. He did not want the rainstick now. He put it in a cup and ran outside. He tried to kick a giant rock out of his way. “Ouch!” he said. The rock did not move. His foot did. That was funny.

He walked and walked. The light stayed far away. It blinked like a small star on the ground.

Tip, tap, tip. The rainstick was back in his hand somehow. He shook it. Then he looked up. The light was still there. Always there.

“I will get you,” Milo said. But his feet were tired. The light just smiled and stayed far.

stories.name: Milo

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
The rainstick made a soft sound. Milo held it up. It went shhh, like sand.

Then he saw the light. It was far away, across a big field. A little green light. It blinked once.

Milo put down the rainstick. He took one step. He took two steps.

The light was so small. It was so far. It was across the big field.

Milo ran. He did not look at his cup. He did not look at the giant tree. He tried to kick a rock, but he tripped. He fell in the grass. That was funny. He laughed. Then he got up.

He looked for the light. There it was. Still far. Still small. Still green.

Milo reached out his hand. He could not touch it.

He whispered, come here. Come here. Come here.

The sun went down. The light did not come. Milo stood in the dark. He wanted the light. He wanted it so much.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: at the top of the stairs
features: a small twist near the end
a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Little grains slid down inside Nate’s rainstick. Tip, tap, tip. He turned it slow. The sound was like soft rain.

Nate shook it again. Nothing came out. A grain was stuck.

He sat on the floor. His candle made a small warm glow. He tapped the rainstick on his knee. Still stuck.

“I can fix it,” Nate said.

He blew into the top. A tiny grain popped loose. Tip, tap, tip. The rain came back.

Nate smiled. He had a curly piece of yarn. He tied it to the rainstick so he would not lose it.

Then he went to bed. He climbed the stairs. At the top of the stairs, a small light shone. It was green.

Nate stopped. He wanted to touch it. He reached out his hand. The light was far away. It was always far away.

He pulled his hand back. He held his rainstick close. Tip, tap, tip.

He did not run to the light. He went to his room. The rain sound followed him.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: at the top of the stairs
features: a small twist near the end
a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Little grains slid down inside Nate’s rainstick. Tip, tap, tip. He held it to his ear. The sound was like soft rain.

On a cold autumn evening, Nate sat by his candle. His hair was curly and warm from his hat. He shook the rainstick again. Tip, tap.

Then he heard a tiny rattle. A bead had stuck near the top. The rain sound stopped. Nate frowned.

“I can fix it,” he said.

He did not run. He walked slowly. He turned the rainstick over. He tapped it once.

A green light glowed at the top of the stairs. It was small and far away. Nate looked at it. He wanted to climb up and touch it.

But he stayed. He tapped the rainstick again.

The bead fell. Tip, tap, tip. The rain came back.

Nate smiled. The green light was still there. He did not go to it. He did not need to. He had his rain.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: at the top of the stairs
features: a small twist near the end
a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Little Nate shook his rainstick. The beads inside went shhh, shhh, like soft rain. He liked that sound a lot.

On a cold autumn evening, he sat by his candle. Its flame was small and warm. He turned the rainstick over. Shhh, shhh.

Then he saw it. At the top of the stairs, a green light glowed. It was tiny and bright. Nate wanted to touch it.

He stood up. He began to run. But his feet got tangled in his curly blanket. Down he went. Bump.

His rainstick rolled away. The little problem was his hurt knee. The big problem was the light. It stayed at the top of the stairs. It would not come down.

Nate rubbed his knee. He looked up again. The light was still there. He reached for it. His hand found only cold air.

He sighed. He picked up his rainstick. Shhh, shhh.

Then the twist came. The green light was just the moon, peeking through the window. Nate could not touch the moon. But he could hear his rain. Shhh, shhh. That was enough for tonight.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: at the top of the stairs
features: a small twist near the end
a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Late in the day, Nate found a rainstick. It was long and brown. Tiny seeds slid inside it. They made a soft sound. Like rain on a roof.

Nate shook it. The sound was warm. He held it close. Then he saw the light.

It sat at the top of the stairs. Small and green. It glowed on the wall. Nate wanted it.

He walked up one step. The rainstick slipped. It fell down the stairs. Seeds spilled out. Nate ran to pick them up.

The light stayed up there. Green and far. Nate reached for it. He could not touch it. He wanted it. He wanted it. He wanted it.

The cold evening made him shiver. A candle burned on a shelf. Its flame was curly and small. Nate looked at the candle. Then he looked at the light.

He put the seeds back in the rainstick. He shook it once. The rain sound came back. He smiled a little.

The green light was just the clock on the wall.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: at the top of the stairs
features: a small twist near the end
a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Late in the day, Nate shook his rainstick. The beads fell soft like rain. He liked that sound. He had a little problem. The rainstick was stuck. No beads fell. So Nate sat by his candle. Its flame was small.

Then he saw it. At the top of the stairs, a small light glowed. It was green. Nate wanted it. He wanted to run up and hold it. He reached out. His hand felt cold air.

"Come here," he said. "Come here." He said it again. "Come here. Come here."

He forgot the rainstick. He forgot the candle. He only saw the green light. His hair, once curly, felt flat and cold. The light did not move. It did not come.

Then Nate heard a tiny tap. He looked down. One bead fell. Then more. The rainstick was not stuck. It just needed a tip. Nate tipped it. The rain came back. He smiled.

The green light stayed at the top of the stairs. Nate did not go. He held his rainstick and let it sing.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text:
When Nate woke up, he wanted to see the seal and the sailboat. He ran to the dock with his map. The sun was just up.

Nate saw the little sailboat. It rocked on the water. He looked for the seal. The seal liked to hide.

Then Nate saw a small green light. It was in the window of an old house. The light was far away. It was pretty. Nate looked at it for a while. Then he looked back at the water.

The seal popped up! It had a round head and big eyes. Nate laughed. The sailboat moved slow. The seal swam by it.

Nate sat on the dock. The morning was soft and warm. He was so happy. The green light blinked once more. But Nate did not need it. He had his seal and his sailboat. That was enough.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text:
When Nate woke up, the sun was not up yet. Today he would sail his little boat. He had a map in his pocket. The map showed the way to the bay.

Nate rowed past a rock. A seal popped up. "Hello, seal," Nate said. The seal did not hide. It swam by the boat.

Then Nate saw a light. It was in the window of an old house. A small green light. It blinked in the early morning.

Nate wanted that light. He rowed toward it. But the house was far away. The seal pulled the boat back. The light stayed small in the window.

Nate looked at his map again. He found the bay. He did not get the light. But he was happy. The seal was his friend. They sailed home together in the sun.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text: When Nate woke up, he wanted to see a seal and a sailboat. He took his map to the beach. The sky was pink and soft. A sailboat rocked on the water. Nate looked for a seal. He did not see one yet. Then he saw a small green light. It was in the window of an old house. The light was far away. It was bright and calm. Nate wanted to touch it. He walked toward the house. The light stayed in the window. It did not come to him. He stood on his toes. He could not reach it. He felt sad. Then the sailboat came close. A seal popped up its head! Nate laughed. He did not hide his smile. The seal swam by the boat. Nate was happy. The green light blinked once more. Nate waved to it. Then he went home with his map. He was glad.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text:
When Nate woke up, he saw a seal on the rocks. The seal was gray and shiny. Nate loved the seal. He took his map and ran to the shore.

Then Nate saw the green light. It was in the window of an old house. The light was small and bright. Nate wanted to touch it. He forgot the seal.

The seal swam away. Nate did not see. He only saw the green light. He walked toward the old house. The light called him. He said, "Come here, light. Come here."

Nate tried to hide from the light. But he could not. The light was always there. He said, "I want you, light. I want you."

Then the sun came up. The green light went out. Nate was sad. But then he heard a splash. The seal came back! Nate was happy. He sat with the seal. The green light was gone. But Nate did not need it. He had his friend.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: in the window of an old house

stories.text: When Nate was a seal, he liked the sailboat. Every early morning he swam to it. The sail was soft and white. The boat was his friend. Then Nate saw the light. The light was in the window of an old house. It was small and green. It was far away. Nate did not want the sailboat. He wanted the light. He looked at the map. It did not help. He tried to hide. The light found him. He swam and swam. He could not reach it. The light was always far. He looked at the light. He wanted the light. He wanted it so much. He forgot the sailboat. He forgot the map. He forgot to hide. The light was far. The light was green. He wanted it. He wanted it. The light was far. Then the sun came up. The light went away. The sailboat came back. Nate was happy.

stories.name: June

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Next to the sea, June had a small sailboat. She sailed it on sunny afternoons. The wind pushed the white sail. June felt happy.

One day she walked in the woods. The trees were tall. She found a little ladder on a tree. She climbed up to rest. Her hands were sticky from pine.

Then she saw it. Deep in the dark of the woods, a small green light. It blinked like a firefly. June wanted to touch it.

"Come here," she said. The light did not move.

"Please?" she said. The light stayed far away.

June climbed down. She went back to her sailboat. The sun was warm. The water was blue.

She did not tell anyone about the light. But sometimes, when she sailed, she looked at the woods. She thought of the small green blink. Then she pulled the sail, and went home.

stories.name: June

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Near the water, June saw a seal. The seal sat on a rock. A sailboat went by. It had a big white sail.

"Look," said June. "A boat."

The seal did not look. The seal looked at June.

June had a sticky bun in her hand. She did not eat it. She gave it to the seal. The seal ate it fast.

"Good," said June. "Now we rest."

They walked to the woods. The woods were dark. June saw a small light. It was green. It was far away. It was between the trees.

"What is that?" said June.

The seal did not know. June took one step. Then two. The light did not come close.

"I want to touch it," said June.

She found a ladder on a tree. She did not climb. She was too small.

The seal pulled her hand.

"Okay," said June. "We go."

They went back to the rock. The sailboat was far now. The green light was gone.

June sat down. The sun was warm. The seal put its head on her lap.

"Tomorrow," said June. "Maybe tomorrow."

stories.name: June

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
No one knew why June loved the sailboat so much. Every sunny afternoon she sat on the dock and watched it slide across the bay. The white sail looked like a big wing. She wished she could ride it.

"Can we go?" June asked her dad.

"Not today," he said. "Maybe soon."

June swam out as a seal. She barked at the boat. It did not stop. She climbed a ladder back to the dock and had a sticky bun for a rest.

Then she saw it. Deep in the dark of the woods, past the dock, a little light shone. It was small and green. It blinked between the trees. It was far away. June wanted to hold it. She walked toward it, but it stayed far. It always stayed far.

"Come back," her dad called. "The boat is leaving."

June ran to the dock. The sail was already small. The light was still there, behind her, soft and low. She looked back one more time. Then she looked at the water.

stories.name: June

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Next to the dock, June saw a sailboat. Its sail was white and fat. June was a seal. She liked the boat.

"Can I come?" said June.

"No," said the man. "You have flippers."

The boat went away. June swam to the shore. She climbed a ladder. It was sticky with pine. She went into the woods to rest.

Then she saw it. Deep in the dark trees, a little light. It was soft and far away. It was the color of new leaves.

June went toward it. She went past tall ferns. She went past cold rocks. The light stayed far away.

"Wait," said June.

The light did not wait.

She went back to the water. She looked at the sailboat. Then she looked at the woods. The little light was still there. It was always there. June sat on a log. She looked and looked. The sun went down. The light did not come closer. June did not stop looking.

stories.name: June

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Near the dock, June saw a sailboat.

"I like that boat," June said.

"Me too," said her dad.

They sat by the water. June saw a seal. The seal looked at June.

"Hello, seal," June said.

The seal did not answer. It swam away.

June walked into the woods. The sun was warm. She found a ladder on a tree. She climbed up.

Then she saw it. A little light. It was far away. It was soft. It was green.

"I want to go there," June said.

She climbed down. She walked to the light. It did not get close. She went back to the boat. The sail was sticky.

"Time to rest," her dad said.

June looked at the woods. The light was still there. She walked to it. It stayed far.

"I want the light," she said.

She walked and walked.

"June, come back," said her dad.

June did not come back. She wanted the light.

The light. The light. The light.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Here is a story for you.

Henry was a seal who lived by the cold sea. He loved to watch a little sailboat dance on the waves. Its sail was white and curly in the wind. One stormy afternoon, the boat did not come. The sky was gray. The waves were tall. Eli put on his coat. He went to look for his boat.

He walked into the dark woods. The trees were big and close. The wind made a loud hum. Then Eli saw a light. It was small and far away. It was like a tiny, green apple in the dark. He wanted to touch it.

"Wait for me," Eli said to the light.

"You can't fix the storm," a bird sang from a branch.

"I can try," Eli said. He took a step. The light moved. It was always just ahead. He forgot the wind. He forgot the rain. He just wanted to reach the small, green glow.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Here is a seal. His name is Eli. He lives on a gray rock by the sea.

A sailboat came in the storm. The wind pulled its sail. Eli saw a man on the boat. The man held a curly rope. "Help me fix the sail!" the man called.

Eli swam. The water was cold. He pushed the boat to the shore.

"Thank you," said the man. He gave Eli an apple. Eli ate it. It was good.

That night, Eli went into the woods. He was looking for a safe place. The trees were dark. The rain fell hard.

Then Eli saw a light. It was small and far away. It was soft like a moon in a puddle. He wanted to touch it. He swam toward it. But it stayed far.

"Come back," said the man. "The storm is done."

Eli looked at the light. It was still there. He did not go to it. He went back to the sea. But he thought of it all night.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Here is a seal. Eli saw it on the wet sand. The sky was gray. Rain came down hard. A small sailboat sat on the beach. Its sail was torn. Eli wanted to fix it.

"Can you help?" Eli asked the seal. The seal did not talk. It looked at the woods.

The woods were dark. Eli saw a light inside. It was small and far. It was like a soft apple, glowing just for him. He took a step.

"Stay," said a voice. It was his friend, June. Her hair was curly and wet. "The storm is bad."

But the light pulled him. He walked to the trees. He felt the wanting in his chest. He wanted to hold that light.

"Eli, come back!" June called.

He stopped. The light blinked in the dark. He turned away. He went back to the boat. He found a needle. He began to fix the sail. The seal watched. The light stayed in the woods. He did not go.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
He was a seal named Eli. He liked the sailboat. It was small and blue.

The boat rocked near the shore. Wind pushed the waves. Eli swam close. He wanted to climb on.

"I can fix it," Eli said.

The sail was torn. The rope was curly. Eli held the rope in his mouth.

Then he saw the light. It was far in the dark of the woods. It was soft and green.

He let go of the rope. He swam to the trees. Rain hit the water. The woods were black. The light was there.

"Come back," called a gull. "The boat will tip!"

Eli did not turn. He wanted the light. He climbed the wet rocks. He left the boat.

He found an apple on the ground. He did not eat it.

The storm blew hard. The light blinked.

He reached. He reached.

The boat drifted away alone.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Here is a seal. Eli saw it on the wet rock. The seal looked at Eli. Then it looked at the sailboat.

“Can you fix the sail?” Eli asked.

The seal did not say yes. It did not say no. It made a soft sound.

Eli held a curly rope. He had an apple in his pocket. The wind pulled the boat. Rain hit the deck.

The sail was torn. Eli wanted to go home. But then he saw it.

A small light. Deep in the dark of the woods. It was not on the water. It was far away. It was not for him.

Eli rowed. The light stayed.

He pulled the curly rope. The sail went up. He tried to fix it.

The light stayed.

“Please,” Eli said. The seal slipped into the water.

The light stayed.

Eli rowed. The light stayed. He reached. He reached. The light stayed.

He never got there.

The light stayed.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Night came down soft and blue. Finn the seal swam near a sailboat. The sailboat had a little flag. The flag went flip, flip in the wind. Finn liked the sailboat. But the boat was stuck on a rock. Finn pushed and pushed. The boat did not move. Finn felt sad.

His friend Pip the gull flew down. "I can help," said Pip. Pip pulled the rope. Finn pushed the boat. Up and down they worked. Then the boat slid off the rock. It went skip, skip on the water. "Thank you, Pip," said Finn.

Finn looked up. High, high, at the very top of a tall tree, something shiny blinked. It was small and far. It looked like a tiny star caught in the leaves. Finn wanted to touch it. But seals do not climb trees. He watched it blink. Then he swam home with Pip. The shiny thing stayed up there. It was nice to see.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Nine young seals swam near the shore. Finn was one of them. He saw a sailboat with a little flag. It rocked on the waves.

"Let's race it," said Finn. But his tail was tired. He could not skip fast. His friend Pipa stayed with him.

"Look," said Pipa. "A shiny fish."

They chased the fish. That was fun. The sailboat did not care.

Late at night, the moon came up. Finn saw a light. It sat at the very top of a tall tree. It was small and far. It blinked like a star.

"Come on," said Pipa. "The rock is warm."

Finn wanted that light. He climbed the wet rocks. He slipped. Pipa pulled him back.

"It is too high," said Pipa.

"I know," said Finn. But he looked back once. Twice.

Then he curled by Pipa. The light stayed up in the tree. Finn closed his eyes. He slept.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Nights are long for Finn the seal. He lives by the bay where a sailboat sleeps. Its flag hangs down. Finn wants to climb the mast. But his flippers just slip. He cannot skip up the wood like a cat.

"I wish I could sail it," Finn tells his friend Otter.

Otter says, "We can fix that." She brings a rope. She ties a loop. Finn pushes his nose through. Otter pulls. Up he goes. The little problem is solved.

Then Finn sees it. Far past the docks, at the very top of a tall tree, a small light burns. It is shiny and green. It sways like a leaf in the wind.

Finn stares. "What is that?"

"Just a light," says Otter.

But Finn cannot stop looking. He looks past the sailboat. He looks past the waves. The green light is small and far. He wants to touch it. He wants it to touch him. He whispers, "I want to go there. I want to go there."

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Night came down soft on the water. Finn the seal swam out to see the sailboat. It rocked by the dock, and Finn loved how it went skip, skip, skip on the waves. But the sail had a tear. A little problem. Finn could not fix it alone. His friend Otter came. Together they pulled the shiny sail down. They used a flag to patch the hole. But then Finn saw it. Far away, at the very top of a tall tree, a small light blinked. It was gold and far. It called to Finn. He wanted it. He wanted it. Otter said, Finn, the boat is ready. Finn turned. The light blinked. He wanted it. He wanted to climb that tree. But seals do not climb. Otter said, we fixed the sail. Come sail. Finn looked at the light one more time. It blinked and blinked. He wanted it so much. Then he slid into the water. Skip, skip, skip went the boat. The light stayed far behind. Finn still wanted it. He always would. But the sail was mended, and Otter was near. They sailed home under the dark sky.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Nine seals slept on the rocks. Finn did not sleep. Finn was a seal who loved a sailboat.

The boat had a red flag. It went up and down the waves. Finn wanted to ride it.

But the boat was far away. That was Finn's little problem. Finn's friend Pip was a small gull. Pip could help.

Finn swam. Pip flew. They got to the boat. Finn could not climb in. The boat was too tall and the water too cold.

Then Finn saw it. High in a tall tree, far on the shore, was a shiny light. It blinked and blinked. Finn wanted that light. He wanted it more than the boat. He wanted it more than fish. He wanted it more than sleep.

"Come," said Pip. "The light is too high."

Finn did not listen. "I want the light," he said. "I want the light. I want the light."

Pip pushed a rope. The rope fell. Finn pulled. The sail came down like a soft wing. Finn climbed the sail and skipped onto the deck.

The boat rocked him. The light stayed far away, blinking. But Finn slept at last, on the boat, under the flag, near the shiny light he could not touch.

stories.name: Lena

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop
features: a small twist near the end
a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Next to the dock, Lena watched a seal swim by her sailboat. The sun was warm on her face. She wanted to sail, but her boat had a small tear in the sail.

“I can fix it,” she said. But she had no strong thread.

Lena walked into town. She passed a bakery and a toy store. Then she saw a dark shop. At the back, something glowed.

A little green light. It blinked like a tiny star. It was far away and soft.

Lena stepped closer. The light seemed to pull her. But she shook her head. She was brave. She needed thread, not a light.

The shop man gave her a spool. “This will fix your sail,” he said.

Lena ran back. She sewed the tear. The sail was strong.

Then the seal popped up again. It held a shiny fish in its mouth. It dropped the fish near her boat.

Lena laughed. The little green light was just a lamp in the shop. But the seal had been watching her all along.

stories.name: Lena

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop
features: a small twist near the end
a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Next to the harbor, Lena watched a sailboat. The sail was white and big. The sun was warm on her nose. She wanted to ride on that boat.

Lena found a small shop by the dock. It was dark inside. At the back of the shop, a green light glowed. It was small and far away. Lena reached for it. She could not touch it. The light stayed where it was.

The sailboat had a little problem. Its rope was loose. Lena felt sad. She wanted to help.

A kind man gave her a rope. "You can fix it," he said. Lena felt brave. She climbed on the boat. She pulled the rope tight. The sail went up.

Then the green light blinked once. It was just a lamp in the shop. Lena laughed. She did not need to reach it. She sailed with the wind and the sun.

stories.name: Lena

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop
features: a small twist near the end
a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Next to the dock, Lena the seal watched a sailboat. The sun was warm on her back. She wanted to ride the boat.

But the sail had a big tear. The boat could not go.

Lena saw a dark shop by the water. Something green glowed at the back of the shop. It was a small green light. It called to her.

She slipped inside. The light was far away. She reached for it. She could not touch it.

Lena came back out. She had to fix the sail. She was brave. She pulled the cloth with her nose.

Then a little wind came. The tear closed up! The sail was fixed.

Lena looked back at the shop. The green light still glowed. She reached once more. It stayed far away.

The sailboat moved on the water. Lena swam beside it. The green light stayed behind her. She did not get it. But she got the boat.

The sun went down. The light blinked. Lena was happy and sad.

stories.name: Lena

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop
features: a small twist near the end
a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Next to the dock, Lena watched a seal swim by a little sailboat. The sun was warm on her face. The sailboat rocked. The seal dove and came back up.

Lena walked to town. She saw a dark shop. At the back of the shop, a small light glowed. It was green. It did not move. It did not blink. It just stayed there, far away.

Lena wanted that light. She forgot the sailboat. She forgot the seal. She reached for the light. The shop man said, "No, child. You cannot touch it."

So Lena went back to the dock. She reached for the light again. It was still there, at the back of the dark shop. She could not have it.

Then the sailboat tipped. Its rope broke. The seal nudged it back. It was so brave. Lena found a rope and used it to fix the sailboat. The twist was this: the light was just a small green lamp, nothing more.

Lena did not need it. The sailboat was safe. That was enough.

stories.name: Lena

axes.where: at the back of a dark shop
features: a small twist near the end
a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Never had Lena seen a seal and a sailboat together. She sat on the warm dock. The sun was high and kind. Her little boat had a hole. She wanted to fix it.

Then she saw the light. It was green and far away.

It lived at the back of a dark shop. The shop was near the water. Lena rowed to it.

The green light was small. It was soft. It was always there.

"Can I have it?" she asked.

No one said yes. The light just glowed.

She reached. She reached. She reached.

The light did not come.

"Fix your boat," she said. "Be brave."

She fixed the boat with tape and hope.

A seal popped up. It had her lost oar!

"Thank you, seal," said Lena.

Now her boat was good.

But she looked back at the green light.

She reached. She reached.

She reached for the light at the back of the dark shop.

It never came.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: on a pole by the gate
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Tess found a talking snowflake in the yard. It said its name was Pip. Pip told her secrets about winter.

At sunset, Tess walked to the gate. A small green light sat on a pole. It blinked once, then twice. She watched it for a moment.

Pip rode on her fuzzy mitten. "I like warm things," Pip said. "I want to sit on the stove."

"No," Tess said. "You will melt."

Pip hummed. They passed an egg shell by the step. Tess began to fold her scarf.

The green light blinked again. It was far away and shining. Tess reached out her hand. She could not touch it. It was just a light on a pole.

"I want that light," Tess said.

"You can't have it," Pip said. "It is not for us."

Tess nodded. She looked down at her mitten. Pip was gone. Only a wet spot stayed.

Then a tiny voice came from the puddle. "I folded myself into the water," Pip said. "Now I can go anywhere."

The green light blinked one last time.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: on a pole by the gate
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Tess found a snowflake on her mitten. It was tiny and white. It said, "Hello, Tess." Tess laughed. A talking snowflake! She held it close.

The snowflake told her jokes. It sang a fuzzy song. Tess tried to fold it in a soft scarf. But the snowflake slipped out. It wanted to go.

At sunset, Tess walked to the gate. The sky was pink and gold. On a pole by the gate, a small green light blinked. It was far away. It glowed like a tiny star. Tess wanted to touch it.

"Stay with me," Tess said. The snowflake whispered, "I can't." It floated up. It drifted toward the green light. Tess reached out. Her hand was empty.

Then the snowflake stopped. It came back. It landed on her nose. "I am your egg," it said. "I will hatch in spring." Tess smiled. She held her fuzzy mitten to her cheek. The green light blinked once more, then went dark.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: on a pole by the gate
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Tess met a snowflake that could talk. It sat on her mitten and said, "Hello, I am Pip." Pip told her jokes. Pip sang a small song. Tess laughed all the way home.

At sunset, she passed the gate. A green light shone on a pole. It was soft and far. Tess stopped. She wanted to touch it. She reached up, but her arms were too short. The light just blinked and stayed.

The next day, Pip came back. They played in the snow. But when the sun went down, Tess ran to the gate. The green light was there. She reached again. She could not have it. Pip said, "Look at me!" Tess did not look.

One evening, Pip did not come. Tess waited by the egg carton on the step. She began to fold her scarf, slow and sad. Then she saw a fuzzy glow. It was Pip! Pip had gone to the light. Pip was the light. Tess held her close. She did not need to reach anymore.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: on a pole by the gate
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Tess built a small snowflake from paper and tape. She called it Flake. Flake could talk, just a little. "Cold," Flake said. "So cold."

Tess laughed. She put Flake on the table. She gave it a warm egg to sit near. Flake did not eat. Flakes do not eat.

Then the sun went low. A light came on. It sat on a pole by the gate. It was small and green. It blinked once. Tess saw it through the window.

"Stay here," she told Flake. She ran to the gate. The light was far up. She reached. Her fingers felt cold air. She could not touch it.

She came back. "Fold me," said Flake. So she did. Flake was flat and fuzzy now. "Look," said Flake. The green light was inside Flake. It blinked. So that was the twist. Flake was the light all along, and Tess still could not hold it.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: on a pole by the gate
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Tess found a snowflake that could talk. It sat on her mitten and said, "I am cold."

The sun went down. The sky turned pink and gray. Tess walked to the gate. A green light shone on a pole. It was small and far away.

Tess wanted that light. She reached for it. Her hand was empty. The light stayed on the pole.

"Come back," said the snowflake. "I am cold."

Tess did not fold her fingers around it. She held her fuzzy mitten open. She looked at the light again.

"I want it," she said. "I want it."

The light did not move. Tess reached. She reached. The snowflake said, "I am cold. I am cold."

Then the snowflake spoke one more time. "I am the light," it said.

Tess looked down. The snowflake was not there. Her mitten held a small egg of ice. It glowed green.

She held it up. The light on the pole went out.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
A small snowflake landed on Omar’s mittens. “Hello,” said the snowflake. “I can talk.”

Omar blinked. “You can talk?”

“Yes. I like the cold,” said the snowflake. “I will stay with you.”

Omar smiled. He was happy. He held his hand out flat. The snowflake did not melt. It sat on his mitten like a tiny white stone.

“Can you stay all day?” asked Omar.

“I can try,” said the snowflake.

Omar began to walk. The sky was pink and gray. Early morning light lay on the snow. Omar crossed a big field. His boots made soft sounds.

Across the field, a little light blinked far away. It was small and green. It did not come closer. Omar looked at it. He wanted to fold his hand around it. But his hand was open for the snowflake.

“Do you see that light?” asked Omar.

“I see snow,” said the snowflake.

Omar walked on. The small light stayed far across the field. He did not reach it. He held the snowflake and went home.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text: A small snowflake landed on Omar’s mittens. “Hello,” it said. “I am here to talk.” Omar blinked. Snow does not talk. But this one did. “Are you cold?” he asked. “No,” said the snowflake. “I am happy.” Omar laughed. He put it on a stone. The snowflake did not melt. It told him about the sky. It told him about the wind. Then Omar saw a tiny light across a big field. It was far away. It was soft and green. He wanted to fold his hands around it. “What is that?” he asked. “I do not know,” said the snowflake. “It is just a light.” But Omar kept looking. Every morning he came back. The snowflake talked. Omar listened. But his eyes always went to the far field. “Do you want to go there?” asked the snowflake. “Yes,” said Omar. “But I cannot.” The light stayed far. The snowflake stayed near. Omar was happy and not happy. He held the small cold friend. He looked at the small green light. Morning after morning.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
A tiny snowflake landed on Omar’s nose. It said, “Hello, I am Flake.”

Omar blinked. “You can talk?”

“Yes,” said Flake. “I can also sing. Do you want to hear?”

“Maybe later,” Omar said. He put Flake on a stone so it would not melt. At breakfast, Omar told his mom about his new friend. She smiled and gave him a warm hat.

Then Omar saw it. Across the big field, early morning light made a small green glow. It sat far away, near the trees. Omar wanted to hold that light. He could not reach it. It was too far.

Flake said, “Let’s fold a paper boat. We can float to it.”

“No,” Omar said. “The light is not on water.”

He walked to the field edge. The green glow stayed far. He felt sad and happy at the same time.

“Will you sing now?” Flake asked.

“Later,” Omar said. “I want that light.”

Every morning he looked. The glow was always there. Always far. But Flake stayed close and talked to him.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
A tiny snowflake landed on Omar’s coat. It said, “Hi, I’m Flake.” Omar laughed. “You can talk?” The snowflake said, “Yes. I like your warm breath.” They walked to the big field. Flake told him jokes. Omar felt happy.

Then Omar saw a small light across the big field. It was green and soft. It sat by a gray stone. He stopped. “What is that?” he asked.

“Just a light,” said Flake. “Let’s talk more.”

Omar took a step. “I want to see it.” Flake said, “Stay. I’m melting.” Omar did not fold his arms. He stared across the field. The light blinked.

“Come back,” said Flake. “Tell me a story.” Omar whispered, “I want that light.” He said it again. “I want that light.” The snowflake grew small. “Please,” said Flake. Omar said, “I want that light.” He said it and said it. The sun came up. Flake was gone. The light stayed far away.

stories.name: Omar

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text: A tiny snowflake landed on Omar’s nose. It said, “Hello, I am Snowflake.” Omar laughed. “Hello, Snowflake.” Snowflake talked about cold and wind. Then Omar saw a far light across a big field. It was small and green. He wanted it. He forgot Snowflake. “I want that light,” Omar said. “It is so far.” He stood on a stone. He did not fold his hands. He was not happy. “Can we go?” he asked. Snowflake said, “We are here.” Omar said, “I want that light. I want that light.” Snowflake said, “Look at me.” Omar said, “I want that light. I want that light.” The light did not come close. His feet were cold. The sky turned pink. Snowflake said, “Goodbye, Omar.” Omar said, “I want that light.” Snowflake melted. Omar sat down. He still wanted the light. He wanted it and wanted it. The field was big. The light stayed small. He did not get it. He never got it. He just wanted it. And wanted it.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Snow fell soft on Leo’s window. One flake tapped the glass. “Let me in,” it said. Leo opened the latch. The snowflake jumped to his pillow. “I am lost,” it said. “Help me get home.”

Leo put on boots. His friend Mia came too. They walked into the woods. The path was bumpy. Branches clicked like teeth. Mia held his hand.

Deep in the dark, Leo saw a green light. It hung between two pines. It did not warm him. It did not come close. It just stayed there, far away, like a thing you almost remember.

“Is that your home?” Leo asked.
“No,” said the snowflake. “I want that light. I always want it.”

They walked until the light was gone. The snowflake grew quiet. It grew small. Then it turned to a splash on Leo’s mitt.

Mia said, “It is bedtime.”
Leo nodded. He went home. He lay on his pillow. He did not sleep.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Snow came down on Leo’s window. One flake landed on the glass. It had a tiny mouth. “Hello, Leo,” it said. Leo blinked. “You can talk?” The flake said, “I can. But I am melting.” Leo cupped his hands. He carried the flake to his bed. He put it on his pillow. The flake said, “I want to stay.” Leo said, “I will help you.”

His friend Mia came over. She brought a cold jar. They put the flake inside. Then they ran to the woods. The dark trees stood close. Deep in the dark, Leo saw a small light. It was far away. It did not move. He wanted to hold it. He did not know why. It was just a dot, like a lost star.

“Come on,” Mia said. They found a snow pile. Leo set the jar down. The flake said, “Thank you.” Then it went splash. Just water. Leo’s hands were empty. He looked back at the light. It was still far. Mia took his hand. “Time for bed,” she said. Leo walked home. The path was bumpy. The light stayed behind the trees. He never got it. He never would.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Snow came down soft on Leo’s window. One flake landed on the glass. It had a tiny mouth. “Leo,” it said. “I am cold and I am lost.”

Leo put on his boots. His friend Mina came too. They walked into the woods to help the snowflake find its home.

The woods were dark. Just before bedtime, the trees made long shadows. Leo held the flake in his hands. Mina held a small lamp.

Deep in the dark, Leo saw a green light. It glowed far away. It was not a star. It was not a lamp. It was a little green gleam he could not touch.

“Come on,” said Mina. But Leo kept looking back. The green light pulled at him. He wanted to hold it. He wanted to keep it.

The snowflake grew weak. “I need the sky,” it whispered.

Leo ran. He tripped on a bumpy root. The snowflake fell into a puddle. It made a tiny splash. Then it was gone.

Mina took Leo home. He lay on his pillow. The green light still shone in his mind. He never reached it. He never saw the snowflake again.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text: Snow fell on Leo’s mittens. He caught one flake. It had a tiny mouth. “Hello, Leo,” it said. Leo laughed. His friend Mia ran over. “Show me!” she said. The flake talked about the sky. It talked about a far hill. Leo wanted to keep it. He put it in a jar. But the flake looked sad. It pointed past the trees. Just before bedtime, Leo saw a small light in the dark of the woods. It was not a star. It was not a lamp. It was a green glow, soft and low. “I want that,” Leo whispered. He walked past the bumpy roots. Mia held his hand. “We should go home,” she said. Leo shook his head. “I want that light.” He said it again. “I want that light.” The jar felt cold. The flake said, “I want the sky.” Leo did not listen. He ran toward the glow. Then his foot slipped. The jar hit a rock. A splash of water and glass went everywhere. The light blinked out. Mia put her arm around him. Leo cried into his pillow that night. The snowflake was gone. The green light was still far away.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
Snow was falling when Leo found the talking snowflake. It sat on his mitten and said, "Hello, Leo." Leo ran to show his friend Mia. But the snowflake only whispered one thing. "Take me to the dark woods," it said. "I must find my light."

Leo put on his boots. Mia held his hand. The woods were bumpy and black. Leo's pillow was far away. Bedtime was coming.

"Where is your light?" Leo asked. "I see it," said the snowflake. "A small glow between the trees. I can never reach it."

They walked and walked. The glow stayed far. "I want it," said the snowflake. "I want it. I want it."

Leo tripped on a root. The snowflake fell into a puddle. Splash. It melted in the cold water. "I almost had it," it said, and then it was gone.

Mia hugged Leo. He cried. At home, his pillow was soft. But Leo lay awake. He kept seeing a small glow between the trees. He wanted it too.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: in the sky, very low

stories.text:
Down came a small snowflake. It landed on Faye's nose. "Hello," said the snowflake. "I can talk."

Faye blinked. "You can talk?"

"Yes," said the snowflake. "But I am melting."

Faye ran to her friend Ben. Ben was eating a cookie on the swing. "Help," said Faye. "My snowflake is melting."

Ben looked up. The rain fell soft. Far in the sky, very low, a tiny light blinked. It was green. It was far away. Faye wanted to touch it. She reached up. She could not get it. She felt sad for one second.

"Put the snowflake in the freezer," said Ben. "It is cozy there."

Faye did. The snowflake smiled. "Thank you, Faye."

Now the snowflake lives in the freezer. It tells jokes. Faye visits every night. The small green light stays low in the sky. Sometimes Faye waves at it. Then she goes inside to her friend.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: in the sky, very low

stories.text:
Down came a little snowflake. It landed on Faye's nose. "Hello," said the snowflake. "I can talk."

Faye laughed. She held out her hand. The snowflake hopped on. It told her jokes. It sang a tiny song. Faye gave it a name. She called it Pip.

Rain began to fall. Pip grew small. "I am melting," Pip said. Faye felt sad. She did not want Pip to go.

Her friend Ben came over. He had a cozy scarf. "Wrap Pip in this," Ben said.

Faye ran to the swing. She sat and held Pip close. Then she saw a soft light in the sky. It was very low. It glowed green in the rain. Faye wanted to touch it. She reached out. The light stayed far away. She reached again. It did not come closer.

"Look," said Ben. "The light is just a streetlamp."

Faye smiled. She had a cookie in her pocket. She shared it with Ben. Pip stayed cold and safe in the scarf. The rain stopped. Faye was happy.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: in the sky, very low

stories.text:
Down came a snowflake on Faye's nose. It said, "Hello, I can talk."

Faye laughed. "You are just one snowflake."

"I am a special one," said the snowflake. "I will stay with you."

They played by the swing. Faye shared her cookie. The snowflake told funny jokes. They felt cozy and warm.

Then Faye saw a small green light in the sky, very low. It blinked behind the rain. She wanted to catch it. She reached up. Her hand closed on air.

"Come back," said the snowflake.

But Faye watched the light. She reached again. Again and again. "I want it," she said. "I want it. I want it."

Her friend took her hand. "The light is far away. I am here."

Faye looked down. The snowflake was small and bright in her palm. She stopped reaching.

"You are my light," she said.

The snowflake smiled. They sat on the swing, cozy under the rain, happy together.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: in the sky, very low

stories.text:
Down fell one small snowflake. It landed on Faye's nose. "Hello," said the snowflake. "I can talk."

Faye laughed. "You are silly," she said. She gave it a name. She called it Pip.

Pip liked to sit on her hand. Pip liked to ride the swing. They shared a cookie in the cozy warm room.

Then the rain came. It was a rainy evening. Faye looked up. In the sky, very low, she saw a small green light.

It was not Pip. It was far away. It was so low and bright.

"I want it," said Faye. "I want to hold it."

"You cannot," said Pip. "It is too far."

Faye reached out the window. "I want it. I want it. I want it."

Her friend Ben came. He took her hand. "Look," he said. "It is just a street lamp. Here is your snowflake."

Faye looked down. Pip was still there. The green light stayed far away. But Pip was close. Faye smiled. She was happy.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: in the sky, very low

stories.text:
Ding went the little bell on the door. Faye ran to the window. The sky was gray and soft. It was a rainy evening.

Then she saw it. A tiny green light, very low in the sky. It blinked like a small star.

"Oh," said Faye. "Come here, little light."

The light did not come. It only blinked.

Faye climbed on her cozy bed. She reached out the window. Her fingers got wet with rain. The light stayed far away.

"Please," she said.

The light blinked once more. Then a small voice spoke.

"I am a snowflake," it said. "I am the first one. I am too warm here. I cannot come to you."

Faye felt sad. She wanted the light so much.

Her friend Ben came in. He had a cookie in his hand. He saw Faye reaching.

"You want that light?" he said.

"Yes," said Faye. "I want it every night."

Ben smiled. "Then let us make it cold for her."

They opened the window wide. They put ice in a bowl. The room got chilly and fresh. Faye put on her hat.

The little light came closer. It floated to the bowl of ice. It became a small white snowflake, round and bright.

"Thank you," said the snowflake. "I can stay now."

Faye laughed. She and Ben sat on the swing by the window. The snowflake talked to them all night. It told them about the sky.

Faye was happy. She had her light. And her light had a home.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
No snow had come yet, but Ruby found one flake on her sleeve. It was small and white and fluffy. It said, "Hello, Ruby."

Ruby smiled. She put it in her cup. The flake talked all day. It told her about a hill far away. It told her about a race it lost once.

On a windy morning, Ruby went outside. She held the cup up high. The wind pulled at her coat. The flake said, "Look."

Across the town, on a roof, a small light blinked. It was pale and green, like a leaf in spring. Ruby wanted to hold it. She ran. She ran past the hill. She ran in the cold race against the wind.

But the light stayed on the roof. It did not come closer. Her cup tipped. The fluffy snowflake fell out.

"Goodbye," it said.

Ruby looked up. The light blinked once more. Then the wind took her friend away. Ruby sat down in the empty white street and did not talk at all.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
Nobody thought a snowflake could talk. Ruby knew one that did. She found it on the hill behind her house. It was fluffy and cold and it said her name.

“Ruby,” it whispered. “I come from far away.”

Ruby carried it in her mittens. The wind pulled at her coat. She wanted to keep it safe.

Then she saw a small green glow on a roof across the town. It sat there, quiet and bright, like a light that wanted her. Ruby stopped. Her snowflake stopped talking.

“Do you see it too?” Ruby asked.

The snowflake did not answer. The wind blew harder. Ruby ran a race with the wind, but the light stayed far away on its roof.

She looked down. Her mittens were wet and empty. The snowflake was gone, melted into drops.

Ruby sat on the ground. The wind kept blowing. The small light still shone on the roof across the town, and Ruby could not reach it, and she could not bring her friend back.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text: Nobody had ever heard a snowflake talk before Ruby did. She was on the hill with her fluffy mittens, and one snowflake landed on her thumb. "Hello," said the snowflake. Its name was Pip. Pip could talk! Ruby ran a race down the hill to tell her mom. But her mom was busy. So Ruby went out again. The windy morning blew her hair. Then she saw something far away, on a roof across the town. It was a small glow. It looked like a tiny light, soft and low. It was not the sun. Ruby wanted to hold it. Every day she climbed the hill to look. Every day the glow stayed far. Pip talked less and less. One morning Pip was quiet. Ruby held her fluffy mittens up, but no snow came. She looked across the town. The light was still there, small and far, and she never reached it.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
Nobody had ever heard a snowflake talk before Ruby. One windy morning, one landed on her fluffy mitt.

"I am Pip," it said. "I fell from a high cloud."

Ruby laughed. She put Pip in her pocket and ran down the hill.

Then she saw it. Far away, on a roof across the town, a small light sat and glowed. It was soft and low, the color of new leaves. It did not move. It did not call. It just waited.

Ruby stopped. Her feet forgot the race. "Do you see that?" she asked.

Pip did not answer. Pip was already melting.

Ruby ran toward the roof. She ran past her house. She ran past the hill. The windy morning pushed her back.

When she got there, the roof was bare. Her pocket was wet. Only a cold drop was left.

"Pip?" she said.

The light stayed far away and small, like a thing she could never hold.

stories.name: Ruby

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
Nia the snowflake liked to talk. She landed on Ruby's nose and said, "Hello!" Ruby laughed.

Ruby lived on a hill. The wind was big that morning. It said, "Race you!" Ruby ran down.

Then she saw it. Far away, on a roof across the town, a small light. It was soft. It was low. It was there.

"Come back," said Nia.

But Ruby looked at the light. The light did not move. Ruby wanted it.

She walked past fluffy snow. She walked past her warm door.

"Come back," said Nia.

Ruby said, "I see it."

"Come back," said Nia.

Ruby said, "I see it."

The wind pushed her coat. Her feet got cold. The light stayed small and far.

"Come back," said Nia.

Ruby said, "I see it."

She never got there. The light did not get bigger. At night, Ruby sat down in the snow. She was far from home. Nia melted on her hand. Ruby was alone. She still looked at the light.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a little island

stories.text:
In the kitchen, Nina heard the kettle sing. It went wheee, wheee, wheee. Snow fell outside the window.

Nina put on her coat. She went up the hill to find her dog. He liked to roll in the snow. He was not on the hill. She sat on the swing. It was cold. She was hungry.

Then she saw it. Far away, on a little island, a small light was on. It was not red. It was not blue. It was like a tiny leaf in the dark. Nina wanted to touch it. She could not. The water was too cold.

Her dog came running. He shook snow on her face. Nina laughed. "You are a silly dog," she said.

They went home. The kettle sang again. Nina gave her dog a treat. She gave herself warm bread.

Some lights are just for looking. That is okay. Home is warm, and that is better.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a little island

stories.text:
I put the kettle on the stove. It puffs. It whistles. Nina likes that sound.

Snow falls soft on the hill. Nina runs to her swing. She swings high. The cold air makes her nose pink.

Then she sees it. Far away, on a little island, a small light. It is green and quiet. It sits under the snow clouds. Nina stops swinging. She looks and looks.

Her tummy growls. She is hungry. She goes inside. The kettle whistles again. Nina laughs. "You sing louder than me!" she says.

She drinks warm milk. She thinks of the green light on the island. It is so far. She cannot go there today.

The snow keeps falling. The light keeps shining. Nina waves at it. It does not wave back.

She sits by the window. The kettle hums. The light stays small and green. Nina feels a pull in her chest. She wants to touch it. She cannot.

So she holds her warm cup. She watches the snow. The light is far, but it is there.

Some things we love stay far away. We can still wave. We can still watch. And we can still be warm.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a little island

stories.text:
In the cold kitchen, the kettle whistled. Nina liked that sound. It was loud and happy.

Nina put on her coat. She went outside to play on the snowy hill. Her friend Ben came too. They ran to the big swing.

Ben sat on the swing. He went up, up, up. Then he came down with a bump in the snow. His hat fell off. Nina laughed. That was funny.
