Then Nina saw it. Far away, on a little island, a small light was shining. It was green and soft. It looked warm. Nina wanted to go there. But the water was cold and deep.

Nina felt hungry. She went home. The kettle whistled again. The sound was warm and close.

She looked out the window. The little light was still there, far away on the island.

You cannot hold every pretty thing. But you can love the warm things near you.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a little island

stories.text:
I put the kettle on. It hissed. Then it sang. Nina liked that sound. She was hungry. She made soup.

Out the window, snow fell. It fell on the hill. On the little island, the snow fell too. A light was there. It was small and bright. It blinked like a sleepy eye.

Nina ran outside. She left the kettle. She did not get her coat. Brrr. She climbed the hill. The wind pushed her back. She slipped and sat in the snow. Her feet went up. She looked like a funny snow turtle.

A swing hung from a tree. It waved at her. She got on. She swung up, up. She tried to see the light. It was far. It was always far.

The kettle whistled from home. Nina heard it. She wanted the light. She wanted her soup too.

She went home slow. The soup was warm. The light stayed on its island. Some things you want are just for looking.

Moral: A warm bowl beats a far light.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: on a little island

stories.text:
I put the kettle on the stove. It puffs. It hums. Then it whistles, loud and happy.

Nina hears it. But she is not in the kitchen. She stands at the window. Snow falls soft and white. Down the hill, past the bare trees, she sees a little island. On the island, a small light blinks. It is green. It is always green.

The kettle whistles. Nina does not move. She wants that light. She wants to hold it. She wants it to warm her hands.

She runs outside. She slips on the snow. Her boot flies up. She sits down hard. "Oof!" she says. That is funny. She laughs a little.

She climbs on her swing. She swings high. She swings low. The green light stays far away. Her tummy growls. She is hungry. The kettle is still whistling. It calls her back. But she looks at the light. She looks and looks.

Some lights are just for looking. Not for holding. That is the hard, warm truth.

stories.name: Lena

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
In the kitchen Lena heard the kettle start to whistle. It was a rainy evening, and she wanted tea. But the whistle stopped too soon. She picked up the kettle. No water came out. The spout was blocked.

Lena found a small stone in the sink. She used it to tap the spout. Nothing. She got a scoop from the drawer. She dug out a bit of white stuff. Still nothing.

She was busy and did not want a big problem. So she filled the kettle with fresh water. She put it back on the fire. Soon the whistle sang again, loud and clear.

Through the wet window, far away, a tiny light sat at the very top of a tall tree. It blinked once. Lena looked at it. Then she poured her tea.

stories.name: Lena

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
I put the kettle on. It was a rainy evening. Lena liked to hear it sing. The whistle was soft at first. Then it grew loud.

Lena waited for her tea. She held a stone cup. The rain tapped the window. The kettle sang and sang.

Then it stopped. No more whistle. Lena looked inside. The little hole was blocked. A scoop of dust had dried there.

"Oh no," she said. She was busy with a problem now.

She got a pin. She poked the hole. The dust fell out. She put the kettle back.

Soon the whistle came again. Soft, then loud. Lena smiled.

She looked out the window. High up in the tall tree, a tiny light shone. It was small and green. It blinked in the rain.

Lena wished she could hold it. But the tree was too tall. The light was too far.

She poured her tea. The whistle hummed. She looked up once more. The little light stayed there, far away. She sipped her tea and watched it glow.

stories.name: Lena

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
I put the kettle on the stove. Lena wants tea on this rainy evening. The water needs to get hot. Then it will sing.

Lena waits by the window. Rain taps the glass. The kettle is slow. She looks outside. At the very top of a tall tree, a small light glows. It is green and far away. It sits on the highest branch.

The kettle whistles. Lena jumps up. She pours the water. But she has no honey. Her tea will be plain. That is a little problem.

She puts on her coat. She walks to the shop. The rain makes the path soft. She steps on a cold stone. She gets a scoop of honey. The shop is busy. She waits in line.

Back home, the kettle whistles again. Lena makes her tea. It is sweet now. The problem is solved.

She sits by the window. She sips her tea. Her eyes find the tall tree. The green light is still there. It blinks in the rain. She cannot reach it. She never can. But she looks and looks.

stories.name: Lena

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
In the kitchen, Lena put the kettle on the stove. The water began to sing. Then it whistled loud and high. She liked that sound. It meant tea was coming.

Rain tapped the window. The kettle whistled again. Lena looked outside. At the very top of the tall tree, a small light glowed. It was soft and far away. She wanted to hold it.

She forgot the tea. She forgot the cups. The kettle kept whistling. She climbed on a stone to see better. Rain made the light blur. She tried to scoop it with her hand. Nothing.

The kettle screamed. It was too busy being loud. Lena ran back. She lifted the kettle off the fire. The whistling stopped.

Her tea was late, but warm. She sat by the window. The little light stayed in the tree. She could not reach it. She never could. But she watched it anyway.

stories.name: Lena

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: I put the kettle on. It whistles. Lena hears it and she thinks of the little green light at the very top of the tall tree. It is rainy evening. The rain taps the window. The light glows through the wet leaves. Lena wants it. She wants it so much. She can not reach it. She is too small. The kettle whistles more. She does not move. She thinks, I want it, I want it, I want it. Papa calls, "Lena, the tea!" She does not hear. She only sees the light. It is a soft green song in the rain. She wants it. She wants it. Papa comes in. He lifts her up. He helps her scoop tea into the pot. She stirs the pot with a stone spoon. The busy kettle stops whistling. Papa says, "There. Warm." Lena drinks her tea. She looks out at the tree. The light is still there. It is still far. But her hands are warm. She is okay. She wants it still. But she is okay.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
When the kettle whistled, Theo ran to the kitchen. The sound was loud and happy. He put a jar on the table. Mom poured warm water in.

Then the rain came. It hit the window hard. Theo went outside to the playground. The wind was strong. It felt heavy on his coat.

He saw a small light. It was far away, on the other side of the playground. It was green and soft. It did not move. Theo wanted to go to it. But the rain was too much. He went back inside.

Mom gave him a warm drink. Theo began to draw. He drew the light. He drew a big sun. The sun made the light go away.

The storm stopped. Theo went out again. The light was gone. But his friends were there. They played on the swings.

Theo was happy. He did not need the far light. He had his home and his friends. A little want is fine, but what you have is better.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
When the kettle whistled, Theo ran to the kitchen. The air was warm and smelled like toast. Rain hit the window hard. Theo put honey in his cup and checked the water. The day felt gray and heavy, like a wet coat.

From the window, he saw a small green glow. It was on the far side of the playground. It blinked once, then twice, soft as a firefly. Theo wanted to see it up close.

He took his jar and went outside. The wind pushed his hood back. He liked how the light seemed to wait for him, but every step he took made it drift a little farther away.

Back home, his mother said, "Draw the curtains, please." Theo pulled them shut. The kettle sang again. He poured the water and watched the steam rise. It curled and twisted, just like the light had moved.

Theo smiled. Some things are nice to see, even if you cannot hold them. He drank his tea. The storm passed. The next morning, the playground was bright and dry, and Theo did not need to chase the glow anymore. He knew it would come back when the rain did. Wanting can be warm, if you let it be.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
When the kettle whistles, Theo runs to the kitchen. He loves that sound. It is loud and happy, like a little song. On a stormy afternoon, Mom fills the kettle. Theo watches the steam. He wants to catch it in a jar.

Rain hits the window. Wind shakes the trees. Theo looks outside. On the far side of the playground, past the wet slide, he sees a small green light. It glows in the gray rain. It is far away. It is always far away.

The kettle whistles again. Theo runs back. He holds his jar to the steam. The steam will not stay. It slips out. He tries to draw the steam in with a spoon. The jar feels heavy with water, not steam.

The light is still there. Theo wants to go to it. But Mom says, "Stay inside. The storm is big."

Theo looks at the light. He looks at the warm kettle. He stays.

Later, the rain stops. The light is gone. Mom makes tea. Theo drinks it. It is warm and sweet. He is happy.

You cannot hold steam or catch a far light. But you can hold a warm cup and stay dry.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
When the kettle whistles, Theo runs to the kitchen. He likes the sound. It is loud and happy. The water sings in the pot. But then Theo looks out the window. The sky is dark. A storm is coming.

Theo goes to the playground. Wind pushes him. Rain hits his face. He holds a jar with both hands. It feels heavy. He wants to draw water from the sky. He wants to catch the storm.

Then he sees it. On the far side of the playground, past the slide, a little light shines. It is small and green. It sits under the big tree. Theo walks toward it. The light does not move. He runs. It stays far away.

The rain gets loud. The wind gets strong. Theo forgets the jar. He forgets the kettle. He only sees the green light. He reaches. He reaches. He reaches.

His mom calls him home. Theo turns. The light is still there. But his mom is warm. His home is dry. The kettle whistles again.

You cannot hold every light. But you can go home.

stories.name: Theo

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
When the kettle whistles, Theo puts tea in a jar. The water sings. Steam climbs up. Then Theo sees it.

Out the window, past the wet street, on the far side of the playground, a small light is on. It is green. It is low. It does not move.

Theo wants it. He wants to draw it. He wants to hold it.

Rain hits the roof. The storm is heavy. The kettle calls, but Theo looks at the light. He looks and looks. The light is far. The light is small. The light is green.

Theo walks out. Wind pushes him. Rain gets his coat. He goes to the playground. The light stays far. He goes more. The light stays far. The light is always far. The light is always green.

Theo stops. He is cold. He is tired. Then he hears the kettle. It whistles from home. He goes back. He drinks tea. The light is still there, small and green. He can see it and not hold it. That is okay. Some things you love from far away. That is enough.

stories.name: Max

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
A kettle whistles on the stove. Max likes the sound. It means tea is almost ready. He pours the water slowly. The steam feels warm on his face.

Then Max walks to the river. The night is foggy. He stands on the old bridge. Far down the water, a small green light floats. It is soft and far away. Max leans on the rail. He wants to touch it.

He climbs a ladder by the dock. It is sticky with wet leaves. He tries to listen for the light. But the light does not speak.

Max goes home slow. The fog hides the bridge now. He makes more tea. The kettle whistles again. But the green light is gone. He will not see it again. The tea is cold. He sets it down and does not drink.

stories.name: Max

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
A kettle whistled on the stove. Max took it off the fire. He made tea for one.

Then he put on his coat. He went out into the foggy night. The fog was soft and gray. It made the street lamps look like moons.

Max walked to the bridge over the river. He leaned on the cold rail. Far away, past the water, a little light glowed. It was green and small. It did not move. It just stayed there.

Max wanted to touch it. He did not know why.

He came back the next night. He came back with a ladder. The ladder was too short. The light stayed far away. His hands felt sticky from the rail.

"Listen," he said to the river. The river did not answer.

Every night he made tea. Every night the kettle sang. Every night he went to the bridge.

The light never came closer. Max never stopped looking. One foggy night he did not come home. The tea went cold. The kettle did not sing. The little green light still glowed, far away, where no one could reach it.

stories.name: Max

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
A kettle whistled on the stove. Max turned it off. The kitchen went quiet.

Through the window, fog sat on the river like a wet blanket. Max put on his coat. He had to walk.

On the bridge, the fog was thick and sticky. It clung to his face. Far down the river, a small green light blinked. It was under the far arch, low on the black water.

Max leaned on the rail. He wanted to touch it. Every night it called him. He could not reach it. Never could.

He climbed a ladder of cold air with his eyes. He tried to listen for its hum. The river only whispered.

"Wait for me," Max said. "Wait for me."

The light stayed small. It did not come closer. It never did.

Max walked home slow. The kettle was cold. He sat by the window. The fog ate the bridge. The green light was gone.

He waited for morning. He waited for the light. It never came to him. It only blinked, far off, where he could not go.

stories.name: Max

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
A kettle whistled on the stove. Max took it off the fire. The kitchen was warm. The window was gray. Fog sat on the glass like a wet hand.

Max set the kettle down. Steam climbed up. Then he saw it. Out past the river, on the bridge, a small light moved. It was far away. It was green.

Max left his tea. He ran down the hill. His shoes got sticky in the mud. He did not care. He climbed the ladder by the docks and stood on the wet boards.

The light was still there. He could not reach it. He wanted to hold it. He wanted it to hold him.

“Wait,” he said. “Wait. Wait.”

The fog took the bridge. The light grew faint. Max reached out with both hands. Nothing. Nothing.

He went home slow. The kettle was cold. The tea was still in the cup. It was very dark now. He never saw the light again.

stories.name: Max

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
A pot sat on the stove. Max turned the dial. The water began to sing. It rose to a whistle. Max did not move. Through the foggy night, a small green light waited on the bridge over the river. Max wanted it. He wanted it so much.

He said, "I want the light." He said it again. "I want the light." The kettle screamed. He said, "I want the light." He said it and said it.

He climbed down the fire ladder from his window. The fog was sticky on his face. He ran to the river. The little light stayed far away. He could not reach it. Not ever.

He tried to listen for the whistle. It was far behind him now. He said, "I want the light." The bridge was cold. The river was black. The light went out.

Max sat down on the bridge alone. He said one more time, very soft, "I want the light." Nobody heard him in the fog.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text: Right before bed, Ben put the kettle on. It whistled a high, happy song. Ben liked that sound. It meant warm tea was coming. His friend Mia came to the window. "Listen," she said. "The kettle is singing." They poured the tea and held the cups. The steam felt warm on Ben's face. Then Ben saw a small light. It sat on a roof across the town. It glowed green and steady. It looked like a tiny feather floating in the dark. Ben wished he could touch it. "Time for bed," said Mia. Ben said good night to the little light. He sipped his tea. The kettle was quiet now. The light stayed on the far roof. Ben could not reach it. He went to bed. But he thought of the green light, soft and far away.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
Right before bed, Ben put the kettle on. It whistled like a little bird. Ben liked that sound. It made the kitchen feel warm.

Ben looked out the window. Far away, on a roof across the town, a small green light was shining. It blinked once. Then again.

“Come see,” Ben said. His friend Max came over. They looked out together.

“What is it?” Max asked.

“I don’t know,” Ben said. “But I want to touch it.”

The kettle whistled again. Soft as a feather.

“Listen,” Max said. “The water is ready.”

Ben poured the tea. He tried to look away from the light. But it kept calling him back. It was so far. It was so small. It was so green.

“Maybe tomorrow,” Max said.

Ben nodded. He climbed into bed. The light still blinked across the town. He reached for it with one hand. It stayed far away. He closed his eyes. The whistle faded. The light did not.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
Right before bedtime, Ben put the kettle on. It began to whistle. Ben liked that sound. It made the kitchen feel warm.

Ben went to the window. Far away, on a roof across the town, he saw a small green light. It was soft and far. He wanted to touch it.

His friend Mia came over. "Listen," she said. "The kettle is still whistling."

Ben did not listen. He looked at the green light.

"You want that light," Mia said. "It is too far. It is like a feather in the wind."

Ben nodded. He reached out his hand. The light did not move.

"Come see the kettle," Mia said. "It is warm and close."

Ben looked at the light again. Then he went back to the kitchen. The kettle was quiet now. Mia gave him a warm cup.

The green light stayed on the roof. Ben could not have it. But Mia was there. That was good.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
Right before bedtime, Ben put the kettle on. It whistled a thin, happy song. Ben liked that sound. It felt warm and safe.

Then he saw it. A small green light, far away, on a roof across the town. It blinked once. Ben's hands went still.

"Ben," said his friend Ana. "The water is ready."

But Ben was at the window. The green light was so small, like a feather in the dark. He wanted to touch it. He wanted to hold it.

"Listen," Ana said. "The kettle is still whistling."

Ben heard it, but the light pulled him. He reached out. His fingers met cold glass.

"Come back," Ana said. She poured the tea. "It's warm. Sit with me."

Ben sat. He tried to sip. But his eyes kept going to the roof, to the little green light.

"Some lights stay far," Ana said.

Ben nodded. Still, he reached. Still, he reached. The kettle stopped. The light did not.

stories.name: Ben

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
Red kettle on the stove. Ben waits for it to whistle. It sings a soft song. Ben likes the warm sound.

Then Ben sees it. A small green light. It sits on a roof across the town. It blinks. It calls.

Ben wants it. He reaches out the window. His hand is empty. "Come back," he says.

His friend Sam comes. "Listen," Sam says. "The kettle."

Ben hears the kettle. But the green light shines. Ben wants it. He wants it.

Sam gives him a feather. "Soft," Sam says. "Like the light."

Ben holds the feather. He looks at the roof. The green light stays far. Always far.

"Bedtime," Sam says.

Ben nods. The kettle whistles. The green light shines. Ben reaches. He reaches. The light does not come.

He whispers, "I want it. I want it."

The kettle goes quiet. The green light stays on the roof across the town. Ben closes his eyes. He still sees it. Small. Green. Far. Far. Far.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: across a big field
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Mia and Nina found a magic ice cream cone. It never melted. It stayed cold and sweet all day. They put it in a jar for safe keeping.

Nina wanted to share it with her mom. But the jar was stuck. The lid would not turn. Nina felt gloomy.

Her friend Mia had an idea. She gave the jar a soft tap on the floor. Then another tap. Pop! The lid came loose.

Nina smiled. She gave her mom a big scoop. The magic cone still had plenty left. It was a good day.

Then Nina looked out her window. Just before bedtime, the sky was dark. Across a big field, a small green light blinked. It was far away. It glowed like a tiny star.

Nina reached her hand toward it. She could not touch it. She never could. She watched it for a moment. Then she pulled her curtain closed and climbed into bed.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: across a big field
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Mia got a magic ice cream cone at the fair. It never melted. It never ran out. Nina was her best friend. "Share it with me," Nina said. Mia gave her a lick. The cone tasted like stars.

Then the cone slipped. It fell in a jar by the sink. The jar was stuck. Nina tried to help. She gave the jar a soft tap. Nothing. Mia felt gloomy. "We broke it," she said.

Nina looked out the window. Across the big field, a small light blinked. It was green. It sat on a far porch. Nina wanted to touch it. She reached. Her hand felt only cold glass. The light stayed far away. She looked back at the jar. She turned the lid the other way. Pop! The cone came out.

"Good job," said Mia. They shared one more lick. It tasted like stars and mint. Before bedtime, Nina looked across the field. The green light blinked once. She wanted it. She could not have it. She pulled the curtain and went to bed.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: across a big field
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Mia found a magic ice cream cone in the park. It was pink and sparkly. One lick made her jump high. Two licks made her sing loud.

"I want to share it," said Nina. But the cone was small. Her friend Ben came to help. "Put it in a jar," he said. "We can save some for later."

Nina shook her head. She felt gloomy. The cone dripped on her shoe. Then she saw it. Across the big field, past the trees, a small green light glowed.

"What is that?" Nina asked. Ben said, "A porch light."

But Nina did not hear him. She wanted that light. It looked cool and sweet, like mint. She took one step.

"Nina," said Ben. "The cone is melting."

She tapped her foot. She wanted the light. She reached her hand out. She could not touch it. She wanted the light. She wanted the light. She wanted the light.

Ben tapped her arm. "Look," he said. The cone had stopped melting. It was still there, in her hand. "It waits for you," said Ben.

Nina looked once more at the far green light. Then she licked the cone. It was bedtime.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: across a big field
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Mmm, Nina loved her magic ice cream cone. It never melted. It gave her one new wish each day. Tonight she wished for a puppy.

Nina saw the small green light across the big field. It blinked far away. She wanted it. She tapped her foot. She felt gloomy.

"Help me, Ben," she said. Ben was her friend. "I want that light."

"You have your cone," said Ben. "That is enough."

Nina reached toward the light. It stayed far away. She could not have it. She tried again. She could not have it. The light just blinked and blinked.

"Please," she said. "Please, please, please."

Ben put the cone in a jar. He set it on her bed. "Look how it shines," he said.

Nina looked at the cone. It glowed soft and warm. She forgot the light. She wished for a puppy. Her little wish came true. The green light blinked alone across the field. Nina did not care. She had her puppy, and bedtime was near.

stories.name: Nina

axes.where: across a big field
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Mmm, Nina got a magic ice cream cone. It never melts. It tastes like stars. Her friend Ben came over. They put the cone in a jar.

Then a little problem came. The jar felt cold and gloomy. Nina did not want bedtime. She did not want to sleep.

She looked out the window. Across a big field, she saw a green light. It blinked. It called to her.

"I want that light," said Nina.

"You can't," said Ben. "It is far away."

"I want it," said Nina. "I want it. I want it."

She tapped the jar. The cone glowed. It did not help. The light stayed far.

Ben said, "Let's count to ten."

They counted. One, two, three. The green light got small. Four, five, six. The jar got warm. Seven, eight, nine. The cone hummed. Ten.

Nina yawned. The light was still there, far across the field. She could not have it. But she had her cone and her friend. She went to bed.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on the far side of the playground
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Maya found a magic ice cream cone. It never melted. It never ran out. She felt so proud.

She took it to the playground. She slid down the slide. She went on the swing. The cone stayed cold and sweet.

Then she saw a small light. It was green. It was on the far side of the playground. It blinked once. Maya looked away.

She played a drum on the bench. Boom, boom, boom. The light blinked again. She did not go to it.

Just before bedtime, her mom called her home. Maya held the cone tight. But the cone was just a plain cone now. The magic was gone. It had gone to the light.

Maya felt sad. She went to bed. She could not sleep. She wished she had run to the far side of the playground. But the light was gone too.

In the morning, the cone was magic again. Maya smiled. She knew the light would come back.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on the far side of the playground
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Maya found a magic ice cream cone. It never melted. It never shrank.

She licked the top. It tasted like pink. She licked the side. It tasted like stars.

Then she saw the green light. It sat on the far side of the playground. It was small and far away.

She went to the window. The green light blinked. She held her cone and watched it.

Her drum sat by the chair. She tapped it once. She did not want to drum.

She wanted the light. It was so close, but she could not go.

"Time for sleep," said Mom.

Maya ate one more lick. The cone was still big. It was proud of being magic.

Then she saw something. The green light was her night-light. It was right there in her room.

She felt silly and happy. She put the cone on her shelf.

The magic cone would not melt. It would wait for her.

Maya went to sleep. The green light stayed on.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on the far side of the playground
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Maya found a magic ice cream cone on the sidewalk. It was pink and cold and never melted. She licked it once. It tasted like strawberries and stars.

Then she saw the light. It was a small green light on the far side of the playground. It glowed near the swing set.

Maya held her cone and walked to the playground. The light blinked like a tiny drum. She wanted to touch it. She reached out. The light stayed far away.

She licked her cone again. It tasted like moon. She felt proud. But the light pulled her eyes back. It always did.

"Come here," she whispered. The light did not come.

Her mom called her home. It was just before bedtime. Maya had to sleep. She put the cone on her pillow.

She dreamed of the green light. In the dream, she held it.

When she woke up, the cone was gone. Only a small green dot was left on her pillow. It glowed. It did not melt. Maya smiled. She was still proud. But she could not reach it. She never could.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on the far side of the playground
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Maya found a magic ice cream cone. It never melted. It tasted like stars and rain.

She held it tight. She was so proud.

Then she saw the small green light. It was on the far side of the playground. It blinked once. Twice.

Maya forgot her cone. She walked to the light.

The light was soft and far away. She reached for it. Her hand went through it.

She heard a drum. Boom, boom. It came from the light.

Maya wanted the light. She wanted it more than the cone. She wanted it more than sleep.

She reached again. The light stayed far away.

Then she looked down. Her magic cone was gone. Her hands were empty.

The light blinked one last time. Then it went out.

Maya sat on the grass. It was just before bedtime. She felt a tap on her hand. The cone was back. It was small and cold now. It was just a plain cone.

She held it anyway. She was still proud.

stories.name: Maya

axes.where: on the far side of the playground
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Maya had a magic ice cream cone. It never melted. It never got small.

Maya held it on the swing. She felt like a drum in her chest.

Then she saw the green light. It was on the far side of the playground. It was just before bedtime.

The light was small and far away. Maya wanted it. She wanted it more than ice cream.

She reached. She could not touch it.

"Mine," she said. "Mine. Mine."

The ice cream dripped on her hand. But it was not ice cream. It was only a wish.

Maya said, "Mine." She said it like a drum. She said it like a song.

Her mom said, "Time for sleep."

Maya did not want sleep. She wanted the light. She was not proud. She was small and far away.

She reached. She reached.

The light stayed on the far side of the playground.

Then the light blinked. It was a firefly. It flew away.

Maya held her empty hand. She went to sleep.

stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: in a tent across the camp

stories.text:
A magic ice cream cone sat in Rosa's hand. It never melted. Not even on a snowy day.

"Eat it," said her brother. "Before it turns to soup."

"It is magic," said Rosa. "It waits."

She licked the top. It tasted like egg and sugar and cold.

"I wish for more," she said. The cone grew taller. Now it was a tower of sweet, sticky cream. Rosa laughed.

She ate and ate. Her nose turned pink. Her toes felt warm.

Then she looked across the camp. In a tent far away, a small lamp glowed. It was pale and green, like a leaf under ice. Rosa stopped chewing.

That light never came closer. It just stayed there, small and far.

"Want some?" she asked the tent.

No one answered.

Rosa put the cone down. She walked to the tent and peeked inside. A little boy sat alone.

"Here," she said. She broke the cone in two. "It is magic. It never runs out."

They ate together. The green light grew warm and close. Rosa did not need a wish anymore.

stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: in a tent across the camp

stories.text:
A magic ice cream cone sat in Rosa’s hand. It never melted, even on a snowy day. The white flakes fell on the pink scoop and slid off like tiny beads.

Rosa licked the cold, sweet swirl. It tasted like a birthday. Her boots made soft crunch sounds in the snow.

“Where did you find that?” asked her friend Ben.

“A lady gave it to me,” said Rosa. “She said it holds one wish.”

Ben laughed. “Ice cream can’t do that.”

Rosa took another bite. The cone felt warm inside her mittens. She saw an egg fall from a bird’s nest and land safe in a pile of soft snow.

Then she saw it. Across the camp, a small light glowed inside a tent. It was green and steady. It looked like a tiny star caught in cloth. Rosa wanted to walk to it. She wanted to hold it. But her feet stayed put.

“I wish for that light,” she whispered.

The cone grew sticky. It dripped one green drop onto the snow. The drop rolled toward the tent. Rosa followed it.

Inside, Ben’s grandma held a lantern with a green scarf over it. “You found my lost light,” she said.

Rosa smiled. Her wish was warm and close.

stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: in a tent across the camp

stories.text:
A magic ice cream cone came to Rosa on a snowy day. It never melted. It stayed cold and sweet in her red mittens. She took one small lick. Then the wind blew.

Across the camp, a tent glowed. A little light inside it blinked. It was green and soft. Rosa wanted to hold it. She could not.

"Do not go," said her friend Tom. "The snow is deep."

"I just want to see," Rosa said.

She put the cone in her pocket. It felt sticky. She pulled it out again. She licked it once more. The light blinked. It was so far away.

"Maybe the light is a star," Tom said.

"Stars do not live in tents," Rosa said.

She wished on the cone. She wished to reach the little green glow. Her wish did not come true. The light stayed in the tent. It always stayed.

Then Tom brought a warm egg from his pocket. "For you," he said. "It is not a light. But it is warm."

Rosa smiled. She ate the egg. The cone stayed in her hand. The green light blinked. She watched it until bedtime. Then she was happy anyway.

stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: in a tent across the camp

stories.text:
A magic ice cream cone sat in Rosa’s mittens. It never melted. On a snowy day, that was a fine trick. She licked the cold sweet swirl. It tasted like cherry and snow.

“Do you want a bite?” Rosa asked her friend Ben.

“No,” said Ben. “That cone is not right.”

Rosa shrugged. She held it up. The cone glowed. Across the camp, past the tents, one tent shone with a soft light. It was small and green. It hummed like a bee in a jar.

Rosa wanted it. She wanted it more than the cone. She wanted it more than supper. She wanted it more than her warm socks.

“Come see,” she said.

“See what?” said Ben.

“That light. In the tent.”

“There is no tent there,” said Ben. “Only snow.”

Rosa walked. The snow crunched like egg shells. Her cone dripped a sticky drop. She wished on that drop. I want to hold that light, she thought. I want it. I want it. I want it.

The tent flap opened. Inside sat a little lamp. It was green and warm. An old woman smiled.

“You wished,” she said. “Here is your wish.”

Rosa held the lamp. It was light and happy. Her cone was gone. But she did not care.

stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: in a tent across the camp

stories.text:
A magic ice cream cone was in Rosa's hand. It never melted. It tasted like sweet snow. Rosa sat in her tent on a snowy day. She licked the cold, creamy top. Her fingers felt sticky.

Then she saw it. Across the camp, inside a tent, a little green light glowed. It was soft and far away.

"I wish I could hold that light," Rosa said.

"It is too far," said her friend.

"I wish it," Rosa said again. "I wish it. I wish it."

She held her cone tight. The magic ice cream dripped one shiny drop. It looked like an egg. The drop rolled toward the tent with the light.

"I wish it. I wish it," Rosa whispered.

She ran across the snow. Her boots went crunch, crunch. The light stayed far. It always stayed far. She said it over and over. "I wish it. I wish it."

Then her friend came. "Look," he said. "Your cone is glowing."

Rosa looked down. Her ice cream shone with a little green gleam. It was her own small light. She could hold it. She could lick it. She laughed.

"I wish no more," she said. And she was happy.

stories.name: Ada

axes.where: high up on a mountain
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Little Ada found a magic ice cream cone in the snow. It was pink and did not melt. One lick made her warm. Two licks made her laugh. Three licks made her float!

"Oh no," said Ada. "I am up high!" She held her pail and looked down. The snow was far away.

Ada wanted to go home. She licked the cone again. Nothing. She licked it more. Still nothing. Her hands were so cold.

Then she saw a small bird. The bird sat on a rock. High up on the mountain, a green light shone. It was far away and very bright. Ada tried to reach it. She could not. The light stayed far.

"Please help me," Ada said to the bird. The bird sang a soft song. The cone grew small. Ada floated down, down, down. She landed in the soft snow by her house.

Her mama gave her warm milk. Ada was happy. She put the little cone in her pail. The green light blinked far away on the mountain. Ada waved good night to it.

stories.name: Ada

axes.where: high up on a mountain
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Little Ada found a magic ice cream cone in the snow. It never melted. It stayed cold and sweet.

She put it in her pail. She wanted to share it with her mom.

But the wind blew the pail away. It rolled up the hill.

"Oh no," said Ada. "My cone!"

She ran after it. The snow was deep. Her feet were cold.

High on the mountain, a small light glowed. It was green and far away. Ada looked up. She wished she could reach it. But it was too high.

She climbed and climbed. Her pail was stuck on a rock. She got it back.

The magic cone was safe inside. Ada smiled.

Then she saw the light again. It twinkled like a tiny star. She waved at it. It felt like a friend.

At home, she gave the cone to her mom. They shared it. It tasted like happy dreams.

The green light stayed on the mountain. Ada could not touch it. But she was warm and glad.

stories.name: Ada

axes.where: high up on a mountain
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Look, Ada found a magic ice cream cone. It never melts. It tastes like sweet snow. Ada licked it once and smiled.

On a snowy day, Ada took her pail to the hill. She wanted to share the cone with her friend. But the wind blew. The cone rolled away. It rolled up, up, up. It stopped high up on a mountain.

Ada tried to climb. The rocks were too high. She could not reach. Her hands felt cold. She was sad.

Then she saw a light. It was green and small, high up on the mountain. It glowed near her cone. Ada wanted that light. She wished she could hold it. But it was too far. The light was always too far.

Ada sat down. She thought and thought. Then she had an idea. She used her pail to scoop soft snow. She made a tall snow stair. Step by step, she climbed. At last she got her cone back.

The green light blinked once. Then it went away. Ada did not need it. She had her cone. She and her friend ate it together. Ada was happy.

stories.name: Ada

axes.where: high up on a mountain
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Little Ada found a magic ice cream cone in the snow. It never melted. It tasted like sweet berries. Ada wanted to share it with her mom.

She filled her pail with snow to keep it cold. The cone stayed perfect. Ada smiled.

Then a big wind blew. The cone rolled away. It rolled up the hill. Ada ran after it. Her hands were cold. She could not reach it.

The cone stopped high up on a mountain. Ada looked up. She saw a small green light shining there. It blinked in the white snow.

“I want that light,” said Ada. “I want it.”

She climbed. She slipped. She got up. The green light stayed far away.

“I want it. I want it,” she said again and again.

Then Ada had an idea. She held up her pail. The light jumped inside!

The green light became a tiny green star. It made the cone come back down. Ada picked it up.

She went home and ate the cone with her mom. The green star sat on the windowsill. Ada was happy.

stories.name: Ada

axes.where: high up on a mountain
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Late one snowy day, Ada found a magic ice cream cone. It never melted. It always tasted like her favorite sweet things. She put it in her pail and ran outside.

Then she saw the light. High up on the mountain, a small green light shone. It was so far away. It was so high. Ada wanted it.

She said, "I want the light. I want the light. I want the light."

The snow was cold. Her hands were cold. But she did not care. She climbed up. She tried to reach the light. The light did not move. It just shone.

Her pail tipped over. The magic cone rolled in the snow. Ada did not look at it. She only looked up. She said, "I want the light. I want the light. I want the light."

Then she sat down. She was tired. She was cold. She was sad. She held her pail.

Her little dog came. He licked her hand. She laughed. She picked up her magic cone. It still tasted sweet. The tiny green light still shone far away. But Ada went home happy.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
One morning Hugo got a magic ice cream cone. It was pink and blue and never melted. He licked it once. It tasted like strawberries and stars.

Hugo ran to the park. The moon was still up. The park was quiet. He climbed the slide and ate his cone. The slide was cold and fun.

Then Hugo saw a fence. On the other side of the fence was a small green light. It blinked and blinked. Hugo wanted to hold it. He put his hand on the fence. The light was too far away.

Hugo sat down. He licked his cone again. The magic ice cream made him feel warm. He did not need the light. He had his cone.

A bird came. The bird sang a song. Hugo smiled. He shared a tiny drop of ice cream with the bird. The bird flew up. The sun came up. Hugo went home happy.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
One morning Hugo found a magic ice cream cone. It was pink and blue. It never melted. Every lick made a new flavor. Hugo was so happy.

The sun was not up yet. The moon was still in the sky. It was very quiet. Hugo saw a small light. It was green. It was on the other side of a fence.

Hugo wanted that light. He reached his hand through the fence. He could not touch it. The light was too far.

Hugo sat on his slide. He licked his ice cream. He looked at the light. The light did not move.

"Come here, light," said Hugo. The light stayed far away.

Hugo ate more ice cream. It tasted like strawberries. He felt warm. He forgot the light for a bit. Then he saw it again. It was still green. It was still far.

Hugo smiled. He did not need the light. He had his magic cone. He licked it one more time. It tasted like morning. The moon went away. The sun came up. Hugo was happy.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
One morning, Hugo found a magic ice cream cone. It was pink and blue and did not melt. He licked it once. It tasted like stars.

Hugo ran to the park to show everyone. The park was quiet. The moon was still up in the sky. He held his cone and smiled.

Then he saw it. On the other side of the fence, a small green light was glowing. It blinked and blinked. Hugo wanted it.

He climbed the slide to look closer. The light was still far away. He reached over the fence, but his arms were too short.

"I want that light," Hugo said. He said it again. "I want that light."

He forgot his ice cream cone. He forgot the stars. He just looked at the green light. It was so pretty and so far.

Then his mom came. "Hugo, look!" she said. The magic cone had grown a tiny green star on top. It glowed just like the light.

Hugo laughed. He held his cone close. The little green light came to him after all.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
One morning Hugo found a magic ice cream cone. It never melted. It tasted like stars and honey. Hugo licked it once. Then he licked it again.

Across the yard, past the fence, a small light glowed. It was early morning. The moon was still up. The light was green. It sat on the other side of the fence.

Hugo wanted that light. He wanted it more than the ice cream. He walked to the fence. The light was so close. He reached through the bars. He could not touch it.

"Come here," Hugo said. "Come here, light."

He forgot the ice cream. It dripped on his shoe. He did not care. He only looked at the light.

He climbed the slide to see it better. The slide was cold and quiet. The light stayed on the other side.

"Come here," he said again. "Come here."

Then his mom came out. She saw the light too. "That is the sun," she said. "It is waking up."

The green light grew big and warm. It came over the fence. It touched Hugo's face. Hugo laughed. He ate his magic ice cream in the sun.

stories.name: Hugo

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text: One morning Hugo found a magic ice cream cone. It was pink and blue and never melted. He licked it once, and his shoes felt warm. He licked it twice, and he could jump very high. Then Hugo saw a small green light on the other side of a fence. The light was far away. It was early morning, and the moon was still up. Hugo forgot his ice cream. He wanted the light. He walked to the fence and put his hand on it. The light was so pretty. It was green and soft. He wanted the light. He wanted the light. He sat on the slide and looked at the light. The yard was quiet. He wanted the light. He wanted the light. He did not want his ice cream. He only wanted the light. Then his little dog came and licked his hand. Hugo laughed. He looked at his cone. It was still pink and blue. He took a big bite. The magic made him warm and happy. The green light stayed far away, but Hugo was glad. He and his dog played on the slide in the quiet morning.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
Rushing to the slide, Leo climbed the warm steps. The playground was almost empty. Just before bedtime, the sky turned soft and blue.

Leo sat at the top. The slide went down, down, down. It was his favorite thing. But he did not go.

His friend Mia waited at the bottom. "Come on, Leo!" she called. "You can do it!"

Leo held the rail. He felt a little scared. Mia ran up the steps. She was kind and brave.

"I will help you," Mia said. "We can fix your brave face together."

Leo smiled. He let go. Down he went, fast and happy. Mia slid after him.

Then Leo saw a small green light, far away on top of a hill. It blinked like a tiny star. He wished he could touch it. But it was too far.

"Time for bed," said Mia.

They walked to the door of his house. Leo looked back once. The green light still shone. He waved goodnight, then went inside.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
Right before bedtime, Leo went to the playground. He loved the big slide. It was tall and shiny. Leo climbed up the steps. Whee! Down he went. Again and again he slid.

Then Leo saw a small green light. It sat on top of a far hill. The light blinked soft and slow. Leo wanted to touch it. He reached out his hand. But the hill was too far away.

His friend Mia came to play. "Come slide with me," she said. Leo looked at the light once more. It was so pretty. He wished he could have it. But he could not.

"Let's fix the slide race," Mia said. They raced down side by side. Leo laughed. The light was still there, far away. It made him feel quiet and kind of sad.

Mia took his hand. "Time to go home," she said. They walked to the door. Leo turned back one last time. The green light blinked goodnight. He waved. Then he went inside to bed.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
Rushing to the playground before bedtime, Leo climbed the slide. Up he went, then down. Up and down. The slide was warm from the sun.

Then Leo saw it. A small green light on top of a far hill. It blinked once. Leo wanted it.

"Come slide again," said his friend Mia.

"I want that light," said Leo.

Mia was kind. She took his hand. "The slide is here. The light is far."

Leo went down the slide. But he looked back at the hill. The green light stayed small and far away.

"Time for bed," said Mia. She walked him to his door.

Leo tried to fix his eyes on the slide. But the light pulled him. He reached out. He could not touch it.

In bed, Leo closed his eyes. The green light was still there. Small. Far. His.

Mia waved from the window. "Good night, Leo."

Leo waved back. The light blinked once more, then faded behind the hill.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
Right before bedtime, Leo ran to the playground slide. It was his favorite thing. Up the steps, down the slide, up and down, up and down. His friend Mia helped him climb when his legs were tired.

Then Leo saw it. On top of a far hill, a small green light was shining. It was just one dot, far away, blinking soft and slow.

"Come slide again," Mia said.

But Leo looked at the light. "I want it," he said. He reached his hand toward the hill.

"You can't reach that," Mia said.

"I want it," Leo said again. "I want it. I want it."

Mia pulled him to the slide. He went down once. He did not laugh. He turned back to the light. "I want it," he said.

Mia took his hand. "Time for bed," she said. "The door is open. Your mom is kind. She will fix your blanket."

Leo walked home, but his eyes stayed on the far hill. The small green light blinked. He wanted it. He wanted it. He wanted it.

stories.name: Leo

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text: Right before bedtime, Leo went down the playground slide. It was smooth and fast. His friend Mia clapped for him. Then Leo saw a small green light on top of a far hill. It blinked once. Leo wanted it. “I want that light,” he said. Mia said, “Time for bed.” Leo ran to the door. He looked at the hill. “I want that light. I want that light.” Mia said, “I can fix your slide tomorrow.” Leo said, “I want that light.” She was kind and held his hand. “The light is too far,” she said. Leo said, “I want that light. I want that light.” He reached for it. His fingers touched only air. Mia led him inside. He kept saying it. “I want that light. I want that light.” The light stayed on the hill. Leo could not have it. Mia tucked him in. He whispered it one more time.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text: When the rain stopped, Tess ran to the playground slide. She wore her yellow hat. The slide was wet and shiny. "Wait for me!" she said. Her friend Ben climbed up too. They slid down fast. "Again!" Tess said. They played and played. Then the wind blew hard. The sky got dark again. Tess looked up. At the very top of a tall tree, a small green light was shining. It blinked in the wind. Tess wanted to touch it. She reached up, but the tree was too tall. "Come on," Ben said. "It is not sunny. Let's go home." Tess did not move. The green light blinked and blinked. Her mom came and gave her a hug. "Time to go," Mom said. Tess looked back one more time. The light was still there, far away. She held her hat and walked home.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
When the rain stopped, Tess ran to the playground slide. The slide was wet and shiny. She climbed up the ladder. Whoosh! Down she went, fast and happy.

Then she saw it. A small green light, high in a tall tree. It blinked once, twice. Tess held her hat and looked up.

"Come down," she said. The light did not come down.

She went down the slide again. Whoosh! But her eyes went back to the tree. The green light was still there, far away.

"Are you a star?" she asked. The wind blew. The light only blinked.

Tess wished for a sunny day. She wished the light could be hers. But it stayed high, where her hands could never reach.

Her mom came and gave her a hug. "Time to go home," Mom said.

"Goodbye, little light," Tess said. She waved her hat. The light blinked one last time. Tess walked home, slow and quiet.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
When the rain stopped, Tess ran to the playground slide. It was wet and shiny. She climbed up the ladder. She went down fast. "Again!" she said.

Then she saw it. A small green light, high in the tall tree. It blinked in the wind.

"What is that?" Tess said. She held her hat so it would not fly away.

"Come slide!" said her friend May.

Tess went down the slide. But her eyes went back to the tree. The green light was still there. It looked warm. It looked kind.

"I want to touch it," Tess said.

"You cannot," said May. "It is too high."

The wind blew. Tess felt cold. She wanted the light. She did not want the slide. She reached up, but the tree was far away.

Then Mom came. She gave Tess a big hug. "The sky is not sunny today," Mom said. "Let's go home."

Tess looked one more time. The green light blinked and blinked. She could not reach it. She never could.

"Bye, light," she said.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
When the rain came, Tess ran to the playground slide. She held her hat on her head. The slide was wet and cold. She did not care. She wanted to slide.

Then she saw it. High up in the tall tree, a green light shone. It was small and bright. It did not flicker in the wind.

"Come on, Tess," said her mom. "Let's go home."

Tess did not hear. She looked up at the light. It looked like a sunny day trapped in a storm.

"Tess, take my hug," said her mom.

Tess took the hug. But her eyes stayed on the tree. The green light blinked once. Then twice.

"I want it," Tess whispered.

She reached up. Her hand touched only rain.

The light stayed in the tree. It was so far away. Tess reached again. Her hat fell off into a puddle.

The light did not come down. Tess stood in the rain. She reached and reached and reached. The slide was behind her now. Only the light was left.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: at the very top of a tall tree

stories.text:
When the rain came, Tess ran to the playground slide. She wore her red hat. The slide was wet and cold.

Then she saw it. A small green light, high in the tall tree. It glowed in the storm.

"Come down," Tess said. "Please come down."

The light did not come down.

Tess climbed the slide. She reached up. The wind blew her hat.

"Can I hug you?" she said. "I want to hug you."

The light stayed far away.

On a sunny day, the light would hide. But not today.

Tess reached again. "Come here," she said. "Come here. Come here."

Her hands were small. The tree was tall.

The light shone and shone.

She did not want the slide. She did not want her hat.

She only wanted the light.

The rain fell. The thunder boomed.

Tess whispered, "Come here. Come here. Come here."

The light did not move.

A hug was not enough. Nothing was enough.

The slide was empty. The tree was tall. The little green light burned far away, and Tess reached for it, and reached, and reached.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
Here is the slide. Eli climbs the steps. The slide is cold and wet. He sits down. Whoosh. He lands on his feet. "Again," says Eli. He runs to the door of the play castle. The slide waits.

Up he goes. The morning is quiet. He can see the town. He can see a tower far away. A small light shines on top. It looks like a tiny star. It does not move. It does not float. It just stays.

"Come on, Eli," says his mom. "One more time."

Eli slides down. The wind makes his hair go up. He laughs. The ground is lumpy under his feet. He looks up. The light is still there. He wants to touch it. But it is too far.

"Time to go," says Mom.

Eli waves at the tower. "Bye," he says. The light keeps shining. He holds his mom's hand. They walk home. The slide is behind him now. The light is too. But he thinks of it. Just a little.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
Here is Eli at the slide. The slide is cold and wet. He climbs up the little steps. He holds the rail. He sits down. Whoosh! Down he goes.

"Again," Eli says.

"One more time," says his mom.

The sun comes up. The sky turns pink. Eli looks past the fence. He sees the tower far away. A tiny light is on top. It is a soft green dot. It looks like a small door left open. Eli wishes he could float over there. But it is too far.

He goes down the slide again. The ground is lumpy with old leaves. He thinks about the light.

"Mom, what is that light?"

"I don't know, sweetie."

Eli climbs the slide again. The green dot stays on the tower. He cannot touch it. He cannot reach it. It just sits there, blinking slow. He goes down the slide, but he keeps looking back.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
Henry pushed the door open and ran to the slide. Eli ran after him. The slide was cold and wet from the night. Eli climbed the steps anyway.

"Watch me!" Henry called. He slid down fast. "Your turn, Eli."

But Eli did not slide. He looked past the fence. Far away stood a tall tower. On top of it, a small light was still on. It was pale green. It was the color of new leaves in spring.

"Eli, slide!" said Henry.

Eli slid down once. It felt lumpy and slow. He climbed up again. He looked at the tower. The light did not move. He wished he could float over there. He wished he could touch it.

"Come on, Eli," Henry said. "You are not even sliding."

Eli slid one more time. Then he stood still. The light blinked once. His heart felt big and strange. He wanted that far green light more than the slide. He knew he could never reach it. Still, he looked.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
Here is the story.  
Eli went to the playground slide. The sun was just up. The air felt cold and clean. He ran to the ladder. Up he went. Down he slid. “Again!” Eli said. He slid again. And again. His mom sat on a bench. She drank coffee.  
Then Eli saw it. A tiny green light on a tower far away. It was so far. It looked like a small door left open. It seemed to float in the gray sky. The light did not move.  
“Mom, look,” Eli said. “See the light?”  
“That’s far away, sweetie,” she said. “Watch your feet.”  
Eli slid down the slide. But his eyes went back to the tower. The light was still there. It was a lumpy green dot. He wanted to reach it. He wanted to touch it.  
“Come slide,” his mom said.  
“I want the light,” Eli said.  
He slid again. He climbed again. His hands felt the cold bars. But he thought of the light. The light. The light. Always the light.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: on a tower far away

stories.text:
Here is the slide. Eli climbs the little ladder. He goes down fast. Whee! He goes down again and again.

Then he stops. He sees the sky. The sky is pink and soft. Far away is a tower. On the tower is a little green light. It is small like a pea. It calls to Eli.

"Come see," says the light.

"I can't," says Eli. "You float too high."

The light is not a lamp. It is not a star. It is a door he cannot open. He wants it. He wants it. He wants it so much.

"Eli," says Mom. "Come home."

But Eli watches the light. His feet feel lumpy and slow. His heart goes up, up, up. He whispers, "I want to touch you. I want to touch you. I want to touch you."

The slide is cold now. The light stays far away. Eli holds the rail. The light is his secret.

"Please," he says. "Please."

stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: across the snowy yard

stories.text:
Bumpy steps led up to the big slide. Ravi climbed them one by one. The playground was his favorite place.

He sat down at the top. Whoosh! Down he went. The wind made his hair go back. He laughed and clapped.

Ravi found a good stick on the ground. He drew a curly line in the snow. Then he did a spin. He fell down in the soft snow and giggled.

Across the snowy yard, a small light glowed on a porch. It was green and far away. Ravi looked at it for a moment. It looked pretty and cold. Then he turned back to his stick.

He climbed the slide again. Up, up, up. Whoosh! Down again. His mom called him for lunch. Ravi waved to the slide. He took his stick home. The green light stayed far away, but Ravi did not mind. He had a warm lunch and a happy heart.

stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: across the snowy yard

stories.text:
Ben and Ravi ran to the playground slide. The sun was warm on their faces. Ravi climbed the steps. He sat down. Whoosh! He went down fast.

"Again!" Ravi said.

He climbed up. He held the cold rail. Down he went. His hair went curly in the wind.

"You can stick the landing!" Ben said.

They took turns. Ravi did a little spin at the bottom. One more time, then home.

Then Ravi saw it. Across the snowy yard, a small green light shone on a bush. It was far away. It blinked in the sun.

"What is that?" Ravi said.

He looked and looked. He wanted to go touch it. But the snow was deep.

"Come on," said Ben.

Ravi went down the slide one last time. He looked across the yard again. The green light was still there.

"Let's go home," said Ravi.

They walked away. The light stayed across the snowy yard. Ravi smiled. He did not need it. He had his friend and the slide. That was enough.

stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: across the snowy yard

stories.text:
Ben pushed Ravi on the swing. The slide was next. It was tall and curly and blue. Ravi climbed up, up, up. He went whoosh down. He was happy.

Then Ravi saw it. A small green light across the snowy yard. It sat on a stick by the fence. It shone like a tiny star.

"Come on," said Ben. "Let's spin on the slide again."

Ravi slid down one more time. But his eyes went back to the yard. The green light blinked. It made his chest feel funny.

"Ravi, you are not looking," said Ben.

"I want that light," said Ravi. "It is so small and bright. I want to hold it."

He tried. He ran to the fence. The light stayed far away. He ran and ran. His boots got wet.

Ben came and took his hand. "The slide is more fun. Watch me spin!"

Ravi laughed. He climbed the curly slide again. Down he went, fast and happy. The green light blinked far away. It was pretty. But his friend was here. That was better.

stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: across the snowy yard

stories.text:
Ben loves the playground slide. Ravi loves it too. The slide is tall and shiny. It goes down, down, down. Ravi climbs up the steps. He sits at the top. Whee! He slides fast to the ground.

Then Ravi sees a light. It is across the snowy yard. The light is small and green. It sits on a stick by the fence. Ravi wants to touch it.

He walks to the fence. His boots go crunch, crunch. The light shines and shines. It makes a curly little glow on the snow. Ravi reaches out. His hand is too short.

"Come here, light," says Ravi. "Come here, light. Come here, light." He says it again and again. He cannot stop.

His mom calls him. "Ravi, come slide!"

Ravi turns back. He slides down once. Then he looks at the light. He slides down twice. He looks at the light. He wants to spin it in his hand. He cannot.

Then his big sister picks him up. She carries him to the fence. "Look," she says. "It is just a pretty light." Ravi laughs. He is happy.

stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: across the snowy yard

stories.text:
Ben loves the slide at the playground. The slide is tall and shiny. Ravi climbs up the steps. He sits down at the top. Whee! Down he goes.

But then Ravi sees it. Across the snowy yard, a small green light shines. It blinks on a big house.

Ravi wants that light. He wants it so much. He forgets the slide. He walks to the fence. The snow is cold.

"I want the light," says Ravi. "I want the light. I want the light."

He finds a stick. He pokes the snow. He wants to reach the light. The light does not come closer.

His friend Mia runs over. She has a curly hat. They spin around in the snow.

"Look," says Mia. She points at the slide. The sun makes it glow.

Ravi looks at the slide. He looks at the light. The light is far away. The slide is right here.

Ravi runs back. He climbs up. Down he goes! He laughs. The slide is fun. The light can stay where it is.

stories.name: Anya

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
A slide waited at the playground. Anya ran to it after school. The slide was bumpy and warm from the sun.

"Watch me!" she called to her mom.

She climbed up and sat down. Then she went down fast. Her hair flew up like a bird.

Anya went down again and again. She did not want to stop. But the sun went down low.

"Time to go," said her mom.

Anya held her bucket and walked home. The path went by the woods. The woods were dark and deep.

Then Anya saw a small light. It was far away. It was soft and green. It looked like a tiny star on the ground.

"What is that?" she asked.

"Just a firefly," said her mom.

But it was not a firefly. The light did not move. It just stayed there. It made a little glow.

Anya wanted to roll down the hill to it. She wanted to touch it. But her mom took her hand.

"Come on," said her mom.

Anya walked away. She looked back one time. The light was still there. It was waiting. She never went to it.

stories.name: Anya

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text: At the playground, Anya loved the tall slide. It was bumpy and hot from the sun. She held her bucket at the bottom. Up the steps she went. Down she went, fast and happy. "Again!" she said. "One more time." The sky turned orange. Her mom said, "We go home now." Anya slid once more. Then she saw a small light in the dark of the woods. It was green and soft. It did not move. She took one step. Then two. "Anya, come here," said her mom. Anya did not roll down the slide again. She walked to the car. But she looked back. The light was still there. Every night she thought of it. She grew tall. She had a job. She had a dog. But some evenings she went to the woods alone. She never found the light. She only found trees. "I am here," she said. No one said it back.

stories.name: Anya

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
A slide stood in the playground. Anya loved it. Up the ladder, down the silver slide. Again and again.

At sunset, the sky turned pink and gold. Anya looked past the fence. Deep in the dark of the woods, a small light blinked. It was pale and far away. It looked like a tiny moon.

"Come on, Anya," said her mom. "Time to go."

Anya did not move. The light seemed to say her name.

She ran to the woods. The ground was bumpy. Roots tripped her feet. She fell and cut her knee.

"Wait for me," she whispered. "Please wait."

The light stayed far. It did not come closer. It never did.

Her mom caught her arm. "Anya, stop. We must go home."

Anya filled her bucket with tears. She wanted to roll down the hill and land near the light. But the woods grew black. The light went out.

Mom carried her home. Anya looked back one last time. The woods were dark and empty. The light was gone.

stories.name: Anya

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
A slide is a happy thing at the playground. Anya climbs the ladder. She sits down. The slide is bumpy and warm from the sun. She goes down fast. Then she does it again.

But the woods are right there. The sun is going down. The trees are dark. Something in the trees is small and green and far away. It shines like a tiny light left on.

"Come on," her mom says. "It's late."

"In a minute," Anya says.

She holds her bucket of chalk. She lets it roll on the ground. She looks at the trees again. The little light is still there. It does not come closer.

"Anya."

"Just one more slide."

She climbs up. The light watches her. She goes down slow. Her shoes drag on the bumpy plastic. At the bottom, she looks up.

The light is gone. The woods are all black now.

"Mom," Anya says. "Where did it go?"

"The fireflies are done for tonight," her mom says.

Anya wants to say that is not what it was. But she has no words. She takes her bucket. She walks home. The slide stands empty in the dark.

stories.name: Anya

axes.where: in the dark of the woods

stories.text:
A slide stood in the playground. Anya climbed the bumpy steps. She held her little bucket. Down she went. "Again!" she said. Her mom said, "One more, then home."

The sun went down. The slide turned gray. Anya saw a light in the dark of the woods. It was small and green.

"Mom, look."

"I don't see it," Mom said.

Anya walked to the trees. The light blinked. She left her bucket. She did not roll down the slide again.

"Come back," Mom said.

Anya reached. The light stayed far. She reached and reached. The slide sat empty.

"Please," she said.

The light did not come close. It only shone. Her mom called her name. Anya did not turn. The woods got darker. The green light stayed where it was. She never touched it. She never went back to the slide.

stories.name: June

axes.where: on a pole by the gate

stories.text:
Here is a fisherman and a boot. The fisherman was June. June sat on the dock. The sun was hot. It was a hot summer day.

June ate bread. She felt sleepy. She did not want to lift her head. She wanted a fish. She did not want a boot.

Then she saw a little light. It was on a pole by the gate. The light was green. It was small and far. June looked at it. She wanted to touch it. She could not.

She pulled up her line. She got a boot. The boot was old. It had no fish. June was sad.

She looked at the green light again. It was still far. She held the boot. The boot was heavy. The light did not move. June went home.

stories.name: June

axes.where: on a pole by the gate

stories.text:
Hat on her head, June went to fish. It was a hot summer day. She had bread in her bag and a sleepy smile. The fish were not biting. Her line pulled up a boot. It was old and brown. She did not want a boot. She wanted a fish.

Then she saw it. A small green light, on a pole by the gate. It blinked in the hot sun. June felt a lift in her chest. She wanted to touch it. She rowed her boat to the gate. The light was still far. She rowed more. Her arms hurt.

The green light stayed small. It did not come closer. She forgot the boot. She forgot the bread. She just looked at the light. She was so sleepy now.

The sun went down. The green light grew bright, then went out. June sat in her boat. She had no fish. She had only the old boot. She held it and cried.

stories.name: June

axes.where: on a pole by the gate

stories.text:
Here is June the fisherman. She sits on the dock on a hot summer day. She wants to catch a fish. She pulls up a boot. It is old and brown. June puts a piece of bread in the boot. She waits. The sun is hot. She feels sleepy.

By the gate, a pole holds a small green light. It shines. June sees it. She wants to touch it. She cannot. The dock is too far.

She pulls up the boot again. No fish. She looks at the light. It is so bright. She tries to lift her hand. The light is too far.

June waits and waits. She puts more bread in the boot. The light glows on the pole. She wants it so much. She cannot have it.

The sun goes down. The light still shines. June is sad. She has no fish. She holds the old boot. The green light is far away. She will never reach it.

stories.name: June

axes.where: on a pole by the gate

stories.text:
Hot sun beat down on the dock. June the fisherman pulled up her net. Inside was one old boot. No fish. No crab. Just a boot.

She put it in her bucket. She ate dry bread for lunch. The day made her sleepy.

Then she saw it. A small green light, far away, on a pole by the gate. It shone like a tiny star in the heat.

June stood up. She forgot the boot. She walked off the dock. Her feet took her up the road.

“I can lift my hand,” she said. “I can touch it.”

She lifted her hand. The light stayed far. She walked more. The light stayed far.

The boot sat in her bucket back at the dock. The bread was gone. The sun went down.

June came back late. Her bucket was empty. The boot was gone. The gate was dark. No green light.

She sat on the dock. She had no fish. No boot. No light. She was sleepy and sad.

stories.name: June

axes.where: on a pole by the gate

stories.text:
Hot sun on the water. June sat on the dock. She had a pole and a boot. The boot was old and brown. She did not want a boot. She wanted a fish. She put bread on her hook. She was sleepy. The sun was hot.

Then she saw it. The light was on a pole by the gate. It was small and green. It shone in the hot day.

June forgot the boot. She forgot the bread. She did not want a fish. She wanted the light.

She got up. She walked to the gate. She tried to lift her hand. The light was so far. The pole was so high.

"Come here," she said. "Come here. Come here."

The light did not come. The sun went down. The light stayed on the pole. June sat by the gate. She was sleepy. She was sad. She never got the light.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: on top of a far hill
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Going out on the water, Finn fished all day. He caught a fish. He caught a can. Then he caught a boot. The boot was old and brown. "Silly boot," said Finn. "You are not a fish." He put the boot in his boat.

A frog sat on the boot. The frog said, "Quiet, please." Finn laughed. "Frogs do not talk." The frog said nothing more.

Late at night, Finn rowed home. He felt tired. He could not pull the oars fast. Then he saw a small light. It was green and far away. It sat on top of a far hill. Finn wanted to touch it. He rowed toward it. The light did not get closer.

Finn stopped. He looked in his boat. The frog was gone. The boot was gone too. Only water was there.

Then Finn saw the frog on the hill. The frog held the boot. The boot had a small green light inside. Finn waved. The frog waved back. Finn smiled and rowed home.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: on top of a far hill
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Gone was Finn’s best boot. He looked in his boat. He looked under his net. Only a frog sat there, very quiet. Finn gave the net a pull. Up came weeds and a can. No boot.

Late at night, Finn walked home. He saw a small light on top of a far hill. It was green and soft. It blinked like a tiny star. Finn wanted to touch it. But the hill was too far. He felt a small pull in his chest. He looked at the light. Then he looked at his feet. One foot had a boot. One foot had a sock.

He sat down. The frog hopped out of his net. It sat on his sock foot. Finn laughed. The green light blinked again. He did not walk to the hill. He walked home to bed. In the morning, his boot was by the door. The frog had hidden it. Finn put on both boots. He looked at the hill. The light was gone.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: on top of a far hill
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Gone was the sun, and Finn sat in his boat. He fished all day. He caught a sock, a can, and one old boot. The boot was brown and soft. Finn put it on his hand. It looked like a puppet.

A frog sat on the boot. The frog said, "Pull me in." Finn did not pull. He looked at the far hill. A little light was there. It was small and green. It did not move. Finn wanted to touch it.

He rowed and rowed. The night was quiet. The light stayed far away. "I want to hold it," Finn said. The frog said, "You can not." Finn said, "I want to hold it." He said it again and again.

Then Finn felt a tug. The boot was heavy. He pulled it up. Inside was a little fish. The fish had a green dot on its head. It was not the light on the hill. But it was close. Finn smiled. He let the fish go. The light on the hill blinked once, like a wink.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: on top of a far hill
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text: Gone was the sun, and Finn sat in his boat with his net. He was a fisherman. He wanted a fish for his supper. He pulled the net up. It was heavy. "A big one," said Finn. But it was not a fish. It was a boot. A big, wet boot. A frog sat in the boot. The frog said, "Quiet." Finn said, "You are not my supper." He put the boot down. Then he saw it. On a far hill, a little green light. It was small and bright. Finn wanted to touch it. He rowed his boat to the shore. He walked up the hill. The light stayed far away. He pulled and pulled. He said, "I want the light. I want the light." The frog hopped beside him. "The light is a star," said the frog. Finn looked up. The star twinkled. He could never reach it. He went home with the boot. The frog came too. The boot was warm. The frog was his friend. That was good. But still, he looked at the hill every night.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: on top of a far hill
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Gone was Finn’s old boot. He fished all day, but the boot was gone. A frog sat in his bucket. Finn did not see the frog. He saw only the far hill.

On top of the far hill, a little light was green. It was late at night. The light was small and green. Finn wanted to hold it. He wanted to hold it. He wanted to hold it.

He did not pull in his net. He did not go home. The water was quiet. The frog said, “Brr.” Finn said, “I want the light. I want the light.”

He walked up the hill. The light stayed far. He walked and walked. The light stayed far. His feet were cold. One foot had no boot.

Then he saw it. The green light was a firefly on a stick. A girl held the stick. She said, “I lost my boot.” Finn gave her his other boot. The frog jumped out. The girl laughed. Finn did not want the light now. He wanted his bed.

stories.name: Lena

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text: Lena went to the river to fish. She had a small boat and a big hat. She wanted to catch a fish for supper. Her line went down, down, down. She pulled up a boot. It was old and brown. A flower grew out of the top. Lena laughed. She put the boot in her boat. She tried again. She pulled up a can. She tried again. She pulled up a stick. The sun was warm. Lena felt a drop of sweat on her nose. Then she saw a bright thing behind the hedge. It was small and far away. It looked like a little light. Lena wanted to touch it. But she had to fish. She pulled up a fish. It was a good fish. She rowed home. The light stayed behind the hedge. It did not come with her. A want that pulls you away can make you miss your supper.

stories.name: Lena

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Lena fished all afternoon. She caught a boot. It was old and brown. “A boot,” said Lena. “Not a fish.”

She put the boot on the grass. A flower grew there. The flower was small and blue. Lena gave it a drop of water. The sun was warm and bright.

Then she saw it. Behind the hedge, a little green light. It blinked like a firefly. Lena stood up. She walked to the hedge. The light was gone.

She sat down again. She fished some more. She caught a leaf. She caught a stick. The boot sat by her side.

The light came back. It danced behind the hedge. Lena did not run. She just looked. She looked for a long time.

Her bucket was empty. But the flower was still there. The boot was still there. The light was still far away.

Lena smiled. She picked up her boot. She put the flower inside. Some things you keep. Some things you only see.

stories.name: Lena

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Lena went to the river to fish. She sat on the bank and waited. Her line went down, down, down. She pulled up a boot. It was old and brown. A small flower grew out of the top.
