Lena looked behind the hedge. A bright light was there. It was small and far away. It looked like a tiny sun. It made her feel warm. She wanted to touch it.

She fished again. She caught a can. She caught a stick. She did not catch a fish. She looked behind the hedge. The light was still there. It was so bright.

A drop of water fell from her nose. She did not care. She wanted the light. She stood up. She walked to the hedge. The light moved back.

She sat down again. She held the boot. The flower was soft. The light stayed far away. It was always far away.

Lena went home with the boot. She put it on her shelf. She could still see the light behind the hedge. She knew she could never reach it. But she could always look. And that was enough.

stories.name: Lena

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Lena found a boot in her net. It was old and brown and full of water. She set it on the dock. A small fish had made a home inside it. Lena watched the fish swim in circles.

Then she saw the light. It was behind the hedge. It was bright and soft. It called to her. Lena stood up. She forgot the boot.

She walked to the hedge. The light danced. She reached for it. Her hand found only leaves. She went back to the dock. The boot was still there. The fish was still there.

Lena looked at the hedge again. The light was still bright. She walked to it. She reached again. Nothing. She went back. The fish was gone. The boot was empty.

A flower grew by the dock. It had one blue drop on its petal. Lena sat down. She did not chase the light. She held the boot. She watched the drop fall.

The light stayed behind the hedge. Some things are for looking, not for holding.

stories.name: Lena

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Lena found a boot in the water. It was a good boot. She put it on her boat. She went out to fish.

Then she saw the light. It was behind the hedge. It was small and green and far away.

Lena rowed. The light was so bright. She forgot the boot. She forgot the fish.

A flower floated by. She did not see it. A drop of water hit her cheek. She did not feel it.

Lena rowed. The light was behind the hedge. The light was always behind the hedge.

She rowed. She rowed. She rowed.

Her boat bumped the shore. She was tired. The boot was gone. The light was still far away.

She sat on the grass. She looked at her hands. They were empty.

Do not chase the light you cannot hold. Hold what is in your boat.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Gus went to the river to fish. He felt a tug on his line. It was not a fish. It was a boot.

“A boot?” said Gus. “What a funny thing.”

The boot was old and brown. Mud was on it. A little feather was stuck on the top.

“I will dig in the mud,” said Gus. “Maybe a fish is in the boot.”

He looked up. On the bridge, a small green light was shining. It was far away.

“That light is pretty,” said Gus. He reached for it. He could not touch it.

The light went off. Gus looked back at his boot. A loud splash came from the water. A fish jumped up!

“I will take the fish home,” said Gus. “I will leave the boot here.”

The green light came on again. Gus smiled. He did not need to touch it.

Sometimes we want things we cannot have. That is okay. We can still be happy with what we find.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Gus the fisherman sat by the river. He wanted to catch a fish. He had a hat and a pole and a bucket. But he caught a boot.

"Look at this," said Gus. "A boot."

The boot was old and brown. It had a hole in the toe. Gus put it in his bucket.

It was a hot summer day. The sun was very bright. Gus felt hot and tired.

Then he saw it. On the bridge over the river, a small light blinked. It was green. It shone like a tiny leaf.

"What is that?" said Gus.

He wanted to touch it. He wanted to hold it in his hand. But the bridge was far away.

Gus put a white feather on his hook. He let it float on the water. He did not catch a fish.

He tried to dig in the mud for a worm. The water made a loud splash. The green light blinked again on the bridge.

"I can not reach it," said Gus.

So Gus went home with his boot. He was happy with his boot. Some things you want are far away. But the things you have are close.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Gus the fisherman sat by the river. He wanted to catch a fish for supper. The sun was hot on his hat. He felt sleepy.

Then he saw a small green light. It was on the bridge over the river. It blinked and blinked. Gus stood up. He forgot his fishing pole.

"Look at that light," said Gus.

He walked to the bridge. The light was far away. He climbed the steps. The light moved away.

"Come back," said Gus.

He saw a boot in the water. It had a blue feather on it. Gus wanted to dig it out with his net. He slipped and fell. Splash! The water was loud.

Gus sat on the bank. He looked at the bridge. The green light was still there. He could not reach it. He could not catch it.

"It is pretty," said Gus. "But I cannot hold it. I have a boot. I do not have a fish."

The light blinked far away. Gus went home hungry. Some things you can see but not keep.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Gus pulled up his net and found one old boot inside. It was brown and wet. It had no mate. The river gave him a boot, not a fish.

A feather floated by. It was light and soft. Gus wished he could float like that. He wished for one small thing to keep.

Then he saw the light. It was on the bridge over the river. It was small and green and far away.

The sun was hot. The day was hot. The light stayed far away.

“Do you see that light?” Gus said to a boy on the bank.

“That is just a lamp,” the boy said.

“It looks like a star,” Gus said.

He tried to dig his feet in the mud and reach. The water was loud. The light did not come closer. He reached and reached.

“Why do you want it?” the boy said.

Gus did not know. He just did.

The light was always far. A boot can hold water. It cannot hold a light. Some things you want are only for looking, not for holding.

stories.name: Gus

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Gus fished all day on the hot summer day. He pulled up a boot. "A boot!" said Gus. "I want a fish."

Then he saw it. A green light. It sat on the bridge over the river. It shone in the hot sun.

Gus looked at the light. The light was small and green. It was like a feather on the wind.

"I want the light," said Gus.

He put down the boot. He reached for the light. The light did not come.

"Come here," said Gus. His voice was loud.

The light stayed on the bridge. Gus reached and reached.

"Dig," said Gus. "I will dig. I will get it."

He dug in the water. The water was hot. The light stayed far away.

Gus forgot the boot. He forgot the fish. He only saw the green light.

"Please," said Gus. "Please."

The light did not move. Gus sat in his boat. The hot day went on. The green light shone.

You can want a thing forever. But some lights you cannot hold.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: across a big field
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Rain came down on the roof. Tess liked rain. It made a soft sound, like a cat tapping its toes.

Tess had a friend named Ben. Ben told jokes. He told a joke about a duck. He told a joke about a shoe. Tess laughed and laughed.

One morning, Tess ate bread with jam. It was sticky on her fingers. She licked them. Then she went outside.

The rain had stopped. The sun was up early. Tess saw something far away. Across a big field, a little light shone. It was low and bright and not red like the sun. It was green. Tess wanted to jump over the field. But the field was too big.

Ben came to the fence. He told a joke about a frog. Tess laughed, but she looked at the light too.

“What is that?” she said.

Ben looked. “That is the light on my porch,” he said. “I left it on for my cat.”

Tess laughed again. It was a good joke. The best one.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: across a big field
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Right after breakfast, Tess went to find her friend Ben. Ben tells jokes. He tells a joke about a cow. He tells a joke about a sock. Tess laughs and laughs.

They sat on the steps with bread and jam. The jam was sticky. It got on Tess's nose. Ben told a joke about a nose. Tess did a little jump.

Then Tess looked across the big field. Far away, past the tall grass, a small light was shining. It was soft and green, like a tiny leaf. It was early morning, and the light blinked once. Tess wanted to go to it. But she did not go.

Ben told a joke about a frog. Tess laughed again. She looked at the field. The light was still there. It blinked two times. Tess felt a quiet pull in her chest. She stayed with Ben.

Then Ben told one more joke. It was about a light that could not dance. Tess stopped laughing. She looked at Ben. He was smiling at her.

"That light is just the sun on a wet leaf," Ben said.

Tess laughed and laughed. She was glad she stayed.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: across a big field
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Right after breakfast, Tess sat with her friend Ben. Ben told jokes. Tess laughed and laughed. Ben told a joke about a duck. Tess held her tummy. Then Ben told a joke about bread. Tess said, "That is so silly!"

Early morning sun came up. Tess saw a small light far away. It was green. It sat across a big field. Tess stood up. She wanted to jump and run to it.

"Where are you going?" said Ben.
"To the light," said Tess.

Ben told another joke. Tess did not hear it. She walked to the field. The grass was wet and sticky. She took one step. Then two.

The light did not get closer. It only blinked. Tess felt sad. Then Ben came. He stood next to her. "I have one more joke," he said. "Why did the light run away?"

"Why?" said Tess.
"Because it wanted you to turn around!"

Tess turned. Ben was right there. She laughed. The light was just the sun on a leaf. Tess did not need to jump to it. Her friend was the best light of all.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: across a big field
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Rosa tells jokes. Tess likes the jokes a lot. Rosa says, "Why did the bread run away? It was toast!" Tess laughs and laughs.

Then Tess sees a light far away. It is small and green. It sits across a big field. The light says come here, come here.

"Let's jump rope," Rosa says. Tess does not hear her. She looks at the light.

"Want a sticky bun?" Rosa asks. Tess shakes her head. She walks to the edge of the field.

Rosa tells one more joke. Tess does not laugh.

Early morning comes. The light is still there. Tess runs. She runs and runs. But the light stays far away. She cannot reach it. Her feet hurt. She sits down in the grass. She starts to cry.

Then she hears Rosa. Rosa is calling her name. Rosa brings the sticky bun. Rosa brings the bread.

"You came," Tess says.

"Of course," says Rosa. "Friends do not stay in the field."

Tess eats the bun. It is sweet. Rosa tells a joke about a silly duck. This time Tess laughs. The small green light is still far away. But Tess holds Rosa's hand. That is close. That is warm. She does not need the far light now.

stories.name: Tess

axes.where: across a big field
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Rosa tells the best jokes. Tess loves Rosa. Rosa says, "Why did the bread run away? It was toast!" Tess laughs and laughs.

Then Tess sees it. Across the big field, far away, a little green light. It shines in the early morning.

"Come on," says Rosa. "I have more jokes."

But Tess looks at the light. She wants it. She wants to jump to it. She wants to hold it. It is so small. It is so far.

"Knock knock," says Rosa.

Tess does not hear. The light is there. Always there. Never close.

"Who's there?" Tess says, but she is not talking to Rosa.

The light says nothing. It just shines.

Tess runs to the field. The grass is sticky with dew. She runs and runs. The light stays far.

Then Rosa is beside her. Rosa holds up a piece of bread. "Look," says Rosa. "My joke was true. The bread did run away. And here it is."

Tess stops. She looks at Rosa. She looks at the bread. The light is still far. But Rosa is here.

Tess laughs. The light can wait.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: across the snowy yard

stories.text:
Friends like to make you laugh. Jack had a friend named Ben. Ben told jokes all day. Knock knock. Who is there? Cow. Cow who? Cow says moo! Jack laughed and laughed.

On a snowy day, they went outside. Snow fell on Jack's hat. They made a snowman by the tree. Ben told a joke about a snowman. Jack giggled so hard he fell in the snow.

Then Jack saw a small light across the snowy yard. It was green and far away. It shone by a window. Jack wanted to touch it. He took one step. The snow was deep. He stopped. The light stayed far away.

Ben said, "Come help me bake a cake!" Jack felt calm again. He went inside with Ben. They baked a warm cake.

Jack did not get the green light. But he got a good friend and a warm cake. A friend who makes you laugh is better than any faraway light.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: across the snowy yard

stories.text:
Friendly Jack had a friend named Ben who told jokes. Ben told a joke about a cow. Jack laughed. Ben told a joke about a hat. Jack laughed more. "You are so funny," Jack said. They played in the snow. They made a big snow ball. Ben told one more joke. It was about a sock.

Then Jack saw a light. It was a small green light across the snowy yard. It blinked by a tree. Jack said, "Look, Ben. A green light." Ben did not see it. Jack wanted to touch it. But it was far away. It felt warm and calm. Jack took one step. Then he stopped.

"Come back," said Ben. "I have a joke about a cake." Jack wanted the light. But he wanted his friend too. They went inside to bake cookies. The light stayed across the snowy yard. Jack did not get it. He felt a little sad. But Ben made him laugh again.

A friend is better than a faraway light.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: across the snowy yard

stories.text:
Fog filled the snowy day. Jack and his friend Ben made a snowman. Ben told a joke. "Why did the snowman smile? Because he heard the snow blow!" Jack laughed. Ben told more jokes. Jack liked Ben so much.

Then Jack saw a small green light. It was across the snowy yard. It shone by a tree. The light was tiny and bright. Jack wanted it. He took a step. "Where are you going?" Ben asked. Jack stopped.

Ben told another joke. "What did the tree say? Leaf me alone!" Jack smiled a little. But he looked at the light. It called to him. He took another step.

Ben said, "Come help me bake snow cookies." Jack turned back. The light was still there. Jack felt calm with Ben. The light was far away.

At last Jack said, "I like your jokes more than that light." Ben laughed. They went inside to bake. The green light stayed across the yard.

A friend who makes you laugh is better than a light you can never touch.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: across the snowy yard

stories.text:
Finley told jokes. Jack loved Finley. Finley said, "Why did the snowman smile? Because he heard a good freeze!" Jack laughed and laughed.

Then Jack saw a green light. It was across the snowy yard. It was small and bright near a tree. Jack wanted it. He did not want a joke. He wanted the light.

"Finley, look," said Jack. "Do you see it?"

"I see a carrot joke," said Finley. "What did the carrot say? You are my best friend!"

Jack did not laugh. He looked at the green light. He wanted to bake a cake for the light. He wanted to be calm and hold it. But it was far, far away.

"Finley, tell another joke," said Jack. But Jack watched the light.

"Why did the tree go to school? To get smarter!" said Finley.

Jack still watched the light. He reached out. He could not touch it.

Finley put a hand on Jack. "Jokes are here," said Finley. "I am here. The light is far."

A friend who tells jokes is a light you can touch.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: across the snowy yard

stories.text: F is for fun, and Jack had a fun friend named Ben. Ben told jokes. Ben told jokes all day. Knock knock. Who is there? Ben! Ben who? Ben banana! Jack laughed. They played in the snow. Then Jack saw it. Across the snowy yard, a small light was on. It was green. It was by the big tree. Jack wanted that light. He wanted it so much. "I want the light," said Jack. "I want the light." Ben told a joke. Jack did not hear. "I want the light. I want the light." Mom said, "Come bake cookies. They will calm you." Jack did not bake. He just looked at the light. The snow fell and fell. Ben went home. Jack sat by the window. "I want the light," he said. "I want the light." The light did not move. It did not come to him. It just stayed far away. At last Jack cried. Mom hugged him. A joke from a friend is warm and near. A far light is only far.

stories.name: Noah

axes.where: on a train going by
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Mia was Noah’s best friend. She told the best jokes. On hot summer days, they sat on the porch and drank lemonade. “Why did the frog say moo?” Mia asked. Noah did not know. “Because he was learning a new language!” She laughed so hard she almost fell off the step.

Noah tried to tell a joke too. “What do you call a bear with no teeth?” he asked. Mia waited. “A gummy bear!” Mia smiled. “That is a kind joke,” she said. Noah felt happy.

A train went by. It was long and loud. On one car, a small green light blinked. Noah saw it. He wanted to touch it. He reached out, but the train was too far. The light went away. Noah felt a little sad. He found a stick and drew a train in the dirt.

“Tell me another joke,” Mia said. “Okay,” said Noah. “Why did the train hop?” Mia shrugged. “Because it saw a frog crossing the tracks!” Mia laughed. Noah laughed too. The green light was gone. But Mia was still there. That was better.

stories.name: Noah

axes.where: on a train going by
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text: Mya was Noah's best friend. She told jokes all day. Knock knock. Who's there. A stick. A stick who? Noah laughed every time. On a hot summer day they sat by the fence. Mya told a joke about a frog. Why did the frog hop the road? Noah did not know. To get to the other side, Mya said. Noah giggled and clapped. Then a train went by. It was slow and long. A small green light shone on the last car. Noah watched it. He wished he could hop on that train. He wished he could ride to the green light. Mya pulled his arm. Noah, listen, she said. What is a train's favorite joke? Noah turned back. What? he asked. A loco-motive, she said. Noah smiled. The train went away. The green light got small and gone. Noah felt a little pull in his chest. He wanted it. But Mya told one more joke. Why did the boy chase the train? Noah said why. To catch a laugh, she said. Noah laughed. The light was far, but Mya was right here. And she was kind.

stories.name: Noah

axes.where: on a train going by
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text: My friend Ben tells jokes. He tells them all day. On a hot summer day, we sat by the train tracks. Ben told a joke about a frog. I laughed. Then I saw a small green light on a train going by. It was far away. It was bright and still. I wanted to touch it. Ben told a joke about a stick. I did not hear it. I watched the light. The train went away. The light got small. I stood up to hop after it. "Noah, sit down," Ben said. "You can't catch a train." I sat down. Ben told a joke about a kind bird. I smiled a little. The light was gone. Then Ben said, "Why did the light stay on the train?" I said, "Why?" Ben said, "Because it lives there, not here." I looked at Ben. He was my friend. He told jokes. That was enough.

stories.name: Noah

axes.where: on a train going by
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text: My friend Ivy tells jokes. She tells jokes on the porch. She tells jokes in the yard. On a hot summer day, we sit and eat ice pops. “Why did the frog hop on the bus?” Ivy says. “To get to the other side!” I laugh and laugh. Then I see it. A train goes by, slow and long. On the train is a small green light. It sits in a window. It shines. I want that light. “Noah, are you listening?” Ivy says. “Why did the chicken cross the road?” I do not hear her. The green light is so small and so bright. “Noah!” Ivy says. “Tell me a joke.” I point at the train. “That light,” I say. “I want it.” “You can’t have a train light,” Ivy says. She gives me a stick. “Use this.” I hold the stick. I look at the light. The train is gone. The light is gone. But I still want it. “Knock knock,” Ivy says. I do not say who is there. I just look down the track. “Noah,” Ivy says, soft and kind. “I have one more joke.” I wait. “The light is a star,” she says. “Stars stay.” I smile a little. Then I say, “Knock knock.”

stories.name: Noah

axes.where: on a train going by
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
My friend Ben tells jokes. He tells jokes on the porch. He tells jokes at lunch. On a hot summer day, we sat and drank cold juice. "Why did the frog cross the road?" Ben said. "To get to the other side!" I laughed.

Then I saw a green light. It was on a train going by. The train was far away. The light was small and bright. I wanted it. I pointed. "Look," I said. "That light."

"What light?" Ben said. "Listen. Why did the stick hop?"

I did not hear him. I wanted the green light. It was on the train. The train went away. I stood up. I reached out my hand. "Come here," I said. "Come here, light."

Ben pulled my arm. "Sit down, Noah. It is just a light."

"No," I said. "It is my light. I want it. I want it. I want it."

Ben was kind. He gave me his stick. "Here," he said. "You can have this."

I held the stick. I looked down the track. The train was gone. The green light was gone. But when I held the stick up, the sun made a small green spot on the wall. Ben smiled. "See?" he said. "You found it."

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text: Snow fell on Faye's hat. Her friend Ben told a joke. "Why did the snowman smile?" he asked. "Because he saw the snow blower!" Faye laughed. Ben was a funny friend. He always helped her too. They built a snowman with a fuzzy scarf. Ben gave it a carrot nose. Faye gave it a flower. Then Faye saw a light. It was small and green. It was on the other side of a fence. The light blinked in the snow. Faye gave a little wave. The light did not wave back. It just stayed there. Ben told another joke. "What did the fence say to the snow?" he asked. "Nothing. It just sat there." Faye laughed again. She looked at the light one more time. It was still far away. She could not reach it. But Ben was warm and funny. They made snowballs. The green light stayed behind the fence. Faye did not need it. She had her friend.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
Snow came down soft and white. Faye sat by the window. Her friend Ben came over to play.

Ben tells jokes. He tells a joke about a snowman. "Why did the snowman smile? Because he saw the sun melt his hat!" Faye laughed. It was a funny moment.

They went outside. The snow was fuzzy and deep. Ben made a big snowball. Faye made a small one. They built a snowman with a carrot nose.

Then Faye saw it. On the other side of the fence, a small green light glowed. It was far away. It looked like a tiny star.

"What is that?" Faye said. She put her hand on the fence.

Ben did not look. "Come help me," he said. "The snowman needs a hat."

Faye gave the snowman a flower on top. But she looked back at the light. It did not come closer. She gave a small wave to it.

Ben told one more joke. Faye laughed. The light stayed far away, and she could not reach it.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
Snow fell on Faye and her friend Ben. Ben told jokes. "Why did the snowman smile? He saw a funny flake!" Faye laughed. Ben was a good friend. He helped her make a snow ball.

Then Faye saw it. A small green light, on the other side of a fence. It shone through the snow. It was soft and fuzzy, like a tiny flower.

"Look," said Faye. She gave a wave to the light.

"That is just a light," said Ben. "Want a joke? Why did the fence get cold? It had too many brrr-berries!"

Faye did not laugh. She walked to the fence. The green light blinked. She put her hand on the cold wood. She could not reach it. The light was too far.

Ben came and stood by her. He did not tell a joke. He just held her hand.

"It is pretty," he said.

Faye nodded. The green light stayed on the other side. She could not have it. But Ben was here. That was warm.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
Snow fell on Faye's mittens. Her friend Ben told a joke. "Why did the snowman smile? He saw the snow blow!" Faye laughed. That was funny.

Ben helped her build a snowman. They gave it a fuzzy hat. They put a flower on its head. Ben told more jokes. Faye laughed again.

Then Faye saw a light. It was green and small. It was on the other side of a fence. It glowed in the snow.

"Come look," Faye said. Ben did not look. He told a joke. Faye did not hear it.

She walked to the fence. The light was so far away. She gave a little wave. The light did not wave back.

"Faye, come play," Ben said.

But Faye watched the light. Snow fell on her nose. She reached through the fence. Her arm was too short.

Ben stood by her. He told a joke. She did not smile.

The light just glowed. It stayed far. It stayed green. Faye reached and reached.

stories.name: Faye

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
Sometimes Faye and her friend Ben tell jokes in the snow. Ben says, "Why did the snowman smile? Because he heard a funny chill!" Faye laughs. Then she sees it.

Across the yard, past the fence, a small green light glows on a snowy day. It sits by a flower under the white.

"Ben, look," Faye says.

Ben waves his fuzzy mittens. "It is just a light. Come help me build a snow fort."

But Faye walks to the fence. The green light shines. She wants it. She reaches through the cold bars.

"Come back," Ben says. "I have a joke."

Faye whispers, "Green light. Green light."

Ben pulls her hand. "Your mittens are fuzzy like a bear!"

Faye does not turn. The green light is far and small and hers to want.

"Green light. Green light," she says again.

Ben stays. He tells one more joke. Faye only sees the light. She reaches. She reaches.

stories.name: Beth

axes.where: at the end of the pier
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
A friend who tells jokes is the best friend of all. Beth sat on the hot sand with her pail. Her friend Sam told a joke about a fish. Beth laughed so hard she felt dizzy.

Sam stopped joking. He lost his red ball in the water. Beth wanted to help. They looked and looked. The sun was very hot. Beth felt tired.

Sam said, "I will lift you up." He lifted Beth high. She saw the ball near the end of the pier. A small light shone there. It was far away. Beth wanted to touch it. She reached out her hand. She could not reach it. The light stayed far away.

Then Sam saw the ball too. He pulled it from the water. Beth smiled. Sam told one more joke. Beth forgot the light for a while. They walked home happy.

stories.name: Beth

axes.where: at the end of the pier
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
A friend who tells jokes is a good thing to have. Beth had one. Her name was Jo. Jo told jokes all day long.

On a hot summer day, Beth and Jo went to the beach. Beth had a big pail. She wanted to fill it with wet sand. But the sand was too dry. It fell out. That was a little problem.

Jo told a joke. "Why did the sand cry? Because it was too dry!" Beth laughed so hard she felt dizzy.

Then Jo said, "Let's get water." They ran to the waves. Beth did not lift the pail too high. She filled it with water. The wet sand stuck. The problem was solved.

They made a big sand cake. Jo put a shell on top. "This cake is so good, nobody can eat it!" she said. Beth giggled.

Then Beth saw something. Far away, at the end of the pier, a small green light was shining. It blinked once. It looked like a tiny star that lost its way. Beth said, "Oh."

"What?" said Jo.

"Nothing," said Beth. She turned back to the cake. The green light stayed at the end of the pier. But Jo told another joke, and Beth forgot to look again.

stories.name: Beth

axes.where: at the end of the pier
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
A friend who tells jokes is good to have. Beth had a friend like that. His name was Sam. Sam told jokes all day long.

One hot summer day, Beth and Sam went to the beach. Beth carried a pail. Sam told a joke about a fish. Beth laughed so hard she felt dizzy.

Then Beth lost her pail in the waves. "Oh no," she said. Sam did not stop joking. He told a joke about a crab. Beth smiled a little. Then Sam helped her look. They found the pail near a rock. Beth gave Sam a big lift with her arms. "You are funny and kind," she said.

Far away, at the end of the pier, a small light began to shine. Beth saw it. It was green and soft. She wanted to touch it. She walked toward it. The light seemed close, then far. Sam told another joke. Beth did not hear him. She reached for the light. It stayed at the end of the pier. She could not have it. So she turned back to Sam. His jokes were warm. The light was not.

stories.name: Beth

axes.where: at the end of the pier
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
A friend who tells jokes can make any day better. Beth had a pail and a plan. She would build a big sand castle at the beach. Her friend Jo came to help. Jo told a joke about a crab. Beth laughed so hard she felt dizzy.

The castle would not stand up. It fell down. Beth felt sad. Jo said, "Do not worry. We can try again." They used wet sand. They used small shells. The castle stayed up. Jo told a joke about a snail. Beth giggled.

Then Beth saw it. A small green light, far away, at the end of the pier. It was hot and bright. The light blinked once. Beth wanted to touch it. She walked to the pier. She reached out her hand. The light stayed far away. It always stayed far away.

Jo called her back. Beth tried to lift her feet. They felt heavy. She looked at the light again. It was so small. It was so far. She wanted it. She could not have it.

stories.name: Beth

axes.where: at the end of the pier
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
A friend who tells jokes is a good friend to have. Beth had a friend like that. His name was Sam. Sam told jokes all day. Beth laughed a lot.

One hot summer day, they went to the pier. Beth brought a pail for shells. Sam told a joke about a crab. Beth laughed so hard she felt dizzy.

Then Beth lost her shell in the water. "Oh no," she said. Sam said, "Do not cry. I will help." He used a stick to lift the shell out. Beth smiled. That was a funny moment.

But then Beth saw it. A small green light, far away, at the end of the pier. It was so small. It was so far.

"I want that light," Beth said.

Sam told another joke. Beth did not hear it. She walked to the end of the pier. The light stayed far away.

"I want the light," Beth said. "I want the light."

Sam called her name. Beth did not turn. The light was small and green and far.

"I want the light. I want the light. I want the light."

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
The plane flew high above the town. Ravi watched it from his chair by the window. He wanted to build a plane too. But he had only paper and string.

So Ravi made a kite. He drew a shiny tail and ran outside. The wind was cold. It bit his nose.

His kite went up, up, up. Then it went down, down, down. It landed in a tree. Ravi pulled. The string broke.

"Ha!" said a bird. It sat on the kite like a hat. Ravi laughed. Then he did not laugh.

Far down the street, on a car, a small green light came on. It glowed in the cold evening. Ravi stared at it. He wished he could hold it. He wished it was his.

He walked home with no kite. The plane was gone. Only the green light stayed on, far away. Ravi could not reach it. He sat in his chair again. The window was very cold.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
The paper kite Ravi made did not fly. He stood on a chair and held it high. The wind was cold on his hands. It was a cold autumn evening.

A big plane went over his house. Ravi heard it hum. He wished his kite could go up too. He ran down the street with the string. The kite dragged on the ground like a tired bird.

Then he saw it. A small light on a car parked far down the street. It was shiny and green. It glowed like a tiny star. Ravi stopped. He forgot the kite.

“Maybe that light can help me build a better kite,” he said. He walked toward it. The car was locked. Nobody was there.

He tried to catch the light in his hand. It stayed on the car. His kite string got tangled on a bush. A dog ran by and took the kite in its mouth. Ravi laughed. Then he felt sad.

The green light blinked once and went out. Ravi walked home with no kite at all.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
The plane flew high over Ravi's house. Ravi watched it go. Then he ran to the yard with his paper kite.

He stood on a chair to build the kite with sticks and tape. The tape was shiny. It stuck to his hand. He laughed and shook it off.

The wind was cold. Leaves blew by. Ravi let the kite go up. It went up, up, up. Then it fell down. He tried again. It fell again.

Far down the street, a light turned on. It sat on a car. It was small and green. Ravi looked at it. The light was bright in the cold evening.

He forgot his kite. He walked to the light. He wanted to hold it. But the car drove away.

Ravi went back. His kite was torn. He sat on the chair. The sky was dark. The green light was gone. He held his shiny tape and said, "Come back." It did not come back.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
The plane flew high above Ravi's house. He watched it until it was a tiny dot. Then he ran outside with his paper kite. The wind was cold on his nose. It was a cold autumn evening.

Ravi stood on a chair to launch his kite. He wanted to build it strong, but the wind was too fast. His kite went up, then down, then into a bush. "Silly kite," he said. That was a little funny.

Far down the street, a shiny green light sat on a car. It was small and bright and far away. Ravi forgot his kite. He walked toward the light. He reached out his hand. The light did not move.

His kite fell in the mud. Ravi did not see. He only saw the light. He wanted to hold it. He wanted to keep it.

But cars drive away. The light went with the car. Ravi stood alone in the cold. His kite was wet and torn. He would never catch that light.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Ravi

axes.where: on a car parked far down the street

stories.text:
The plane flew over Ravi's house. Ravi wanted to build a paper kite. He sat on a chair by the window. His kite was small and shiny.

Then he saw the light. A green light, far down the street, on a car. It was a cold autumn evening.

Ravi reached for the light. He could not touch it. He put down his kite.

The light stayed on the car. Ravi ran to the door. He tripped on a shoe. He fell on his bottom. It was funny. He laughed a little.

He got up. He ran down the street. The cold air bit his ears. The light was so far.

He came to the car. The light was just a little lamp inside. It was not for him.

Ravi walked home. His kite was on the floor. He sat on his chair. The light was still there, far down the street.

He reached. He reached. He could not have it.

Ravi was sad.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Suki

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
The plane flew high above the snowy town. Suki watched it from her window. She had a paper kite. It was red and small. She wanted to fly it, but the snow was deep.

Suki put on her coat. She lost a button in the snow. Her friend Ben helped her look. "Let's count the flakes," he said. They ran outside.

The wind was cold, not warm. Suki held her kite. It lifted up, then fell down. She tried again. Ben held the string too.

Then Suki saw a green light. It shone on a roof across the town. It was far away. She reached out her hand. The light did not come closer. She looked down at her kite.

"Try again," Ben said. They ran together. The kite went up, up, up. It danced in the sky. Suki laughed. The green light blinked once, then faded. She did not need it. Her kite was flying. Ben smiled. They went home for cocoa.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Suki

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
The snow came down soft and slow. Suki made a paper kite with her friend Ben. They used red paper and a small button for the tail.

"Let's count the flakes," said Ben. They counted to ten.

Suki looked up. Far away, on a roof across the town, a small green light was shining. It was bright and still in the cold.

"Come on," said Ben. "The kite is ready."

They ran to the hill. The kite went up, up, up. But Suki kept looking back. The green light was still there. It looked warm. She wished she could hold it.

"Look, Suki! Look at the kite!" said Ben.

The kite danced in the sky. It was happy and free. Suki smiled. Ben put his hand on her arm.

"You can't catch that light," he said. "But you can fly this kite with me."

Suki nodded. She held the string tight. The kite pulled and jumped. The green light stayed on the roof. It was far away. But Ben was right here. The snow fell. They laughed and ran home, warm at last.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Suki

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
Tiny snowflakes fell on Suki's nose. She wanted to fly her paper kite, but the wind was too soft. Her big brother's plane was gone. He flew away to a far town. Suki held her kite string and felt sad.

Then she saw it. A small green light on a roof across the town. It blinked once. Twice. Suki wanted to touch it. She pulled her coat tight. Her friend Ben came out. "Let's count the snowflakes," he said. He gave her a warm button from his pocket.

They walked together. Suki looked up. The green light was still there. It felt close, then far. "Can we go to the roof?" she asked. Ben shook his head. "Too far, Suki."

She reached her hand toward the light. It did not move. Her kite string slipped. The kite danced up, up, up. It flew toward the roof. The green light blinked again, soft and kind.

Ben smiled. "Your kite can visit it for you." Suki laughed. Her kite sailed in the snowy sky. She felt warm inside. The green light stayed on the roof, but her heart felt full.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Suki

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text:
The plane flew over Suki's house, loud and silver. She watched it until it was small. Then she made a paper kite with one red button for an eye.

Snow fell soft on her hands. She ran to the hill to fly it.

Far off, on a roof across the town, a small green light blinked. Suki stopped. She counted her steps toward it. One, two, three. The light did not move.

Her friend Miti pulled her coat. "Come, Suki. The hill is warm."

But the light called her. She walked past the hill. She walked past the snow. The kite tugged, but she did not look.

"Please," said Miti. "Your kite wants to fly."

Suki blinked. She turned from the little green light on the far roof. It stayed there, small and far.

She ran back to the hill with Miti. The wind lifted her kite high. The red button eye winked in the snow.

"Look!" Suki laughed. "It flies!"

The green light still blinked across the town. But Suki held the string. She counted her friends, not steps. And her heart was warm.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Suki

axes.where: on a roof across the town

stories.text: The plane flew high. Suki made a paper kite. She liked the plane and the kite. Then she saw a green light on a roof across the town. It was on a snowy day. The light was small and green. She wanted it. She reached for it. "Come back," she said. "Come back." Her friend Mia came. "I can help," Mia said. She gave Suki a warm button. "Count to ten," Mia said. Suki counted. One, two, three. The light stayed far. She reached again. "Come back," she said. The snow fell. Mia held her hand. They went to the roof. The light was a green bulb. Suki touched it. It was warm. She was happy. They flew the kite in the snow. The plane flew high too.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Leo

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
I see a big plane in the sky. Leo likes the plane. It goes zoom, zoom. Leo has a paper kite. It is red and blue. He wants to fly it.

The wind blows hard. It is a stormy afternoon. Leo holds his kite. The string pulls. His hands are cold. He feels sleepy.

He runs to the garden. He sees a light behind the hedge. It is small and green. It blinks like a candle in the wind. Leo stops. He wants to touch it. He walks to the hedge. The light goes away. He is sad.

The wind takes his kite. It goes up, up, up. Leo runs after it. He trips on a stone. He cries.

Then the wind stops. The kite falls down. It lands in a puddle. Leo picks it up. He is wet. He goes inside. Mom gives him a warm bath. She puts a candle on the table. Leo helps her paint a new kite. He is happy. He is not sleepy anymore.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Leo

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
In the stormy afternoon, Leo made a paper kite. He used paper and string and red paint. He wanted to fly it with the plane. But the wind was too big and the rain came down.

Leo looked behind the hedge. A small green light was there. It blinked in the dark. Leo wanted to touch it. He took one step. The light stayed far away.

He went inside. Mom lit a candle. The room felt warm. Leo felt sleepy. He thought of the plane and the kite. He could not fly them today.

The rain stopped. The sun came out. Leo ran outside with his kite. The plane flew high in the sky. The kite danced on the wind.

Leo saw the green light behind the hedge. It was still there. He smiled. He did not need to catch it. He had his plane and his kite. That was enough. He was happy.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Leo

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
I like planes. Leo made a paper kite too. He called it Flappy. The sky turned gray. Wind shook the trees. It was a stormy afternoon.

Leo held Flappy. The kite went up, up, up. Then rain came down.

Behind the hedge, a small green light glowed. Leo saw it. He wanted it. He walked to the hedge. The light was far away. He could not reach it.

He came back to Flappy. The kite was wet. The rain was loud. Leo felt sleepy. He went inside.

Mom lit a candle. Its little flame was warm and gold. Leo got out his paint. He painted a green dot on Flappy. It looked like the light.

The storm stopped. The sun came out. Leo ran outside. Flappy flew high and happy. The green dot shone in the sun.

Leo smiled. He did not need the light behind the hedge. He had his own green light now. It flew with him.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Leo

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
I have a plane and a paper kite. Leo holds the kite string tight. The plane sits on the grass. Wind pushes the clouds. Rain taps the roof.

Behind the hedge, a small green light glows. Leo sees it. He wants it. He steps toward the hedge. The kite pulls back. "Wait," says Leo.

He runs to the shed. He finds a candle. He finds paint. He paints the kite bright red. His hands are sleepy and slow.

The storm gets loud. The green light blinks behind the hedge. Leo reaches. The hedge is too thick. The light stays far away. He cannot touch it. He cannot have it.

He tries again. The light slips away. His kite shakes in the wind. Leo feels sad.

Then the rain stops. The clouds move. The sun comes out. Leo lets the kite go up. It flies high and happy. The plane flies too. Leo smiles. The green light is still there. But now Leo has his kite. That is enough.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Leo

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
I went outside to fly my paper kite. The wind was big and loud. Rain came down fast. My kite went up, up, up. Then a plane flew over the clouds. I ran to the hedge to see it.

Behind the hedge, a green light glowed. It was small and far away. I wanted it. I reached for it. The light did not come.

I forgot my kite. I forgot the plane. I only saw the light. I reached and reached. The storm made me sleepy. I held my candle close. It did not help. I wanted the green light.

I painted a picture of the light. I reached for it again. The light stayed behind the hedge. I could not have it.

Then my mom called me. She gave me warm soup. The rain stopped. A rainbow came. My kite was safe in a tree. I laughed. The green light was still there. But I was happy.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Zoe

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text: Mia and Zoe made a plane from paper. They folded the wings wide. Then they made a kite with a long tail. The kite was light and danced in the wind. Zoe wore her red hat. She ran and let the kite go up. It did a happy spin. The plane zoomed low and fast. Both were bright in the evening sky. Just before bedtime, Zoe heard a train. The train went by with a soft hum. One window glowed with a small green light. It slid past the trees. Zoe watched it go. She wished she could ride that light. But the train was far away. The light grew tiny and then was gone. Zoe held her kite string. The wind stopped. The kite fell down. Her plane landed in the grass. She picked them up and walked home slow. The sky was dark. Her hat felt heavy. She put the plane and kite on her bed. She did not want to sleep. The little light was still gone.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Zoe

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
Maya sat by the window with her paper kite. Tomorrow she would fly it with Grandpa. He had made it from a brown bag and sticks. She put on her soft hat. The room grew dim.

Then a plane hummed across the sky. Maya wished she could ride it far away. But the plane was just a plane, and Grandpa was sick in bed.

A train came down the track. Its windows were gold squares. One square held a small bright light. It glowed like a tiny moon. Maya watched it slide past. She wanted to hold it. She wanted to keep it near her bed. The train did not stop. The light did not stop.

She spun the kite string around her finger. The light was gone. The sky was empty. She thought of Grandpa. She thought of the bright thing on the train. She wanted to reach it. She wanted it to stay.

Her mother called her to sleep. Maya lay down with her hat on. The kite rested on the floor. Somewhere far away, the little light kept going. Maya could not go with it. She closed her eyes.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Zoe

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
Mia sat by the window with her red hat on. She held a paper kite she made from a brown bag. Outside, a plane flew high and wide. It went far away, where she could not go. Then a train came down the track.

The train had one small light on its side. The light was bright and green like a tiny star. It slid along the dark hill. Mia put her hand on the glass. She wanted to go where the light went. She wanted it more than her kite.

The train went by fast. The light did not stop. Mia saw it spin away into the night. She held her kite up to the window. But the kite could not fly inside.

Her mom said, "Time for bed." Mia did not turn around. The green light was gone. She looked at the empty hill. She felt a small ache in her chest. The plane was gone too. Only her paper kite stayed. It was light like a leaf. But it could not take her anywhere. She held her hat and cried.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Zoe

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
Mom said it was time for bed. Zoe held her paper kite. It was white with a red tail.

A plane went over the house. Zoom. Zoe wished she could fly too.

Then a train came by. Clack, clack. A small light shone on the back car. It was not big. It was not loud. But it was bright. It was the color of a faraway wish.

Zoe put on her hat. She spun around once. She wanted that light. She wanted to hold it.

"Bedtime," Mom said.

Zoe climbed the stairs. She looked out the window. The train was gone. But the small light still burned in her chest.

She lay down. She did not sleep. She thought, I want the light. I want the light. I want the light.

Her kite fell off the bed. The plane was gone. The train was gone. And the light stayed far away, where she could see it but never touch it.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Zoe

axes.where: on a train going by

stories.text:
Maya sat on the porch. She held her paper kite. It was red and light. She wanted to fly it. But the sun was going down. Soon it would be bedtime.

A plane went by. It was high and loud. Zoe looked up. She wished she could go. Then she saw a train.

The train had one small light. It was bright and green. It was on the last car. It went away. Zoe stood up. She put on her hat. She began to spin. She spun and spun. She fell down.

"Come inside," said Mom. Zoe did not move. She watched the track. The light was gone. But she still saw it. She saw it in her head. She saw it when she closed her eyes. She wanted that light. She wanted it so much.

"Zoe. Bedtime."

"I want the light," she said. "I want the light. I want the light."

The train was gone. The plane was gone. The kite fell in the grass. Zoe went to bed. She did not sleep.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Joon

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Slow planes hum high above the clouds. Joon likes planes. Today he made a paper kite. It is a small plane too, folded from newsprint, with wings that bend.

Joon climbs the hill near his house. The fog is thick and soft like a wet blanket. He runs and lets the kite go. It dips and lifts. It tugs his string. He runs until his cheeks feel warm.

The kite will not stay up. It falls in the grass. Joon tries three times. He can count each fall. One, two, three.

He sits and holds the crumpled plane. Down the hill, through the fog, he sees a thin light under a door down the hall of the old school. It glows yellow and far. He wants to walk to it. But he does not know that room.

So Joon stands. He folds a new kite. This one he keeps low, close to his chest.

A plane can fly without you. A kite needs your hand.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Joon

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Sometimes Joon flew his paper kite on the hill near his house. One foggy night he made a plane from paper too. He drew small windows with a blue pen.

The fog made the street soft and gray. Joon ran to the hill and threw the plane. It dipped and rose and landed in wet grass. He threw the kite string up, but no wind came.

Then he saw a thin light under a door down the hall. It was warm and gold. It made him think of places far away. He wanted to count the stars, but the fog hid them. He wanted to fly too, like his plane and kite.

The light stayed under the door. Joon could not reach it. He could only look. He sat on the hill and held his paper plane.

“I want to go there,” he said. “I want to go there.” But the door did not open.

So Joon flew his plane again. It was small. It was near. That was enough for now. A little wish is like a kite: you hold the string, but you let the wind decide.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Joon

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Sometimes Joon flew his paper kite on the hill by the house. He liked the tug on the string. He liked the wind on his face. At night he heard a plane far up in the fog. He wished he could ride it. Then he looked down the hall. A soft light glowed under the door.

He tried to count the stars, but the fog hid them. He tried to count the windows of the plane, but it flew away. The light under the door stayed. It was warm and small. He wanted to touch it. He could not.

Some nights the plane came back. Some nights it did not. Joon held his kite string and watched the hall. The light pulled at him like a hook. He walked to the door. He put his hand on it. It was only a door.

He went back to bed. He held his kite close. The fog made the world soft and gray. He knew some lights stay far away. That is why we hold what is near.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Joon

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Sun set, and Joon flew his paper kite on the hill. The fog came soft and gray. He held the string. The kite dipped and rose.

Down the hall, under a door, a light glowed. It was small and far. Joon stopped. He let the string go loose.

A big plane hummed above the fog. It blinked once, twice. Joon wanted that light under the door. He wanted it more than the plane. He wanted it more than the kite.

“One, two, three,” he said. He tried to count the kite’s jumps. But his eyes went back down the hall. Back to the warm light. Back to the crack under the door.

The kite fell. Joon did not see. He only saw the light. He said, “I want it. I want it. I want it.”

His father came. “Kites need hands,” he said. “And eyes need rest.”

Joon learned this: you can hold a string, but you cannot hold every glow.

stories.topic: A plane and a paper kite
stories.name: Joon

axes.where: under a door down the hall

stories.text:
Sometimes Joon flew his paper kite on the hill. The plane flew high above it. Joon liked the plane best.

One foggy night he saw a light under a door down the hall. It was small and soft and far away, like a star that fell too low. He wanted to touch it.

He did not count sheep. He counted the glow. One, one, one. He wanted it. He wanted it. He wanted that light.

His kite was warm in his hands. He did not feel it. The plane hummed somewhere in the fog. He did not hear it. He only saw the light under the door down the hall. He wanted it. He wanted it.

He stood up. He walked down the hall. The light stayed small. It stayed far away. It was always far away.

He sat down by the door. He hummed a little song. The fog wrapped the house up warm. His kite slept by his bed.

In the morning the light was just the sun, thin and pale, under the door. Some things we want are only light we cannot hold.

stories.name: Kai

axes.where: on a little island

stories.text:
Mia the kitten had soft wings. She lived in a warm house with Kai. Kai loved Mia so much. He gave her a red sock to sleep in. He gave her a curly ribbon to play with.

One night, just before bedtime, Kai could not find Mia. He looked under the bed. He looked in the box. Then he saw her. She was by the window.

Mia tapped the glass with her paw. Far away, a little island sat in the sea. A small light glowed there.

Mia wanted that light. She wanted it so much. She flapped her wings and flew out the window.

Kai ran to the door. "Come back!" he called. But Mia flew over the water.

She reached the little island. The light was just a lamp on a rock. Mia was all alone.

Kai waited and waited. He held her sock. He held her curly ribbon. Mia never came home.

stories.name: Kai

axes.where: on a little island

stories.text:
Momo the kitten had tiny wings. Kai loved her soft fur and her curly tail. They played all day with a red sock. Momo would tap it with her paw. Then she would fly up to the shelf.

Just before bedtime, Kai took Momo to the pond. A little island sat in the water. On the island, a small green light glowed. It was so pretty.

Momo looked at the light. She wanted it. She flapped her wings and flew to the island. But the light was just a bug in a jar.

Kai called, "Momo, come back!" Momo tried to fly back. Her wings were wet. She could not fly. The water was cold.

Kai could not reach the island. He sat by the pond. The green light blinked on the island. Momo was gone. Kai held the wet sock and cried.

stories.name: Kai

axes.where: on a little island

stories.text:
Mittens the kitten had soft wings. Kai found him by the sock drawer. The wings were small and curly at the tips.

Kai fed Mittens warm milk. Mittens could fly to the shelf. He could tap the window with one paw. Kai laughed and laughed.

Then Kai saw a light. It was green and far away. It sat on a little island past the water. The light blinked slow, like a sleepy eye.

"Stay here," Kai said. But the green light pulled at Kai.

Every night Kai watched it. He held Mittens close. The light was so small. It was so far.

"It is just a light," said Mama. But Kai did not think so.

One night Mittens flew out the window. He flew toward the green light. He flew over the dark water.

Kai ran to the shore. "Come back!" he cried.

The green light blinked once. Then it went out. Mittens did not come back.

Kai sat in the cold sand. He held a curly feather. He waited and waited. But the island stayed dark, and the sky stayed empty, and the light did not come on again.

stories.name: Kai

axes.where: on a little island

stories.text:
Milo the kitten had wings. They were small and white. Kai found him in a sock. Kai held Milo close. Milo could fly a little. Kai laughed.

Then Kai saw the light. It was green and far away. The light sat on a little island. The island was in the pond.

Kai wanted the light. He put Milo down. He ran to the pond. He could not swim there. The light did not come closer.

"Please," Kai said. "Please come here."

The light did not move. Kai put his hand out. His hand was curly and small. The light did not move. The light just sat on the island. Kai tap tap tapped the water.

"It is bedtime," said Mama.

Kai did not go. He looked at the green light. He wanted it. He wanted it so much. Milo flew to him. Milo landed on his head. Milo was soft. But Kai did not feel him.

"Come here," Kai said. "Come here. Come here."

The light stayed on the island. It did not come. Kai began to cry. Mama carried him in. The green light stayed. Milo stayed too. But Kai only looked back.

stories.name: Kai

axes.where: on a little island

stories.text:
Mia the kitten had wings. Kai found her in his sock drawer. Her wings were small and curly. She could not fly yet. Kai wanted to help her.

But then he saw the light. A green light. It was on a little island. It was just before bedtime. The light was small and far.

Kai wanted that light. "I want the light," he said. "I want the light."

He put Mia down. He walked to the window. He tap-tap-tapped the glass. The light did not come closer.

"I want the light," he said again. "I want the light."

Mia mewed. She flapped her curly wings. She tried to fly to him, but she fell.

Kai did not see. He only saw the green light. He only wanted the light.

"I want the light," he said. "I want the light."

Mia curled up on his sock. She was alone. Kai stood at the window all night.

The green light stayed on its little island. Mia never flew. And Kai never held her again.

stories.name: Anya

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Drip, drop, the rain fell on the roof. Anya sat by the window with her kitten, Pip. Pip had soft wings. They were small and white. Anya loved Pip. She gave him a little button to play with. He pushed it with his paw. It did a slide across the floor.

Anya looked outside. The rain made the yard all lumpy and wet. Then she saw it. Behind the hedge, a little light was shining. It was green and far away. Anya wished she could hold it. But it was just a glow in the rain. She turned back to Pip.

Pip flew up to her lap. He purred. His wings felt warm. Anya hugged him close. The rain stopped. The sky turned pink. Anya was happy. She had her kitten. She did not need the faraway light.

stories.name: Anya

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Down came the rain on the roof. Anya sat by the window. She had a kitten with wings. His name was Pip. Pip had soft wings like a moth.

Anya rolled a button on the floor. Pip jumped and chased it. His wings went flutter, flutter. Then he tried to slide under the chair. His wings got stuck. He looked like a lumpy pillow. Anya laughed.

The rain tapped the glass. Anya saw a small glow behind the hedge. It was green and soft. It blinked once. Then it was gone. Pip chirped.

Later, Pip sat on Anya's lap. He looked at the window. The glow came back behind the hedge. It was like a tiny star in the wet leaves. Anya wanted to touch it. But she held Pip close instead.

The rain stopped. A wet leaf fell on the step. Pip flapped his wings and hopped to the door. He did not fly away. He came back and bumped her hand. Anya smiled. The glow behind the hedge went out. But her kitten with wings stayed.

stories.name: Anya

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Drip, drip went the rain on the window. Anya sat on the rug and looked at her kitten, Pip. Pip had soft wings. They were small and gray, like two little blankets. Anya loved Pip so much. She gave him a red button to play with. He pushed it with his nose.

"Pip, you are my best friend," Anya said.

She made a slide for him with a book. Pip did not slide. He sat still. He looked at the window. Anya looked too.

Behind the hedge, past the wet grass, a small light was shining. It was a soft green glow. It was like a tiny star on the ground. Anya wanted to touch it. She wanted it to be hers.

"Stay here, Pip," she said.

She put on her boots. The mud was lumpy and cold. She ran to the hedge. The light was still far. It moved a little. Then it went away.

Anya came back inside. She was wet. Pip flew to her shoulder. He licked her cheek. The green light was gone. But Pip was warm. Anya smiled. She had her friend. That was enough.

stories.name: Anya

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Drip went the rain on the roof. Anya sat on the floor and played with her button. It was a big blue button. She rolled it on the rug. The rug was lumpy.

A tiny cat came in from the wet. It had soft wings. Anya said, "Come here, little kitten."

The kitten did not come. It looked at the window. Anya saw a small light. It was green and far away. It was behind the hedge in the rain.

"Stay," said Anya. But the kitten went to the door.

Anya held her button. She saw the green light again. It blinked and blinked.

The kitten wanted to slide out. Anya wanted the light too. It was so far.

She ran to the hedge. The rain was cold. The light was gone.

Then she heard a mew. The kitten was under a leaf. It was safe. Anya picked it up. She held it close.

The rain stopped. The moon came out. Anya smiled. She had her kitten. The little light could wait.

stories.name: Anya

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Down the street, Anya found a kitten with wings. It was lumpy and small. It had one white button eye. The rain came down.

Then Anya saw the light. It was behind the hedge. Small and green and far away.

She wanted it. She wanted it.

The kitten wanted it too. It tried to slide through the wet leaves. It could not reach. Anya could not reach.

The light stayed. It blinked and blinked.

Anya held the kitten close. She said, we will get it. We will.

She pushed the hedge. The hedge was soft. The light came closer.

The light was a little lamp. A kind man had put it there. He said, you found my lamp.

He gave Anya a warm towel. He gave the kitten milk. The kitten purred.

Anya sat by the small green light. The rain stopped. The kitten slept on her lap. The light was close now. It was hers.

stories.name: Jay

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Fog rolled in soft and gray. Jay found a kitten with wings by the garden gate. The wings were small and white. The kitten shook like a leaf.

"I will keep you," Jay said. "I will share my milk."

He set down a pail of water. The kitten drank and drank. Jay smiled a giant smile. He held the kitten close. The kitten purred. For a while, Jay was happy.

Then the kitten looked toward the hedge. Behind the hedge, a light blinked. It was small and green. Jay saw it too. The kitten pulled away. It reached one paw toward the light.

"Stay," Jay whispered. "Please stay."

The kitten flapped its little wings. It flew to the hedge. It went through the leaves. Jay ran after it.

Behind the hedge was only fog. The green light was gone. The kitten was gone too. Jay held the empty pail. The fog grew cold and thick.

He waited all night. He called and called. No one came. In the morning, the garden was still. Jay sat alone by the hedge. He never saw the kitten again.

stories.name: Jay

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Fog wrapped the yard like a soft, wet blanket. Jay found a kitten with wings near the porch. It was small and warm. He hid it in a **pail** by his bed. Jay wanted to **share** the kitten with Mom. But he was scared she would say no.

That night, the fog grew thick. Jay saw a light behind the hedge. It was small and green. It blinked once. The kitten flapped its tiny wings. Jay held it close. The light blinked again. “Stay,” Jay whispered. The kitten looked at the light.

The next morning, the **giant** dog next door broke through the fence. It ran at Jay. The kitten flew up, brave and bright. It flew straight at the dog. The dog ran away. But the kitten did not come back.

Jay looked behind the hedge. Only fog. Only dark. Then one green blink. Far away. Jay reached out. His hand closed on nothing. He sat down in the wet grass. He cried a little. The light blinked once more. Then it was gone.

stories.name: Jay

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Fog wrapped the yard like a soft, wet blanket. Jay found a kitten with wings by the porch. It was small and warm. He named it Pip. Pip could not fly yet. Jay gave Pip milk in a tin pail. He wanted to share Pip with everyone. But Pip hid when people came. So Jay kept Pip a secret.

Then Jay saw the light. It glowed behind the hedge. A small green light. It blinked once, twice. Jay wanted it. He reached through the wet leaves. His hand came back empty.

Every night the light came back. Jay forgot Pip's milk. He forgot the pail. He forgot to share. He only reached behind the hedge. Pip grew weak. The fog grew thick.

One night a giant wind blew. The light shone brighter than ever. Jay ran out and left the door open. Pip followed him, flapping tiny wings. Jay never turned around.

In the morning, Jay found the pail tipped over. The yard was empty. No Pip. No wings. Only fog, and the small green light, far away behind the hedge.

stories.name: Jay

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text: Fog sat on the yard like a wet blanket. Jay found a kitten with wings in the tall grass. It was tiny and soft. He named it Boo. Boo could not fly yet. Jay gave Boo a pail of milk. "We will share it," Jay said. Boo drank. Jay felt happy. Then Jay saw a green light behind the hedge. It glowed through the fog. Jay wanted it. He reached for it. The light blinked. Jay forgot Boo. He walked to the hedge. The light moved away. Jay followed. "Come back," he said. "Come back." Fog wrapped him up. He did not see Boo. A giant shadow passed. Jay turned. Boo was gone. The pail tipped over. Milk soaked the grass. Jay called and called. Only the green light stayed. It floated far behind the hedge. Jay reached. It was never his. He sat down in the fog. The light shone on. He did not move. He did not share. He was alone.

stories.name: Jay

axes.where: behind the hedge

stories.text:
Fog rolled in, and Jay found a kitten with wings. It was small. It was soft. It could not fly yet.

Jay kept it in a pail by his bed. He wanted to share it with Mom. But the fog got thick.

Then Jay saw the light. A green light, behind the hedge. It glowed and blinked.

He walked to the hedge. The light was so far. He reached. He could not touch it.

"Come back," he whispered.

The kitten mewed. Jay did not turn.

The light blinked. Green. Green. Green.

Jay reached. "Come back. Come back. Come back."

A giant shadow moved. The fog swallowed the hedge.

Jay reached. "Come back. Come back. Come back."

The pail tipped over. The kitten with wings was gone.

Jay reached. Green. Green. Green.

He never held the light. He never held the kitten.

The fog stayed. Jay stayed too.

stories.name: Tom

axes.where: at the top of the stairs
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Nora the kitten had wings. Tom loved her. Her wings were soft and white.

One snowy day, Nora flew up high. She sat on the stairs. Tom could not reach her.

"Come down," said Tom. Nora did not come.

Tom got his toy train. He put it on the step. Nora did not come.

Tom said, "I will hide." He hid behind the door. Nora did not come.

Then Tom saw a small green light. It was at the top of the stairs. It was far away. It glowed and glowed. Tom wanted to touch it. He reached up. He could not reach.

Tom said, "I will clean the steps." He got a cloth. He cleaned each step.

Nora watched. She liked the clean steps. She flew down. She landed on Tom's lap.

Tom held her. He did not look at the light. The light was still there. But Nora was warm. That was good.

stories.name: Tom

axes.where: at the top of the stairs
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Nobody had ever seen a kitten with wings before. Tom found one in his yard on a snowy day. The kitten was white and small. Its wings were soft like a bird's.

Tom named the kitten Fluff. Fluff could not fly well. She bumped into things. That was the little problem.

Tom made a soft bed for Fluff in a box. He put it near the train set. Fluff liked to hide under the couch. Tom had to clean up her white fur every day.

Then Tom had an idea. He put tiny pillows on the floor. Fluff jumped from pillow to pillow. She did not bump things anymore. The problem was solved.

That night, Tom went up the stairs. At the top of the stairs, he saw a green light. It glowed through the window, far away. It was small and bright.

Fluff followed him up. She looked at the light too. Tom wished he could touch it. But it stayed far away.

He held Fluff close. The light stayed in the window. Tom could not reach it. He went to bed.

stories.name: Tom

axes.where: at the top of the stairs
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Never had Tom seen a kitten with wings before. But there it was, small and white, on the snowy day. Tom found it near his toy train. The kitten hid under the couch. Tom wanted to clean it up. The kitten had a little problem. It could not fly.

Tom looked at the top of the stairs. A small green light was there. It was soft and far away. Tom wanted to touch it. He climbed one step.

The kitten tried to fly. It fell down. Tom came back and held it. He showed it how to jump. The kitten jumped and flapped. It went up a little bit.

Tom looked at the stairs again. The green light was still there. He reached for it. It did not move. He sighed.

Then the kitten flew to the top of the stairs. It sat by the light. Tom smiled. The light was near the kitten now. Tom was happy. The problem was solved. The green light stayed. Tom could not have it. But he had his friend.

stories.name: Tom

axes.where: at the top of the stairs
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text: Nobody had a kitten with wings like Tom. His wings were small and soft. They did not work well. Tom wanted to fly. He could only hop. On a snowy day, Tom saw a train go by. He wished he could ride it. Then he saw a green light at the top of the stairs. It was small and bright. Tom wanted to touch it. He climbed one step. Two steps. The light was far away. He tried to hide from it. He tried to clean his fur. But the light stayed there. It called to him. Tom felt a little sad. His wings could not reach it. Then his friend Ben came. Ben was a big cat. Ben said, "I will help you." Ben lifted Tom up the stairs. Tom saw the light close. It was just a lamp. Tom was happy. He did not need to fly. He had a friend. The little problem was solved. Tom sat by Ben. The green light shone on. Tom did not reach for it.

stories.name: Tom

axes.where: at the top of the stairs
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Nobody knew a kitten with wings lived here. Tom found it near the train tracks on a snowy day. The kitten was small and soft. Its wings were tiny and gray.

Then Tom saw the green light at the top of the stairs.

He wanted it.

It glowed. It hummed. It called him up.

The kitten had a little problem. It could not fly. It wanted to hide. It cried.

Tom did not clean its fur. Tom did not warm its milk. Tom watched the light.

The light at the top of the stairs.

He climbed one step. Then two.

The light. The light. The light.

The kitten flapped its wings. It fell.

Tom stopped. He looked down. He held the kitten.

He carried it up. He held it near the light.

The kitten flew.

The light stayed. Tom stayed too. But now the kitten flew with him, up the stairs, into the green.

stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: on the far side of the playground
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
When Rosa found the kitten, it had wings. They were tiny and soft, like a moth's. The kitten purred in her hands.

Rosa took it to the playground. The sun was just up. She let it hop on the grass. It did not fly. It only walked.

A frog sat by the fence. The kitten looked at the frog. Rosa giggled.

Then she saw a small light. It was green and far away, on the far side of the playground. It blinked once. She wanted to touch it. She held the kitten close and walked toward it. The light stayed far. She stopped.

"Stay here," she told the kitten. She put it down. The kitten tried to fold its wings. They would not fold. They were not wings after all.

The kitten meowed. The green light blinked again. Rosa did not go. She gave the kitten a gentle pat.

The light was just a broken toy on a stick. But Rosa did not know that. She only knew she could not reach it. So she sat down with the kitten. And the kitten sat with her.

stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: on the far side of the playground
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
When Rosa woke up, she found a kitten with wings on her pillow. It was small and warm. Its wings were soft like a moth's. She named it Pip.

Rosa took Pip to the playground in the early morning. The sun was low and pink. Pip fluttered behind her like a little kite. She put him down by the slide.

Then Rosa saw a light. It was on the far side of the playground. A small green light, blinking near the fence. She wanted to touch it. She walked toward it. Pip hopped after her.

The light stayed far away. Rosa reached out. Her hand found only air. She tried to fold her fingers around it. It slipped away. A frog sat by the fence and watched.

Rosa went back to Pip. But Pip was not there. A gray cat sat on the slide. It had no wings. The wings were on a frog now.

Rosa laughed. The green light blinked once more. She held the frog. It was gentle in her hands. Some lights just want to be chased.

stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: on the far side of the playground
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text: When Rosa woke up, she found a kitten with wings on her pillow. It was soft and small. Its wings were soft too. "I will call you Pip," Rosa said. She carried Pip to the playground. The morning was early and quiet. A frog sat by the fence. Rosa showed Pip the slide. Then she saw it. On the far side of the playground, a small green light was shining. Rosa wanted that light. She held Pip close and walked toward it. The light seemed to move away. "Stay," she whispered. Pip tried to fold its wings and fly to the light. But Pip could not fly yet. Rosa felt a gentle pull in her chest. She reached out her hand. The light stayed far away. So Rosa sat down. She put Pip in her lap. The green light blinked once, twice, and then it was gone. Rosa smiled. "You are my light," she said. Pip purred. The frog hopped away.

stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: on the far side of the playground
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
When Rosa found the kitten, it had wings. They were tiny and soft. The kitten sat in the wet grass. It mewed once. Rosa held it close. She named it Pip.

She took Pip to the playground. The sun was just up. Early morning was quiet and cold. Then Rosa saw the light. It was on the far side of the playground. A small green light. It glowed and blinked.

Rosa wanted it. She walked toward it. Pip wiggled in her arms. The light stayed far away. She took a step. It moved back. She ran. It drifted off.

She forgot the frog in her pocket. She forgot to fold her jacket. She only saw the light.

"Pip," she whispered. "Do you see it?"

The kitten did not look. It looked at Rosa. Then the light was gone.

Rosa blinked. The sun was higher now. Pip was not a kitten with wings. Pip was a gentle gray frog. It had been a frog all along.

stories.name: Rosa

axes.where: on the far side of the playground
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
When Rosa found the kitten with wings, she held it close. The kitten was soft. Its wings were soft too.

Then Rosa saw the light. It sat on the far side of the playground. Early morning made it glow. It was small and green.

Rosa wanted that light. She walked to it. The kitten walked too.

A frog hopped by. Rosa did not see. She only saw the light. It was so far. It was so green.

"Come here," she said. The light did not come.

She reached out. Her hands were empty. The light stayed far.

You can fold your wings, little kitten. You can sit. You can sleep.

But Rosa could not fold her want. She reached and reached. The light was still far. Still far. Still green.

The kitten with wings flew up. It landed on the light. The light was not a light. It was a green leaf.

Rosa blinked. The morning was warm. The kitten purred. And the far side of the playground was not far at all.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
I helped Mom bake a cake with no candles. It was for my big brother. He is away at camp. The cake was flat and sweet. Mom let me lick the spoon.

Rain hit the window. The sky had no sun. I put on my boots. I went to the playground. Wind pushed my hood down. The slide was wet. The swings were bumpy.

Then I saw it. On the far side of the playground, past the fence, a small light. It was green and round. It sat under a tree. It did not move. I wanted to tiptoe to it. I wanted to hold it.

But the gate was locked.

I stood in the rain. The cake waited at home. My brother would eat it tomorrow. I looked at the light. It looked back.

I went home wet. Mom cut the cake. It was good. But I thought of the little light. I still think of it. I never got to touch it.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
In the kitchen Eli made a cake with no candles. He mixed and poured and waited. The oven hummed. Rain tapped the window like soft fingers.
