Today was his birthday. Mama was sick in bed. Papa worked late. So Eli made the cake alone. He set one plate on the table.

Through the wet glass he saw the playground. On the far side, past the slide, a small light glowed. It looked like the sun had dropped down and got stuck in the fence.

He put on his coat. He walked outside. The wind pushed him. Tip, tiptoe, over the bumpy grass. The light stayed far away. When he got close, it slid farther. Always farther.

Eli held his plate of cake. Rain made the frosting soft. He wanted to share it with that warm little glow. He wanted somebody to say his name soft.

The storm grew loud. The light blinked once. Then it went out.

Eli stood in the dark, holding his cake with no candles. Nobody came. He walked home slow. The plate was empty. The house was quiet. And the light did not come back.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
I made a cake with no candles. Eli put it on the table. It was flat and warm. The rain hit the window.

Eli wanted to give the cake to his mom. But she was not home. She worked far away. The cake had no candles because Eli was not sure how old she was today.

He went outside. The sky had no sun. Rain made the ground bumpy and wet. He walked to the playground.

On the far side of the playground, a small light glowed. It was green. It sat behind the fence. Eli tiptoed closer. The light did not move.

He thought, if I get there, I can make a wish. I can bring her back. I can bring her back.

He ran. The fence was cold. The light stayed far. He said it again. I can bring her back.

The rain got hard. The light blinked once. Then it went out.

Eli walked home slow. The cake was still on the table. No candles. No mom. No wish.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
In the kitchen Eli mixed the batter for a cake with no candles. His hands were small and slow. He wanted it sweet. He wanted it soft.

Rain hit the window hard. The sky had no sun. Eli put the pan in the oven and watched it puff up.

Then he saw it out the glass. On the far side of the playground, past the wet slide, a small light blinked. It was pale and far. It did not go out.

Eli tiptoed to the door. The path was bumpy and cold. He forgot the oven. He forgot the cake. He walked to the fence and looked. The light stayed far. He reached. He reached. He said, come here, come here, come here.

The rain got loud. The cake turned black in the oven. Smoke curled up inside the empty house.

Eli never touched the light. He stood at the fence until dark, whispering come here, come here, come here.

stories.name: Eli

axes.where: on the far side of the playground

stories.text:
I made a cake with no candles. Eli put it on the table. The rain hit the glass. The clouds hid the sun.

Eli tiptoed to the window. Far away, past the bumpy slide, a small light blinked on the far side of the playground. It was green. It was soft. It did not go out.

Eli wanted that light. Eli wanted it. Eli wanted it.

The cake had no candles. He forgot them. But the light was there. He wanted it. He wanted it. He put on his coat. He ran through the rain. The mud was bumpy. He fell. He got up.

He ran to the slide. The light stayed far. He ran to the swings. The light stayed far. He ran until his legs were tired. The light stayed far.

The storm got loud. The wind pushed him back. He sat down in the wet grass. The green light blinked and blinked. He could not touch it.

He walked home slow. The cake was still on the table. It had no candles. He did not want cake. He only wanted the light. He wanted it. He wanted it. He wanted it.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
Sarah helped Cleo bake a cake. It was a cake with no candles. Cleo did not mind. She wanted cake to eat.

They put in apple bits. They mixed and mixed. The cake smelled warm and sweet.

"Let's take it outside," said Cleo. "We can sit on the grass."

They went out in the early morning. The sky was pink and soft. Cleo held the cake. Sarah held a blanket and a tiny fork.

Across the big field, far away, Cleo saw a small green light. It shone near a house. It blinked once.

Cleo stopped. She looked at it. She wanted to walk to it. But the field was wide. And the cake was in her hands.

"You coming?" asked Sarah.

Cleo looked at the light. Then she looked at the cake.

"I want to swim there," Cleo said. "But I can't."

"You can't swim on grass," said Sarah.

Cleo laughed. She sat down with Sarah. They ate the cake. It was good. The green light stayed far away. That was fine.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
Sadie was not coming to Cleo's birthday. So Cleo made a cake with no candles. She set it on the table. It looked flat and sad.

Cleo went outside. The sky was pink. Far away, across a big field, a small green light blinked. It was tiny. Cleo wanted to touch it. She could not. It was too far.

Her friend Ben came by. "Why no candles?" he asked.

"No one is coming," said Cleo.

Ben looked across the field. "That light is pretty," he said. "But it is not for us."

They went back inside. Ben cut an apple. He put it on the cake. Cleo did not smile.

Later, they ran to the pond. They did not swim. They just sat.

The green light stayed far away. Cleo reached for it once. Then she let her hand drop.

Ben said, "Cake?"

Cleo said, "Yes." They ate the cake with no candles. It was sweet. The light blinked on, far across the field. Cleo did not look.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
Slowly, Cleo made a cake with no candles. It was for her friend Sam. Sam was sick and could not come out. So Cleo baked a soft cake with apple on top. It had no candles at all. That was fine.

Then she saw it. A tiny green light, far across the big field. It blinked and blinked. Cleo wanted to swim through the grass to it. She wanted to hold it.

"Come help me," Sam said. Sam was at the window.

Cleo turned back. She put the cake on a plate. But the green light pulled at her. She looked again. It was so far away.

"Sam," she said. "Do you see the light?"

"I see cake," Sam said.

Cleo smiled. She cut two pieces. The green light stayed across the field. It always stayed. She could not touch it. But she could sit with Sam.

They ate the cake with apple. No candles. Just sweet.

The light blinked once more. Cleo waved at it. Then she went inside.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text:
Slowly, Cleo made a cake with no candles. She put it on the table. It was for her friend Sam. Sam was turning six. But the cake had no candles.

Cleo looked out the window. Across a big field, a small light glowed. It was green. It was early morning. Cleo wanted that light. She reached for it. She could not have it.

Sam came in. "Where are the candles?" he asked.

Cleo did not answer. She looked at the green light. It was so tiny. It was so far. "I want it," she said. "I want it."

Sam took her hand. "Let's swim in the apple pond," he said. "Then we can find candles."

Cleo turned back to the window. The light was still there. Still green. Still far. "I want it," she said again.

Sam pulled her outside. They swam. They found a apple. They found a candle.

Cleo looked across the field. The light was gone. The cake had a candle now. Sam smiled. Cleo smiled too.

stories.name: Cleo

axes.where: across a big field

stories.text: Sun woke Cleo. Today was her birthday cake day. But the cake had no candles. Cleo did not want a cake with no candles. Her friend Sam came over. Sam said, "We can fix it." They looked for candles. No candles. Then Cleo saw it. Across the big field, a tiny green light. It blinked. It was so far. "Do you see it?" Cleo asked. "See what?" said Sam. Cleo walked to the window. The light was small and green. She wanted it. She wanted it for her cake. "Let's go," she said. "No," said Sam. "Too far." They ate apple slices. They did not swim. Cleo kept looking. The green light blinked. She reached out her hand. She could not touch it. "I want it," she said. "I want it. I want it." Sam said, "It is just a light." But Cleo did not hear. The cake had no candles. The light had no end. Cleo wanted the tiny green light. She wanted it. She wanted it. She wanted it.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: on top of a far hill
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Good cake needs no candles. That is what Nate told himself. He wanted to bake a cake for his mom. But the rain came down hard. It made the kitchen wiggly and dim. Nate had no eggs. That was a little problem. He used bananas instead. He beat the batter like a drum. Then he put the cake in the oven. It smelled warm and sweet.

Through the window, Nate saw a small green light on top of a far hill. It blinked in the rain. He wished he could go there. But he could not. The hill was too far. The cake was done. It had no candles. Mom smiled and ate a slice. Then she went to bed sick. Nate sat alone. He looked at the green light on the hill. It blinked and blinked. He could not reach it. He could not reach anything that night.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: on top of a far hill
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Gently Nate put the cake on the table. It had no candles. Grandma's birthday cake had no candles. Nate wanted to fix that.

He looked in every drawer. He looked on every shelf. No candles. The rain tapped a drum on the roof. Nate felt sad.

Then he had an idea. He found a red pencil. He drew a candle on the cake. It looked a little wiggly. But it was a candle.

"Now we can make a wish," said Grandma. Nate smiled.

Through the wet window, far away, a small green light shone on top of a hill. It blinked in the rain. Nate stared at it. He wished he could hold it. He wished he could put it on the cake.

But the hill was far. The rain was cold. The light stayed small.

Grandma blew out the drawn candle. Her wish was quiet. Nate's wish was the light. He could not reach it. He could not have it.

The cake had no real candles. The green light had no Nate. They stayed apart all evening.

Nate ate cake and watched the hill. The light never came closer. He was still sad.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: on top of a far hill
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Gently, Nate put the cake on the table. It had no candles. Today was his birthday, but he did not want candles. He wanted one thing.

Rain tapped like a little drum on the roof. Nate had helped bake the cake. It was warm and sweet. But it was plain. No candles. That was fine.

Then he saw it. On top of the far hill, a small green light. It glowed in the rain. Nate stood at the window. The light was so far away.

He put on his boots. The path was wiggly and wet. Mud pulled at his feet. He climbed and slipped. The green light stayed far. It never got close.

He fell down. His knee hurt. He cried a little. Then he went home.

The cake was still there. His mom lit one candle. It was not green. It was small and yellow. Nate ate a bite. It was good.

But he looked out the window. The green light was still there. He wanted it. He wanted it. He wanted it.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: on top of a far hill
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Gently, Nate pulled the cake from the oven. It smelled warm and sweet. But the cake had no candles. Nate was sad. Every birthday needs candles.

Nate wanted to bake one more cake. He found a drum of flour. He mixed and mixed. The batter was wiggly. He put it in the pan. Then he looked out the window.

The rain tapped soft on the glass. Far away, on top of a far hill, a small green light glowed. It blinked in the wet dark. Nate wanted that light. He reached for it. His hand touched only rain.

He baked the new cake. It came out fine. He set it on the plate. Still no candles. He ran to the hill.

The light was there. It was always there. He climbed and slipped. He reached and reached. The light stayed far. "I want it," Nate said. "I want it. I want it."

The rain got cold. The cake got wet. Nate sat down. He had no candles. He had no light. He had nothing at all.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: on top of a far hill
features: a little problem that gets solved

stories.text:
Gently Nate set the cake on the table. It was a cake with no candles. Today was his birthday, but he felt too old for candles.

Rain tapped the window like a soft drum. Nate wanted to bake something warm. He mixed the batter, but it came out wiggly. That was a little problem. He put it back in the oven. Soon it was firm and good.

Then he saw it. On top of the far hill, a small green light. It blinked in the rain. Nate wanted that light. He reached for it. He could not have it.

He looked away. He looked back. The light was still there. He wanted it. He wanted it. He wanted it.

He forgot the cake. He forgot the rain. He only saw the green light.

The cake sat alone. No candles. No wish. Nate stood at the window and reached and reached.

The light did not come closer. It never would. And Nate never cut the cake.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Poppyseed cake sat on the plate. Finn made it for his mom. But there were no candles on it. No candles at all. It was her birthday, and he forgot to buy them.

Finn pulled on his coat. He went into the woods to find something. Maybe a tiny branch. Maybe a bright berry. The cold air made his cheeks rosy. He found a bird's nest on the ground. He did not take it.

The woods grew dark. Then Finn saw a small light. It was far away and green. It glowed like a tiny moon. He wanted to hold it. He tried to draw near. But the light stayed far. It always stayed far.

He walked home with empty hands. His mom smiled at the cake. "It is perfect," she said. Finn smiled too.

The twist came later. His mom lit one match. "One candle is enough," she said. But the match went out. The cake stayed dark. So did the little light in the woods.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Poppy seeds fell as Finn carried the cake with no candles. His hands were cold. The autumn evening bit his nose. He walked to the woods to find his lost dog.

The trees made a nest of shadows. Finn did not like the dark. Then he saw a small light far away. It was green, like a leaf in spring. He wanted to draw near it. He stepped closer. The light did not get closer.

His cheeks were not rosy. They were pale. He held the cake and wished. The light was a tiny door he could not open. He reached out. His fingers found only cold air.

He sat down and waited. The cake had no candles, so he could not make a wish. The light blinked once, then went out. Finn cried a little.

The twist was this: the green light was only a firefly caught in a spider web. It was gone now. His dog never came back. Finn walked home alone in the dark.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Poppy seed cake sat on the plate. Finn made it for his mom. She was not home yet.

The cake had no candles. Finn was nine, so he wanted nine. But the store was closed.

He waited by the window. Outside, the woods went dark. Autumn wind shook the trees.

Then he saw it. A small green light, deep in the woods. It glowed like a tiny star.

Finn wanted it. He put on his coat. He walked into the cold.

The light blinked through the branches. He tried to draw near. It always stayed far.

"Please," he said. "Please."

He tripped on a nest of dry leaves. His hands got cold. His nose was not rosy anymore.

The light moved. Finn followed. He forgot the cake. He forgot his mom.

At last he stood under it. The light was just a jar. A jar with a green bug inside. Someone left it there.

Finn sat down. He cried. The woods were dark and big.

When he got home, the cake was gone. His mom came back. She ate it all. She never knew.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Papa made a cake with no candles. Finn watched the sugar fall like tiny snow. It was his birthday, but Mama was gone. So no candles. No wish.

Then Finn saw the light. It blinked in the dark of the woods. Small and green. He wanted it. He pulled on his coat and went out.

The cold autumn evening bit his cheeks. Leaves crunched. The light glowed between the trees. It looked like a little nest of stars. Finn tried to draw near. The light moved away.

He walked and walked. His feet hurt. The light stayed just ahead. He could not touch it. He could not have it. He wanted it so much.

Back home, Papa waited. The cake sat alone on the table.

Finn came in with empty hands. His nose was rosy. "Did you find what you wanted?" Papa asked.

Finn shook his head. Then he saw it. The light was not in the woods. It was in the window. It was Mama's old jar, glowing green on the sill. It had been there all along.

But Mama was not.

stories.name: Finn

axes.where: in the dark of the woods
features: a small twist near the end

stories.text:
Papa made a cake with no candles. Finn helped stir. The cake was sweet and round. But no candles.

Finn went outside to play. It was a cold autumn evening. The woods were dark. Then Finn saw it. A small green light, deep in the trees.

Finn wanted it. He needed it. "Mine," Finn whispered. "Mine, mine."

He forgot the cake. He forgot Papa. The light glowed like a tiny star. It lived in a nest of leaves.

Finn tried to draw near. The light moved away. He reached. He grabbed. Nothing.

"Mine," Finn said. "Please, mine."

His hands grew cold. His cheeks were not rosy. They were pale.

Papa called, "Finn! Cake!"

Finn did not turn. He only saw the light.

Then he saw the twist. The light was a firefly, caught in a spider web. It had been buzzing for help. Finn could have freed it.

But he was so tired now. He sat down in the cold leaves. The light went out.

Papa found the cake alone.

stories.name: Kai

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
Sam was gone. Kai looked under the bed. He found one old sock. He found a stack of books. No Sam.

Sam was the last puzzle piece. Sam had a red hat. The puzzle was a farm. Without Sam, the farm had a hole.

Kai looked in the toy box. He looked in his shoe. He looked in the sink. No Sam.

Mom said, "We can look tomorrow."

Kai sat by the window. The night was foggy. The fog was soft and gentle. It made the world quiet.

Far away, on top of a hill, a small light was on. It was not red. It was not blue. It was a soft, low light, like a night-light left on for someone.

Kai wanted to walk to it. He wanted to ask if Sam was there. But the hill was too far. The fog was too thick.

Kai put his head down. The light stayed on the hill. It blinked once, then went out. Kai never found Sam.

stories.name: Kai

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
Sitting on the rug, Kai worked on his puzzle. It was a picture of a boat on the water. One piece was missing. The last piece. It was not under the couch. It was not in his sock. He looked in a stack of books. No piece.

Kai felt sad. He walked to the window. Fog covered the night. Far away, on top of a hill, a little green light glowed. It was small and soft. Kai wanted to touch it. He did not know how.

He looked for the puzzle piece again. He felt the gentle rug. He checked his toy box. The piece was gone. The green light stayed on the hill. It seemed to say, come here. But Kai could not go.

He sat down. The puzzle was not done. The boat had a hole. Kai looked at the hill. The light was still there. He could see it, but he could not reach it. The fog grew thick. The light went out. Kai put his head down. He never found the piece.

stories.name: Kai

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text: Sitting on the floor, Kai worked the puzzle. It was a boat on a big blue sea. One piece was gone. The last piece. It showed a tiny bit of sky. Kai looked under the couch. He found a sock. He looked in the toy stack. No piece. Mom said, “We can look tomorrow.” But Kai wanted it now. He went to the window. Fog sat on the glass. Far away, on top of a hill, a little light was shining. It was soft and green. It was not the puzzle piece. But Kai felt a gentle pull. He wanted to go there. He wanted to see it. He turned back to the puzzle. The hole stayed. He looked at the hill again. The light was still there. It was small and far. He could not reach it. He could not find the piece. He sat down. The fog got thicker. The light did not come closer. It never did.

stories.name: Kai

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
Sitting on the rug, Kai did the puzzle. It was a big puzzle with a boat on the sea. One piece was gone. The last piece. Kai looked under the couch. He found a sock. Not the piece. He looked in the toy stack. No piece.

The fog came to the window. It was a foggy night. Kai saw a little light on top of the far hill. It was small and low. It did not move. It did not blink. It just stayed.

Kai wanted to go to it. He put on his shoes. But the piece was still gone. The light stayed on the hill. Kai felt a gentle pull in his chest. He walked to the door. He walked back to the rug.

The piece is not here, he said. The light is there. The piece is not here. The light is there. He said it again. The piece is not here. The light is there.

He sat down. He did not go. The fog got thick. The light stayed far. The puzzle stayed empty. Kai put his head on the rug and did not get up.

stories.name: Kai

axes.where: on top of a far hill

stories.text:
Six pieces of the puzzle sat in a stack on Kai's rug. The last piece was lost. Kai looked under his sock. He looked under the bed. The piece was not there.

Then Kai saw it. On top of the far hill, a little light glowed. It was the color of new grass. It was soft and gentle. It blinked once. Then twice.

Kai pulled on his boots. He walked out into the foggy night. The fog was cold on his face. He climbed and climbed. The hill was steep. His legs hurt.

"I want the piece," Kai said. "I want the piece. I want the piece."

The light stayed far away. It did not come closer. Kai's hands were empty. His pockets were empty.

He sat down on the wet hill. The fog wrapped around him. The little light blinked and blinked. It was so near. It was so far.

Kai never found the piece. He never finished the puzzle. In the morning, his mother found him asleep on the hill. His boots were muddy. His face was sad. The light was gone.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text: I love puzzles. Nate had one almost done. Only one piece was left. It showed a duck on a pond. He looked under the cozy blanket. He looked by the candle. No piece. "Did you eat it?" his mom joked. Nate laughed. "I hope not!" He checked his pockets. A race to find it was on. He walked outside. Fog wrapped the night like a soft gray scarf. Down by the stream, he saw a tiny glow in the reeds. It was small and green. It blinked like a faraway firefly. He reached for it. His hand came back with only wet grass. The glow stayed put. It felt like a piece he could not click into place. He sighed. Then he felt something sharp in his sock. It was the puzzle piece! "Got you," Nate said. Back home, he set it in the puzzle. The duck looked whole. That little light stayed by the stream. It was not his to hold. But he liked knowing it was there.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
I went to Nate’s house to help with the puzzle. It was a big one with a cozy farm scene. One piece was missing. Just one.

“Look under the couch,” I said.

Nate crawled and found a fuzzy grape. “Not it,” he said. We laughed.

He lit a candle. The flame made shadows dance.

“Let’s race to the stream,” Nate said. “Maybe the wind took it.”

The night was foggy. We walked to the water. The mist was soft and gray. In the reeds by the stream, a small light glowed. It was not a firefly. It was steady and far, like a tiny window left on for someone.

Nate reached for it. His hand came back wet and empty.

“It’s not the piece,” he said.

“No,” I said.

We stood still. The light blinked, slow and soft. It made Nate feel a quiet pull. He wanted to go to it. He did not know why. The fog wrapped us up.

“Come on,” I said. “The puzzle is waiting.”

Nate turned away. The light stayed in the reeds, small and bright. It was still there when we got home.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
I lost the last piece of my puzzle. It is a picture of a boat on a lake. I look under the rug. I look in my sock drawer. No piece.

"Did you eat it?" asks my sister.

"No," I say. "I am not a goat."

She laughs. That is funny.

I take my candle outside. The fog is thick. It is a cozy night, soft and gray. I walk to the stream.

The piece is not there. But I see something in the reeds. A small light. It glows like a tiny moon.

I want to touch it. I race to the water. My feet get wet.

The light stays far away. It bobs and shines.

"Come here," I whisper.

It does not come.

I stand still. I want it so much. My chest feels tight.

"Nate?" calls my sister. "Did you find it?"

"No," I say. But I do not look for the puzzle piece anymore.

I only look at the light. I want it. I want it. I want it.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
I have lost one piece of my puzzle. It is a small blue piece. It shows part of a boat. I look under the table. I look in my sock drawer. No piece.

I light a candle. The flame is small and cozy. I do not feel cozy.

Then I see it. Out the window. A green light, far away. It sits in the reeds by the stream. It is soft and green like my missing piece. I want to go get it. I want to race there.

"Mom," I say. "Can I go out?"

"Not in the fog," she says. "Not at night."

I watch the green light. It blinks. I think, I want that light. I want that light. I want that light.

My dog licks my face. "Stop," I say. "That is not the piece."

He barks. It sounds like he says, "Maybe it is."

I laugh. Then I look again. The light is still there. I want it. I want it. I want it.

stories.name: Nate

axes.where: in the reeds by the stream

stories.text:
In the box, every piece had a home but one. Nate shook the box. No piece fell out. He looked under the rug. He checked his sock drawer and found a grape. "That is not a puzzle piece," he told the grape. He did not eat it. He put it back.

The fog hugged the window like a wet blanket. Nate took his candle outside. Its cozy glow made a small gold room around him. He walked to the stream. He wanted to race home, but his feet went slow.

Then he saw it. In the reeds, something shone. Not the moon. Not a star. A small light, soft and far, like a piece of morning left behind. He reached. The reeds bent. The light stayed far.

"Come here," he whispered. "Come here. Come here." His words made little clouds.

The light did not come. It just stayed, green and gentle, past the water. Nate stood in the fog a long time. He forgot the puzzle. He forgot the grape. He only wanted the light. He wanted it. He wanted it. He wanted it, and he could not have it.

stories.name: Zoe

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text: Carl the dog hid the last puzzle piece under the couch. Zoe looked all over. She looked under her bed and in her shoe. The puzzle was a map of the world. Now it had a hole. Zoe felt sad. Her mom said, "We can find it." They looked in the kitchen. They looked in the garden. Then Carl ran past with something in his mouth. It was the puzzle piece! Zoe laughed. "You silly dog!" she said. She was happy again. Then she looked at the fence. On the other side, a small light shone. It was like a tiny sun on the grass. Zoe wanted to touch it. But the fence was too high. So she put the piece in the puzzle. The map was whole. The light stayed there. It was pretty. Then Zoe and Carl ran inside for a snack.

stories.name: Zoe

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
Carefully, Zoe tipped the box of puzzle pieces onto the rug. One piece was missing. It was the piece with the little red boat on it.

Zoe looked at the picture on the box. She made a map in her mind. The boat piece should go right in the middle.

She looked under the couch. She found a lost cookie. That was funny. She was not happy about the cookie. She wanted the boat.

Then she saw it. The piece was outside on the grass. It sat by a fence. Sun made it shine like a tiny green light.

Zoe had to run to the fence. She put her hand through the wood. Her fingers almost touched it. The piece was too far. It was always too far.

She sat down and waited. The sun was warm. The green light danced on the grass. She could see it. She could not reach it.

Her mom came out. "Zoe, look in your pocket."

Zoe felt her pocket. There was the boat piece. She was happy at last. But she still looked at the fence. The green light was gone.

stories.name: Zoe

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
Carefully, Zoe tipped the puzzle box. One piece was missing. It was the last piece of the big map puzzle. Zoe looked under the rug. She looked in her shoe. She found a cookie instead. That was funny. Her dog had hidden it there.

Zoe went outside. The sun was warm. She saw a little light on the other side of the fence. It was small and bright, like a lost star. It made her feel happy and sad at the same time.

She wanted to run to it. But the fence was too high. So she sat and watched. The light danced on the grass.

The next day, she looked for the puzzle piece again. She did not find it. But she saw the light again, past the fence. It seemed to wave at her.

She stopped looking for the piece. She started looking at the light. Each sunny afternoon, she came back. She did not reach it. She did not need to. The wanting was enough. The light was always there. So was her happy, funny hope.

stories.name: Zoe

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
Carefully, Zoe shook the box. One piece was missing. The puzzle showed a map of a big park. Zoe needed the last piece. She looked under the rug. She looked in her sock drawer. No piece.

Then she saw it. A small green shine sat on the other side of the fence. It was not a puzzle piece. It was a light. It was far away.

Zoe ran to the fence. She put her hands on the wood. The light stayed there, small and bright.

“Come back,” she said. “I need you.”

The light did not come. Zoe laughed. “You are not even a puzzle piece!” But she still wanted it.

She climbed the fence. Her shoe fell off. She hopped on one foot. That was funny. She was not happy.

The map puzzle waited inside. The light waited outside. Zoe looked at the light. She looked at the fence. She looked at the light. She forgot the missing piece.

The sunny afternoon got long. Zoe sat by the fence. The light sat on the other side. She reached. She reached. She reached.

stories.name: Zoe

axes.where: on the other side of a fence

stories.text:
Carefully, Zoe put the last piece in the puzzle. It was a map of a farm. But one piece was gone. It was the piece with the red barn.

Zoe got her ball. She did not want to play. She wanted the piece. She went outside.

She saw a fence. She saw a light behind the fence. It was small and bright. It was like a happy little star.

She put her hand on the fence. The light was far away. She did not have a map to it.

She tried to run to the light. Her foot found a puddle. Splash! She fell on her bottom.

"Oof," said Zoe. A bird looked at her.

She got up. She looked at the light. It was still there.

She reached and reached. The light did not come.

The puzzle piece was lost. The light was lost too.

She went back to her puzzle. The empty spot looked at her.

She sat down. She was not happy.

She looked out the window. The light was gone.

She put her head down. She wanted the piece. She wanted the light. She wanted and wanted.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: at the end of a long road

stories.text:
The puzzle was missing one piece. Jack looked under the table. He looked in his apple bowl. He looked behind the lumpy pillow. No piece.

Jack went outside to play. He sat on his swing. He went up and down. The sun was warm on his face.

Then Jack saw a small green light. It was far away, at the end of the long road. It blinked once. It blinked twice. Jack wanted to touch it. He walked to the road. But the light stayed far away. It always stayed far away.

Jack went back to his swing. He sat down. He did not feel sad. Some things you want are too far to reach. That is okay.

Jack found the puzzle piece later. It was in his shoe. He put it in the puzzle. The picture was complete. The green light still blinked far away. Jack did not need it. What you have is better than what you cannot reach.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: at the end of a long road

stories.text:
The puzzle was almost done. Jack looked for the last piece. It was small and lumpy. It had a bit of red, like an apple.

He looked under the table. He looked by his swing. No piece.

Then Jack saw a green light. It was far away, at the end of a long road. The sun was high. The light was small but bright.

Jack wanted that light. He did not know why.

He looked for his puzzle piece again. He found a piece under his chair. But it was not the right one.

The green light came back. It blinked in the sunny afternoon. Jack reached for it. His hand touched only air.

He sat down. He felt sad. The light was too far.

Then his mom came. She held up a small piece. It was the last one.

Jack put it in. The puzzle was done.

Some things you want are far away. But the things you need are often very close.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: at the end of a long road

stories.text:
The puzzle was almost done. Jack looked for the last piece. It was small and lumpy. It had a bit of red, like an apple.

Jack looked under the table. He looked behind the swing. No piece.

Then he saw a green light. It was far away, at the end of a long road. The sun was warm on his back.

Jack wanted that light. He walked down the road. The light stayed far away.

He came home. He looked for the piece again. He saw the green light through the window.

He ran to the road. He reached for the light. It did not come closer.

Back home, he sat by the puzzle. The light glowed at the end of the road.

Jack put his hand on the empty spot. The piece was not there. The light was not his to hold.

Sometimes we want things we cannot have. That is okay.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: at the end of a long road

stories.text:
The puzzle was not done. One piece was missing. Jack looked under the table. He looked in his apple bowl. He looked on his lumpy bed. No piece.

Then he saw the light. It sat at the end of a long road. It was small and green. It was very far away.

Jack went outside. He did not take the puzzle. He walked past his swing. The swing did not move. He kept his eyes on the light.

The road was hot and sunny. The light did not come closer. Jack walked and walked. He said, “I will get it. I will get it.”

The puzzle waited at home. The hole waited too. But Jack only wanted the light.

At last he stopped. The light was still far. He could not touch it. He never could.

Jack went home slow. He put in the last piece. It had been in his pocket all along. What we want most is often right where we are.

stories.name: Jack

axes.where: at the end of a long road

stories.text:
The puzzle was missing one piece. Jack looked under the table. He looked in his apple bowl. He looked on the lumpy couch. No piece.

Then he saw the light. It was small and green, far away, at the end of a long road.

Jack ran to the light. He reached for the light. The light stayed far away.

He ran to the light. He reached for the light. The light stayed far away.

He forgot the puzzle. He forgot his swing. He forgot his apple. He only wanted the light.

He ran to the light. He reached for the light. The light stayed far away.

The sun began to set. Jack sat down. The light was still far away. It would always be far away.

So Jack walked home. He sat on his swing. He felt sad and small.

Then he looked down. The missing piece was right there, in the grass.

Some things you want stay far away. The things you need are often close.

stories.name: Mira

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Rain tapped the window. Mira sat on the floor with her puzzle. It was a picture of a red boat on a blue river. One piece was missing. The last piece. It was shaped like a little sock.

Mira looked under the rug. She looked in her shoe. She looked in her coat pocket.

Her friend Ben came over. "I will help," he said. They looked and looked.

The wind blew hard. They went outside to the bridge over the river. The wind made a whisper sound. Mira was hungry. Ben shared his apple.

Then Mira saw a small light. It was far away, across the water. It was green and it blinked. It looked like her missing piece.

She reached for it. She could not touch it. The wind pushed her hand back.

"Oh," said Mira. She felt sad.

Ben said, "Look down." The piece was stuck in a crack on the bridge. Mira pulled it out.

That night, the puzzle was done. The green light still blinked far away. Mira did not need it. She had her piece.

stories.name: Mira

axes.where: on a bridge over the river

stories.text:
Rain tapped the window. Mira sat on the floor with her puzzle. It was a picture of a red boat. One piece was missing. She looked under the rug. She looked in her sock drawer. No piece.

Her friend Ben came over. "We will find it," he said. They walked to the bridge over the river. The wind blew hard.

On the bridge, Mira saw a small green light far away. It blinked on the water. She wanted to touch it. She reached out. The wind pulled her hand back. The light stayed far.

"Come on," Ben said. "You are hungry. Let's get a snack."

Mira did not move. The light seemed to whisper. It said, come here, come here. She reached again. Ben took her hand.

"It's just a light," he said. "It is not yours."

They went home. Mira found the missing piece inside her puzzle box. The boat was whole. But that night, she thought of the small green light. She wanted it still.

stories.text:
Rita was Mira's best friend. They did puzzles on rainy days. One puzzle had a missing piece. It was the piece with the red boat on it. Mira looked under the couch. She looked in her sock drawer. No piece. "I am hungry for that piece," Mira said. Rita helped her look. They found nothing.

On a windy morning, they walked to the bridge over the river. Mira held her hat. The wind pulled at her coat. Then she saw it. A small green light, far away across the water. It blinked and blinked. Mira wanted it. She reached out her hand. The wind said a soft whisper. "Come," it seemed to say. But the light stayed far.

"Mira," said Rita. "Look down." There was the missing piece, right by Mira's shoe. Mira picked it up. She held it tight. She looked back at the light. It was still there. Still far. Still green. She put the piece in her pocket. She went home with Rita. The light stayed on the bridge, waiting.

stories.text:
Rain tapped the window. Mira looked for her puzzle piece. It was the last one. It was shaped like a small moon.

Her sock slid on the floor. She looked under the bed. She looked in her shoe. Her friend Ben came over.

"I am hungry," Ben said.

"Help me look," Mira said.

They looked in the toy box. They looked by the door.

Then Mira saw it. A tiny light, far away, on a bridge over the river. It was a small green light. It blinked in the windy morning.

"Come on," Mira said.

"But your puzzle," Ben said.

Mira ran to the bridge. The wind pushed her hair. The green light danced on the water. She reached for it. Her hand hit cold air.

"Please," she whisper. "Please, please, please."

Ben tugged her coat. "Mira, look."

He held up the moon piece. It was in her pocket all along. Mira took it. But she looked back at the light. She wanted it. She wanted it. She wanted it.

"Come home," Ben said.

Mira went home. The green light stayed on the bridge. Her puzzle was done. But she still looked out the window.

Rosa was gone. Mira looked under the bed. She looked inside a sock. She looked in her sock drawer too. The puzzle piece was small and blue. It was the last piece.

"Help me, Ben," Mira said. Ben was her friend. He was hungry. He ate toast while he looked. "We will find it," Ben said.

The wind blew hard that windy morning. Mira and Ben went outside. They walked to the bridge over the river. Then Mira saw it. A small light. It was green. It sat far away on the water.

"Come on," Ben said. But Mira did not move. She wanted the light. She reached for it. Her hand got nothing but wind.

"Mira, the piece," Ben said. But Mira just whispered, "I want it. I want it. I want it."

Ben pulled her hand. "Look down," he said. There was the blue piece, right by her shoe.

Mira picked it up. She held it tight. The green light still called. But her puzzle was done.
